Initially created: 2026-03-31T17:27:12.965+09:00 by CH Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Generally, those who possess territory and shepherd the people,
their duty lies in the four seasons,
and their protection lies in the granaries.
If the state has much wealth,
then those from afar will come;
if the lands are opened and cultivated,
then the people will remain and dwell;
if the granaries are full,
then they will know *Lǐ* and etiquette;
if food and clothing are sufficient,
then they will know honor and shame.
If those above follow the regulations,
then the six relations will be stable;
if the *Sì Wéi* are extended,
then the ruler's orders will be carried out.
Therefore, the essential of reducing punishments
lies in prohibiting superficial cleverness;
the regulation for protecting the state
lies in cultivating the *Sì Wéi*;
the principle for following the people
lies in clarifying the spirits and gods,
revering the mountains and rivers,
respecting the ancestral temples,
and honoring ancestors and elders.
If one does not attend to the seasons of heaven,
then wealth will not be produced;
if one does not attend to the benefits of the earth,
then the granaries will not be filled.
If the wilds are overgrown and desolate,
then the people will become neglected;
if those above have no measure,
then the people will become reckless;
if superficial cleverness is not prohibited,
then the people will become licentious;
if the two sources are not blocked,
then punishments will become numerous.
If the spirits and gods are not clarified,
then the ignorant people will not be enlightened;
if the mountains and rivers are not revered,
then majestic orders will not be heard;
if the ancestral temples are not respected,
then the people will challenge their superiors;
if ancestors and elders are not honored,
then filial piety and fraternal duty will be incomplete.
If the *Sì Wéi* are not extended,
the state will perish.
To the right is the *Guó Sòng*.
The state has the *Sì Wéi*:
if one dimension is severed, the state leans;
if two are severed, it is endangered;
if three are severed, it is overturned;
if four are severed, it is extinguished.
What leans can be straightened;
what is endangered can be secured;
what is overturned can be raised;
but what is extinguished cannot be established again.
What are the *Sì Wéi*?
The first is *Lǐ*,
the second is *Yì*,
the third is *Lián*,
the fourth is *Chǐ*.
With *Lǐ*, one does not exceed the proper limits;
with *Yì*, one does not promote oneself;
with *Lián*, one does not conceal evil;
with *Chǐ*, one does not follow the crooked.
Therefore, if limits are not exceeded,
then those in high positions are secure;
if one does not promote oneself,
then the people will be without artifice and deception;
if evil is not concealed,
then conduct will naturally be perfect;
if one does not follow the crooked,
then wicked deeds will not arise.
To the right are the *Sì Wéi*.
The success of government
lies in following the hearts of the people;
the failure of government
lies in opposing the hearts of the people.
The people detest sorrow and toil,
so I provide them with ease and joy;
the people detest poverty and lowliness,
so I make them wealthy and honored;
the people detest danger and downfall,
so I preserve and secure them;
the people detest extinction,
so I allow them to give birth and grow.
If one can provide ease and joy,
then the people will endure sorrow and toil for him;
if one can make them wealthy and honored,
then the people will endure poverty and lowliness for him;
if one can preserve and secure them,
then the people will face danger and downfall for him;
if one can allow them to give birth and grow,
then the people will face extinction for him.
Therefore, punishments are not enough to intimidate their will,
and executions are not enough to subdue their hearts.
Thus, if punishments are frequent but the will is not fearful,
then orders will not be carried out;
if executions are numerous but hearts are not subdued,
then those in high positions are in danger.
Therefore, by following their four desires,
then those from afar will naturally become close;
by practicing their four dislikes,
then those nearby will rebel.
Therefore, knowing that giving is taking
is the treasure of government.
To the right are the *Sì Shùn*.
Place the state on ground that does not tilt.
Accumulate in granaries that do not run dry.
Store in treasuries that are not exhausted.
Issue orders from the source of flowing water.
Employ the people in offices where there is no contention.
Clarify the path of certain death.
Open the gate of certain gain.
Do not attempt the unachievable.
Do not seek the unobtainable.
Do not occupy what cannot be held long.
Do not perform what cannot be repeated.
Placing the state on ground that does not tilt
means bestowing power upon the virtuous.
Accumulating in granaries that do not run dry
means attending to the five grains.
Storing in treasuries that are not exhausted
means cultivating mulberry and hemp and raising the six domestic animals.
Issuing orders from the source of flowing water
means orders follow the hearts of the people.
Employing the people in offices where there is no contention
means letting each person do what they are best at.
Clarifying the path of certain death
means being strict with punishments.
Opening the gate of certain gain
means being trustworthy with rewards and honors.
Not attempting the unachievable
means measuring the people's strength.
Not seeking the unobtainable
means not forcing the people to do what they detest.
Not occupying what cannot be held long
means not seeking temporary gain for one generation.
Not performing what cannot be repeated
means not deceiving one's people.
Therefore, if power is bestowed upon the virtuous,
the state will be secure.
If one attends to the five grains,
food will be sufficient.
If one cultivates mulberry and hemp
and raises the six domestic animals,
the people will be wealthy.
If orders follow the hearts of the people,
then majestic orders will be carried out.
If each person is made to do what they are best at,
then supplies will be complete.
If punishments are strict,
the people will keep away from wickedness.
If rewards and honors are trustworthy,
the people will make light of difficulties.
If the people's strength is measured,
then nothing will fail to be accomplished.
If one does not force the people to do what they detest,
then deception and falsehood will not arise.
If one does not seek temporary gain for one generation,
then the people will have no resentment in their hearts.
If one does not deceive the people,
then those below will feel close to those above.
To the right is the *Shí Yī Jīng*.
If one treats a household as a village,
the village cannot be governed;
if one treats a village as a state,
the state cannot be governed;
if one treats a state as the world,
the world cannot be governed.
Treat a household as a household,
a village as a village,
a state as a state,
and the world as the world.
Do not say they are not of the same birth,
or those far away will not listen;
do not say they are not of the same village,
or those far away will not go forth;
do not say they are not of the same state,
or those far away will not follow.
Be like the Earth and like Heaven;
what partiality or favoritism could there be?
Be like the Moon and like the Sun;
such is the integrity of a ruler.
The reins for managing the people
lie in what the one above values;
the gate for leading the people
lies in what the one above prioritizes;
the road for summoning the people
lies in what the one above likes and dislikes.
Therefore, if the ruler seeks it,
then the ministers will obtain it;
if the ruler relishes it,
then the ministers will eat it;
if the ruler likes it,
then the ministers will wear it;
if the ruler dislikes it,
then the ministers will hide it.
Do not conceal your faults,
and do not change your standards,
or the worthy will not assist you.
When words spoken in the room fill the room,
and words spoken in the hall fill the hall,
this is what is called a Shèng Wáng.
Inner and outer city walls and moats
are not enough to ensure a firm defense;
weapons, armor, and great strength
are not enough to respond to the enemy;
vast lands and much wealth
are not enough to hold the masses;
only those who possess the Dào
can prepare for disasters before they take shape,
so that calamity does not sprout.
The world does not suffer from a lack of ministers,
but from a lack of a ruler to employ them;
the world does not suffer from a lack of wealth,
but from a lack of people to distribute it.
Therefore, one who understands the times
can be established as a leader;
one who is selfless
can be placed in charge of government;
one who is discerning of the times and observant of utility
and who can provide for the various offices
can be honored as a ruler.
Those who are dilatory fall behind in their affairs;
those who are stingy with wealth lose their kinsmen;
those who trust petty men lose true scholars.
To the right are the Liù Qīn and Wǔ Fǎ.
Yán Èr.
Mountains are
the highest of things;
kindness is
the highest conduct of a lord;
compassion is the highest conduct of parents;
loyalty is the highest conduct of ministers;
filial piety is
the highest conduct of children and daughters-in-law.
Therefore, if a mountain is high and does not collapse,
then the sacrificial sheep will arrive;
if a lord is kind and does not slacken,
then the people will offer support;
if parents are compassionate in nourishment and do not slacken,
then children and daughters-in-law will be obedient;
if ministers are loyal and do not slacken,
then rank and salary will arrive;
if children and daughters-in-law are filial and do not slacken,
then a fine reputation will be attached to them.
Therefore, if integrity is high and one does not slacken,
then what is desired will be obtained;
if one slackens, it will not be obtained.
Thus it is said: If a mountain is high and does not collapse,
then the sacrificial sheep will arrive;
if an abyss is deep and does not dry up,
then the submerged jade reaches its limit.
An abyss
is where the myriad things are born;
if it can be deep and not dry up,
then the submerged jade will arrive.
A ruler
is the one upon whom people look up to for life;
if he can be broad-minded, pure, and generous without being harsh or malicious,
then the people will attach themselves to him.
Parents
are those from whom children and daughters-in-law receive instruction;
if they can be compassionate and kind in teaching and instruction without losing reason,
then children and daughters-in-law will be filial.
Ministers
are those who are used by the lord;
if they can exhaust their strength in serving the one above,
then they will be in accord with the lord.
Children and daughters-in-law
are the means by which parents find peace;
if they can be filial and fraternal and obey their parents,
then they will be in accord with the parents.
Therefore, if the abyss dries up and has no water,
then the submerged jade will not arrive.
If the lord is harsh and lacks generosity,
then the myriad people will not attach themselves.
If parents are violent and lack grace,
then children and daughters-in-law will not be close.
If ministers follow along but are not loyal,
then they will be lowly, disgraced, and impoverished.
If children and daughters-in-law do not provide peace for their parents,
then calamity and sorrow will arrive.
Therefore, if the abyss does not dry up,
then what is desired will arrive;
if it dries up,
then it will not arrive.
Thus it is said:
"If an abyss is deep and does not dry up,
then the submerged jade reaches its limit."
Heaven does not change its constancy.
Heaven covers the myriad things,
regulates cold and heat,
moves the sun and moon,
and orders the stars;
such is the constancy of Heaven.
It governs them by principle,
ending and then beginning again.
A ruler shepherds the myriad people,
governs the world,
and oversees all officials;
such is the constancy of a ruler.
He governs them by law,
ending and then beginning again.
Harmonizing descendants
and gathering kinsmen
is the constancy of parents.
They govern them by righteousness,
ending and then beginning again.
Sincerity, respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness
are the constancy of ministers.
With these they serve their lord,
ending and then beginning again.
Loving parents and being good at providing for them,
thinking of respect and following instructions,
are the constancy of children and daughters-in-law.
With these they serve their parents,
ending and then beginning again.
Therefore, if Heaven does not lose its constancy,
then cold and heat obtain their season,
and the sun, moon, and stars obtain their order.
If a ruler does not lose his constancy,
then the ministers obtain their righteousness,
and the various officials maintain their duties.
If parents do not lose their constancy,
then descendants are harmonious and obedient,
and kinsmen are joyful with one another.
If ministers do not lose their constancy,
then affairs will have no faults,
and official posts and government will be orderly.
If children and daughters-in-law do not lose their constancy,
then the elder and younger will be in order and the distant and close kinsmen will be harmonious.
Therefore, those who use constancy are well-governed,
and those who lose constancy are in chaos.
Heaven has never changed that by which it governs;
therefore it is said:
Heaven does not change its constancy.
Earth does not change its rules.
Earth gives birth to and nourishes the myriad things;
this is the rule of Earth.
Bringing peace and order to the common people
is the rule of the ruler.
Instructing and protecting the affairs of the family
is the rule of parents.
Providing upright remonstrance and dying for one's integrity
is the rule of ministers.
Exhausting one's strength in reverent provision
is the rule of children and daughters-in-law.
Earth does not change its principles,
therefore the ten thousand things are born from it.
The ruler does not change his principles,
therefore the common people are at peace.
Parents do not change their principles,
therefore family affairs are managed.
Ministers and subordinates do not change their principles,
therefore the ruler has no errors.
Children and daughters-in-law do not change their principles,
therefore the care of parents is complete and provided for.
Thus, those who use principles are secure;
those who do not use principles are in danger.
The Earth has never changed;
that is why it is secure.
Therefore it is said:
Earth does not change its principles.
Spring, autumn, winter, and summer
do not change their seasons;
past and present are the same.
Spring:
the yáng qì begins to ascend,
therefore the ten thousand things are born.
Summer:
the yáng qì fully ascends,
therefore the ten thousand things grow.
Autumn:
the yīn qì begins to descend,
therefore the ten thousand things are harvested.
Winter:
the yīn qì fully descends,
therefore the ten thousand things are stored.
Thus spring and summer are for birth and growth,
autumn and winter are for harvesting and storing;
these are the nodes of the four seasons.
Rewards and punishments
are the nodes of the ruler.
The four seasons have never failed to give life or take it away;
the ruler has never failed to reward or punish.
Therefore it is said:
Spring, autumn, winter, and summer
do not change their seasons.
Heaven covers the ten thousand things and regulates them;
Earth carries the ten thousand things and nourishes them;
the four seasons produce and grow the ten thousand things and harvest and store them.
From ancient times until now,
they have not changed their Dào.
Therefore it is said:
“Past and present are the same.”
When a jiāolóng gains water,
its divinity can be established.
The jiāolóng
is the divine among aquatic creatures;
when it rides upon water,
its divinity is established;
when it loses water,
its divinity is discarded.
The human ruler
is the one who possesses majesty in the world;
when he gains the people, his majesty is established;
when he loses the people, his majesty is discarded.
The jiāolóng waits to gain water before establishing its divinity;
the human ruler waits to gain the people before completing his majesty.
Therefore it is said:
“When the jiāolóng gains water,
its divinity can be established.”
When tigers and leopards gain secluded places,
their majesty can be sustained.
Tigers and leopards
are the fierce ones among beasts;
when they dwell within deep forests and wide marshes,
then people fear their majesty and sustain it.
The human ruler
is the one who possesses power in the world;
when he dwells in seclusion, then people fear his power.
Thus, if tigers and leopards leave their secluded places and approach people,
then people capture them and disregard their majesty.
If the human ruler leaves his gates and presses close to the common people,
then the people slight him and are arrogant toward his power.
Therefore it is said:
Tigers and leopards rely on secluded places,
and their majesty can be sustained.
Wind and rain have no fixed direction,
so resentment and anger do not reach them.
Wind
is what blows things away;
what the wind blows
does not avoid the noble or the lowly, the beautiful or the ugly.
Rain
is what moistens things;
where the rain falls
does not avoid the small or the great, the strong or the weak.
Wind and rain are perfectly impartial and without selfishness;
they travel without a constant direction;
although people encounter blowing or moistening,
none resent them.
Therefore it is said:
“Wind and rain have no fixed direction,
and resentment and anger do not reach them.”
The noble have the means to execute orders;
the lowly have the means to forget their lowliness.
The reason the human ruler’s orders are followed
and his prohibitions are obeyed
is that he must base his orders on what the people like
and his prohibitions on what the people hate.
In the human condition, none do not desire life and hate death;
none do not desire benefit and hate harm.
Therefore, when the superior orders things that grant life and benefit people,
the orders are followed.
When he prohibits things that kill or harm people,
then the prohibitions are obeyed.
The reason orders are followed
is that the people must find joy in his administration.
Then the orders are indeed followed.
Therefore it is said:
“The noble have the means to execute orders.”
The reason the human ruler is able to make subordinates exert their strength and feel close to the superior
is that he must bring benefit and remove harm for the world.
Thus his virtue and bounty extend to the world,
and his benevolence is bestowed thickly upon the ten thousand things.
Fathers and sons gain security,
and all living things gain nourishment.
Therefore the ten thousand people joyfully exert their strength
and take pleasure in being used by the superior.
Internally, they devote themselves to the fundamental and work diligently
to fill the granaries;
externally, they exhaust their integrity and die against the enemy
to secure the Shèjì.
Although they experience toil, bitterness, lowliness, and humiliation,
they do not dare to complain.
This is how the lowly forget their lowliness.
Therefore it is said:
“The lowly have the means to forget their lowliness.”
Longevity, premature death, poverty, and wealth
do not come without reason.
If rising and resting are timely,
if eating and drinking are moderate,
and if cold and heat are properly adjusted,
then the body is benefited and the lifespan is increased.
If rising and resting are untimely,
if eating and drinking are immoderate,
and if cold and heat are not adjusted,
then the physical form is burdened and the lifespan is diminished.
If people are lazy and extravagant, they will be poor;
if they are diligent and frugal, they will be wealthy.
Things do not arrive for no reason;
there must be a cause.
Therefore it is said:
“Longevity, premature death, poverty, and wealth
do not come without reason.”
Cherishing the mandate
is the ruler’s dignity.
When laws are established and the people find joy in them,
when orders are issued and the people cherish them,
when the laws and orders harmonize with the hearts of the people
like two halves of a tally,
then the ruler is honored and prominent.
Therefore it is said:
“Cherishing the orders
is the ruler’s dignity.”
Receiving petitions
is the operation of reputation.
When the superior has no trivial affairs
then the people test their own abilities.
In the enlightened ruler’s governing of the world,
he quiets his people and does not disturb them,
he eases his people and does not toil them;
not disturbing them,
the people follow their own course;
not toiling them,
the people test themselves,
therefore it is said:
“When the superior has no trivial affairs,
the people test themselves.”
Holding the Bàoshǔ without speaking
yet the ancestral temple is already well-ordered.
The ruler of men establishes his measures,
sets forth the distribution of offices, and clarifies
his laws and patterns
to oversee his people.
If he does not precede them with words,
then the people will follow what is correct.
That which is called Bàoshǔ
refers to ritual vessels.
Therefore it is said:
"Holding the Bàoshǔ without speaking,"
and yet the ancestral hall is already ordered.
"The hónghú sound qiāngqiāng;
only the people sing of them."
The stately hónghú in their enclosures
are those with beautiful appearances.
Because their appearance is beautiful,
the people sing of them.
Virtue and righteousness
are the beauty of conduct.
Because virtue and righteousness are beautiful,
the people rejoice in them.
That which the people sing of and rejoice in
are beautiful conduct, virtue, and righteousness.
And the enlightened ruler possesses these caged hónghú.
Therefore it is said:
"The hónghú sound jiāngjiāng;
only the people sing of them."
"Stately are the many officers;
the people of Yīn are transformed by them."
"Stately" (jìjì) means
being sincere, solemn, and decisive in affairs.
"Many officers" means
having many elders.
Zhōu Wén Wáng was sincere, solemn, and decisive in affairs;
therefore the state was well-governed.
His various ministers understood principles to assist the ruler;
therefore the ruler was enlightened.
When the ruler is enlightened and the state is well-governed,
everyone within the borders receives his benefits and bounty.
The people of Yīn raised their heads and looked toward Wén Wáng,
wishing to become Wén Wáng's subjects.
Therefore it is said:
"Stately are the many officers;
the people of Yīn are transformed by them."
This was Zhòu’s failure.
As a ruler, Zhòu
exhausted the people's strength,
seized the people's wealth,
and endangered the people's lives.
Unjust and violent orders
were imposed upon the common people.
Cruel and poisonous agents
were deployed throughout the world.
Therefore, the great ministers were not close to him,
the common people were resentful,
and the world rebelled against him.
That they wished to be Wén Wáng's subjects
was brought upon Zhòu by himself.
Therefore it is said:
"This was Zhòu’s failure."
Among the drifting tumbleweeds
is not where one finds guests.
Having no ritual laws,
standards, or patterns, flying and wavering without being fixed,
is what is called "the questions of drifting tumbleweeds; the questions of drifting tumbleweeds"
which an enlightened ruler does not listen to.
Speech that lacks measure
is not permitted by an enlightened ruler.
Therefore it is said:
"Questions like drifting tumbleweeds are not among those to be treated as guests."
When swallows and sparrows gather,
one who walks the Way does not look at them.
If the Way is walked, then ruler and ministers are close,
fathers and sons are at peace,
and all living things flourish.
Therefore, the task of an enlightened ruler
lies in practicing the Way
and not looking at small things.
Swallows and sparrows
are small things.
Therefore it is said:
"When swallows and sparrows gather,
one who walks the Way does not look at them."
Sacrificial animals, jade tablets, and bi-disks
are not sufficient to please the ghosts and spirits.
If an enlightened ruler's actions and stillness attain principle and righteousness,
his orders accord with the people's hearts,
his executions fit the crimes,
and his rewards fit the merits.
Thus, even if he does not use sacrificial animals and jade tablets to pray to the ghosts and spirits,
the ghosts and spirits will assist him,
Heaven and Earth will favor him,
and his undertakings will bring good fortune.
If a chaotic ruler's actions and movements lose righteousness and principle,
his orders go against the people's hearts,
his executions do not fit the crimes,
and his rewards do not fit the merits,
then even if he uses sacrificial animals and jade tablets to pray to the ghosts and spirits,
the ghosts and spirits will not assist him,
and Heaven and Earth will not favor him.
His undertakings will bring calamity.
Therefore it is said:
"Sacrificial animals, jade tablets, and bi-disks are not sufficient to
please the ghosts and spirits."
If the ruler's achievements have a foundation,
what use are precious coins?
That by which a ruler achieves success
is wealth and strength.
Therefore, if the state is wealthy and the army strong,
then the feudal lords will submit to his government,
and neighboring enemies will fear his majesty.
Even if he does not use precious coins to serve the feudal lords,
the feudal lords will not dare to violate him.
That by which a ruler commits a fault
is poverty and weakness.
Therefore, if the state is poor and the army weak,
it will not be victorious in battle
and its defenses will not be firm.
Even if he presents famous vessels and heavy treasures to serve neighboring enemies,
he will not escape the disaster of death and destruction.
Therefore it is said:
"If the ruler's achievements have a foundation,
what use are precious coins?"
The Way of Yì
was not merely shooting.
Yì
was a skilled archer of antiquity.
He harmonized his bow and arrows and held them firmly.
In his handling of the bow,
he examined height and depth,
and he possessed the Way to certainly hit the mark.
Therefore, he could shoot many times and hit many times.
An enlightened ruler is like Yì.
He brings peace and harmony to his laws,
examines what to discard or establish, and holds firmly to them.
He possesses the Way to certainly govern.
Therefore, he can undertake many things and have many of them be appropriate.
The "Way"
is how Yì certainly hits the mark
and how a ruler certainly governs.
"Shooting"
is the bowstring launching the arrow.
Therefore it is said:
"The Way of Yì was not merely shooting."
The art of Zào Fù
was not merely driving.
Zào Fù
was a skilled driver of horses.
He looked after his horses well,
regulated their food and drink,
measured the horses' strength,
and examined their gait.
Therefore, he could take long journeys without the horses becoming exhausted.
An enlightened ruler is like Zào Fù.
He governs his people well,
measures their strength,
and examines their skills.
Therefore, he establishes merit without the people becoming distressed or harmed.
Therefore, "art"
is how Zào Fù undertook long journeys
and how a ruler establishes merit and name.
"Driving"
is holding the reins.
Therefore it is said:
"The art of Zào Fù was not merely driving."
The skill of Xī Zhòng
was not merely carving and paring.
When Xī Zhòng made carriages and vessels,
the square, round, curved, and straight
all matched the compass, square, hook, and line.
Therefore, the mechanisms rotated and complemented each other,
their use was firm and advantageous,
and the finished products were sturdy.
An enlightened ruler is like Xī Zhòng.
His words and actions
all match the arts and calculations.
Therefore, the various principles are appropriate,
and those above and below are close to each other.
Skillfulness is
that which Xī Zhòng used to construct implements
and that which a ruler uses to govern.
As for cutting and carving,
these are the work of axes and knives.
Therefore it is said:
"The skill of Xī Zhòng
did not lie in cutting and carving."
To summon those from afar, act such that it seems effortless;
to keep those nearby close, speak as though there is no business.
Only the one who walks at night possesses this.
If the people benefit from it, they come;
if they are harmed by it, they leave.
The people's pursuit of benefit
is like water running downward;
they make no choice between the four directions.
Therefore, those who wish to attract the people
first initiate benefits for them,
and even without being summoned, the people will arrive of their own accord.
If what they hate is established,
even if summoned, the people will not come.
Therefore it is said:
"To summon those from afar, act such that it seems effortless."
Oversee the people like a father and mother,
and the people will love and be close to you.
When the Dào is pure and generous
and one treats them with substance,
even if one does not say, "I love the people,"
the people will already be close.
Oversee the people like enemies,
and the people will distance themselves from you.
When the Dào is not generous
and one treats them without substance,
then deception and falsity arise together.
Even if one says, "I love the people,"
the people will not be close.
Therefore it is said:
"To keep those nearby close, speak as though there is no business."
When an enlightened ruler causes those afar to come and those nearby to be close,
it is done within the heart.
What is called "walking at night"
is the action of the heart.
If one can practice virtue in the heart,
then no one in the world can compete with him.
Therefore it is said:
"Is it only the one who walks at night who possesses this!"
In a gorge upon a flat plain,
how could there be any height?
To be a ruler yet be a predator,
to be a parent yet be cruel,
to be a minister
yet be disloyal, to be a son or daughter-in-law
yet be unfilial—these four are the great failures of humanity.
If these great failures reside in one's person, even if there is small goodness, one cannot be considered worthy.
What is called a "flat plain" is low marshland;
even if there is a small mound, it cannot be
high.
Therefore it is said: "In the marsh of a flat plain,
how could there be any height?"
In the recess of a great mountain,
how could there be any depth?
To be a ruler yet be kind,
to be a parent yet be compassionate,
to be a minister yet be loyal,
to be a son or daughter-in-law yet be filial—these four are the high conducts of humanity.
If high conduct resides in one's person,
even if there are small faults,
one is not considered unworthy.
What is called a "great mountain"
is the highest of mountains;
even if there is a small recess,
it is not considered deep.
Therefore it is said:
"In the recess of a great mountain,
how could there be any depth?"
People of Zǐ and Wèi
should not be entrusted with great responsibility.
Slandering the worthy is called Zǐ;
promoting and praising the unworthy is called Wèi.
If people of Zǐ and Wèi are employed,
then the ruler's clarity is obscured,
and words of slander and praise arise.
If entrusted with great matters,
then the work will not be accomplished and disaster will arrive.
Therefore it is said:
"People of Zǐ and Wèi
should not be entrusted with great responsibility."
Those who plan for the great can be joined in far-reaching undertakings;
those who consider worries can be joined in attaining the Dào.
Those whose plans are hasty and whose worries are immediate
should be let go and not summoned.
When an enlightened ruler considers matters,
those who plan for the world are called Mú officials.
With Mú officials, the lands within the seas are covered
by their bounty; their bounty is spread throughout the world, and future generations enjoy their achievements for a long time, the benefits becoming ever more numerous.
Therefore it is said: "Mú officials can be joined in far-reaching undertakings."
The Sage chooses what can be spoken before speaking
and chooses what can be done before acting.
Seeking temporary benefit that later brings harm,
or seeking temporary joy that later brings worry—
these the Sage does not do.
Therefore, when the Sage chooses words, he must consider the burdens;
when choosing actions, he must consider the worries.
Therefore it is said:
"Those who consider worries can be joined in attaining the Dào."
As for the petty person,
he twists the Dào to seek acceptance,
conforms to the ruler's intent to seek temporary pleasure,
and prepares for benefit to seek temporary gain.
For those like this,
though their gains are fast,
the arrival of disaster is also swift.
Therefore the Sage dismisses and does not use them.
Therefore it is said:
"Those whose plans are hasty and whose worries are immediate
should be let go and not summoned."
Promoting the long-term can be seen from afar.
Promoting one thing that becomes a long-term benefit for the world
is called "promoting the long."
When the long is promoted, those who receive its benefit are numerous,
and the manifestation of virtue and righteousness is seen from afar.
Therefore it is said:
"Promoting the long-term can be seen from afar."
One who measures greatly is what the masses align with.
Heaven's measure is great,
so it can cover all things.
Earth's measure is great,
so it can sustain all things.
The ruler's measure is great,
so he accommodates many things and the masses can align with him.
Therefore it is said: "One who measures greatly is what the masses align with."
To desire people to cherish you,
resolutely practice and do not grow weary.
Nobility, wealth, honor, and prominence—
the people return to and enjoy these,
and no ruler does not desire them.
Therefore, one who wants the people to cherish and enjoy him
must practice virtue and the Dào without weariness,
and the people will cherish and enjoy him.
To make the cherishing of people beautiful,
resolutely practice and do not grow weary.
Matters that must be gained
are not worthy of reliance.
In the Sage's pursuit of matters,
he first deliberates on the principles and righteousness,
and calculates whether they are possible or not.
Thus, if it is righteous, he seeks it;
if it is not righteous, he stops.
If it is possible, he seeks it;
if it is not possible, he stops.
Therefore, the matters he attains
are always treasures for his person.
In the petty person's pursuit of matters,
he does not deliberate on the principles and righteousness,
and does not calculate whether they are possible or not.
He seeks it even if it is not righteous;
he seeks it even if it is not possible.
Therefore, the matters he attains
have never been worthy of reliance.
Matters that must be gained
are not worthy of reliance.
Words that must promise
are not worthy of trust.
In the Sage's promises,
he first deliberates on the principles and righteousness,
and calculates whether they are possible or not.
If it is righteous, he promises;
if it is not righteous, he refrains.
If it is possible, he promises;
if it is not possible, he refrains.
Therefore, his promises are never untrusted.
The xiǎorén agrees even to what is unrighteous,
and agrees even to what is impossible.
If his words always promise agreement,
then his agreement cannot necessarily be trusted.
Therefore it is said:
"Words that always promise agreement
are not worthy of trust."
Those who are cautious only in small matters will not establish themselves in a grand way.
If one is cautious within a single household,
then one establishes oneself in one household;
if one is cautious in a single xiāng,
then one establishes oneself in one xiāng;
if one is cautious in a single guó,
then one establishes oneself in one guó;
if one is cautious throughout Tiānxià,
then one establishes oneself throughout Tiānxià.
Therefore, if that which one is cautious about is small,
then that which one establishes will also be small;
if that which one is cautious about is great,
then that which one establishes will also be great.
Therefore it is said:
"Those who are cautious only in small matters will not establish themselves in a grand way."
One who is picky about food does not fatten the body.
The sea does not reject water,
and thus it can achieve its greatness.
The mountain does not reject earth and stones,
and thus it can achieve its height.
A míngzhǔ does not tire of people,
and thus he can achieve his multitude.
A shì does not tire of learning,
and thus he can achieve his shèng.
A picky eater
is one who dislikes many things.
Jiàn
is the means by which a zhǔ is secured.
Food
is the means by which the body is fattened.
If a zhǔ dislikes jiàn, he will not be secure;
if a person is picky about food, he will not be fat.
Therefore it is said:
"One who is picky about food does not fatten the body."
He who possesses words that are never discarded
must be in harmony with Tiāndì.
When speech discusses Dàodé, loyalty, trustworthiness, filial piety, and fraternal respect,
these are the words that are never discarded.
Heaven is fair and without selfishness,
so there is nothing beautiful or ugly that it does not cover.
Earth is fair and without selfishness,
so there is nothing small or large that it does not carry.
Words that are never discarded
are fair and without selfishness;
thus, there is no one worthy or unworthy who is not employed.
Therefore, one who has words that are never discarded
corresponds to the lack of selfishness of Tiāndì;
therefore it is said:
"He who possesses words that are never discarded
must be in harmony with Tiāndì."
A cliff three rèn high
is a great difficulty for humans,
yet gibbons and macaques drink there.
When a míngzhǔ manages things,
he employs them for their strengths
and does not employ them for their weaknesses;
thus, there is no task that is not completed
and no merit that is not established.
A luànzhǔ does not know that things each have their own strengths and weaknesses,
and demands perfection in everything.
Planning affairs and determining things,
or clarifying rites and righteousness,
are strengths of humans
but weaknesses of gibbons and macaques.
Scaling heights and traversing danger
are strengths of gibbons and macaques
but weaknesses of humans.
If one demands from humans the strengths of gibbons and macaques,
then his orders will be abandoned and responsibilities will not be fulfilled.
Therefore it is said:
"A cliff three rèn high
is a great difficulty for humans,
yet gibbons and macaques drink there."
Therefore it is said: Boasting of oneself and being fond of autocracy
are the calamities of undertaking affairs.
When a míngzhǔ undertakes an affair,
he relies on the deliberations of the shèngrén,
uses the strength of the masses,
and does not involve his own self;
thus, the task is successful and blessings are born.
A luànzhǔ considers himself wise
and does not rely on the deliberations of the shèngrén.
He boasts and exerts himself for his own merit,
and does not rely on the strength of the masses.
He uses himself exclusively
and does not listen to upright jiàn.
Thus, the task fails and calamity is born.
Therefore it is said:
"Boasting of oneself and being fond of autocracy
are the calamities of undertaking affairs."
If one does not travel the wilderness,
one still does not neglect his horse.
The horse
is that which is ridden to travel the wilderness.
Therefore, although one is not currently traveling the wilderness,
one's nurturing and feeding of the horse
is never remiss or lazy.
The mín
are those who defend and fight.
Therefore, although they are not currently defending or fighting,
the governing and nurturing of the mín
is never remiss or lazy;
therefore it is said:
"If one does not travel the wilderness,
one still does not neglect his horse."
To be able to give without taking
is to match Tiāndì.
Heaven produces the four seasons,
and Earth produces the myriad riches,
to nurture the myriad things,
yet they take nothing from them.
A míngzhǔ matches Tiāndì.
He teaches the mín according to the seasons,
encourages them in plowing and weaving
to enrich the livelihood of the mín,
and does not boast of his merit
nor take their profit for himself;
therefore it is said:
"To be able to give without taking
is to match Tiāndì."
Those who are idle and weary will not reach their goal.
Remissness, laziness, neglect, and arrogance—
to use these to serve a zhǔ is to be disloyal;
to use these to serve parents is to be unfilial;
to use these to start an undertaking is to fail.
Therefore it is said:
"Those who are idle and weary will not reach their goal."
One who is not diffuse seems like a shén.
The shén is within,
and those who cannot keep up are at the gate.
What is within will be applied;
those at the gate must wait.
Be cautious at dawn and do not be idle,
for those who are late will encounter misfortune.
To forget one's tasks in the morning
is to lose one's merit by the evening.
Using a compass and square to make circles and squares results in success.
Using feet and inches to measure length results in accuracy.
Using laws and numbers to govern the mín results in peace.
Therefore, when affairs do not deviate from principle,
their success is like that of a shén;
therefore it is said:
"One who is not diffuse seems like a shén."
To serve a zhǔ without exerting full effort
results in punishment.
To serve parents without exerting full effort
results in a lack of intimacy.
To receive instruction and ask after learning without diligence
results in a lack of achievement.
Therefore, if in the morning one does not strive to advance,
by the evening no merit will be seen.
Therefore it is said:
"To forget one's tasks in the morning
is to lose one's merit by the evening."
When xiéqì enters within,
the zhèngsè then declines.
If the inner sentiments are trustworthy and sincere,
then one's reputation will be beautiful.
If one's cultivation of conduct is cautious and respectful,
then honor and prominence will follow.
If there is no genuine sentiment within,
then one's reputation will be bad.
If one's cultivation of conduct is negligent and lax,
then disgrace and humiliation will arise.
Therefore it is said:
"When xiéqì invades the interior,
the zhèngsè then declines."
If the jūn does not act as a jūn,
then the chén does not act as a chén.
For one who is a ruler, if he is not enlightened about the righteousness between ruler and minister to correct his ministers,
then the ministers will not know the principles of being a minister to serve their lord;
therefore, it is said:
“If the ruler does not act as a ruler,
then the minister will not act as a minister.”
If the father does not act as a father,
then the son will not act as a son.
For one who is a father, if he is not enlightened about the righteousness between father and son to teach and organize his son,
then the son will not know the way of being a son to serve his father.
Therefore, it is said:
“If the father does not act as a father,
then the son will not act as a son.”
If those above lose their positions,
then those below will exceed their proper bounds.
If superiors and inferiors are not in harmony,
then orders will not be carried out.
If ruler and minister are close,
if superiors and inferiors are in harmony,
and if the myriad people are unified,
then when the lord issues an order, the people will carry it out;
when those above issue a prohibition, the people will not violate it.
If ruler and minister are not close,
if superiors and inferiors are not in harmony,
and if the myriad people are not unified,
then orders will not be carried out,
and prohibitions will not be observed;
therefore, it is said:
“If superiors and inferiors are not in harmony,
then orders will not be carried out.”
If attire is not correct,
then the attendants will not be solemn;
if speech is trustworthy,
if movements are dignified,
and if attire is correct,
then the ministers and subordinates will be solemn.
If speech is disrespectful,
if movements are deficient,
and if attire is slovenly,
then the ministers and subordinates will slight them;
therefore, it is said:
“If attire is not correct,
then the attendants will not be solemn;
if advancing and retreating are without ritual decorum,
then government orders will not be carried out.”
Ritual decorum is
the standard for the myriad things.
Laws and regulations are
the model for the myriad people.
Ritual and righteousness are
the model for the noble and the humble.
Therefore, if actions possess ritual decorum, then orders will be carried out;
if there is no ritual decorum, then orders will not be carried out;
therefore, it is said:
“If advancing and retreating are without ritual decorum,
then government orders will not be carried out.”
If one is both kind and awe-inspiring,
then the way of the ruler is complete.
As for the lord of men,
if he is gentle, kind, and generous,
then the people will love him.
If he is orderly, strict, and dignified,
then the people will fear him.
Thus, if the people love him, they will be close to him;
if they fear him, they will be of use to him.
For the people to be close and of use
is the urgent concern of the lord;
therefore, it is said:
“If one is both kind and awe-inspiring,
then the way of the ruler is complete.”
If no one brings them joy,
then no one will mourn for them;
if no one gives them life,
then no one will die for them.
If the lord of men can bring peace to his people,
then the people will serve their lord as they serve their parents;
thus, if the lord has worries, they will worry with him;
if he has difficulties, they will die for him.
If the lord treats the people like dirt,
then the people will not be of use;
if the lord has worries, they will not worry;
if he has difficulties, they will not die;
therefore, it is said:
“If no one brings them joy,
then no one will mourn for them;
if no one gives them life,
then no one will die for them.”
Those who go out do not arrive;
those who come in do not reach the limit.
The reason why the people guard and fight even unto death without flagging
is because that which those above bestow upon the people is generous;
thus, if those above bestow generously,
then the people’s repayment to those above will also be generous;
if those above bestow meagerly,
then the people’s repayment to those above will also be meager.
Therefore, if one bestows meagerly but demands generously,
the ruler cannot obtain it from the minister,
and the father cannot obtain it from the son;
therefore, it is said:
“Those who go out do not arrive;
those who come in do not reach the limit.”
That which the Dào speaks of is one,
but those who use it are different.
The Dào is
that which supports the myriad things,
enables them to be born and grow,
and allows each to complete its life and destiny.
Thus, some use it to govern a village,
some use it to govern a state,
and some use it to govern the world.
Therefore, it is said:
“That which the Dào speaks of is one,
but those who use it are different.”
There are those who hear of the Dào and enjoy managing a family;
they are the people of one family.
There are those who hear of the Dào and enjoy managing a village;
they are the people of one village.
To hear of the Dào and use it to govern a village,
to make their fathers and sons close,
to make their brothers harmonious,
to correct their customs,
to make the people delight in those above,
to make them secure on their land,
and to be the mainstays of a village—
these are the people of the village.
Therefore, it is said:
“There are those who hear of the Dào and enjoy managing a village;
they are the people of one village.”
There are those who hear of the Dào and enjoy managing a state;
they are the people of one state.
There are those who hear of the Dào and enjoy managing the world;
they are the people of the world.
There are those who hear of the Dào and enjoy establishing the myriad things;
they are the counterparts of Tiān and Earth.
Where the Dào departs,
the people do not come;
where the Dào arrives,
the people do not leave.
The people following one who possesses the Dào
is like the hungry seeking food,
like the cold seeking clothes,
and like those in the heat seeking shade;
therefore, if there is Dào, the people will return to it;
if there is no Dào, the people will leave it;
Therefore, it is said:
“Where the Dào departs,
the people do not come;
where the Dào arrives,
the people do not leave.”
That which the Dào establishes
is the transformation of the self.
The Dào is
that which transforms the self and leads it toward correct principles;
thus, if the Dào is within the self,
then speech will naturally be harmonious,
conduct will naturally be upright,
serving the ruler will naturally be loyal,
serving the father will naturally be filial,
and treating others will naturally be reasonable;
therefore, it is said:
“That which the Dào establishes
is the transformation of the self.”
Maintaining fullness accords with Tiān;
securing peace and danger accords with men.
The way of Tiān
is to be full without overflowing
and to be at its peak without declining.
The enlightened ruler emulates the Dào of Tiān;
thus, he is noble but not arrogant,
rich but not extravagant,
and acts according to principle without being idle.
Therefore, he can long preserve his nobility and wealth,
and long possess the world without losing it;
therefore, it is said:
“Maintaining fullness accords with Tiān.”
An enlightened ruler is one who rescues the world from calamity
and stabilizes the world from danger;
for those who rescue from calamity and stabilize from danger
must wait for the ten thousand people to be utilized
before they can achieve it.
Therefore it is said:
“Safety and danger depend on others.”
If one loses the measure of Heaven,
even if full, one must dry up.
A large territory and a wealthy state,
a numerous population and strong soldiers—
this is a state at the peak of fullness.
Although it is already at the peak of fullness,
if there is no deep virtue to stabilize it
and no systematic measures to govern it,
then the state will not be its state,
and the people will not be its people.
Therefore it is said:
“If one loses the measure of Heaven,
even if full, one must dry up.”
If those above and below are not in harmony,
even if secure, they will certainly be in danger.
If ministers are not close to their ruler,
and the common people do not trust their officials,
and those above and below are estranged and not in harmony,
then even if they consider themselves secure,
they will certainly be in danger.
Therefore it is said:
“If those above and below are not in harmony,
even if secure, they will certainly be in danger.”
If one wishes to rule as king over the world
but loses the Way of Heaven,
the world cannot be gained and ruled as king.
If the ruler possesses the Way of Heaven
to direct his people,
then the people will be of one heart in serving their superior.
Therefore he can be noble and wealthy and rule as king over the world for a long time.
If he loses the Way of Heaven,
then the people will become estranged and rebellious and will not obey.
Therefore the ruler will be in danger and cannot rule as king over the world for a long time.
Therefore it is said:
“If one wishes to rule as king over the world,
but loses the Way of Heaven,
the world cannot be gained and ruled as king.”
If one attains the Way of Heaven,
his affairs will seem natural;
if one loses the Way of Heaven,
even if established, he will not be secure.
Once the Way is attained,
no one knows who brought it about;
once the merit is accomplished,
no one knows who bestowed the bounty.
Storing it without form
is the Way of Heaven.
If a ruler of men devotes himself to learning methods and techniques
and strives to practice correct principles,
then transformation and change will progress daily
until great merit is achieved,
yet the ignorant will not know of it.
A chaotic ruler is licentious, dissipated, depraved, and crooked,
daily acting without the Way,
until he reaches destruction and yet is unaware of it himself.
Therefore it is said:
“No one knows who brought it about;
once the merit is accomplished,
no one knows who bestowed it;
it is stored without form.”
Those who doubt the present
should examine antiquity;
those who do not know the future
should look to the past.
Of old, the Sān Wáng and Wǔ Bà
all were rulers of men who benefited from
the Way of Heaven.
Therefore their persons were noble and illustrious,
and their descendants received their bounty.
Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì
all were rulers of men who harmed the world.
Therefore their persons were troubled and injured,
and their descendants suffered their misfortune. Therefore it is said: “Those who doubt
the present should examine antiquity;
those who do not know the future should look to the past.”
The arising of all matters
may have different paths but share the same destination;
past and present are one.
Shénnóng taught plowing and the growing of grain
to bring benefit to the people.
Yǔ personally channeled the ditches,
cutting through the high and bridging the low,
to bring benefit to the people.
Tāng and Wǔ campaigned against those without the Way
and executed the violent and rebellious
to bring benefit to the people.
Therefore, although the actions of enlightened kings were different,
their benefiting of the people was the same.
Therefore it is said:
“The carrying out of all matters
may arise differently but shares the same destination;
past and present are one.”
When a fresh ridgepole collapses a house,
resentment and anger do not follow;
but when a young child drops a tile,
a compassionate mother grasps the whip.
When a ridgepole is fresh and warps,
it cannot bear the burden and the house collapses,
yet the reason people do not feel resentment
is that the principle makes it so.
A young child
is what a compassionate mother loves,
but if he drops a tile without reason,
then the compassionate mother will flog him.
Therefore, for those who act according to principle,
even if they collapse a house, it does not cause resentment.
For those who do not act according to principle,
dropping a tile will certainly result in flogging.
Therefore it is said:
“When a fresh ridgepole collapses a house,
resentment and anger do not follow.
When a young child drops a tile,
a compassionate mother grasps the whip.”
When the Way of Heaven reaches its limit,
those who are distant naturally become close;
when human affairs arise,
those who are close and kin create resentment.
If one practices the Way of Heaven
and manifests public principles,
then those who are distant will naturally become close.
If one abandons the Way of Heaven
and practices private actions,
then child and mother will resent each other.
Therefore it is said:
“When the Way of Heaven reaches its limit,
those who are distant naturally become close;
when human affairs arise,
those who are close and kin create resentment.”
All things, in relation to people,
have no private closeness
and no private distance.
The skillful have a surplus,
while the clumsy have a deficit.
Of old, Wǔ Wáng's territory did not exceed one hundred lǐ,
and his host of fighting soldiers did not exceed ten thousand men;
yet he was able to win battles and seize territories
and was established as the Son of Heaven,
and the world calls him a Sage King because
he knew the techniques for doing so.
Jié and Zhòu were as noble as the Son of Heaven,
wealthy within the four seas,
their territory was extremely large,
and their fighting soldiers were extremely numerous;
yet they died and their states perished,
and they became objects of humiliation for the world, because
they did not know the techniques for doing so.
Therefore, if one can do it,
then the small can become great
and the lowly can become noble;
if one cannot do it,
then even if one is the Son of Heaven,
people will still take it away.
Therefore it is said:
“The skillful have a surplus,
while the clumsy have a deficit.”
Those whose achievements follow Heaven, Heaven assists them;
those whose achievements oppose Heaven, Heaven surrounds them.
That which Heaven assists,
even if small, must become great;
that which Heaven surrounds,
even if accomplished, must fail.
Anciently, Wǔ Wáng
was one whom Heaven assisted;
therefore, although his land was small and his people few,
he still became the Son of Heaven.
Jié and Zhòu
were those whom Heaven opposed;
therefore, although their land was vast and their people numerous,
they still suffered distress and humiliation, and perished.
Therefore it is said:
"Those whom Heaven assists,
though small, will certainly become great.
Those whom Heaven opposes,
though great, will certainly be diminished."
Those who follow Heaven achieve success;
those who defy Heaven harbor misfortune,
and cannot rise again.
The craftiness of crows
is such that even if they seem friendly, they are not intimate.
In social interactions,
being full of deceit and lacking genuine sincerity,
seeking only to get by for the moment;
this is called an "association like a gathering of crows."
An association like a gathering of crows
may be joyous at first,
but later they will certainly rebuke each other.
Therefore it is said:
"An association like a gathering of crows,
though seemingly friendly, is not intimate."
An alliance that is not solemn,
though it seems firm, will certainly be dissolved.
In the application of the Dào,
solemnity is valued.
When a sage forms an alliance with others,
he observes from above how they serve their lord
and observes from within how they serve their parents;
there must be a principle that can be known
before he forms an alliance.
If an alliance is formed without following principle,
they will certainly turn against each other later.
Therefore it is said:
"An alliance that is not solemn,
though firm, will certainly be dissolved.
In the application of the Dào,
solemnity is valued."
Do not associate with the unsuitable.
An enlightened ruler deliberates with sages;
therefore his plans succeed.
He undertakes tasks with them;
therefore his tasks are accomplished.
A chaotic ruler deliberates with the unworthy;
therefore his plans fail.
He undertakes tasks with them;
therefore his tasks are ruined.
Now, when plans fail and tasks are ruined,
this is the fault of associating with the unsuitable.
Therefore it is said:
"Do not associate with the unsuitable."
Do not force the incapable.
An enlightened ruler measures what human power is capable of
and only then employs it.
Therefore, when orders are given for what people can do,
then the orders are carried out.
When people are employed for what they can do,
then the tasks are accomplished.
A chaotic ruler does not measure human power
and gives orders for what people cannot do;
therefore his orders are ignored.
When people are employed for what they cannot do,
then the tasks fail.
Now, when orders are issued but ignored,
and tasks are undertaken but fail,
this is the fault of forcing the incapable.
Therefore it is said:
"Do not force the incapable."
Do not inform the ignorant.
To those who are deluded and confused,
if you tell them of the righteousness between lord and subject,
the principles of father and son,
and the distinctions between noble and base,
they will not believe the words of the sage
but will instead cause him harm.
Therefore the sage does not inform them.
Therefore it is said:
"Do not inform the ignorant."
Associating with the unsuitable,
forcing the incapable,
and informing the ignorant
are called "laboring without success."
Undertaking tasks with the unworthy
leads to failure.
Employing people for what they cannot do
leads to the ignoring of orders.
Informing the deluded and confused results in harm to oneself.
Therefore it is said:
"Associating with the unsuitable,
forcing the incapable,
and informing the ignorant
are called 'laboring without success.'"
A friend who makes a show of giving
is close to not being intimate.
An association that makes a show of affection
is close to not being bonded.
Virtue that makes a show of being bestowed
is close to not being requited.
That to which the four quarters gravitate
is the conduct of the heart.
If one constantly uses words to flaunt and highlight what they give to others,
their affection for others,
and the virtue they have toward others,
and uses this to make friends,
then there is no intimacy.
If one uses this to form associations,
then there is no bond.
If one uses this as having virtue toward others,
then there is no requital.
Therefore it is said:
"A friend who makes a show of giving
is close to not being intimate.
An association that makes a show of affection
is close to not being bonded.
Virtue that makes a show of being bestowed
is close to not being requited.
That to which the four quarters gravitate
is the conduct of the heart."
A state ruled in isolation
is toilsome and plagued by disasters.
An enlightened ruler does not use his own wisdom
but relies on the wisdom of sages.
He does not use his own strength
but relies on the strength of the multitude.
Therefore, when one deliberates using the wisdom of sages,
there is nothing unknown.
When one initiates tasks using the strength of the multitude,
there is nothing unaccomplished.
Being able to set oneself aside and rely on the wisdom and strength of the world to rise,
one's person is at ease and blessings are many.
A chaotic ruler uses only his own wisdom
and does not rely on the wisdom of sages.
He uses only his own strength
and does not rely on the strength of the multitude.
Therefore his person is toiled and his disasters are many.
Therefore it is said:
"A state ruled by reliance on oneself alone
is toilsome and plagued by disasters."
The ruler of an isolated state
is lowly and lacks majesty.
An enlightened ruler internally implements laws and standards
and externally practices principles and righteousness.
Therefore neighboring states are close to him
and allied states trust him.
When there is trouble, neighboring states worry for him;
when there is difficulty, neighboring states rescue him.
A chaotic ruler internally loses his common people
and externally is not trusted by neighboring states.
When the state has trouble, no one worries for him;
when there is difficulty, no one rescues him.
Losing both the external and internal,
he is solitary and without allies.
Therefore the state is weak and the ruler is humiliated.
Therefore it is said:
"The ruler of an isolated state
is lowly and lacks majesty."
A woman who acts as her own matchmaker
is considered ugly and is not trusted.
In an enlightened ruler's governance of the world,
he must employ sages
and only then is the world well-governed.
When a woman seeks a husband’s family,
she must use a matchmaker
and only then are the domestic affairs successful.
Therefore, if one governs the world without using sages,
then the world will be perverse and chaotic and the people will not be close.
If one seeks a husband’s family without using a matchmaker,
then it is ugly and shameful and people will not trust her.
Therefore it is said:
"A woman who acts as her own matchmaker
is considered ugly and is not trusted."
If people feel close to someone before even seeing them,
then they can go to him;
as for an enlightened ruler,
people have not yet seen him,
yet they have a feeling of closeness toward him
because he possesses the way to make the people feel close to him;
therefore, his position is secure and the people flock to him.
Thus it is said:
"If people feel close to someone before even seeing them,
then they can go to him."
If after a long time people do not forget him,
then they can be made to come to him.
Yáo and Shùn were enlightened rulers of antiquity;
the world promoted them without weariness
and praised them without boredom,
and the reason they were not forgotten even after a long time
is that they possessed the way to make the people not forget them;
therefore, their positions were secure and the people came to them.
Thus it is said:
"If after a long time people do not forget him,
then they can be made to come to him."
When the sun and moon are not bright,
the sky has not changed;
the sun and moon are what illuminate and observe the myriad things,
but if the sky has many clouds and mists
and those that screen and cover are numerous,
then the sun and moon will not be bright.
A ruler of men is like the sun and moon;
if the ministers are mostly treacherous and established in their positions,
privately obstructing and screening the ruler,
then the ruler cannot illuminate and observe his subordinates;
the sentiments of the subordinates
cannot be communicated upward,
therefore treachery and wickedness increase daily
and the ruler is further screened.
Thus it is said:
"When the sun and moon are not bright,
the sky has not changed."
When a mountain is high but cannot be seen,
the earth has not changed.
A mountain
is a thing of height;
if the terrain is treacherous, overgrown, and uneven,
then the mountain cannot be seen.
A ruler of men is like a mountain;
if those on his left and right form cliques and factions to obstruct their ruler,
then the ruler cannot be seen.
Thus it is said:
"When a mountain is high but cannot be seen,
the earth has not changed."
Regarding words that should not be repeated,
the lord does not speak them;
when a ruler of men utters words that do not oppose the people's hearts
and do not contradict reason and righteousness,
and what he says is sufficient to bring peace to the world,
then people only fear that he will not speak them again.
To utter words that alienate the intimacy between father and son,
distance the way between lord and minister,
or harm the masses of the world—
these are words that should not be repeated,
therefore an enlightened ruler does not speak them.
Thus it is said:
"Regarding words that should not be repeated,
the lord does not speak them."
Regarding actions that should not be redone,
the lord does not perform them.
If a ruler of men's own conduct is upright,
employing others with ritual propriety
and treating others with reason,
such that actions originating from himself
serve as a model for the world,
then people only fear that he will not perform them again.
If his own conduct is not upright,
employing others with cruelty
and treating others with bad faith,
such that actions originating from himself
become a laughingstock for the world,
these are actions that should not be redone,
therefore an enlightened ruler does not perform them.
Thus it is said:
"Regarding actions that should not be redone,
the lord does not perform them."
In general, words that should not be repeated
and actions that should not be redone
are the great prohibitions for one who possesses a state.
The reason words should not be repeated
is that the words are untrustworthy.
The reason actions should not be redone
is that the actions are harmful and violent;
therefore, if words are untrustworthy,
then the people will not adhere;
if actions are harmful and violent,
then the world will be resentful.
If the people do not adhere
and the world is resentful,
this is where destruction and downfall originate,
therefore an enlightened ruler prohibits them.
Thus it is said:
"In general, words that should not be repeated
and actions that should not be redone
are the great prohibitions for one who possesses a state."
In a state of ten thousand chariots,
the army cannot be without a leader;
if the land is vast and wide,
the countryside cannot be without officials;
if the common people are numerous and prosperous,
the government offices cannot be without heads;
to hold the lives of the people in hand,
the court cannot be without policies.
When the land is vast but the state is poor,
it is because the countryside is not cultivated;
when the people are numerous but the army is weak,
it is because the people have nothing to gain.
Therefore, if secondary production is not prohibited,
then the countryside will not be cultivated;
if rewards and punishments are not trustworthy,
then the people will have nothing to gain.
If the countryside is not cultivated
and the people have nothing to gain,
externally one cannot respond to enemies,
and internally one cannot firmly defend.
Thus it is said, if one has the title of ten thousand chariots
but lacks the utility of one thousand chariots,
yet seeks for one's power not to be diminished,
it cannot be achieved.
When the land is cultivated but the state is poor,
it is because boats and carriages are decorated
and towers and pavilions are expansive;
when rewards and punishments are trustworthy but the army is weak,
it is because the masses are used recklessly,
causing the people to be exhausted.
If boats and carriages are decorated
and towers and pavilions are expansive,
then taxes and levies will be heavy;
if the masses are used recklessly
and the people are made to labor,
then the people's strength will be exhausted.
When taxes and levies are heavy,
then those below will resent those above;
when the people's strength is exhausted,
then orders will not be carried out.
When those below resent those above
and orders are not carried out,
yet one seeks for enemies not to plot against oneself,
it cannot be achieved.
One who wishes to rule the world
must value the use of their state;
one who wishes to rule their state
must value the use of their people;
one who wishes to care for their people
must be serious about not exhausting the people's strength.
If there is no means to sustain them,
then they will leave and cannot be stopped;
if there is no means to shepherd them,
then they will remain but cannot be commanded.
That people from afar arrive and do not leave
is because there is a means to sustain them;
that the masses of people can be unified
is because there is a means to shepherd them.
When he sees what is acceptable,
his pleasure has visible signs;
when he sees what is unacceptable,
his dislike has a visible form.
If rewards and punishments are trustworthy regarding what is seen,
then even in what is not seen,
would anyone dare to act wrongly?
Seeing what is acceptable,
show joy without outward evidence;
seeing what is unacceptable,
show dislike without external form.
If rewards and punishments are not trusted in what is seen,
then seeking for the people to be transformed in what is not seen
is impossible.
Deep love and benefit
are sufficient to endear them;
clear wisdom and *lǐ*
are sufficient to teach them.
The superior practices these personally to lead them,
examines measures and standards to restrain them,
and appoints teachers in the *xiāng* to explain the *Dào* to them.
Only then should one apply laws and orders,
encourage them with rewards,
and stimulate them with punishments.
Thus, when the common people all delight in doing good,
then violent and chaotic conduct will have no way to arise.
The earth produces wealth at certain times,
the people's labor has its exhaustion,
yet the ruler's desires are endless.
Using what is seasonal and what is exhaustible
to support an endless ruler,
without establishing measures between them,
results in mutual resentment between superiors and inferiors.
Because of this, there are ministers who kill their rulers
and sons who kill their fathers.
Therefore, if taking from the people has a limit
and spending has a stop,
the state will be secure even if small;
if taking from the people has no limit
and spending has no stop,
the state will be in peril even if large.
Land that is not reclaimed
is not our land;
people who are not shepherded
are not our people.
In all shepherding of the people,
feeding them according to what they have accumulated
must be carefully examined.
Those whose accumulation is much eat much,
those whose accumulation is little eat little,
and those with no accumulation do not eat.
If there are those who have accumulation but do not eat,
then the people will distance themselves from the superior;
if there are those with much accumulation who eat little,
then the people will not exert effort;
if there are those with little accumulation who eat much,
then the people will be full of deceit;
if there are those with no accumulation who eat for free,
then the people will be opportunistic.
Therefore, when people distance themselves from the superior, lack effort,
are full of deceit, and are opportunistic,
undertakings will not succeed,
and they will be of no use when facing an enemy.
Therefore it is said:
examining ability to grant office
and distributing stipends and gifts
are the keys to employing the people.
The countryside and the market compete for people,
the household and the treasury compete for goods,
gold and grain compete for value,
and the *xiāng* and the court compete for governance.
Thus, that the countryside does not accumulate weeds
means agricultural matters are prioritized;
that the treasury does not accumulate goods
means wealth is stored among the people;
that the market does not form rows of stalls
means household supplies are sufficient;
that the court does not gather crowds
means the *xiāng* are governed separately.
Thus, when the countryside does not accumulate weeds,
the treasury does not accumulate goods,
the market does not form rows of stalls,
and the court does not gather crowds,
it is the height of governance.
Human nature is not double-minded;
therefore, the people's nature can be managed.
By examining their likes and dislikes,
their strengths and weaknesses can be known;
by observing their associates,
their worthiness or unworthiness can be discerned.
If these two are not lost,
then the people's abilities can be harnessed for office.
The defense of land lies in the city,
the defense of the city lies in the soldiers,
the defense of the soldiers lies in the people,
and the defense of the people lies in grain.
Thus, if the land is not reclaimed,
the city will not be secure.
If one's own self is not governed,
what can be expected of others?
If people are not governed,
what can be expected of the household?
If the household is not governed,
what can be expected of the *xiāng*?
If the *xiāng* is not governed,
what can be expected of the state?
If the state is not governed,
what can be expected of *Tiānxià*?
*Tiānxià*
is the basis of the state;
the state
is the basis of the *xiāng*;
the *xiāng*
is the basis of the household;
the household
is the basis of the person;
the person
is the basis of the self;
the self
is the basis of governance.
Thus, if the superior does not favor the fundamental business,
then secondary occupations cannot be prohibited;
if secondary occupations are not prohibited,
then the people will be slow in seasonal matters and slight the benefits of the land;
if they slight the benefits of the land
and yet seek the reclamation of fields
and the fullness of granaries,
it is impossible.
If merchants are in the court,
then wealth flows upward;
if women speak on human affairs,
then rewards and punishments are not trusted;
if there is no distinction between men and women,
then the people will have no sense of integrity or shame.
If wealth flows upward,
rewards and punishments are not trusted,
and the people have no sense of integrity or shame,
yet one seeks for the common people to face difficulties with ease
and for soldiers to die for their integrity,
it is impossible.
If the court is not solemn,
noble and lowly are not distinguished,
elder and younger are not divided,
measures are not examined,
clothing has no rank,
and superiors and inferiors overstep their status,
yet one seeks for the people to respect the ruler's decrees,
it is impossible.
If the superior favors trickery and deceit,
and subordinates compete for taxes,
making the people opportunistic,
then the common people will be resentful,
and seeking for inferiors to be close to the superior
is impossible.
If one has land but does not work at the fundamental business,
or rules a state but cannot unify the people,
and yet seeks to keep the *Zōngmiào Shèjì* from danger,
it is impossible.
If the superior relies on tortoise shells and stalks
and favors shamans and healers,
then ghosts and spirits will frequently cause misfortune.
Therefore, that achievements are not established
and fame is not manifest
is due to three afflictions:
those who act as lone kings,
those who are poor and lowly,
and those for whom the days are insufficient.
For a plan of one year,
nothing is as good as planting grain;
for a plan of ten years,
nothing is as good as planting trees;
for a plan of a lifetime,
nothing is as good as planting people.
That which is planted for a single harvest is
grain;
that which is planted for ten harvests is
trees;
that which is planted for a hundred harvests is
people.
If I were to plant them,
and use them as if with divine power,
handling affairs with divine skill—
this is solely the gate of a *Wáng*.
Generally, for those who shepherd the people,
let the men have no wicked conduct
and the women have no licentious affairs.
Men having no wicked conduct
is the result of education;
women having no licentious affairs
is the result of instruction.
When education and instruction form customs
and punishments are reduced,
it is the natural consequence of strategic calculation.
Generally, for those who shepherd the people,
they desire the people to be upright.
To desire the people to be upright,
then even slight wickedness must not go unforbidden.
Slight wickedness
is that from which great wickedness arises.
If slight wickedness is not forbidden,
yet one seeks for great wickedness not to harm the state,
it cannot be attained.
Generally, for those who shepherd the people,
they desire the people to possess ritual propriety.
To desire the people to possess ritual propriety,
then small rituals must not be neglected.
If small rituals are not treated with care in the state,
yet one seeks for the common people to practice great ritual propriety,
it cannot be attained.
Generally, for those who shepherd the people,
they desire the people to possess righteousness.
To desire the people to possess righteousness,
then small acts of righteousness must not go unpracticed.
If small acts of righteousness are not practiced in the state,
yet one seeks for the common people to practice great righteousness,
it cannot be attained.
Generally, for those who shepherd the people,
they desire the people to possess integrity.
To desire the people to possess integrity,
then small integrity must not go uncultivated.
If small integrity is not cultivated in the state,
yet one seeks for the common people to practice great integrity,
it cannot be attained.
Generally, for those who shepherd the people,
they desire the people to possess a sense of shame.
To desire the people to possess a sense of shame,
then small matters of shame must not go unrefined.
If small matters of shame are not refined in the state,
yet one seeks for the common people to practice a great sense of shame,
it cannot be attained.
Generally, for those who shepherd the people,
desiring the people to be careful with small rituals,
practice small righteousness,
cultivate small integrity,
refine small shame,
and forbid slight wickedness—
this is the way to sharpen the people.
For the people to be careful with small rituals,
practice small righteousness,
cultivate small integrity,
refine small shame,
and forbid slight wickedness—
this is the root of governance.
Generally, for those who shepherd the people,
they desire the people to be controllable.
