To desire the people to be controllable,
then the law must not be treated lightly.
The law
is that which establishes the court.
To establish the court,
then ranks and uniforms must not be made common.
If ranks and uniforms are bestowed upon the unrighteous,
then the people will despise those ranks and uniforms;
if the people despise those ranks and uniforms,
then the ruler of men will not be honored;
if the ruler of men is not honored,
then orders will not be carried out.
The law
is that which uses the strength of the people.
To use the strength of the people,
then stipends and rewards must not be light.
If stipends and rewards are bestowed upon those without merit,
then the people will make light of those stipends and rewards;
if the people make light of those stipends and rewards,
then the superior will have no means to encourage the people;
if the superior has no means to encourage the people,
then orders will not be carried out.
The law
is that which uses the abilities of the people.
To use the abilities of the people,
then the conferring of offices must be scrutinized.
If the conferring of offices is not scrutinized,
then the people will criticize the administration;
if the people criticize the administration,
then reason will not communicate upward;
if reason does not communicate upward,
then those below will resent their superiors;
if those below resent their superiors,
then orders will not be carried out.
The law
is that which uses the lives of the people.
To use the lives of the people,
then punishments must be scrutinized.
If punishments are not scrutinized,
then there will be bias and avoidance;
if there is bias and avoidance,
then the innocent will be killed and the guilty pardoned;
if the innocent are killed and the guilty pardoned,
then the state will not escape traitorous ministers.
Therefore, if ranks and uniforms are despised,
stipends and rewards are made light of,
the people criticize the administration,
and traitorous ministers lead in causing trouble,
this is called the instruction that ruins a state.
There are three things by which a state is governed or falls into chaos,
but executions and punishments
are insufficient to be used alone.
There are four things by which a state is made secure or endangered,
but city walls and strategic passes
are insufficient for defense alone.
There are five things by which a state is made rich or poor,
but light taxes and rents
and low levies
are insufficient to rely upon alone.
Governing a state has three roots,
securing a state has four foundations,
and enriching a state has five matters.
These five matters are the five constants.
There are three things the ruler must scrutinize:
the first is virtue not matching the position,
the second is merit not matching the stipend,
and the third is ability not matching the office.
These three roots
are the origins of order and chaos.
Therefore, if there are those whose virtue and righteousness are not yet manifest in the court,
they must not be placed in honored positions;
if there are those whose merit and effort are not yet seen in the state,
they must not be granted heavy stipends;
if there are those who, when facing matters, are not trusted by the people,
they must not be assigned to high office.
Therefore, for virtue to be deep but the position low is called an oversight,
while for virtue to be thin but the position high is called a loss.
It is better to have an oversight regarding a *Jūn zǐ*,
than to have a loss regarding a *Xiǎo rén*.
Having an oversight regarding a *Jūn zǐ*,
the resulting resentment is shallow;
having a loss regarding a *Xiǎo rén*,
the resulting calamity is deep.
Thus, if the state has those whose virtue and righteousness are not manifest in the court yet occupy honored positions,
then good ministers will not advance;
if there are those whose merit and effort are not seen in the state yet receive heavy stipends,
then hardworking ministers will not be encouraged;
if there are those who, when facing matters, are not trusted by the people yet hold high office,
then talented ministers will not be employed.
When these three roots are scrutinized,
then those below will not dare to make improper requests.
If these three roots are not scrutinized,
then wicked ministers will communicate with the top,
and favorites will wield authority.
If it is like this,
then the ruler's clarity will be blocked above,
governance will be obstructed below,
the upright path will be cast aside,
and wicked deeds will grow daily.
If the Three Foundations are scrutinized,
then favorites and sycophants will have no power in the state,
on the roads there will be no lawless beasts,
the distant and unrelated will have no suppressed lawsuits,
and the orphaned and widowed will have no hidden suffering.
Therefore it is said:
"Punishments are sparse and administration is minimal;
the court does not gather crowds."
The above are the Three Foundations.
There are four things that a Ruler must be cautious of:
First, if one of great virtue is not perfectly humane,
they cannot be granted the handle of the state;
second, if one sees the worthy but cannot yield to them,
they cannot be given a high position;
third, if punishments avoid relatives and the noble,
they cannot be put in command of the military;
fourth, if one does not love the fundamental tasks,
does not strive for the advantages of the land,
and treats taxes and levies lightly,
they cannot be given cities and towns.
These four tasks
are the basis of security or peril.
Therefore it is said:
"If the Qīngxiàng do not win the masses,
it is a peril to the state;
if the high officials are not in harmony,
it is a peril to the state;
if the commander of the army is not feared,
it is a peril to the state;
if the people do not cherish their property,
it is a peril to the state."
Thus, if those of great virtue are perfectly humane,
then in managing the state they will win the masses;
if they see the worthy and can yield,
then the high officials will be in harmony;
if punishments do not avoid relatives and the noble,
then authority will prevail over neighboring enemies;
if they love fundamental tasks,
strive for the advantages of the land,
and value taxes and levies,
then the people will cherish their property.
These are the Four Solidifications.
There are five tasks the Ruler must attend to:
First, if mountains and marshes are not protected from fire,
and the vegetation cannot grow to maturity,
it is the poverty of the state;
second, if ditches and canals do not flow through narrow passes,
and dammed waters are not kept in their reservoirs,
it is the poverty of the state;
third, if mulberry and hemp are not cultivated in the fields,
and the five grains are not suited to the soil,
it is the poverty of the state;
fourth, if the six domestic animals are not raised in households,
and melons, gourds, pungent vegetables, and the hundred fruits are not fully provided,
it is the poverty of the state;
fifth, if craftsmanship competes in intricate carving,
and women's work is preoccupied with decorative patterns,
it is the poverty of the state.
Therefore it is said:
"If mountains and marshes are protected from fire,
and vegetation is cultivated to maturity,
it is the wealth of the state;
if ditches and canals flow through narrow passes,
and dammed waters are kept in their reservoirs,
it is the wealth of the state;
if mulberry and hemp are cultivated in the fields,
and the five grains are suited to the soil,
it is the wealth of the state;
if the six domestic animals are raised in households,
and melons, gourds, pungent vegetables, and the hundred fruits are fully provided,
it is the wealth of the state;
if craftsmanship avoids intricate carving,
and women's work avoids decorative patterns,
it is the wealth of the state."
The above are the Five Matters.
Divide the state into five Xiāng,
and for each Xiāng appoint a Shī.
Divide each Xiāng into five Zhōu,
and for each Zhōu appoint a Zhǎng.
Divide each Zhōu into ten Lǐ,
and for each Lǐ appoint a Wèi.
Divide each Lǐ into ten Yóu,
and for each Yóu appoint a Zōng.
Ten households form a Shí,
five households form a Wǔ,
and each Shí and Wǔ has its own head.
Build barriers to block off those in hiding,
unify the roads,
and regulate entry and exit.
Examine the village gates,
be careful with the locks and keys,
and keep the keys in the custody of the Lǐwèi.
Appoint a Lǘyǒusī,
to open and close them at the proper times.
The Lǘyǒusī observes those who enter and exit,
and reports back to the Lǐwèi.
Whenever entry or exit is at improper times,
clothing is inappropriate,
or associates and groups
do not conform to the norm,
the Lǘyǒusī, upon seeing this,
reports it immediately.
If it involves the sons or younger brothers of a household head, servants, subordinates, or guests,
then the Lǐwèi uses this to reprimand the Yóuzōng,
the Yóuzōng reprimands the Shíwǔ,
and the Shíwǔ reprimands the household head.
Reprimand with respect and do not report further;
for a first or second offense, show leniency,
but for a third, there shall be no pardon.
Whenever there is filial piety, fraternal duty, loyalty, trustworthiness,
virtue, goodness, or exceptional talent,
occurring among the sons or younger brothers of a household head, servants, subordinates, or guests,
then the Shíwǔ report it to the Yóuzōng,
the Yóuzōng reports it to the Lǐwèi,
the Lǐwèi reports it to the Zhōuzhǎng,
the Zhōuzhǎng provides an account to the Xiāngshī,
and the Xiāngshī records it with the Shìshī.
Whenever there is an offense in a group,
if it involves a family member,
responsibility extends to the household head;
if it involves the household head,
responsibility extends to the head of the Shíwǔ;
if it involves the head of the Shíwǔ,
responsibility extends to the Yóuzōng;
if it involves the Yóuzōng,
responsibility extends to the Lǐwèi;
if it involves the Lǐwèi,
responsibility extends to the Zhōuzhǎng;
if it involves the Zhōuzhǎng,
responsibility extends to the Xiāngshī;
if it involves the Xiāngshī,
responsibility extends to the Shìshī.
Every three months a report is made,
every six months an accounting is done,
and every twelve months a record is finalized.
In promoting the worthy, do not bypass ranks;
in employing the capable, do not let them hold concurrent offices;
in punishing the guilty, the consequence should not reach them alone;
in rewarding merit, the benefit should not be given exclusively.
At the dawn of the first month of spring,
the Ruler personally presides over the court,
discussing ranks and rewards and evaluating officials,
for a total of five days.
At the close of the last month of winter,
the Ruler personally presides over the court,
discussing punishments, crimes, and executions,
also for a total of five days.
On the first day of the first month,
all the officials are at court,
and the Ruler then issues orders and promulgates the laws to the state.
The Shī of the five Xiāng
and the Dàfū of the five dependencies
all receive the laws from the Tàishǐ.
On the day of the Great Audience,
the Shī of the five Xiāng
and the Dàfū of the five dependencies
all personally practice the laws before the Ruler.
After the Tàishǐ has promulgated the laws,
they are registered in the Tàifǔ,
and the law registers are distributed in the Ruler's presence.
The Shī of the five Xiāng depart from court,
proceed to their township offices,
summon their township subordinates and the Yóuzōng,
and all receive the laws.
Once the laws have been promulgated,
they then return and report that the orders have been delivered;
only after this do they dare return to their residences.
If the laws have not been promulgated
and the orders have not been delivered,
they do not dare return to their residences.
Returning to one's residence prematurely
is called "obstructing orders,"
a capital crime that shall not be pardoned.
The *Wǔ shǔ dà fū*,
all travel in their carriages to attend the court.
After leaving the court, they do not dare go to their lodgings
but set out immediately.
On the day they reach the capital city,
they proceed to the temple and summon their subordinate officials,
and all receive the laws.
Once the laws have been distributed,
they then dispatch messengers to deliver the orders,
specifying the day the laws were distributed and the time of day, whether early or late.
Once the laws have been distributed
and the messengers have been dispatched,
only then do they dare go to their lodgings.
If the laws have not been distributed
and the messengers have not been dispatched,
they do not dare go to their lodgings;
going to their lodgings
is called "delaying the order,"
a crime punishable by death without pardon.
Once the laws have been distributed,
if there are those who do not implement the laws,
it is called "disobeying the order,"
a crime punishable by death without pardon.
If, upon checking the laws, there are those that do not match the records in the *Tài fǔ*,
it is called "extravagant arbitrary rule";
if they are insufficient, it is called "deficient order,"
a crime punishable by death without pardon.
Only after the primary laws have been distributed
can the laws then be implemented.
To the right is "Promulgating the Primary Laws."
Whenever an affair is about to be undertaken,
the order must first be issued.
It states what the affair to be done is,
and the amounts for rewards and punishments
must first be made clear.
Those establishing the affair
must carefully follow the orders to carry out rewards and punishments;
they shall account for the affair and submit the orders,
and report back on where rewards and punishments were applied.
If there is anything that does not match what was specified in the order,
even if there is merit or profit,
it is called "arbitrary rule,"
a crime punishable by death without pardon.
Only after the primary instructions for an affair have been distributed
can the affair then be undertaken.
To the right is "Promulgating the Primary Affairs."
Maintain the fire laws
and respect the mountains, marshes,
forests, thickets, and accumulated grass.
Where natural resources are produced,
prohibit or allow their harvesting according to the seasons,
so that the people have sufficient materials for building houses
and for the accumulation of firewood and kindling;
these are the duties of the *Yú shī*.
Draining floodwaters,
clearing ditches and canals,
repairing embankments and dikes,
and securing water storage,
so that even if the seasonal rains are excessive,
they do not harm the five grains,
and though the year may be one of drought,
there is still some harvest;
these are the duties of the *Sī kōng*.
Evaluating high and low ground,
examining fertile and barren soil,
observing the suitability of the land,
and clearly announcing the deadlines,
the former and latter farmers
are uniformly regulated according to the seasons
to make the five grains, mulberry, and hemp
all flourish in their proper places;
these are the duties of the *Sī tián*.
Traveling through the townships and villages,
inspecting the houses,
observing the planting of trees and crops,
and checking the six kinds of livestock,
they are uniformly regulated according to the seasons,
encouraging and urging the common people
to work hard and not be idle,
to cherish and find joy in their homes,
and to be reluctant to leave their villages;
these are the duties of the *Xiāng shī*.
Evaluating the various craftsmen,
examining seasonal tasks,
distinguishing between quality and poor workmanship,
and valuing durability and utility,
they supervise and unify the five townships,
regulating them according to the seasons
so that ornate carving and patterns
dare not be produced in the countryside;
these are the duties of the *Gōng shī*.
To the right is "Inspecting the Officials."
Establish the dress according to the rank
and measure expenditures according to the stipend.
There are measures for food and drink,
regulations for clothing,
standards for houses,
numbers for livestock and servants,
and restrictions on boats, carriages, and display vessels.
In life, there are distinctions in carriages and caps, clothing and rank, grain stipends, and fields and houses;
in death, there are standards for inner and outer coffins, shrouds and coverlets, and the size of grave mounds.
Even if one has a worthy person or noble body,
if one does not hold the rank,
one does not dare wear the corresponding clothing;
even if one has a wealthy family and many resources,
if one does not have the stipend,
one does not dare use that wealth.
The *Tiān zǐ* has patterns and emblems on his clothing,
which the ladies dare not wear for banquets or at the ancestral temple;
generals and grand officers use them to attend court,
officials use them by mandate,
and the lower officers are limited to belts and borders.
Common people dare not wear mixed colors,
and craftsmen and merchants may not wear long robes or marten fur.
Former convicts and punished people dare not wear ceremonial caps or keep a train of carriages.
To the right is "Dress Regulations."
If the theory of "laying down arms" prevails,
then strategic passes will not be defended.
If the ruler of men merely listens to "laying down arms,"
then the ministers and guests will not dare speak of military matters.
In such a case, internally they will not know whether the state is in order or chaos,
and externally they will not know the strength of the feudal lords.
If it is like this,
then the city walls will fall into ruin
and no one will build or repair them;
armor will be worn out and weapons blunt,
and no one will maintain them.
If it is like this,
then the preparations for defense are destroyed.
Distant lands will plot,
and the soldiers of the borders will prepare,
while the common people will have no heart to resist the enemy.
Therefore it is said:
"If the theory of 'laying down arms' prevails,
then strategic passes will not be defended."
If the theory of "universal love" prevails,
then the soldiers will not fight.
If the ruler of men merely listens to the theory of "universal love,"
he views the people of the world as his own people
and views other states as his own state.
If it is like this,
then he has no heart for annexation or seizure
and no instances of overthrowing armies or defeating generals.
Consequently, soldiers with skills in archery, charioteering, and strength will not receive generous stipends,
and ministers who overthrow armies and kill generals will not be honored with noble rank.
If it is like this,
then soldiers with skills in archery, charioteering, and strength will go abroad.
I may be able to refrain from attacking others,
but I cannot make others refrain from attacking me.
If they demand land and I give it,
it is not what I desire.
If I do not give it and go to war with them,
I will certainly not win.
The other side uses trained soldiers,
while I use a driven mob;
the other side uses fine generals,
while I use the incompetent.
The defeat will certainly involve the overthrow of the army and the killing of the general.
Therefore it is said:
"If the theory of 'universal love' prevails,
then the soldiers will not fight."
If the theory of "preserving life" prevails,
then integrity and a sense of shame will not be established.
If the ruler of men merely loves "preserving life,"
then the ministers will all preserve their own lives.
And since life further nourishes life—
what does it nourish?
It is said:
"Rich flavors,
sounds and colors,"
then these are pursued for the cultivation of life.
If so, then one follows desires and acts recklessly,
there is no distinction between men and women,
and they revert to the level of birds and beasts.
Then ritual, righteousness, integrity, and shame are not established,
and the ruler of men has no means to maintain himself.
Therefore it is said:
"When the theory of preserving life prevails,
then integrity and shame are not established."
When the theory of private opinion and self-exaltation prevails,
then the orders of the superior are not carried out.
If the ruler of men listens to private opinion and self-exaltation,
then the people will withdraw into quietude and hide away,
living in caves and going to the mountains,
criticizing the world and looking down on the superior,
slighting titles and emoluments while despising the officials.
In such a case, orders are not carried out,
and prohibitions do not stop actions.
Therefore it is said:
"When the theory of private opinion and self-exaltation prevails,
then the orders of the superior are not carried out."
When the theory of cliques and factions prevails,
then the worthy and the unworthy are not distinguished.
If the ruler of men listens to cliques and factions,
then the various ministers will form partisan groups,
obscuring the good and publicizing the evil.
Consequently, the truth and falsehood of the state are not seen by the superior.
If it is like this,
then those with partisans take the lead,
while those with few partisans are left behind.
When those with partisans take the lead
and the worthy and the unworthy are not distinguished,
then the chaos of struggle and seizure arises,
and the ruler is in the midst of danger.
Therefore it is said:
"When the theory of cliques and factions prevails,
then the worthy and the unworthy are not distinguished."
When the theory of gold, jade, goods, and wealth prevails,
then titles and robes flow downward.
If the ruler of men is fond of gold, jade, goods, and wealth,
he must want to obtain what he is fond of.
Thus, he must have something to exchange for them.
What does he use to exchange for them?
Great offices and honorable positions;
if not these,
then noble titles and heavy emoluments.
If it is like this,
then the unworthy will be in high positions.
Consequently, the worthy will not serve under them,
the wise will not plan for them,
the trustworthy will not make agreements,
and the brave will not die for them.
If it is like this,
then it is driving the state away and abandoning it.
Therefore it is said:
"When the theory of gold, jade, goods, and wealth prevails,
then titles and robes flow downward."
When the theory of spectacles, music, and pastimes prevails,
then treacherous people are in high positions.
If the ruler of men listens to spectacles, music, and pastimes,
then there will be ruin.
Generally, spectacles and music involve
palaces, towers, and ponds,
pearls, jade, sounds, and music.
All these waste wealth and exhaust strength,
and are ways of harming the state.
Those who serve the ruler with these things
are all treacherous people.
If the ruler of men listens to them,
how can he not be ruined?
Consequently, the treasuries and granaries will be empty,
and the reserves will be exhausted.
Furthermore, when treacherous people are in high positions,
they block the worthy and prevent them from advancing.
Thus, when the state happens to have a disaster,
then actors and dwarves will arise to discuss state affairs.
This is driving the state away and abandoning it.
Therefore it is said:
"When the theory of spectacles, music, and pastimes prevails,
then treacherous people are in high positions."
When the theory of personal solicitations and recommendations prevails,
then the ink-line is not straight.
If the ruler of men listens to personal solicitations and praise,
then all the ministers will make requests for one another.
Thus, solicitations are successful with the superior,
and partisan groups are formed in the villages.
If it is like this,
then bribes will circulate in the state,
and the legal system will be destroyed in the offices.
The ministers will strive to be clever to seek employment.
Consequently, there will be honor without titles,
and wealth without emoluments.
Therefore it is said:
"When the theory of personal solicitations and praise
prevails,
then the ink-line is not straight."
When the theory of flattery and covering up faults prevails,
then artful sycophants are employed.
If the ruler of men listens to words of flattery and the covering up of faults,
then there will be ruin.
How is this known to be so?
Flattering ministers
always cause their lord not to regret his faults
and not to change his mistakes.
Therefore the lord is deluded and does not know it himself.
If it is like this,
then planning ministers will die and flattering ministers will be honored.
Therefore it is said:
"When the theory of flattery and covering up faults
prevails,
then artful sycophants are employed."
The above are the Nine Ruinations.
To have them arrive at the appointed time,
to have them go when sent,
and for the common people to set aside themselves and take the superior as their heart
is what is expected of teaching.
Beginning from what is not enough to be seen,
ending in what cannot be reached;
if one person submits to it,
ten thousand people will follow it;
this is what is expected of instruction.
To act without being ordered,
to go without being sent,
for the superior not to add encouragement
yet for the people to exhaust themselves,
this is what is expected of custom.
When likes and dislikes take shape in the heart,
and the common people are transformed below,
so that punishments are not yet carried out and the people are in awe,
and rewards are not yet added and the people are encouraged,
this is what is expected of sincerity and trustworthiness.
To act without harm,
to succeed without being criticized,
to gain so that no one can compete,
this is what is expected of the *Tiāndào*.
To act and succeed,
to seek and obtain,
so that whatever the superior desires,
whether small or large, is surely accomplished,
this is what is expected of affairs.
Orders are followed and prohibitions are stopped;
wherever the statutes reach
and wherever the customs cover,
it is like the hundred parts of the body following the heart;
this is what is expected of government.
The above are the Seven Observations.
Generally, in establishing a state capital,
if it is not at the foot of a great mountain,
it must be on a broad river.
If high, do not let it be near drought
so that water use is sufficient;
if low, do not let it be near water
so that ditches and embankments are minimized.
Relying on natural materials
and following the advantages of the terrain,
therefore the inner and outer city walls need not perfectly match the compass and square,
and the roads need not perfectly match the level and line.
The above is on establishing a state.
One who acts through non-action is a *Dì*;
one who acts but does not act for a specific purpose is a *Wáng*;
one who acts but does not value himself is a *Bà*.
Not regarding oneself as the one to be valued
is the Way of the Ruler;
being valued but not exceeding proper measure
is the Way of the Minister.
The above are the Great Principles.
Land
is the foundation of government,
the court
is the orderer of righteousness,
the market
is the standard of goods,
gold
is the measure of utility,
and the land of the Zhūhóu,
a state of a thousand chariots,
is the regulation of the apparatus.
The principles of these five can be known,
and there is a way to manage them.
Land is the foundation of government,
therefore land can be used to rectify government.
If the land is not balanced and harmonized,
then government cannot be rectified.
If government is not rectified,
then affairs cannot be ordered.
Spring, autumn, winter, and summer
are the shifts of Yīnyáng;
the length or shortness of the seasons
is the beneficial use of Yīnyáng;
the change of day and night
is the transformation of Yīnyáng.
Thus, Yīnyáng is rectified;
even if it were not rectified,
what is in excess cannot be reduced,
and what is insufficient cannot be increased.
It is Heaven; none can reduce or increase it.
Therefore, that which can rectify government is land.
Thus it must be rectified.
In rectifying land,
its reality must be rectified.
Long is rectified,
short is rectified,
small is rectified,
large is rectified;
long, short, small, and large are all fully rectified.
If rectification is not correct,
then officials will not be ordered;
if officials are not ordered,
then affairs will not be governed;
if affairs are not governed,
then goods will not be abundant.
Therefore, how do we know that goods are abundant?
It is said:
affairs are governed;
how do we know affairs are governed?
It is said:
goods are abundant.
When goods are abundant and affairs are governed,
then what is sought from the world is little.
There is a way to manage this.
The above concerns Yīnyáng.
The court
is the orderer of righteousness.
Therefore, when ranks and positions are rectified, the people do not feel resentment;
when the people do not feel resentment,
then there is no disorder;
only then can righteousness be ordered.
If not rectified,
then it cannot
be ordered.
Therefore, the people of a whole state
cannot all be noble;
if all were noble,
then affairs would not be completed and the state would not benefit.
Because affairs would not be completed
and the state would not benefit,
if there were no noble ones,
then the people could not order themselves.
Therefore, by distinguishing the honor and meanness of ranks and positions,
one knows the sequence of precedence
and the righteousness of the noble and the humble.
There is a way to manage this.
The above concerns ranks and positions.
The market
is the standard of goods.
Therefore, if all goods are cheap,
then all profits cannot be obtained;
if all profits cannot be obtained,
then all affairs are governed;
if all affairs are governed,
then all expenditures are moderated.
Thus, affairs arise from planning,
are completed through diligence,
and are lost through arrogance.
Without planning they do not arise,
without diligence they are not completed,
without arrogance they are not lost.
Therefore it is said:
the market allows one to know order and disorder,
allows one to know abundance and scarcity,
but it cannot create abundance or scarcity.
There is a way to manage this.
The above concerns the diligence of market affairs.
Gold
is the measure of utility.
By distinguishing the principles of gold,
one knows extravagance and frugality;
knowing extravagance and frugality,
all expenditures are moderated.
Thus, frugality harms affairs,
and extravagance harms goods.
Frugality makes gold cheap;
if gold is cheap, then affairs are not completed;
thus it harms affairs.
Extravagance makes gold expensive;
if gold is expensive, then goods are cheap;
thus it harms goods.
If one only knows insufficiency after goods are exhausted,
this is not knowing measure;
if affairs are finished,
and only then does one know the surplus of goods,
this is not knowing moderation.
Not knowing measure
and not knowing moderation are unacceptable.
This is called having a way.
Throughout the world, horses are ridden and oxen are yoked,
and there are regulations for the weight of their loads.
For a journey of one night,
the distance of the road has a calculated count.
Thus, knowing the land of the Zhūhóu and a state of a thousand chariots
is how one knows the size of the land
and how one knows the weight of the load.
To reduce it only after it is too heavy
is not knowing the load;
to increase it only after it is too light
is not knowing the apparatus.
Not knowing the load and not knowing the apparatus are unacceptable.
There is a way to manage this.
Land that cannot produce food
and mountains without trees:
one hundred units are equivalent to one.
Dried-up marshes:
one hundred are equivalent to one.
Land without grass or trees:
one hundred are equivalent to one.
Where brush and thorns grow together
and the people cannot enter:
one hundred are equivalent to one.
Reedy marshes
where sickles and ropes can enter:
nine are equivalent to one.
Overgrown mountains
whose wood can be used for timber
and for axles,
and where axes can enter:
nine are equivalent to one.
Deep mountains
whose wood can be used for coffins
and for carts,
and where axes can enter:
ten are equivalent to one.
Running water
where nets can enter:
five are equivalent to one.
Forests
whose wood can be used for coffins
and for carts,
and where axes can enter:
five are equivalent to one.
Marshes
where nets can enter:
five are equivalent to one.
This is called: land equalization
by real numbers.
An area of six square *lǐ*
is named a *pù*;
five *pù* are named a *bù*;
five *bù* are named a *jù*.
A *jù* has a market;
if there is no market, the people will be in want.
Five *jù* are named a certain *xiāng*;
four *xiāng* are named a *fāng*.
This is the administrative system.
Once the administration is established, settlements are organized:
five families form a *wǔ*;
ten families form a *lián*;
five *lián* form a *pù*;
five *pù* have a leader;
this is called a certain *xiāng*.
Four *xiāng* are named a *dū*.
This is the settlement system.
Once settlements are established, tasks are regulated:
four *jù* make one *lí*;
five *lí* make one *zhì*;
five *zhì* make one *tián*;
two *tián* make one *fū*;
three *fū* make one household.
This is the labor regulation system.
Once tasks are established, equipment is regulated:
an area of six square *lǐ*
is the land for one *shèng*.
One *shèng*
consists of four horses.
For one horse, its armor is seven pieces
and its protective coverings are five;
for one *shèng*,
its armor is twenty-eight pieces
and its protective coverings are twenty;
thirty unarmored attendants serve two vehicles.
This is the equipment system.
An area of six square *lǐ*
is the land for one *shèng*;
an area of one square *lǐ*
is the field for nine *fū*.
One *yì* of gold
is what one hundred *shèng* consume for one night's stay.
If there is no gold, then use its silk;
thirty-three lengths of *jì* silk equal one *yì*.
If there is no silk, then use its cloth;
one hundred *liǎng* of coarse linen cloth equal one *yì*.
One *yì* of gold
feeds one hundred *shèng* for one night.
Within the distributed land,
if one *dǒu* of grain is produced for every six paces,
it is called a medium harvest year.
Having a market is essential; without a market,
the people will be in want.
An area of six square *lǐ*
is named a *shè*;
if there is a settlement there,
it is named *yāng*.
Also included are the taxes from passes and markets.
One hundred *yì* of gold make one *qiè*;
as for commodities, one grain basket is worth ten *qiè*.
If there are thirty merchants in the market,
in the first and twelfth months
they pay one *yì* of gold.
This is called the *zhèng* levy.
The spring division is called *shūbǐ*;
the start of summer is called *yuèchéng*;
autumn is called *dàjī*,
when the population count is compared with those present and missing.
Every three years, embankments are repaired;
every five years, boundaries are repaired;
every ten years, the regulations are revised.
This is the regular governance.
If water is found at a depth of one *rèn*, there will be no great floods;
if water is found at five *chǐ*, there will be no great droughts.
If water is found at one *rèn*, the levy is light:
subtract one-tenth; if at two, then subtract two; if at three,
then subtract three; if at four, then subtract four;
if at five, then subtract half.
This is compared to the mountains.
If water is found at five *chǐ*,
subtract one-tenth;
if at four, then subtract two;
if at three, then subtract three;
if at two, then subtract four.
If water is found at one *chǐ*,
it is compared to a marsh.
From outside the capital gates
to the limits of the four borders,
a man works two plows,
and a youth of five *chǐ* works one plow,
which is considered three days' labor.
In the first month,
orders are given for farmers to begin work
and perform plowing on the public fields.
When the snow melts,
plowing begins;
weeding marks the end.
For scholars who are well-informed, widely
learned, and discerning
but do not serve as ministers,
they are credited with achievements but do not receive a share.
For merchants who know the high and low prices
and come to the market daily
but are not state merchants,
they are credited with achievements but do not receive a share.
For artisans who refine appearances and functions
and come to the market daily
but are not state artisans,
they are credited with achievements but do not receive a share.
Those who cannot be made to work as artisans
shall have their actual assets and liabilities examined and provide grain per adult male.
Therefore, what the wise know
but the foolish do not
cannot be used to teach the people.
What the skillful can do
but the clumsy cannot
cannot be used to teach the people.
If it is not a single order that makes the people comply,
it cannot be considered a great good.
If common people cannot do it,
it cannot be considered a great achievement.
Therefore, unless one is a sincere merchant, one may not derive a livelihood from trade;
unless one is a sincere artisan, one may not derive a livelihood from craft;
unless one is a sincere farmer, one may not derive a livelihood from farming;
unless one is a trustworthy scholar, one may not stand in the court.
Thus, though an office be vacant, no one dares to solicit it;
though the ruler has precious chariots and armor, no one dares to appropriate them.
When the ruler initiates an undertaking,
ministers do not dare to falsely claim what they cannot do.
The ruler knows his ministers,
and the ministers also know that the ruler knows them.
Therefore, no minister dares not to exert all his effort and bring all his sincerity.
The Way says:
Equalize the land and divide the labor
to make the people aware of the seasons.
The people will then know the timing of the seasons,
the insufficiency of the days and months,
and the hunger and cold reaching their own bodies.
Therefore, they sleep late and rise early;
fathers, sons, and brothers
do not forget their tasks,
working without fatigue,
and the people do not fear toil and hardship.
Thus, inequality is an evil;
the benefits of the land must not be exhausted,
and the strength of the people must not be depleted.
If they are not told the seasons,
then the people will not know them;
if they are not guided in tasks,
then the people will not act.
By sharing goods with them,
the people will know how to obtain things fairly;
by clarifying their shares,
the people will exert all their strength.
Thus, without being ordered, fathers, sons, and brothers do not forget their tasks.
Above are the scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants.
That which makes a Sage a Sage
is being good at organizing the people.
If a Sage cannot organize the people,
he is no different from the common people.
If he is insufficient himself,
how can he be called a Sage?
Therefore, when there are tasks, use them;
when there are no tasks, return them to the people.
Only a Sage is good at entrusting occupations to the people.
In the lives of the people,
openness brings benefit,
while closure brings stagnation.
The one above acts as one;
the ones below act as two.
Above is the Sage.
The handling of affairs in accordance with timing is precise;
it cannot be hidden or set aside.
Therefore it is said:
If it is not done today,
tomorrow there will be a loss of goods.
The days of the past have already gone and will not return.
The above is on missing the opportunity.
For superior land of eighty *lǐ* square,
there is one state of ten thousand households and
four capitals of one thousand households.
For medium land of one hundred *lǐ* square,
there is one state of ten thousand households and
four capitals of one thousand households.
For inferior land of one hundred and twenty *lǐ* square,
there is one state of ten thousand households and
four capitals of one thousand households.
The superior land of eighty *lǐ* square
and the inferior land of one hundred and twenty *lǐ* square
are both equivalent to the medium land of one hundred *lǐ* square.
The above is on land measurement.
To speak of what is right but be unable to establish it,
to speak of what is wrong but be unable to abolish it,
to have merit but be unable to reward it,
to have guilt but be unable to punish it—
if one could govern the people in such a manner,
it has never happened.
What is right must be established,
what is wrong must be abolished,
merit must be rewarded,
and guilt must be punished.
If it is thus, is order achieved?
Not yet.
Why is this?
It is said:
If strategic configurations and implements are not yet prepared,
it is the same as being unordered.
When strategic configurations and implements are prepared, and these four matters are ready,
then there is order.
To be unable to govern one’s people
and yet be able to strengthen one’s military—
it has never happened.
To be able to govern one’s people
but not be clear on the techniques for managing the military,
this is still not possible.
To be unable to strengthen one’s military
and yet be able to certainly defeat enemy states—
it has never happened.
To be able to strengthen one’s military
but not be clear on the principles of defeating enemy states,
it is the same as not being victorious.
For the military to not necessarily defeat enemy states
and yet be able to rectify the world—
it has never happened.
If the military certainly defeats enemy states,
but one is not clear on the distinctions for rectifying the world,
this is still not possible.
Therefore it is said:
There are implements for governing the people;
there are techniques for managing the military;
there are principles for defeating enemy states;
there are distinctions for rectifying the world.
Rules (*Zé*),
Models (*Xiàng*),
Laws (*Fǎ*),
Transformation (*Huà*),
Decision-making and Obstruction (*Juésè*),
Mental Arts (*Xīnshù*), and
Calculation (*Jìshù*):
To take root in the *qì* of heaven and earth,
the harmony of cold and heat,
the nature of water and soil,
and the life of people, birds, beasts, grasses, and trees—
although things are very many,
all have their regularities
and have never changed;
this is called "Rules" (*Zé*).
Righteousness,
names,
timing,
resemblances,
categories,
comparisons, and
forms;
these are called "Models" (*Xiàng*).
Feet and inches,
the marking line,
the compass and square,
weights and balances,
pecks and bushels, and
capacity measures;
these are called "Laws" (*Fǎ*).
Gradualness,
compliance,
influence,
duration,
submission, and
practice;
these are called "Transformation" (*Huà*).
Granting and seizing,
danger and ease,
benefit and harm,
difficulty and ease,
opening and closing, and
killing and living;
these are called "Decision-making and Obstruction" (*Juésè*).
Reality,
sincerity,
generosity,
bestowal,
measure, and
empathy;
these are called "Mental Arts" (*Xīnshù*).
Hardness and softness,
lightness and weight,
largeness and smallness,
fullness and emptiness,
distance and proximity, and
many and few;
these are called "Calculation" (*Jìshù*).
If one is not clear on Rules (*Zé*),
yet wishes to arrange standards and delineate
systems,
it is like setting up a sundial on a revolving wheel,
or shaking a pole and wishing to fix its tip.
If one is not clear on Models (*Xiàng*),
yet wishes to judge talent and examine utility,
it is like cutting what is long to make it short
or joining what is short to make it long.
If one is not clear on Laws (*Fǎ*),
yet wishes to govern the people and unify the masses,
it is like writing with the left hand and erasing it with the right.
If one is not clear on Transformation (*Huà*),
yet wishes to change customs and alter teachings,
it is like steaming wood for a wheel in the morning and wishing to ride the carriage in the evening.
If one is not clear on Decision-making and Obstruction (*Juésè*),
yet wishes to drive the masses and migrate the people,
it is like making water flow uphill.
If one is not clear on Mental Arts (*Xīnshù*),
yet wishes to issue commands to others,
it is like turning one’s back on the target and insisting on hitting it.
If one is not clear on Calculation (*Jìshù*),
yet wishes to undertake great affairs,
it is like having no boat or oars and wishing to cross dangerous waters.
Therefore it is said:
To arrange standards and delineate systems
is impossible without knowing Rules (*Zé*);
to judge talent and examine utility
is impossible without knowing Models (*Xiàng*);
to govern the people and unify the masses
is impossible without knowing Laws (*Fǎ*);
to change customs and alter teachings
is impossible without knowing Transformation (*Huà*);
to drive the masses and migrate the people
is impossible without knowing Decision-making and Obstruction (*Juésè*);
to issue commands and ensure they are followed
is impossible without knowing Mental Arts (*Xīnshù*);
to undertake affairs and ensure success
is impossible without knowing Calculation (*Jìshù*).
The above is the Seven Laws (*Qī Fǎ*).
Numerous concealments wound the authority of the superior;
corrupt officials wound the laws of the office;
wicked people wound the customs and teachings;
thieves and robbers wound the state's populace.
When authority is wounded,
weight rests with those below;
when laws are wounded,
wealth flows upward;
when teachings are wounded,
those who follow commands will not be in harmony;
when the populace is wounded,
the common people will not be at peace in their dwellings.
When weight rests with those below,
commands will not be carried out.
If wealth flows to the upper classes,
the virtue of officials is destroyed;
if those who follow orders are not harmonious,
then the hundred tasks will yield no success;
if the common people are not secure in their dwellings,
then those with few possessions will settle while those with assets will disperse.
When those with few possessions settle
and those with assets disperse,
the land will not be cultivated;
if the land is not cultivated,
the six types of livestock will not be bred;
if the six types of livestock are not bred,
the state will be poor and its resources insufficient;
if the state is poor and its resources insufficient,
the military will be weak and the soldiers will not be encouraged;
if the military is weak and the soldiers are not encouraged,
battles will not be won and defenses will not be firm;
if battles are not won and defenses are not firm,
then the state will not be at peace.
Therefore it is said:
If standing orders are not scrutinized,
then the hundred deceptions will prevail;
if official ranks and titles are not scrutinized,
then corrupt officials will prevail;
if tallies and registers are not scrutinized,
then wicked people will prevail;
if punishments and laws are not scrutinized,
then thieves and bandits will prevail.
When these four guiding principles of the state fail,
the ruler of men becomes negligent, and danger appears.
When the ruler of men is negligent,
then men of truthful words do not come forward;
if men of truthful words do not come forward,
then the state's true and false conditions are not fully revealed to the ruler.
What the lords of the world value are treasures;
those they are close to are their kin;
those they love are the people;
what they emphasize are titles and stipends.
A brilliant ruler is not like this.
What he makes truly valuable
is not treasure;
those he makes truly close
are not his kin;
those he truly loves
are not the people;
what he makes truly weighty
are not titles and stipends.
Therefore, he does not diminish his commands for the sake of valuable treasures;
thus it is said:
"Commands are more valuable than treasure."
He does not endanger his Shèjì for the sake of loving his kin;
thus it is said:
"The Shèjì is closer
than kin." He does not bend the law for the sake of loving the people;
thus it is said:
"The law is more beloved than the people."
He does not divide his authority for the sake of emphasizing stipends and titles;
thus it is said:
"Authority is weightier than stipends and titles."
If one does not master these four things,
one returns to a state of having nothing.
Therefore it is said:
Governing people is like managing a flood;
nurturing people is like raising the six types of livestock;
using people is like using grass and trees.
If in his own conduct he evaluates the Dào and acts according to principle,
then the various ministers will submit to instruction,
all officials will be strict in judgment,
and none will dare to open the way for private interests.
When evaluating merit and calculating labor,
the laws and statutes are never violated.
Sycophants,
personal attendants,
great clans,
the noble,
and high ministers
are not allowed to increase their merit beyond the truth.
Those who are distant,
lowly,
or obscure and unknown
do not have their labor forgotten.
Thus, those with guilt do not resent the ruler,
and those who receive rewards have no greedy hearts;
then the soldiers in the ranks
will all treat death lightly and be at peace with hardships
to achieve the tasks of the ruler;
this is the pinnacle of military affairs.
Above are the four injuries.
The methods of military affairs:
they lie in accumulating wealth,
so that wealth is matchless;
they lie in evaluating workmanship,
so that workmanship is matchless;
they lie in manufacturing equipment,
so that equipment is matchless;
they lie in selecting soldiers,
so that soldiers are matchless;
they lie in government and instruction,
so that government and instruction are matchless;
they lie in training and practice,
so that training and practice are matchless;
they lie in all-encompassing knowledge of the world,
so that knowledge of the world is matchless;
they lie in clarity regarding strategic timing and calculation,
so that clarity regarding strategic timing and calculation is matchless.
Thus, before the army even crosses the border,
there are eight ways in which it is matchless.
Therefore, if one wishes to rectify the world,
if one's wealth does not cover the world,
one cannot rectify the world;
if wealth covers the world
but workmanship does not cover the world,
one cannot rectify the world;
if workmanship covers the world
but equipment does not cover the world,
one cannot rectify the world;
if equipment covers the world
but soldiers do not cover the world,
one cannot rectify the world;
if soldiers cover the world
but instruction does not cover the world,
one cannot rectify the world;
if instruction covers the world
but practice does not cover the world,
one cannot rectify the world;
if practice covers the world
but one does not have all-encompassing knowledge of the world,
one cannot rectify the world;
if one has all-encompassing knowledge of the world
but is not clear regarding strategic timing and calculation,
one cannot rectify the world.
Thus, clarity regarding strategic timing and calculation
is the strategic power of employing the military.
The great factor is timing;
the small factor is calculation.
When the Wáng Dào is not discarded,
and none in the world dare to spy upon the state,
this is the rectitude of the King.
To balance the storehouses
is the ritual of the Tiānzǐ.
Therefore, when equipment is prepared and troops are selected,
the soldiers know victory is certain.
With all-encompassing knowledge of the world
and careful scrutiny of strategic timing and calculation,
one can act alone and be matchless.
Toward the state one loves,
one alone grants benefit;
toward the state one hates,
one alone inflicts harm;
then orders will be followed and prohibitions obeyed.
Thus, the Shèng Wáng values this.
To defeat one and submit a hundred
makes the world fear one;
to establish a few and observe the many
makes the world cherish one;
to punish the guilty
and reward the meritorious
makes the world follow one.
Therefore, gather the elite wealth of the world,
and evaluate the sharpest equipment of the hundred craftsmen;
conduct competitions and tests in spring and autumn
to train them,
giving precedence to the elite and sharp.
Finished equipment that is not inspected is not used;
if it is not tested, it is not stored.
Gather the heroes of the world
and possess the champions of the world.
Thus, their mobilization is like flying birds,
their movement like thunder and lightning,
their release like wind and rain;
none can withstand them in front,
none can harm them from behind;
they advance and retreat alone,
and none dare to resist or obstruct them.
Success in establishing affairs
must follow logic and righteousness.
Therefore, without logic one cannot conquer the world,
and without righteousness one cannot conquer people.
Thus, a worthy and wise ruler
must stand on winning ground;
thus, he rectifies the world and none dare resist him.
The above is the method of military affairs.
As for specific regulations and timely actions,
they must not lose the timing of Heaven,
nor waste the advantages of Earth.
Whether numbers are many or few,
the essence must derive from calculation.
Therefore, in all ways of campaigning and invading,
plans must first be determined internally,
and then the troops go out beyond the borders.
If plans are not yet determined internally
while troops go out beyond the borders,
this is for the battle to defeat itself
and for the attack to destroy itself.
For this reason, to deploy an army and be unable to fight,
to besiege a city and be unable to attack,
or to gain territory and be unable to populate it—
if even one of these three occurs,
then one can be broken and destroyed.
Thus, if one is not clear about the enemy's governance,
one cannot put pressure on them;
if one is not clear about the enemy's situation,
one cannot make agreements;
if one is not clear about the enemy's generals,
one cannot prioritize the army;
if one is not clear about the enemy's soldiers,
one cannot prioritize the formation.
For this reason, using the many to strike the few,
using order to strike chaos,
using wealth to strike poverty,
using competence to strike incompetence,
and using instructed troops and trained warriors to strike a driven mob and raw recruits;
therefore, winning ten times in ten battles
and winning a hundred times in a hundred battles.
If affairs are without preparation
and the military is without a leader,
then there is no early knowledge;
if the wilds are not developed
and the land has no officials,
then there are no accumulated reserves;
if official duties have no constancy
and those below resent those above,
then the equipment and weapons will not be effective;
if the court has no administration,
then rewards and punishments will not be clear;
if rewards and punishments are not clear,
then the people will trust in luck for survival.
Therefore, knowing the enemy early allows one to act alone;
having accumulated reserves
allows for long campaigns without exhaustion;
effective equipment and weapons
allow for invasions without waste;
clear rewards and punishments
ensure that the people do not trust in lucky
survival;
when the people do not trust in lucky
survival,
then brave warriors are encouraged.
Thus, as for military affairs:
scrutinizing maps of the terrain,
planning with the daily
officials, measuring accumulated reserves,
unifying brave warriors,
knowing the world comprehensively,
and carefully managing the mechanics of opportunity—
these are the duties of the military leader.
With movement like wind and rain,
one can disregard the distance of the journey.
With action like flying birds,
one can disregard the dangers of mountains and rivers.
With fighting like thunder and lightning,
one can act alone and be without rival.
With effectiveness like flood or drought,
one can attack states and rescue cities.
With a defense like a metal wall,
one can secure the ancestral temples
and nurture the people.
With the governance of a single body,
one can issue commands
and clarify the constitutional laws.
Movement like wind and rain
means speed.
Action like flying birds
means lightness.
Fighting like thunder and lightning
means the enemy's soldiers cannot keep order.
Effectiveness like flood or drought
means the fields are not harvested
and the plowing yields no crop.
Defense like a metal wall
means using wealth and resources
and establishing ears and eyes.
Governance of a single body
means eliminating eccentric theories
and banning decadent customs.
Disregarding the distance of the journey,
one can overawe the people of remote regions.
Disregarding the dangers of mountains and rivers,
one can subdue states that rely on their fortifications.
Acting alone and without rival,
commands are carried out and prohibitions are obeyed.
Thus, in attacking states and rescuing cities,
one does not rely on allied states,
so that which is pointed at must obey.
Securing the ancestral temples
and nurturing the people,
none in the world can harm them;
only then can one possess a state.
Establishing rituals and laws
and issuing commands
such that all respond—
only then can one govern the people and unify the masses.
Whenever one is about to establish affairs,
one must rectify that Tiānzhí.
As for the recorded laws,
they model the positions of Heaven and Earth,
and image the movement of the four seasons
to govern the world.
In the movement of the four seasons,
there is cold and heat;
the sage models himself after them,
and thus there are Wén and Wǔ affairs.
In the positions of Heaven and Earth,
there is front and back,
there is left and right;
the sage models himself after them
to establish order and discipline.
Spring gives life on the left,
Autumn slays on the right,
Summer grows in front,
Winter hides in the back.
Affairs of birth and growth
are Wén;
affairs of harvesting and storing
are Wǔ;
therefore Wén affairs are on the left
and Wǔ affairs are on the right,
and the sage models himself after this.
Thus he carries out laws and orders
and governs the principles of affairs.
In all legal matters,
the exercise of control cannot be improper;
if the exercise of control is improper,
then judicial governance will not be impartial;
if judicial governance is not impartial,
then governance will not be fully logical.
Affairs will not be fully responded to;
if governance is not fully logical,
then the distant and the lowly will have no way to voice their grievances;
if affairs are not fully responded to,
then merits and profits will not be fully realized;
if merits and profits are not fully realized,
then the state will be poor and the distant will be estranged.
If the lowly have no way to voice their grievances, then those below will be disordered.
Therefore it is said:
"Whenever one is about to establish affairs,
one must rectify that Tiānzhí";
Tiānzhí
is the heart;
when the Tiānzhí is rectified,
then one does not favor close relatives
nor mistreat the distant.
Not favoring close relatives
and not mistreating the distant,
then no benefit is overlooked
and no governance is hidden;
when no benefit is overlooked
and no governance is hidden,
then no affair is left unundertaken
and no object is left behind.
Wind and rain do not deviate;
whether far or near, high or low,
each obtains its continuity.
If one desires to see the mind of *Tiān*,
it is made manifest through wind and rain.
Therefore it is said:
"Wind and rain do not deviate;
far and near, high and low,
each obtains its continuity."
Once the *Sān Jīng* are rectified,
the ruler then possesses the state.
The ten thousand things revere *Tiān*
and value wind and rain.
The reason they revere *Tiān*
is because none do not receive its mandates.
The reason they value wind and rain
is because none do not wait for the wind to move
or wait for the rain to be moistened.
If the ten thousand things were to set aside *Tiān* and receive mandates elsewhere,
set aside the wind and look elsewhere to be moved,
or set aside the rain and look elsewhere to be moistened,
then there would be no cause to revere *Tiān* or value wind and rain.
Now, that which a ruler of men honors and finds security in
is the establishment of his majesty and the execution of his commands.
The reason he can establish majesty and execute commands
is because the control of awe and benefit rests entirely with the ruler.
If the control of awe and benefit were not exclusively with the ruler
but were dispersed,
then the ruler would be increasingly slighted
and his majesty and benefit would daily decline;
this is the path of encroachment and violence.
Therefore it is said:
"Once the *Sān Jīng* are rectified,
the ruler then possesses the state."
In joy, do not reward;
in anger, do not kill.
To reward based on joy
or to kill based on anger
causes resentment to arise
and commands to be discarded.
When hasty commands are not followed,
the hearts of the people turn outward.
When those who turn outward have followers,
calamity begins to sprout.
What the masses are indignant about
cannot be managed even by a multitude.
Taking advantage of the summer as it grows,
carefully manage punishments and rewards,
and one must clarify the principles and regulations.
Display righteousness and establish laws;
decide matters with reason.
Empty the spirit and calm the heart,
then one can put aside anger and joy.
If one turns against the law and abandons commands
to act upon anger and joy,
disaster and chaos will arise,
and the superior position will be endangered.
Therefore it is said:
"In joy, do not reward;
in anger, do not kill."
To reward based on joy
or to kill based on anger
causes resentment to arise
and commands to be discarded.
When commands are issued hastily and not followed,
the hearts of the people turn outward.
When those who turn outward have followers,
calamity begins to sprout.
What the masses are indignant about,
a few cannot plan against.
When promoting what is good,
one must observe its ultimate end.
When discarding what is loathsome,
one must calculate its final outcome.
Once winter has closed and hidden things away,
the hundred tasks all cease;
past matters are completely recorded,
and future matters have not yet arisen.
During winter when there are no affairs,
carefully observe ends and beginnings
and scrutinize the principles of things.
There are matters that are easy at first but difficult later;
there are those whose beginnings are not worth seeing but whose ends cannot be reached.
These are the reasons why constant benefits are not raised
and why affairs become distressed.
Regarding matters that are easy at first,
people undertake them lightly;
because people undertake them lightly,
they will certainly encounter matters difficult to complete.
Regarding those whose beginnings are not worth seeing,
people abandon them lightly;
because people abandon them lightly,
they will certainly lose achievements that cannot be reached.
Now, frequently encountering matters difficult to complete
and regularly losing achievements that cannot be reached
is the path of decline and depletion.
For this reason,
the enlightened ruler scrutinizes the principles of things
and carefully observes ends and beginnings.
To act, he must know what will be accomplished;
to accomplish, he must know what it will be used for;
to use, he must know its benefits and harms.
To act without knowing what will be accomplished,
to accomplish without knowing what it will be used for,
or to use without knowing its benefits and harms
is called reckless action.
For those who act recklessly,
their affairs will not be completed
and their merit will not be established.
Therefore it is said:
"When promoting what is good,
one must observe its ultimate end.
When discarding what is loathsome,
one must calculate its final outcome."
Manifest them with rewards, encouragement, sincerity, and respect;
encourage those with merit with wealth and emoluments;
honor those with reputation with rank and nobility.
Every ruler of men
desires the people to possess ritual and righteousness.
If the people lack ritual and righteousness,
then high and low will be in chaos and the noble and base will struggle.
Therefore it is said:
"Manifest them with rewards, encouragement, sincerity, and respect;
encourage those with merit with wealth and emoluments;
honor those with reputation with rank and nobility."
To love all universally without exception
is called the Mind of the Ruler.
One must first be accordant in instruction,
so that the ten thousand people turn toward the influence like the wind.
Benefit them from morning to evening,
and the masses will then be equal to their tasks.
Every ruler of men
desires the masses to be close to their superiors and turn toward his intentions;
he desires them to be equal to the tasks they undertake.
But if the masses are not loved,
they will not be close;
if they are not close,
they will not be clear.
If instruction is not accordant,
they will not turn toward his intentions.
For this reason, the enlightened ruler uses universal love to draw them close,
clarifies accordant instruction to guide them,
makes their circumstances convenient,
makes their provisions beneficial,
cherishes their strength,
and does not snatch away their time so as to benefit them.
In this way,
the masses will be close to the superior and turn toward his intentions,
and in undertaking affairs, they will be equal to their tasks.
Therefore it is said:
"Love all universally without exception,"
this is called the Mind of the Ruler. One must first be accordant in instruction,
so that the ten thousand people turn toward the influence.
Benefit them from morning to evening,
and the masses will then be equal to their tasks.
Select people based on oneself;
complete affairs based on substance.
The roots of governance are two:
the first is called people,
the second is called affairs.
People must be usable;
affairs must be skillfully done.
People have the contrary and the accordant;
affairs have standards of measurement.
If the hearts of people are contrary,
then the people cannot be used.
If affairs lose their measurement,
then the affairs will not be skillful.
If affairs are not skillful, there is harm;
if people cannot be used, there is resentment.
Therefore it is said:
"Select people based on oneself;
complete affairs based on substance."
Carefully manage the use of wealth,
be cautious in granting rewards,
and examine the standards of weights and measures.
Therefore, in using wealth, one must not be stingy,
and in using labor, one must not be oppressive.
To be stingy with wealth leads to waste;
to be oppressive with labor leads to exhaustion.
To accomplish things with substance
is to use weights and measures.
To judge others by oneself
is to act with empathy and reciprocity.
To act with empathy and reciprocity
is to measure things by oneself.
What one finds uneasy for oneself,
do not impose upon others.
Therefore it is said:
Carefully manage the use of wealth,
be cautious in granting rewards,
and examine the standards of weights and measures.
Therefore, in using wealth, one must not be stingy,
and in using labor, one must not be oppressive.
To be stingy with wealth leads to waste;
to be oppressive with labor leads to exhaustion.
If the people’s resources are insufficient,
then orders will be disgraced;
if the people suffer from calamities,
then commands will not be carried out.
If giving and rewarding are not appropriate,
then misfortune will begin to flourish;
if misfortune flourishes and one does not awaken,
the people will then turn to their own schemes.
This is how one knows it is so:
if the use of labor is oppressive, then tasks will not be skillful. If tasks are not skillful
and must be repeated many times, it is therefore called exhaustion. If the use of wealth is stingy,
it does not accord with the hearts of the people. If it does not accord with the hearts of the people,
then resentment arises. To use wealth and yet generate resentment
is therefore called waste. Once resentment arises,
it does not return; if the masses are exhausted
and cannot find rest,
they will surely have the intent to crumble and collapse.
Therefore it is said: if the people's resources are insufficient, the orders
are disgraced; if the people suffer from calamities, commands are not carried out; if giving and rewarding are not appropriate, misfortune
will begin to flourish. If misfortune flourishes
and one does not awaken, the people will then plot for themselves.
Rectify the laws and straighten the measures;
do not pardon those deserving death;
executions and punishments must be reliable,
so the people feel awe and fear.
Once military prestige is manifest,
orders need not be issued twice.
Generally, if a state has no law,
then the masses do not know what to do.
If there are no measures,
then affairs have no mechanism.
If there are laws but they are not correct,
or measures but they are not straight,
then governance will be perverse;
if governance is perverse, then the state will be in chaos.
Therefore it is said:
"Rectify the laws and straighten the measures;
do not pardon those deserving death.
Executions and punishments must be reliable,
so the people feel awe and fear.
Once military prestige is manifest,
orders need not be issued twice."
Degrade the weary and the lazy to shame them,
punish crimes and pardon
errors to chasten them,
and execute those who violate prohibitions to shock them.
All people dislike punishment and fear crime;
therefore, the ruler establishes strict instructions to show them,
and clarifies penalties to bring them into line.
Therefore it is said:
"Degrade the weary and the lazy to shame them,
punish crimes and
errors to chasten them,
and execute those who violate prohibitions to shock them."
When the foundation is firm and unmoving,
then those leaning toward deviance will be afraid.
When the leaning are corrected and deviance is transformed,
orders go forth and the people follow.
In governing a state, there are three instruments;
in a chaotic state, there are six assaults.
An enlightened ruler can overcome the six assaults and establish the three instruments,
and then the state is well-governed.
An unworthy ruler cannot overcome the six assaults to establish the three instruments,
and therefore the state is not well-governed.
What are the three instruments?
It is said:
"Orders and commands, axes and halberds, and emoluments and rewards."
What are the six assaults?
Relatives, the noble-born, wealth, sensuality,
clever sycophancy, and playthings.
What is the use of the three instruments?
It is said:
"Without orders and commands, there is no way to employ subordinates;
without axes and halberds, there is no way to awe the masses;
without emoluments and rewards, there is no way to encourage the people."
What is the failure caused by the six assaults?
It is said:
"Though one does not obey, one can still survive;
though one violates prohibitions, one can still be spared;
though one has no merit, one can still gain wealth."
In a state where one can disobey and still survive,
orders and commands are insufficient to employ subordinates.
Where one can violate prohibitions and still be spared,
axes and halberds are insufficient to awe the masses.
Where one can have no merit and still gain wealth,
emoluments and rewards are insufficient to encourage the people.
If orders and commands are insufficient to employ subordinates,
axes and halberds are insufficient to awe the masses,
and emoluments and rewards are insufficient to encourage the people,
then the ruler has no means to maintain his position.
What then does an enlightened ruler do?
An enlightened ruler does not change orders because of the six assaults,
does not hesitate in applying punishments because of them,
and does not increase or decrease rewards because of them.
Therefore it is said:
"Establish the foundation firmly without moving,
and those who lean toward deviance will be afraid.
When the leaning are corrected and deviance is transformed,
orders go forth and the people follow."
Emulate Tiān to unite in virtue;
model the laws and have no favorites.
Generally, a ruler
covers and supports the myriad people and possesses them all;
he illuminates and oversees the myriad clans and employs them in service.
Therefore, he uses Heaven and Earth, the Sun and the Moon, and the Four Seasons as his principles and substance
to govern the world.
Heaven covers everything without exception,
and its virtue is everywhere.
Earth supports everything without discarding anything;
it is peaceful, firm, and unmoving.
Therefore, all things grow and multiply.
The Shèng Rén emulates this
to cover and support the myriad people;
thus, none fail to attain their natural functions.
Attaining their natural functions,
none fail to be of use.
Therefore it is said:
"Emulate Tiān to unite in virtue;
model Dì and have no favorites."
Align with the Sun and the Moon,
and be assisted by the Four Seasons.
The brightness of the Sun and Moon is without selfishness,
so nothing fails to receive light.
The Shèng Rén emulates this
to illuminate the myriad people;
thus, he can examine and observe carefully,
so that no good goes unrecorded
and no wickedness remains hidden.
When no good goes unrecorded
and no wickedness is hidden,
then punishments and rewards are reliable and certain.
When punishments and rewards are reliable and certain,
then the good are encouraged and the wicked are deterred.
Therefore it is said:
"Align with the Sun and the Moon."
The progression of the Four Seasons
is reliable, certain, and manifest.
The Shèng Rén emulates this
in managing the myriad people;
thus, he does not miss the seasonal achievements.
Therefore it is said:
"Sync with the Four Seasons."
Pleasure lies in giving;
possessing the masses lies in abandoning selfishness.
Generally, as for the masses,
if you love them, they will be close to you;
if you benefit them, they will come to you.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler provides benefits to attract them
and demonstrates love to make them close.
If there is only benefit without love,
then the masses will come but will not be close.
Mere love without benefit
means the masses will be close but will not come;
if love and giving are both practiced,
then ruler and minister will be pleased,
friends will be pleased, brothers will be pleased, and father and son will be pleased.
Where love and giving are established,
even the four boundaries cannot be held against them.
Therefore it is said:
“Pleasure lies in love and giving.”
The means by which a ruler possesses the masses
is the virtue of love and giving.
If love is shifted elsewhere
and benefits are monopolized,
then he cannot possess them all.
Therefore it is said:
“Possessing the masses lies in abandoning selfishness.”
Summoning those from afar lies in cultivating those nearby.
Though the virtue of love and giving
is practiced without selfishness,
if inner conduct is not cultivated,
then one cannot make the rulers of distant lands pay court.
For this reason, when the righteousness between ruler and minister, superior and inferior is rectified;
when the righteousness between father and son, brothers, husband and wife is refined;
when the distinction between male and female is refined;
when the differences between distant and close relations are distinguished;
so that the ruler is virtuous and the minister loyal,
the father kind and the son filial,
the elder brother loving and the younger brother respectful,
and ritual and righteousness are manifest and clear—
when it is like this,
then those nearby will be intimate with him,
and those afar will return to him.
Therefore it is said:
“Summoning those from afar lies in cultivating those nearby.”
Closing off misfortune lies in removing resentment.
Closing off misfortune lies in removing resentment
does not mean only removing resentment when it exists; rather, the situation one manages
should constantly be free of resentment. Generally, misfortune
and disorder are produced
from resentment and blame.
Resentment and blame
are produced from
that which is contrary to reason. Thus, when an enlightened ruler serves the masses, he must be consistent in his commands,
must follow the way of giving and reciprocation,
must be appropriate in his words,
must be accurate in punishments,
and must be orderly.
In this way, the masses
will have no hearts of stifled resentment
and no intentions of grievance or hatred.
In this way,
misfortune and disorder will not arise,
and the superior position will not be endangered. Therefore it is said: Closing off misfortune lies in removing resentment.
Preparing for the long term lies in employing the worthy.
Generally, the means by which a ruler of men is honored and secure
is the worthy assistant.
If the assistant is worthy,
then the ruler is honored, the state is secure, and the people are well-governed.
If there is no assistant,
then the ruler is debased, the state is in peril, and the people are in disorder.
Therefore it is said:
“Preparing for the long term depends on employing the worthy.”
Securing a high position lies in sharing benefits.
Among all people, there are none who do not desire benefit and dislike harm.
For this reason, he who shares benefits with the world
is upheld by the world.
He who monopolizes the benefits of the world
is plotted against by the world.
What the world plots against,
though it be established, will surely be destroyed.
What the world upholds,
though it be high, will not be in danger.
Therefore it is said:
“Securing a high position lies in sharing benefits.”
If one follows the patterns... (treating people and things, people and things, then one is a Huáng).
In the season of the Five Harmonies,
the ruler wears yellow robes,
tastes sweet flavors,
listens to the Gōng sound,
regulates the harmonious Qì,
uses the number five,
drinks from the Well of the Huáng Hòu,
and cooks with the fire of the Luǒ beasts.
Storing up mildness and gentleness,
practicing nurturing and care,
smoothing the Qì and making it flow through,
all things open and are tranquil,
and forms generate according to principle.
Abiding in emptiness and maintaining stillness,
treating people as people and things as things, then one is a Huáng.
Always reaching the mandate,
honoring the worthy and granting office based on virtue,
then one is a Dì.
Embodying humaneness and practicing righteousness,
clothing oneself in loyalty and using trustworthiness,
then one is a Wáng.
Examining plans and making rituals manifest,
selecting warriors and sharpening weapons,
then one is a Bà.
Determining life and managing death,
treating the worthy with care and organizing the ranks,
then one has the masses.
Being trustworthy in rewards and careful in punishments,
ennobling talent and giving stipends to the capable,
then one is strong.
Calculating the start and providing for the end,
attending to the root and regulating the branch,
then one is wealthy.
Clarifying laws and examining numbers,
establishing constants and preparing capabilities,
then one is well-governed.
Distinguishing offices according to similarities and differences
then one is secure.
Reach them through the Dào,
nurture them through kindness,
be intimate with them through humaneness,
sustain them through righteousness,
repay them through virtue,
bind them through trustworthiness,
engage them through ritual,
harmonize them through music,
expect of them through tasks,
direct them through offices,
arouse them through strength,
and awe them through sincerity.
With one action, the superiors and inferiors find their proper ends;
with two actions, the people all follow;
with three actions, the land is opened and grain is produced;
with four actions, the farmers are at ease and grain is tenfold;
with five actions, tasks are light and gold is ninefold;
with six actions, purity and wisdom deal with changes;
with seven actions, the external and internal are utilized;
with eight actions, victory is achieved and majesty is established;
with nine actions, the works of a Dì take shape.
The Nine Roots are broad and great;
this is what the ruler of men maintains.
The Eight Divisions have their duties;
this is what the ministers and high officials maintain.
The Seven Victories provide majesty;
this is what the generals maintain.
The Six Disciplines are careful and meticulous;
this is what the worthy maintain.
The Five Records are not neglected;
this is what the common people maintain.
When moving, none fail to follow;
when still, none fail to agree.
The roots of order and disorder are three;
the intersection of the lowly and noble is four;
the conclusion of wealth and poverty is five;
the records of prosperity and decline are six;
