the pivot of safety and danger is seven;
the response of strength and weakness is eight;
the number of survival and ruin is nine.
Drill them by dispersing cliques and factions,
and manage the wealth of the departments according to the numbers.
Use penalties to gather wealth,
use encouragement and exhortation to move the masses,
so that the two divisions possess the root.
When initiating goodness, one must be careful about secrecy;
when wielding majesty, one must be clear about being centered.
This is how to dwell within the center of the diagrams.

Implements are perfected through labor,

Movement and stillness are not recorded,

At the first assembly of the *Zhū Hóu*,
the command stated:
“Unless it is the mandate of the *Xuán Dì*,
there shall not be a single day of military service.”
At the second assembly of the *Zhū Hóu*,
the command stated:
“Nurture the orphaned and the elderly,
feed the chronically ill,
and take in the fatherless and the widows.”
At the third assembly of the *Zhū Hóu*,
the command stated:
“The land tax shall be five parts in a hundred,
the market levy two parts in a hundred,
and the border-gate levy one part in a hundred.”
There shall be no shortage of tools for plowing and weaving.
At the fourth assembly of the *Zhū Hóu*,
the command stated:
“Repair the roads,
standardize measurements,
and unify weights and numbers;
let the marshes and wetlands be closed and opened according to the season.”
At the fifth assembly of the *Zhū Hóu*,
the command stated:
“Conduct the regular sacrifices for spring, autumn, winter, and summer;
offer the ancient sacrifices to the heaven, earth, mountains, and rivers;
these must be done according to the proper time.”
At the sixth assembly of the *Zhū Hóu*,
the command stated:
“Bring the products of your lands to the *Xuán Guān*,
and request the *Sì Fǔ*,
so as to perform the rites for *Shàng Dì*.”
At the seventh assembly of the *Zhū Hóu*,
the command stated:
“Officials who occupy positions but lack propriety
shall be banished, for they corrupt their mandate.”
At the eighth assembly of the *Zhū Hóu*,
the command stated:
“Those who establish the *Sì Yì* without dispute
shall be promoted to the *Xuán Guān*
and have their cases heard by the *Sān Gōng*.”
At the ninth assembly of the *Zhū Hóu*,
the command stated:
“Use the resources within your borders
and whatever the state possesses as currency.”
At the ninth assembly,
the *Dà Mìng* was issued
and arrived regularly.
Beyond a thousand *lǐ*
and within two thousand *lǐ*,
the *Zhū Hóu* shall come to court every three years to practice the mandate.
In the second year,

On the first day of the first month of the first year,

They shall receive the mandate from the *Sān Gōng*.
Beyond two thousand *lǐ*

In the third year,

Every ten years,

Every five years,

Beyond three thousand *lǐ*,

Appoint *Dà Fū* to ensure the stability of the court;
they shall enter
and together receive the mandate there.
This resides in the outer regions of the diagram’s northern quadrant.
One must possess civil cultivation, majesty, and military prowess,
and officials must be practiced in the tasks for victory.
Timing is the end-point of victory’s causes;
having no fixed method is the subtle mechanism of victory;
practicing righteousness is the principle of victory;
aligning name and reality is the urgency of victory;
timing and distribution are the tasks of victory;
observing and striking are the actions of victory;
preparation and equipment are the source of victory;
being formless is the root of victory.
Established solitary majesty results in victory;
established planning for resources results in victory;
established intelligence results in victory;
established selection of warriors results in victory;
established regulation of stipends results in victory;
established utilization of methods results in victory;
established logical order results in victory;
established determination over life and death results in victory;
established vision of success and failure results in victory;
established reliance on the extraordinary results in victory;
established knowledge of the solid and the empty results in victory;
established awareness of flourishing and decline results in victory.
If the deployment of the mechanism is truly essential,
then the enemy cannot measure it;
if the use of advantages is perfectly sincere,
then the enemy cannot contest it.
Clarify names and manifest realities,
then the warriors will die for their integrity.
Launch extraordinary maneuvers unexpectedly,
then the warriors will serve with joy.
Handle things according to their methods,
then tools and equipment will be ready.
Rely on ability to sharpen readiness,
then what is sought will surely be obtained.
Perform tasks by clarifying the root,
then the warriors will not be negligent.
Preparation and equipment have no fixed form,
responding without a predetermined method.
Listen to the concise,
thus one can hear what has not yet reached its limit.
Look at the new,
thus one can see what has not yet taken form.
Think of the deep,
thus one can know what has not yet begun.
Strike like a startle,
thus one can reach the immeasurable.
Move in a flourishing manner,
thus one can obtain the treasure.
Stand upon planning,
thus one can be substantial and not easily manipulated.
When implements are perfected and instruction is maintained,
then the distance of the road does not matter;
when signals are precise and instruction is applied,
then the danger of mountains and rivers does not matter;
when broad unity is pure and firm,
then one marches alone and without peer.
Be cautious with signals and precise with insignia,
then the attack does not depend on shifting circumstances.
When the certainty of victory is clear,
then even the compassionate become brave;
when implements have no fixed method,
then even the simple-minded become wise;
when attacking where there is no defense,
then even the clumsy become skillful.
This is the calculation.
In action, be cautious with the *Shí Hào*,

The ruler must always be established;

Seek out the finest talents of the world;

When implements are perfected,
test them to distinguish the bad from the good.
Gather the heroes and outstanding men of the world;
possess the lauded talents of the world.
Persuasion acts like wind and rain;
deployment is like thunder and lightning.

When implements are perfected but not hoarded,

Striking unexpectedly,

Since no one can respond,

since no one can resist,

One must be clear about the situation,

Starting without a beginning,

Harmony and unity allow for training;

none can harm them.

Constantly attaining the mandate,

Embodying benevolence and practicing righteousness,

Carefully planning and making rites manifest,

Determining life and handling death,
being careful of the worthy and regulating the ranks makes one have a following.
Trustworthy rewards and careful punishments,
ennobling talent and enriching the capable makes one strong.
Planning the common and entrusting the end,
attending to the fundamental and refining the peripheral makes one wealthy.
Clarifying laws and carefully calculating,
establishing constants and preparing capabilities makes one orderly.
Distinguishing similarities and differences in official duties makes one secure.
Connect them with the *Dào*,
nurture them with kindness,
befriend them with benevolence,
nourish them with righteousness,
repay them with *Dé*,
bind them with trustworthiness,
receive them with rites,
harmonize them with music,
set expectations with tasks,
attack with words,
act with strength,
and overawe with sincerity.
With the first movement, superiors and subordinates find their end;
with the second movement, the people follow without exception;
with the third movement, the land is opened and grain is formed;
with the fourth movement, farmers are at ease and grain increases tenfold;
with the fifth movement, duties are lightened and gold increases ninefold;
with the sixth movement, pure wisdom understands changes;
with the seventh movement, the internal and external are of use;
with the eighth movement, victory prevails and majesty is established;
with the ninth movement, the *Dì*'s tasks take shape.
The nine fundamentals grasp the greatness;
this is the duty of the lord of men.
The eight divisions have their duties;
this is the duty of the high ministers.
The seven victories provide majesty;
this is the duty of the general.
The six principles are careful and meticulous;
this is the duty of the worthy man.
The five principles are never slackened;
this is the duty of the common people.
The root of order and disorder is three;
the interaction between the lowly and noble is four;
the end of wealth and poverty is five;
the principle of prosperity and decline is six;
the mechanism of security and danger is seven;
the response of strength and weakness is eight;
the number of survival and destruction is nine.
Refine them by dispersing crowds and cliques of officials;
calculate all wealth and offices.
Execute and slaughter to gather wealth;
encourage and exhort to move the masses;
ensure the two divisions possess their fundamentals.
Doing good must be carefully kept secret;
exercising majesty must be clear within the center.

In winter, if autumn administration is carried out, there will be fog;

He treasures compassion and generosity,

Implements are perfected through toil,

Movement and stillness are not recorded,

He is vigilant across the four seasons to distinguish periods of rest,

clarifies the nurturing of life to dissolve stagnation,

At the first assembly of the *Zhū hóu*, the decree says:
"Unless it is a command from the *Xuán Dì*,
there shall not be a single day of military service."
At the second assembly of the *Zhū hóu*, the decree says:
"Care for the orphaned and the elderly,
feed the chronically ill,
and take in orphans and widows."
At the third assembly of the *Zhū hóu*, the decree says:
"The land rent shall be five parts in a hundred,
the market tax shall be two parts in a hundred,
the customs duty shall be one part in a hundred,
and there must be no shortage of tools for plowing and weaving."
At the fourth assembly of the *Zhū hóu*, the decree says:
"Repair the roads,
standardize weights and measures,
and unify numbers;
do not levy taxes on marshes and wetlands, but prohibit or allow their use according to the seasons."
At the fifth assembly of the *Zhū hóu*, the decree says:
"Perform the regular sacrifices for spring, autumn, winter, and summer,
and offer the traditional sacrifices to Heaven, Earth, mountains, and rivers,
always at the proper time."
At the sixth assembly of the *Zhū hóu*, the decree says:
"Provide the products of your land to the *Xuán guān*,
and invite the *Sì fǔ*,
for the purpose of sacrificing to the *Shàng dì*."
At the seventh assembly of the *Zhū hóu*, the decree says:
"For officials who occupy positions but lack propriety,
exile them and treat their lives as weeds."
At the eighth assembly of the *Zhū hóu*, the decree says:
"Establish the *Sì yì*, and for those who act without consultation,
report them to the *Xuán guān*
and let the *Sān gōng* hear the case."
At the ninth assembly of the *Zhū hóu*, the decree says:
"Use the wealth and goods within your fief,
using whatever the state possesses as currency."
When the Great Decree of the Ninth Assembly is issued,
it must always be reached.
Beyond a thousand *lǐ*
and within two thousand *lǐ*,
the *Zhū hóu* shall come to court every three years
to study the decrees.
Every two years,
the *Sān qīng* shall send envoys to the *Sì fǔ*.
On the first day of the first month of every year,
order the *Dà fū* to come for refinement
and to receive commands from the *Sān gōng*.
Beyond two thousand *lǐ*
and within three thousand *lǐ*,
the *Zhū hóu* shall assemble every five years
to study the decrees.
Every three years,
the *Míng qīng* shall request assignments.
Every two years,
the *Dà fū* shall communicate good and bad fortune.
Every ten years,
they shall focus on suitable people
and rectify propriety and righteousness.
Every five years,
the *Dà fū* shall request changes.
Beyond three thousand *lǐ*,
the *Zhū hóu* shall come once per generation,
and a *Dà fū* shall be stationed to ensure the court's peace,
entering to receive commands.

Banners and items favor red,

One must clarify the situation,
clarify the generals,
clarify the government,
and clarify the soldiers.
When these four are prepared,
then use order to strike chaos
and use success to strike failure.
Frequent battles tire the soldiers;
frequent victories make the lord arrogant.
An arrogant lord leading tired people endangers the state.
The ultimate good is to win without fighting;
the next best is to unify it in one.
Regarding a great victory,
if it is the accumulation of many victories without any being unrighteous,
it can be considered a great victory.
A great victory means there is nothing not overcome.
This is located on the map outside the southern region.
To the right is the supplementary map of the southern region.
One must attain civil culture, majesty, and military prowess,
and officials must practice the tasks of victory.
Follow the timing to reach the end of victory,
with no fixed method for the subtle signs of victory,
practice righteousness as the principle of victory,
treat name and reality as the urgency of victory,
divide time for the affairs of victory,
observe attacks for the conduct of victory,
prepare equipment as the source of victory,
and have no fixed form as the root of victory.
Establish solitary majesty for victory,
establish planning and wealth for victory,
establish knowledge and information for victory,
establish the selection of soldiers for victory,
establish the regulation of stipends for victory,
establish the use of methods for victory,
establish organization and principles for victory,
establish life and death for victory,
establish success and failure for victory,
establish reliance on surprise for victory,
establish the substantial and the void for victory,
and establish prosperity and decline for victory.
If the action of the opportunity is truly essential,
then the enemy cannot measure it;
if the use of advantages is perfectly sincere,
then the enemy cannot compete.
Clarify names and manifest realities,
then the soldiers will die for their integrity;
let surprise actions occur unexpectedly,
then the soldiers will serve with joy.
Exchange goods according to the region,
then tools and equipment will be ready;
use ability to facilitate preparation,
then what is sought will surely be obtained.
Hold to tasks and clarify the root,
then the soldiers will not be negligent;
preparations have no fixed form,
and respond in unpredictable ways.
By listening to the essentials, one can hear without limit;
by looking at the new, one can see what has not yet formed;
by thinking deeply, one can know what has not yet begun;
by acting on what is startling, one can reach the immeasurable;
by moving during prosperity, one can obtain treasures;
and by standing on planning, one can make reality impossible to thwart.
When equipment is perfected and instruction is maintained,
then no distance is too great;
when commands are scrutinized and instruction is applied,
then no mountain or river is too treacherous;
when one is broadly unified, pure, and firm,
then one can walk alone and be invincible;
when commands are cautious and regulations are scrutinized,
then their attack does not rely on balancing factors.
Clarifying certain victory makes the compassionate brave;
making equipment without fixed form makes the foolish wise;
attacking where there is no defense makes the clumsy skillful;
such is the method.
In movement, be cautious with the *Shí hào*;
clarify and scrutinize the *Jiǔ zhāng*;
ornament and practice with the *Shí qì*;
master and practice the *Wǔ jiào*;
and carefully maintain the *Sān guān*.
The lord must always be prepared,
and plans must always be decided beforehand.
Seek the finest materials in the world,
discuss the sharpest tools of the various craftsmen,
and once implements are finished, test their quality through competition;
gather the heroes of the world,
possess the materials worthy of the world,
let persuasion and action be like wind and rain,
and outbreaks be like thunder and lightning.

Banners and items favor black,
weapons favor side-shields,

Observe numbers and know governance,
scrutinize equipment and recognize victory,
clarify planning and attain victory,

Establish ancestral temples,
raise sons and daughters,

then one can establish majesty and practice virtue,
regulate laws and ceremonies,
and issue commands.
In the ultimate excellence of military conduct,
it is not land that is sought.
It is the ruler who punishes the people.
Establish righteousness and add victory to it;
reach ultimate majesty and fill it with virtue;
maintain this and then refine victory,
and your mind will burn throughout the world.
Establish what is beneficial to the people.
Remove what harms them,
and the people will follow.
Establish them as lords of six thousand lì,

Allow the rulers of states to achieve their governance,

Gather to request a mandate from Heaven;
when the Earth knows the harmony of qì,

Calculate matters of urgency and leisure,

Be clear about the advantages of tools and weapons,

Examine the principles of precedence,
and when troops go forth, they will not be distressed.
Master the measures of exit and entry,
and you will penetrate deeply without danger.
Be careful about the tasks of movement and stillness,
and success will be achieved without harm.
Be clear about the distinction between taking and giving,
and you will gain land without becoming attached.
Be cautious regarding the offices of commands and orders,
and you will initiate affairs with success.

Unify the interior and empty the periphery;

In movement, none do not follow;

Initiate and release according to ritual;
when ritual is timely, it must succeed.
If harmony and friendship are not established,
and there is no management of the noble and the base,
then changes in affairs will arrive daily.
This resides on the outside of the eastern region of the diagram.
To the right is the main diagram of the east.
Banners and items favor green,
weapons favor spears,
and punishments involve the crossing of cold and harmful shackles.
If tools are made but the principles are not maintained or known,
and instruction is not clear so the release is unexpected:
if the principles are unknown,
none can defend against them;
if the release is unexpected,
none can respond to it.
Since none can respond,
one achieves complete victory without harm;
since none can defend,
one must win and be without rival.
If the four mechanisms are not clear,
in no more than nine days, wandering troops will startle the army.
If barriers and blockades are not scrutinized,
in no more than eight days, outside thieves will hear news.
If the defense is not cautious,
in no more than seven days, there will be slanderous plots within.
If prohibitions against deceit are not maintained,

If the dead are not provided for,

This resides on the outside of the eastern region of the diagram.
To the right is the supplementary diagram of the east.
That the sage kings of old
attained bright names and wide reputations,
achieved great merits and grand undertakings,
became illustrious throughout the world,
and were not forgotten by later generations—
except through winning over the people,
I have never heard of such a thing.
That tyrannical kings lost their states and families,
endangered the altars of soil and grain,
overthrew their ancestral temples,
and were extinguished from the world—
except through losing the people,
I have never heard of such a thing.
Now, rulers who possess land
all desire peace when at rest,
majesty when in motion,
victory in battle,
and firmness in defense.
The greater ones wish to rule as kings over the world,
and the lesser ones wish to be hegemons over the lords.
Yet they do not strive to win over the people.
Thus, the lesser ones find their troops defeated and their land diminished,
while the greater ones perish and their states are lost.
Therefore it is said:
One must strive for the people.
This is the ultimate principle of the world.
It is said:
If that is so, then regarding the way to win over the people,
nothing is better than benefiting them;
regarding the way to benefit them,
nothing is better than instructing them through governance.
Therefore, for one who is good at governance,
the fields are reclaimed and the cities are full,
the court is leisurely and the government offices are well-ordered,
public laws are implemented and private crookedness is stopped,
the granaries are full and the prisons are empty,
and worthy men advance while wicked people retreat.
Their gentlemen value uprightness and despise flattery;
their officers and people value martial courage and despise gain;
their commoners love farming and dislike indulgence in food and drink.
Consequently, resources are sufficient
and food, drink, firewood, and vegetables are abundant.
Therefore, the superiors must be magnanimous
and grant remissions,
and the subordinates must be obedient
and without resentment.
Superiors and subordinates are in harmony
and possess ritual and righteousness.
Thus, they are at peace when at rest and majestic when in motion,
victorious in battle and firm in defense.
In this way, with a single battle, they bring order to the lords.
For those unable to govern,
the fields lie waste and the cities are empty,
the court is turbulent and the government offices are in chaos,
public laws are abandoned and private crookedness prevails,
the granaries are empty and the prisons are full,
and worthy men retreat while wicked people advance.
Their gentlemen value flattery and despise uprightness;
their officers and people value gain and despise martial courage;
their commoners love food and drink and dislike farming.
Consequently, resources are exhausted, and food, drink, firewood, and vegetables are scarce.
The superiors become increasingly cruel and harsh
without granting remissions;
the subordinates become more rebellious and fierce and do not obey.
Superiors and subordinates are at odds and not in harmony.
Thus, they are not at peace when at rest and not majestic when in motion,
unsuccessful in battle and not firm in defense.
In this way, the lesser ones find their troops defeated and their land diminished,
while the greater ones perish and their states are lost.
Looking at it from this perspective,
governance must be approached with caution.
Virtue has six prosperities,
righteousness has seven embodiments,
ritual has eight constants,
law has five tasks,
authority has three measures.
What are the so-called six prosperities?
It is said:
opening up fields,
establishing plots and residences,
cultivating trees and crops,
encouraging the officers and people,
urging diligence in sowing and harvesting,
and repairing walls and houses.
This is called enriching their livelihood.
Revealing hidden resources,
distributing stagnant hoards and repairing roads,
facilitating passes and markets,
and being careful with lodgings—
this is called providing them with wealth.
Channel the floodwaters,
facilitate the use of reservoirs and ditches,
drain the stagnant pools and marshes,
clear away the mud and obstructions,
open up blocked passages,
and be careful with ferries and bridges;
this is called bestowing benefits upon them.
Lighten the levies and collections,
reduce the taxes and duties,
relax the punishments and penalties,
pardon crimes and offenses,
and forgive minor errors;
this is called broadening their administration.
Support the elderly and aged,
show compassion to the young and orphaned,
relieve the widowers and widows,
inquire after the sick and ill,
and offer condolences for misfortunes and funerals;
this is called rectifying their emergencies.
Clothe those who are freezing and cold,
feed those who are hungry and thirsty,
assist the poor and destitute,
provide relief to the exhausted and exposed,
and fund those who are in total lack;
this is called relieving their poverty.
In general, these six items
are the flourishing of *Dé*.
Once these six are spread,
then that which the people desire
will be entirely obtained.
Indeed, the people must obtain what they desire
before they will obey their superiors;
when they obey their superiors,
only then can the administration be well conducted.
Therefore it is said:
*Dé* cannot but be flourished.
It is said:
When the people know *Dé*
but do not yet know *Yì*,
then clearly practice conduct to lead them to *Yì*.
*Yì* has seven substances.
What are these seven substances?
It is said:
Filial piety, fraternal duty, compassion, and kindness,
to nourish one's relatives;
reverence, respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness,
to serve the *Jūn* and superiors;
impartiality, uprightness, and appropriate alignment,
to practice *Lǐ* and moderation;
regulation, order, restraint, and submission,
to avoid punishment and execution;
frugality, thrift, and economizing expenses,
to prepare for famine;
sincerity, simplicity, purity, and steadfastness,
to prepare for disasters and chaos;
harmony, cooperation, unity, and amity,
to prepare for invasions and war.
In general, these seven
are the substances of *Yì*.
Indeed, the people must know *Yì* before they are impartial and upright;
being impartial and upright, they then become harmonious and balanced;
being harmonious and balanced, they can then dwell in peace;
dwelling in peace, they can then exercise authority;
exercising authority, they can then be victorious in battle and firm in defense.
Therefore it is said: *Yì* cannot but be practiced.
It is said:
When the people know *Yì*
but do not yet know *Lǐ*,
then arrange the *Bā Jīng* to lead them to *Lǐ*.
What are the so-called *Bā Jīng*?
It is said:
Superior and inferior have *Yì*;
noble and base have distinctions;
elder and younger have grades;
poor and rich have measures.
In general, these eight
are the *Jīng* of *Lǐ*.
Therefore, if superior and inferior have no *Yì*, there is chaos;
if noble and base have no distinctions, there is strife;
if elder and younger have no grades, there is rebellion;
if poor and rich have no measure, there is loss.
When superiors and inferiors are in chaos,
noble and base strive,
elder and younger rebel,
and poor and rich are without measure,
yet the state is not in disorder—
this has never been heard of.
For this reason, the *Shèngwáng* refined these eight *Lǐ*
to lead their people.
When the eight each attain their proper *Yì*,
then one who is a *Jūn*
is impartial, upright, and without selfishness;
one who is a *Chén*
is loyal, trustworthy, and not partisan;
one who is a father
is compassionate and kind in teaching;
one who is a son
is filial and fraternal with solemnity;
one who is an elder brother
is generous and broad-minded in instructing;
one who is a younger brother
is compliant and yielding with respect;
one who is a husband
is sincere and simple with steadfastness;
one who is a wife
is encouraging and diligent with chastity.
When it is thus, then the inferior do not rebel against the superior,
*Chén* do not kill their *Jūn*,
the base do not overstep the noble,
the young do not insult the elders,
the distant do not come between relatives,
the new do not come between the old,
the small do not impose upon the large,
and licentiousness does not destroy *Yì*.
In general, these eight
are the *Jīng* of *Lǐ*.
Indeed, the people must know *Lǐ* before they are reverent and respectful;
being reverent and respectful, they then value yielding;
valuing yielding, then the young and elder, noble and base, do not overstep one another;
when young and elder, noble and base, do not overstep one another,
then chaos does not arise and calamities do not occur.
Therefore it is said: *Lǐ* cannot but be carefully observed.
It is said:
When the people know *Lǐ*
but do not yet know their tasks,
then distribute laws to employ their strength.
Employing strength has five tasks.
What are the five tasks?
It is said:
The *Jūn* selects *Chén* and assigns offices;
the *Dàfū* handle offices and distinguish matters;
the *Guānzhǎng* handle matters and maintain their duties;
the *Shì* cultivate their persons and perfect their talents;
the *Shùrén* plow, farm, and plant.
When the *Jūn* selects *Chén* and assigns offices,
then matters are not vexing or chaotic;
when the *Dàfū* handle offices and distinguish matters,
then actions and measures are timely;
when the *Guānzhǎng* handle matters and maintain their duties,
then movements and actions are harmonious;
when the *Shì* cultivate their persons and perfect their talents,
then the worthy and good emerge;
when the *Shùrén* plow, farm, and plant,
then wealth and goods are sufficient.
Therefore it is said:
in general, these five
are the tasks of strength.
Indeed, the people must know their tasks
before their hearts become one;
when their hearts are one, then their intent is focused;
when the heart is one and intent is focused,
then their achievements are worthy of observation.
Therefore it is said:
strength cannot but be tasked.
It is said:
When the people know their tasks
but do not yet know the weights of circumstances,
then examine the *Sān Dù* to move them.
What are the so-called *Sān Dù*?
It is said:
Above, measure the auspiciousness of *Tiān*;
below, measure the suitability of *Dì*;
in the middle, measure the compliance of *Rén*;
these are the so-called *Sān Dù*.
Therefore it is said:
when the seasons of *Tiān* are not auspicious,
then there are floods and droughts;
when the ways of *Dì* are not suitable,
then there is famine;
when the ways of *Rén* are not compliant,
then there are disasters and chaos.
The coming of these three
is summoned by the administration.
It is said:
Assess the timing to undertake actions;
use actions to move the people;
use the people to move the state;
and use the state to move the world.
When the world is moved,
only then can achievements and fame be accomplished.
Therefore, the people must understand standards of authority,
and only then will their actions and decisions be correct.
When actions and decisions are correct, the people will be harmonious and united;
when the people are harmonious and united, achievements and fame will be established.
Therefore it is said:
Standards of authority cannot go unmeasured.
Once the Wǔjīng have been promulgated,
then expel the treacherous people,
interrogate the deceitful and false,
banish the slanderous and evil,
do not listen to licentious words,
and do not manufacture frivolous crafts.
If the people have licentious conduct or corrupt natures,
constructing licentious words
and manufacturing frivolous crafts
to flatter the ruler above
and confuse the common people below,
disturbing the state and moving the masses
so as to harm the people's essential tasks,
their punishment shall be death or exile.
Therefore it is said,
as for the reasons why a ruler of men loses the common people within
and loses the feudal lords without,
has his troops defeated and territory reduced,
has his name debased and state diminished,
has the altars of the soil and grain destroyed,
and has his own person put in peril,
it has never been heard that such things did not arise from licentiousness and flattery.
How is it known to be so?
Answer:
Licentious sounds flatter the ear;
licentious sights flatter the eye.
What the ears and eyes like flatters the heart.
What the heart likes in this way harms the people.
If the people are harmed and the ruler's person is not in peril,
it has never been heard of.
It is said:
Fill the wastes and voids,
cultivate the fields,
and repair the walls and houses,
then the state will be wealthy.
Be frugal in food and drink
and modest in clothing,
then resources will be sufficient.
Promote the worthy and good,
encourage merit and effort,
and spread virtue and kindness,
then worthy men will come forward.
Expel the treacherous,
interrogate the deceitful and false,
and remove the slanderous and evil,
then treacherous people will cease.
Prepare for famine,
relieve disasters,
and aid the exhausted and exposed,
then the state will be stable.
The task of an enlightened king
lies in strengthening the fundamental tasks and
eliminating the useless;
only then can the people be made wealthy.
Evaluate worthy men
and employ the capable;
then the people can be made well-governed.
Lighten taxes and levies,
do not be harsh toward the people,
and treat them with loyalty and love;
then the people can be made affectionate.
These three
are the works of a Hegemon or King.
Every matter has a root,
and benevolence and righteousness are its essentials.
Now, though craftsmen are skillful,
the reason why the people lack necessary equipment is that
their delight lies in curios and playthings.
Though farmers are hardworking,
the reason why the world goes hungry is that
their delight lies in rarities and oddities.
Though women are skillful,
the reason why the world is cold is that
their delight lies in ornate embroidery.
For this reason, broad belts are frayed,
large sleeves are torn,
ornate embroidery is stained,
carvings are scraped away,
and sculptures are smoothed.
Inspect the passes but do not levy tolls;
provide market stalls but do not levy taxes.
The good craftsmen of antiquity
did not strain their wisdom and skill to make playthings.
Therefore, useless things
are not produced by those who follow the law.
Grasping the five notes with the left hand,
holding the five flavors in the right.
Carrying the marking cord, level, and hook,
preparing many compasses and axles,
reducing waste to achieve great completion,
this is the regulation of seasonal virtue.
Gather what grows in spring,
gather fruits in autumn,
stay in the shade in summer,
and stay in the sun in winter;
thus the virtue of a great worthy lasts long.
Brightness leads to wisdom,
wisdom leads to brightness,
effort leads to success,
and brightness and wisdom will then flourish greatly.
Dealing with poison without anger,
resenting without words,
and desiring without plotting.
Broadly regulating and measuring ceremonies,
as if waking from sleep,
as if moving from darkness to light,
like Áo in the time of Yáo.
Do not seek counsel from the glib,
do not store up flattery,
do not nurture the malevolent,
and do not take lessons from the slanderous.
If one is not upright, his wasteland will expand.
Do not use their petty schemes.
A bird flies according to a straight line.
Abundant goods fill the ends of the scales;
simplify government and benefit the people.
Do not encounter misfortune,
do not bring your demands too close,
and keep your worries far away.
He who makes his dwelling too high
cannot be saved if he topples in peril.
It can be shallow or deep,
it can float or sink,
it can be curved or straight,
it can be spoken or silent.
Heaven does not have only one season,
earth does not have only one benefit,
and man does not have only one task.
Look uprightly,
tread with stability,
and leave deep traces.
Heaven and earth are sometimes treacherous and sometimes easy,
like a drum having a drumstick;
when it is struck, it resounds.
Heaven and earth are the bag for the myriad things;
the Zhòu Hé contains heaven and earth within its bag.
"Grasping the five notes with the left hand,
holding the five flavors in the right,"
this refers to the division between the ruler and the minister.
The ruler issues orders with ease,
therefore he stands on the left;
the minister takes on the toil of labor,
therefore he stands on the right.
Though the five notes have different sounds, they can be harmonized;
this means that the orders issued by the ruler should not be reckless,
and there is nothing they do not align with;
through alignment, orders are carried out and government is completed.
Though the five flavors come from different things, they can be blended;
this means that the labor undertaken by the minister should not be reckless,
and there is nothing he does not achieve;
through achievement, labor is diligent and wealth is abundant.
Therefore, when the ruler issues orders,
he rectifies his state without making his own desires the standard;
he unifies his love without favoring only this or that.
If a king bestows benefits without selfishness,
then all within the four seas will come as guests.
If ministers exert their strength,
sharing their loyalty without competing for gain,
and performing their duties without claiming fame for themselves;
if respect is divided without jealousy,
then husbands and wives will be harmonious and diligent.
If the ruler loses the correct tone, the winds and laws will surely drift;
if they drift, there will be disorder and ruin.
If ministers deviate from the proper flavor, the common people will not be nurtured;
if the common people are not nurtured,
then the masses will scatter and perish.
When ruler and ministers each fulfill their proper roles,
then the state will be at peace;
therefore, this is called "not manifesting virtue."
"Carrying the cord-line, the level, and the hook;
preparing many compasses and axles;
the slow trickle achieves great success;
this is the measure of timely virtue."
The cord-line corrects deviations;
the level removes hazards to create flatness;
the hook enters crooked and comes out straight.
This refers to the governance and recruitment practiced by sage rulers and worthy assistants.
Being broad without loss,
one relies on this to prepare all abilities without leaving any out.
The state is still the state,
and the people are still the people;
Jié and Zhòu perished through disorder,
while Tāng and Wǔ flourished through order.
By manifesting the Way to teach
and clarifying the laws to set expectations,
the people’s rise toward goodness is like a transformation;
such was the achievement of Tāng and Wǔ.
"Preparing many compasses and axles"
means having complete axles.
When complete axles are numerous,
they are not loose when in large spaces,
and they are not blocked when entering small spaces;
it is like the law of seeking shoes from footprints;
how could they not fit?
Good fitting
comes from good preparation;
it is transcendent;
thus there is no lack.
Therefore, those who illustrate teachings take metaphors from this.
Heaven nurtures
without calculation;
Earth transforms and generates
without boundaries.
So-called right without wrong,
and wrong without right—
right and wrong
will certainly alternate.
If one blindly trusts in "right,"
there will be things that cannot be planned for in advance,
and things that cannot be identified or deliberated upon.
Thus, things will end abruptly without warning.
Therefore, the sage hears broadly and sees much,
accumulating the Way to await things;
when things arrive, they respond to their forms,
and every detail is preserved.
Jiǎn
means "to exhaust";
liù
means "to emit."
It means that from partial to complete,
everything is fully obtained.
Thus it is said:
"The slow trickle achieves great success."
The method of achieving success
must have a great standard.
It must be complete in virtue
and careful regarding the time;
the meeting of time and virtue
is the convergence of affairs,
like the matching of a tally.
Thus it is said:
"This is the measure of timely virtue."
"Gathering the living in spring,
gathering the fruit in autumn,
staying in the shade in summer,
staying in the sun in winter."
This says that the sage's movement and stillness, opening and closing,
contraction and expansion, softness and yielding,
and taking and giving must all follow the times.
If it is the right time, then move;
if it is not the time, then remain still.
Therefore, the scholars of old had intentions but would not manifest them.
Thus they were anxious about their words of governance,
secretly anxious and hiding them.
When worthy people live in a chaotic age,
knowing that the Way cannot be implemented,
they restrain themselves to avoid punishment
and remain silent to escape harm.
Avoiding it is like seeking coolness in summer
and seeking warmth in winter,
so as to avoid the calamities of cold and heat.
It is not that they are disloyal because they fear death.
Forcing speech leads to execution
without adding any merit or benefit;
moving forward, it harms the principle of the ruler's dignity,
and moving backward, it harms the life of the minister;
the disadvantage is extreme.
Therefore, they withdraw their persons without abandoning their uprightness
and cultivate their work without resting their tablets,
awaiting a time of clarity.
Thus Wēizǐ did not participate in the troubles of Zhòu
and was enfeoffed in Sòng
to serve as the lord of Yīn.
The ancestors were not extinguished,
and the later generations were not cut off.
Thus it is said:
"The virtue of a great worthy is long-lasting."
"Clarity leads to wisdom,
wisdom leads to clarity;
exertion leads to falling;
with clarity and wisdom, one can act grandly."
This says that monopolizing beauty and presiding over prosperity while exerting oneself,
using unrestrained ways to trample over others—
this is usually how people meet their downfall.
Therefore, the sages recorded it on bamboo slips
and passed it down to inform later generations,
saying:
"Fèn means prosperity;
líng means to fall."
Of cases of prosperity without falling,
there has never been one.
Therefore, those who possess the Way
do not equalize their reputations,
do not fill their capacities,
do not rely on their pleasures,
and do not reach the limits of their measures.
If their rank is noble, they are respectful to scholars;
if their emoluments are abundant, they strive to bestow them;
if their merit is great, they do not boast;
if their achievements are brilliant, they are not conceited.
Fame and reality have long been at odds with each other;
therefore, they are severed and have no intercourse.
The wise know that both cannot be maintained together,
so they choose one.
Thus they are at peace and without worry.
"Enduring bitterness without anger"—
this refers to stopping impulsive rage
to achieve success.
"Resentful without speaking"—
words must be treated with caution:
if words are not thorough,
they will instead harm oneself.
"Having desires without plotting"—
this means that plans must not be leaked;
if plans are leaked, calamity will reach its peak.
Acting on impulsive rage,
ignoring the law,
and inviting rebels to rise,
speaking lightly and leaking plans—
calamity will surely reach one's person.
Thus it is said:
"Enduring bitterness without anger,
resentful without speaking,
having desires without plotting."
"Greatly considering and measuring the standards,
like waking from sleep,
like dawn coming from darkness"—
this means assuming a profound demeanor to examine oneself,
and using silence to deliberate carefully.
Relying on worthy talents
and employing the benevolent and good;
once clear
and understanding the principles of what is beneficial or harmful,
it is like removing a blindfold.
Thus it is said:
"Like waking from sleep,
like dawn coming from darkness,
like the presence of Áo with Yáo."
“Do not seek counsel from the glib,”
means do not employ glib people;
employing glib people
leads to many private interests being pursued.
“Do not harbor sycophants,”
means do not listen to sycophancy;
listening to sycophancy leads to deceiving those above.
“Do not nurture the violent,”
means do not use cruelty;
using cruelty harms the people.
“Do not look to slanderers,”
means do not listen to slander;
listening to slander leads to losing worthy scholars.
Now, pursuing private interests, deceiving those above, harming the people, and losing worthy scholars—
if these four are practiced,
it is the means by which the lord’s righteousness is harmed and his rectitude is lost.
As for those who are lords and superiors,
once they have lost their righteousness and rectitude,
yet rely on them for their reputation;
those who are ministers are disloyal and wicked,
in order to pursue rank and salary,
disrupting customs and ruining the age,
seeking temporary peace and cherishing pleasure;
though they broaden their prestige,
it lasts only for a brief moment.
Therefore it is said:
“If one is not upright, they only broaden their desolation.”
For this reason, the people of old
blocked such paths
and obstructed such passages,
guarding them so that all things were cultivated.
Therefore, it was recorded on bamboo slips
and passed down to inform later generations, saying:
the resentment caused is deep,
and because of this, their prestige is exhausted.
“Do not use his trifles”
refers to being hollow.
If a person lacks goodness,
they are called hollow.
Generally, if one is rigidly fixed and does not move,
or dammed up and does not flow,
they will surely miss the proper time;
missing it, they will be discarded and fail to achieve success.
If Tiān plants something upright and without error,
it cannot be considered worthy;
if it is straight but lacks ability,
it cannot be considered beautiful.
What is considered worthy and beautiful about the Shèng rén
is that they follow transformations and comply with changes.
Like a deep spring that is never exhausted,
subtle and concise yet flowing and spreading,
thus the flow of their virtue and nourishment is evenly
applied to all things.
Therefore it is said:
The Shèng rén corresponds with Tiān and Dì.
“A bird flies according to the plumb line.”
This speaks of the righteousness of the Great Person.
Now, when a bird flies,
it must circle the mountains and gather in the valleys.
If it does not circle the mountains, it will be exhausted;
if it does not gather in the valleys, it will die.
Where mountains and valleys are located,
they are not necessarily straight.
Yet in circling mountains and gathering in valleys,
though it curves where it must curve,
it is still called following the line.
This is because if the bird starts in the north,
its intent is south and it reaches the south;
if it starts in the south,
its intent is north and it reaches the north.
If the grand intent is achieved,
it is not harmed by minor flaws.
Therefore, the Shèng rén praises and records this,
saying:
A road of a thousand lǐ
cannot be assisted by a plumb line;
a capital of ten thousand households
cannot be leveled by a water level.
This says that the conduct of the Great Person
does not necessarily follow past constants;
establishing righteousness is what is called being worthy.
Therefore, when those above evaluate those below,
they must not lose this method.
“Huàn chōng,”
refers to the heart;
the heart desires loyalty.
“Mò héng,”
refers to the ears and eyes;
the ears and eyes desire to be upright.
Central rectitude
is the foundation of governance.
The ears govern hearing;
hearing must follow what is heard;
to examine what is heard is called Cōng.
The eyes govern seeing;
seeing must follow what is seen;
to observe what is seen is called Míng.
The heart governs deliberation;
deliberation must follow words;
when words are attained, it is called Zhì.
When Cōng and Míng lead to Zhì,
then one is broad;
being broad without being muddled
is the means to simplify governance.
When governance is simple, the people benefit;
when they benefit, they are encouraged;
when they are encouraged, there is good fortune.
If hearing is not careful,
and one does not examine, then one is not Cōng;
if one is not Cōng, then there is error.
If vision does not observe, then one is not Míng;
if one is not Míng, then there are faults.
If deliberation does not attain, then one is not Zhì;
if one is not Zhì, then one is muddled.
Error, fault, and being muddled lead to worry;
worry is the means by which harshness is practiced;
harshness is the means by which governance becomes treacherous.
When governance is treacherous, the people are harmed;
when they are harmed, they resent;
when they resent, there is misfortune.
Therefore it is said:
Huàn chōng and Mò héng
speak of simplifying governance and benefiting the people.
“Do not encounter misfortune,”
speaks of using central rectitude to accumulate caution.
“Do not bring your desires near,”
speaks of the failure of superiors; they are often
greedy for gold, jade, horses, and women,
while being stingy with grain, rice, goods, and wealth.
When heavy taxes are collected from the common people,
then the ten thousand people will feel bitter resentment.
“Keep your worries distant,”
speaks of how superiors lose their states;
they often keep their pleasures near.
They establish entertainers and beauties,
and are externally dissolute in galloping and hunting,
while internally indulging in beautiful women and seductive sounds;
those below then become lax and negligent,
and all officials lose their integrity;
then chaos ensues and they lose their state.
“Build your dwelling high,
and none can save you from a perilous fall,”
this speaks of being honored, high, full, and great,
while liking to boast to others of one’s splendor;
the ruler is excessive and dwells in self-perceived worthiness,
and grants himself the title of a hero.
Therefore, excess must lead to loss, and heroism must lead to defeat.
When a superior is excessive and dwells in self-perceived worthiness
to manipulate the scholars and people,
the state will be chaotic,
and the hearts of the ten thousand people will be resentful;
this will surely lead to ruin.
It is like plunging from a mountain of ten thousand fathoms into a deep abyss;
death without recovery is certain.
Therefore it is said:
“Do not bring your desires near,
keep your worries distant;
build your dwelling high,
and none can save you from a perilous fall.”
“One can be shallow or deep,
can sink or float,
can be curved or straight,
can speak or be silent.”
This speaks of directing the intent to achieve results.
“Tiān does not have only one season,
Dì does not have only one advantage,
and people do not have only one task.”
For this reason, established undertakings must have many divisions,
and names and positions must have different directions.
The enlightened observe affairs,
thus they are not restricted to one thing, but are broadly conversant with the Dào.
The Dào
reaches up to what is without superior,
is detailed to the point of being infinite,
and operates within all living things.
Therefore, those who argue based on a single word,
examine based on a single method of governance,
or specialize in a single task,
can provide partial explanations
but cannot achieve broad application.
From this, the Shèng Rén knows that words cannot encompass everything,
so he extensively establishes governance
and considers its intent;
he knows that tasks cannot be all-inclusive,
so he explains things according to their names
and evaluates their achievements.
The year has spring, autumn, winter, and summer;
the month has upper, middle, and lower ten-day periods;
the day has morning and evening;
the night has dusk and dawn;
the stars
and constellations have their order, each having its own office.
Therefore it is said:
Heaven does not have only one season.
Mountains and hills are steep and rocky;
deep springs flow broadly;
springs overflow and yet are not exhausted;
marshes receive the overflow and yet are not full;
high and low lands, fertile and barren soils—
each thing has its proper place.
Therefore it is said:
The Earth does not have only one benefit.
Villages have customs,
states have laws,
food and drink have different flavors,
clothes have different colors.
The tools used by the world—
compasses, squares, cords, and levels;
weights, measures, numbers, and degrees—
each category has its standard.
Therefore it is said:
People do not have only one task.
These are the standards for various matters,
the details of which cannot be exhausted.
"To be correct and then observed"
refers to examining the beautiful and the ugly,
and distinguishing the fine from the coarse;
this cannot be done without scrutiny.
When roles are held without confusion,
governance will not lead to regret.
"To be fixed and then walked upon"
refers to occupying one's position,
following one's path,
and performing one's duties;
then the people will maintain their roles without disorder;
thus the lineage is preserved and ends well.
"To be deep and leave traces"
refers to clear ink and distinct markings.
When morality is constant,
then everyone in later generations will follow the principles without being lost;
thus fame and reputation will never cease.
"Now, Heaven and Earth are sometimes treacherous and sometimes easy,
like a drum having a mallet;
when it strikes the surface, there is a hit."
This means if there is a call,
there must be an echo;
if the echo does not deviate,
one can thereby exhaust the Dào of Heaven and Earth.
A shadow does not become straight for a crooked object;
an echo does not become beautiful for an ugly sound.
Therefore, the Shèng Rén is clear about the nature of things;
they will inevitably come according to their kind.
Thus the Jūnzǐ is continuously cautious about what he prioritizes.
"Heaven and Earth are the sack for the myriad things,
and the Zhòu Hé contains Heaven and Earth."
Heaven and Earth wrap the myriad things,
so they are called the sack of the myriad things.
The meaning of Zhòu Hé
is that it reaches up above the heavens,
goes down into the springs below the earth,
extends outward beyond the Sì Hǎi,
binds together Heaven and Earth,
and forms a single envelope.
When dispersed, it reaches where there is no space;
it cannot be named and then stopped.
It is so large that nothing is outside it,
and so small that nothing is inside it.
Therefore it is said
to contain Heaven and Earth.
Its principles are not transmitted;
though one may categorize them with a single canon, it does not exhaust even a single thin layer,
yet without categorization, there is no governance.
When much is stored within, there is wealth;
when things are brought out at the right time, it is appropriate.
And the Dào of the Shèng Rén
values being wealthy and appropriate.
What is meant by appropriate?
Rooting oneself in governance without falsehood,
operating in affairs without fixed methods,
and responding to changes without failing—this is called being appropriate.
Changes arrive everywhere;
if there is no appropriate response
and the foundation is misplaced, one cannot be resentful.
Thus it is spoken of and named "Zhòu Hé."
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"The Dào in Heaven is the sun;
in humans, it is the heart."
Therefore it is said:
With Qì there is life,
without Qì there is death;
those who live do so because of their Qì.
With names there is order,
without names there is chaos;
those who govern do so through names.
The Shū Yán says:
"Loving them, benefiting them,
enriching them, and pacifying them—
these four are what the Dào brings forth.
If Dì Wáng use these,
then Tiān Xià will be well-governed.
Dì Wáng
must scrutinize what comes first and what comes last:
if they prioritize the people and the land,
they will succeed;
if they prioritize status and pride,
they will fail.
Therefore, the Xiān Wáng
were cautious about what they put first and what they put last.
A ruler of men cannot but be cautious about status,
cannot but be cautious about the people,
cannot but be cautious about wealth.
Caution regarding status lies in promoting the xián;
caution regarding the people lies in appointing officials;
caution regarding wealth lies in working the land.
Therefore, the lowliness or honor, the lightness or weight of a ruler
depends on these three things;
he cannot but be cautious.
A state has treasures,
has tools,
and has utilities.
City walls,
natural barriers,
and stored reserves
are the treasures;
sagely wisdom
is the tool;
pearls and jade
are the least significant utilities.
The Xiān Wáng valued the treasures and tools
and gave little weight to the utilities;
thus they were able to rule Tiān Xià.
There are two things that lead to life and not death;
there are four things that lead to ruin and not standing:
pleasure,
anger,
hatred,
and desire—
these are the causes of ruin for Tiān Xià,
and the xián keep them to a minimum.
Acting to be good
is not true goodness.
Therefore, goodness should not be done for its own sake.
Thus, the Xiān Wáng valued spontaneous goodness.
Wáng Zhǔ build up their strength among the people;
Bà Zhǔ build up their strength among generals and soldiers;
declining rulers build up their strength among the nobility;
ruined rulers build up their strength among women and pearls and jade.
Therefore, the Xiān Wáng were cautious about what they accumulated.
Striving, striving—
this is the teacher of the myriad things.
Acting, acting—
this is the timing of the myriad things.
Strengthening, strengthening—
this is the richness of the myriad things.
Generally, there are three types of status for a state:
those that control others,
those that are controlled by others,
and those that cannot control others,
nor can others control them.
How can one know this to be so?
When virtue is abundant and righteousness is exalted,
yet one does not delight in imposing one’s reputation upon others;
when the people are numerous and the army is strong,
yet one does not use the state to create difficulties or bring about disasters;
and when the world faces major affairs,
one prefers to place one’s own state last;
one who is like this
is a controller of others.
When virtue is not abundant
and righteousness is not exalted,
yet one delights in imposing one’s reputation upon others;
when the people are not numerous
and the army is not strong,
yet one delights in using the state to create difficulties and bring about disasters;
relying on allied states
and gambling on fame and profit;
one who is like this
is controlled by others.
Advancing when others advance,
retreating when others retreat,
laboring when others labor,
and resting when others rest—
in advancing, retreating, laboring, and resting,
following in step with others;
one who is like this
cannot control others,
nor can others control them.
To love people deeply but be unable to benefit them;
to hate people deeply but be unable to harm them.
Therefore, the former kings valued appropriateness
and valued discretion.
Discretion is that which does not issue from the mouth
and is not visible in the expression;
now a dragon, now a snake,
transforming five times in a single day—
this is called discretion.
Therefore, the former kings did not use one to exceed two,
the former kings did not act alone,
nor did they monopolize merit.
The former kings did not use restrictive oaths
nor did they tie knots of alliance.
Restrictive oaths will be dissolved,
and tied knots will be broken.
Therefore, true intimacy
does not reside in restrictive oaths or tied knots.
The former kings did not use goods for diplomacy
nor did they partition land
to manage the world.
The world cannot be changed by force,
but it can be driven and employed as if with a whip.
Timeliness and righteousness
are what come forth to achieve this.
Redundant eyes are not bright,
redundant ears are not keen;
it is by this
that one can maintain the bearing of the Son of Heaven.
Official posts are likewise.
One who has timeliness gains Heaven;
one who has righteousness gains the people.
When there is both timeliness and righteousness,
one can then gain both Heaven and the people.
The former kings did not use bravery and fierceness to guard the borders,
and thus the borders were peaceful;
when the borders were peaceful,
neighboring states were friendly;
when neighboring states were friendly,
then actions were appropriate.
People naturally hate one another
and the human heart is fierce;
therefore, laws were made for them.
Laws emerge from ritual;
ritual emerges from order.
Order and ritual are the Way.
All things await order and ritual before becoming settled.
Regarding all things,
*yīn* and *yáng* give rise to them as a duality, yet they should be viewed from a third perspective.
The former kings followed this third perspective and were cautious about what entered and what exited.
By treating the lowly merely as lowly,
the lowly cannot be won over;
by treating the exalted merely as exalted,
the exalted cannot be won over.
*Jié* and *Shùn* are examples of this.
This is what the former kings valued most.
That which brings life if attained
and brings death if lost,
what is it?
It is "nothingness." By attaining it,
*Yáo*, *Shùn*, *Yǔ*, *Tāng*, *Wén*, *Wǔ*, and *Xiàojǐ*
all relied on it to achieve success,
and the world must rely on it to live.
Therefore, the former kings valued it.
Going without food for one day
is like a year of poor harvest;
going without food for three days
is like a year of famine;
going without food for five days
is like a year of desolation;
going without food for seven days,
one will have no territory;
going without food for ten days,
one will have no companions and all will die.
The former kings valued sincerity and trust. Sincerity and trust
are the bonds of the world.
Worthy Great Officials do not rely on the royal clan;
scholars do not rely on outside power.
Easy profit is not gained through merit;
easy preparation is not for practical use.
Therefore, preserving the state
and stabilizing the altars of earth and grain
reside within the span of sudden planning.
Sages use their hearts:
nebulously, they are broad and all-encompassing;
undifferentiated, so that no one can find their entrance;
tangled, as if they were chaotic silk;
and yet moving slowly, as if following a pattern of order.
Therefore it is said:
let those who desire knowledge be known;
let those who desire profit be benefited;
let those who desire bravery be brave;
let those who desire nobility be noble.
If another desires nobility
and I treat them as noble,
people will say I have ritual propriety.
If another desires bravery
and I treat them as brave,
people will say I am respectful.
If another desires profit
and I benefit them,
people will say I am benevolent.
If another desires knowledge
and I acknowledge their knowledge,
people will say I am clever.
Be cautious, be cautious!
Observe the subtle and distinguish between things;
when acting, one must reflect upon it;
do not let others recognize your intentions;
be prepared for what comes suddenly.
To be trusted is benevolence.
To be unable to be deceived is wisdom.
When one is both wise and benevolent,
one is called a complete person.
The lowly naturally serve the noble;
the unworthy naturally serve the worthy.
The reason the noble are able to achieve their nobility
is because they use their nobility to serve the lowly.
The reason the worthy are able to achieve their worthiness
is because they use their worthiness to serve the unworthy.
The ugly is the complement to the beautiful;
the humble is the complement to the exalted;
the lowly is the complement to the noble.
Therefore, the former kings valued them.
Heaven employs through the seasons;
Earth employs through materials;
people employ through virtue;
ghosts and spirits employ through omens;
birds and beasts employ through strength.
What is called virtue
means to take the lead.
Therefore, in virtue, nothing is better than leading;
in responding to circumstances, nothing is better than following.
A former king who used one *yīn* and two *yáng* became a Hegemon;
one who used only *yáng* became a King;
one who used one *yáng* and two *yīn* saw their territory diminished;
one who used only *yīn* perished.
When measuring, do not use few or many;
when weighing, do not use light or heavy;
when calculating length, do not use short or long.
If one does not examine these three matters,
one cannot undertake great affairs.
Can you be cautious?
Can you be disciplined?
Can you be hidden and concealed?
Can you be like millet?
Can you be like wheat?
If there is no growth in spring, will there be no harvest in summer?
The Xiānwáng used affairs to join alliances
and virtue to join people.
If these two do not harmonize,
then there will be no success
and no intimacy.
In general, the downfall of a state
is due to its strengths;
a person’s self-failure
is due to what they excel at.
Therefore, those good at swimming die in bridges and pools,
and those good at archery die in the middle of the wilderness.
Life belongs to food,
and governance belongs to affairs.
To have good governance without good affairs
is something that from ancient times until now
has never existed.
The many defeat the few,
the fast defeat the slow,
the brave defeat the cowardly,
the wise defeat the foolish,
the good defeat the evil,
the righteous defeat the unrighteous,
and those with the Tiāndào defeat those without the Tiāndào.
In all these seven victories, the many are valued;
those who use them throughout their lives are many.
If a ruler loves ease and desires
and loses his life and his state,
he is in peril; if his virtue is insufficient to cherish his people,
he is in peril; if he clarifies his punishments but despises his scholars,
he is in peril; if the feudal lords have long borrowed his prestige and he does not know how to restrain himself,
he is in peril; if he grows older and does not know how to respect his shìzǐ,
he is in peril; if he accumulates and stores wealth until it rots and decays
and does not give it to others, he is in peril.
In general, there are three types of reputation for people:
one for governance,
one for shame,
and one for affairs.
Reputations for affairs are twofold:
rectifying them and examining them.
When these five are present, the Tiānxià is governed.
If names are correct, there is order;
if names are biased, there is chaos;
if there are no names, there is death.
Therefore, the Xiānwáng valued names.
The Xiānwáng took the Tiānxià
by treating those far away with Lǐ
and those nearby with Tǐ.
Tǐ and Lǐ
are the means by which to take the Tiānxià;
far and near
are the means by which to distinguish the boundaries of the Tiānxià.
That which increases daily yet one worries is too little
is only loyalty;
that which decreases daily yet one worries is too much
is only desire.
Much loyalty and few desires
constitute wisdom;
it is the broad way for those who serve as ministers.
For one who serves as a minister,
if they have no merit or labor for the state,
yet their family is wealthy and the state is poor,
it is a great crime for a minister;
for one who serves as a minister,
if they have no merit or labor for the state,
yet their rank is noble and the ruler is debased,
it is a great crime for a minister.
For those who are noble and wealthy without merit or labor for the state,
is it only because the ruler values the worthy?
When common people use their minds:
love is the beginning of hatred,
and favor is the root of resentment.
In serving their parents,
once they have a wife and children,
then filial piety declines;
in serving their ruler,
if they have a good profession
and a wealthy household,
then their conduct declines;
when rank and salary are full,
then loyalty declines.
Only the worthy are not like this.
Therefore, the Xiānwáng did not allow for fullness.
When cauldrons and drums are full,
then people level them;
when people are full of pride,
then Tiān levels them.
Therefore, the Xiānwáng did not seek fullness.
The ruler holds the initiative,
and the minister holds submission.
The Xiānwáng gave weight to honor and disgrace;
honor and disgrace lie in action.
In the Tiānxià there is no private love
and no private hatred.
Those who do good have fortune,
and those who do not do good have calamity.
Fortune and calamity lie in action;
therefore, the Xiānwáng gave weight to action.
Clear rewards are not wasteful,
and clear punishments are not violent.
When rewards and punishments are clear,
it is the height of virtue.
Therefore, the Xiānwáng valued clarity.
The Tiāndào is vast and the sovereign uses it; likes and dislikes,
likes and dislikes—the world can be kept secret about them,
and the closure must be firm.
The books of the Xiānwáng
are the respectful adherence of the heart,
yet the common people do not know them.
Therefore, having affairs is an affair;
having no affairs is also an affair.
I fear affairs
and do not wish to create affairs;
I fear words
and do not wish to create words.
Therefore, at sixty years of age, I am an old stutterer.
The inner city walls must be complete;
the outer city walls must not have external connections;
the village boundaries must not have crosswise passages;
the village gates must not be without doors;
palace walls and gates
must be kept in repair.
Therefore, if the inner walls are incomplete,
then rebels and traitors will conspire;
if the outer walls connect externally,
then those who commit treachery, flee, or scale walls will arise.
If village boundaries have crosswise passages,
then those who seize and steal will not stop;
if village gates have no doors
and the outside and inside communicate,
then there will be no distinction between men and women.
If palace walls are not prepared
and gates are not firm,
though one has precious goods,
one cannot keep them.
Therefore, if the situation makes it impossible to do wrong,
then treacherous and evil people will be sincere and honest;
if prohibitions and punishments are majestic and strict,
then the negligent and disrespectful will become orderly.
If laws and orders are clear and prominent,
then the Mányí will not dare to intrude;
if rewards and celebrations are certain and reliable,
then those with merit will be encouraged.
When those who teach and discipline the customs are many,
then the ruler and the people will be transformed without knowing it themselves.
For this reason, when a Míngjūn is in a high position,
punishments are rare and penalties are few;
it is not that he does not punish what should be punished
or does not penalize what should be penalized.
The Míngjūn
closes the gates,
blocks the paths,
and covers his tracks, so that the people have no way to come into contact with places of excess and wrongdoing.
Thus, the people following the correct path and doing good
is as if it were their nature.
Therefore, penalties and punishments are few, and the people are governed.
By walking through the fields,
observing the plowing and weeding,
and calculating the agricultural affairs,
one can know whether a state is hungry or well-fed.
If the plowing is not deep,
the weeding is not careful,
the suitability of the land is not utilized,
and the grassy fields are full of weeds;
if the plowed land is not necessarily fertile
and the uncultivated land is not necessarily barren,
and one calculates the wilderness based on the density of people;
if the grassy fields are many and the reclaimed fields are few,
even without floods or droughts,
it is the wilderness of a hungry state.
If things are like this and the population is small,
then it is insufficient to defend its territory;
if things are like this and the population is large,
then the state is poor and the people are hungry;
if they encounter floods or droughts under such conditions,
then the masses will scatter and cannot be gathered back.
For those whose population is insufficient for defense,
their city walls will not be secure;
for those who are hungry, they cannot be made to fight;
if the masses scatter and cannot be gathered,
then the state becomes a wasteland.
Therefore it is said:
A lord who possesses land and a state
but does not apply himself to plowing and weeding
is a parasitic ruler.
Therefore it is said:
By traveling through the fields and wilderness,
observing the plowing and weeding,
and calculating the agricultural tasks,
a state of hunger or satiety can be known.
By traveling through the mountains and marshes,
observing the mulberry and hemp,
and calculating the production of the six domestic animals,
a state of poverty or wealth can be known.
When mountains and marshes are vast,
then plants and trees easily become abundant;
when the soil is fertile and rich,
then mulberry and hemp easily proliferate;
when fodder grass is plentiful and widespread,
then the six domestic animals easily multiply.
Even if mountains and marshes are wide,
if there are no prohibitions on plants and trees;
even if the soil is fertile,
if mulberry and hemp are not accounted for;
even if fodder grass is abundant,
if the six domestic animals are taxed,
these are the gates to closing off wealth.
Therefore it is said,
"If seasonal goods do not flow smoothly,
even if gold and jade are many,
it is called a poor state."
Therefore it is said:
"By traveling through the mountains and marshes,
observing the mulberry and hemp,
and calculating the production of the six domestic animals,
a state of poverty or wealth can be known."
By entering the state capital and towns,
inspecting the palaces and rooms,
observing the carriages, horses, and clothing,
a state of extravagance or frugality can be known.
In a state where the city walls are large but the fields and wilderness are small and narrow,
the wilderness is insufficient to nourish the people;
where the city area is large but the population is small,
the people are insufficient to defend the walls;
where the palace compounds are large but the rooms and houses are few,
the houses are insufficient to fill the palaces;
where houses are numerous but the attendants and followers are few,
the people are insufficient to dwell in the houses;
where granaries are few but terraces and pavilions are many,
the stores are insufficient to supply the expenses.
Therefore it is said,
"If the ruler above has no accumulation but the palaces and houses are beautiful,
and the common households have no accumulation but their clothing is elegant,
if those riding in carriages decorate them for appearance,
and those traveling on foot display ornate patterns,
where basic resources are few and secondary uses are many,
this is the custom of an extravagant state."
If a state is extravagant, its use of resources is wasteful;
if its use of resources is wasteful, the people are poor;
if the people are poor, treacherous ingenuity arises;
if treacherous ingenuity arises, then wicked artifice is practiced.
Thus, where treachery and wickedness arise,
they are born from shortage and insufficiency;
where shortage and insufficiency arise,
they are born from extravagance;
where extravagance arises,
it is born from a lack of moderation.
Therefore it is said:
"To scrutinize weights and measures,
to economize on clothing,
to be frugal with wealth and usage,
and to forbid extravagance and excess,
are the urgent tasks of governing a state."
Those who do not understand such calculations
cannot be employed to govern a state.
Therefore it is said:
"By entering the state capital and towns,
inspecting the palaces and rooms,
and observing the carriages, horses, and clothing,
a state of extravagance or frugality can be known."
By assessing famines,
calculating military services,
observing terraces and pavilions,
and measuring state expenses,
a state of reality or emptiness can be known.
For a population of ten thousand households in the fields and wilderness,
the land that can produce food
should be fifty *lǐ* square;
this is enough to be sufficient.
For fewer than ten thousand households,
they may move toward mountains and marshes;
for more than ten thousand households,
they should move away from mountains and marshes.
In places where the wilderness is fully cleared but the people have no accumulation,
the state's land is small and the food-producing area is limited;
where half the fields are cultivated but the people have surplus food and grain is abundant,
the state's land is large and the food-producing area is broad;
where the state's land is large but the wilderness is not cleared,
the ruler loves goods and the ministers love profit;
where the cleared land is vast but the people are insufficient,
taxes from above are heavy,
causing their stored wealth to be drained away.
Therefore it is said,
"If grain must travel three hundred *lǐ*,
the state will not have one year's accumulation;
if grain travels four hundred *lǐ*,
the state will not have half a year's accumulation;
if grain travels five hundred *lǐ*,
then the masses will have the look of hunger."
If the harvest is reduced by one-third,
it is called a minor disaster;
three years of minor disasters lead to a major disaster;
in a major disaster
the masses will have abandoned baskets.
With a levy of one out of ten in the army,
and three out of ten idle,
the harvest will be reduced by one-third.
If the harvest is reduced by one-third
and there are no former accumulations,
then there will be emaciated corpses abandoned on the roads.
If a levy of one out of ten is in the army
and not disbanded for three years,
and there is no surplus food,
then the people will sell their children.
Therefore it is said:
"Although the mountains and forests are near,
although the plants and trees are beautiful,
palaces and houses must have moderation,
and prohibitions and openings must have their seasons.
Why is this?"
It is answered:
"A great tree cannot be felled by one alone,
a great tree cannot be lifted by one alone,
a great tree cannot be transported by one alone,
and a great tree cannot be placed upon a thin wall."
Therefore it is said,
"Although mountains and forests are wide,
and plants and trees are beautiful,
prohibitions and openings must have their seasons;
although the state is full and overflowing,
and gold and jade are many,
palaces and houses must have moderation;
although rivers and seas are wide,
ponds and marshes are broad,
and fish and turtles are many,
nets and traps must have their regulations,
for boats and nets cannot be completed with the resources of a single person."
It is not out of personal concern for plants and trees or love for fish and turtles;
it is because one hates to divert the people from producing grain.
Therefore it is said,
"The reason the former kings prohibited working in mountains and marshes
was to concentrate the people on producing grain."
These people cannot eat without grain;
grain does not grow without land;
land does not move without people;
and if the people do not exert effort, there is no way to acquire wealth.
For wealth that is produced
comes from exerting effort;
effort that is produced
comes from laboring the body.
Therefore, if the ruler uses wealth without limit,
it means the people must exert effort without rest.
Therefore it is said,
"When terraces and pavilions overlook each other,
those above and those below will resent each other."
When the people have no surplus accumulation,
prohibitions will not necessarily be effective;
when the masses contain those with leftover bundles,
their battles will not necessarily be victorious;
when the roads contain those discarded and emaciated,
their defense will not necessarily be firm.
Therefore, if orders are not necessarily carried out,
prohibitions are not necessarily effective,
battles are not necessarily won,
and defense is not necessarily firm,
then danger and ruin follow in their wake.
Thus it is said:
“By auditing bad harvests and famines,
calculating military service and labor,
observing the towers and pavilions,
and measuring national expenditures,
a state’s fullness or emptiness can be known.”
Entering the *zhōulǐ*,
observing the customs,
and listening to how the people are transformed by their superiors,
a state’s order or chaos can be known.
If the *zhōulǐ* are not partitioned,
if the *lǘhàn* are not established,
if going out and coming in have no set times,
and if early and late hours are not prohibited,
then people who commit robbery, theft,
assault, and injury
will not be restrained.
If they drink water used to wash grain,
if wells are dug in the alleys,
if threshing floors and gardens are adjacent,
if trees and shrubs are lush,
if palace walls are in ruins,
if doors and gates are not closed,
and if those outside and inside interact freely,
then the distinction between men and women
will not naturally be correct.
If in the *xiāng* there are no elders to guide,
if in the *lǐ* there are no quarters for scholars,
if there are no seasonal assemblies,
if people do not gather for funerals and winter sacrifices,
and if prohibitions and punishments are not strict,
then seniority and harmony
will not naturally arise.
