Therefore, if marriage rites are not handled with care,
the people will not cultivate integrity;
if in the evaluation of the worthy there are no local recommendations,
the scholars will not attain proper conduct;
if wealth and goods circulate within the capital,
then laws and orders will be destroyed in the government offices;
if petitions are granted by the superiors through personal requests,
then factions and cliques will form among the subordinates;
if local officials have no legal systems,
the common people and various groups will not follow.
This is where the ruin of a state and the assassination of a ruler originate.
Therefore it is said:
“Entering the *zhōulǐ*,
observing the customs,
and listening to how the people are transformed by their superiors,
a state’s order or chaos can be known.”
Entering the court,
observing those around the ruler,
seeking out the ministers of the court,
and evaluating who is honored or debased among the high and low,
a state’s strength or weakness can be known.
If many achievements are considered superior
but stipends and rewards are considered inferior,
then ministers with accumulated merit
will not strive to exert their full effort.
If administrative conduct is considered superior
but ranks and titles are considered inferior,
then heroic and talented ministers
will not strive to exhaust their abilities.
If favorites and sycophants around the ruler
are given ranks and stipends
without regard for their merit or ability,
then the common people will feel resentment
and blame the superior, holding ranks in contempt and stipends in low regard.
If merchants and those with gold, jade, and wealth
are given ranks and stipends
without regard for their character or conduct,
then the orders of the superior will be taken lightly
and the legal system will be destroyed.
If those with heavy power
attain high positions
without regard for talent or ability,
then the people will turn away from fundamental conduct to seek external influence.
If those ministers with accumulated merit
do not strive to exert their full effort,
then the soldiers will not fight;
if heroic and talented people do not strive to exhaust their abilities,
then internal governance will not be orderly.
If the common people feel resentment
and blame the superior, holding ranks in contempt and stipends in low regard,
then the superior will have no means to encourage the masses;
if the orders of the superior are taken lightly,
the legal system is destroyed,
then the ruler will have no means to employ ministers,
and the ministers will have no means to serve the ruler.
If the people turn away from fundamental conduct to seek external influence,
then the true and false circumstances of the state will be entirely known by enemy states.
Thus it is said:
“Entering the court,
observing those around the ruler,
seeking the ministers of the court,
and evaluating who is honored or debased among the high and low,
a state’s strength or weakness can be known.”
When establishing laws and issuing orders,
and when presiding over the masses and employing the people,
by measuring whether majesty, severity, leniency, and kindness
are carried out among the people or not, a state’s rise or extinction can be known.
If laws are established in name only and harm falls upon those distant and estranged,
if orders are distributed yet those who do not obey persist,
and if ranks and stipends are held in contempt while those without merit are wealthy,
then the masses will surely treat orders lightly
and the position of the superior will be endangered.
Thus it is said:
“If good fields are not in the hands of fighting men,
the army will be weak in three years;
if rewards and punishments are not trusted,
the state will be broken in five years;
if the superior sells offices and ranks,
it will perish in seven years;
if human ethics are abandoned and animal-like conduct is practiced,
it will be extinguished in ten years.”
Not being victorious in battle
is weakness;
having territory carved away on four sides
and submitting to other feudal lords
is being broken;
abandoning one’s own country
and moving the capital
is perishing;
having the possessor of the state be of a different surname
is being extinguished.
Thus it is said:
“Establish laws and issue orders,
preside over the masses and employ the people,
and measure majesty, severity, leniency, and kindness
being carried out among the people
or not being carried out among the people,
and a state’s rise or extinction can be known.”
By calculating enemy allies,
measuring the ruler’s intentions,
examining the state’s foundations,
and observing whether the people’s production is surplus or insufficient,
a state’s survival or ruin can be known.
If enemy states are strong while allied states are weak,
if remonstrating ministers die while flattering ministers are honored,
and if private interests prevail while public laws are destroyed,
then allied states will not rely on their closeness,
and enemy states will not fear their strength.
Heroic men will not feel secure in their positions,
and those with accumulated merit will not cherish their stipends.
If pleasure is taken in commerce while fundamental goods are not pursued,
then the people will live lazily and not attend to accumulation.
If heroic men do not feel secure in their positions,
then good ministers will leave;
if those with accumulated merit do not cherish their stipends,
then soldiers will not be of use;
if the people live lazily and do not attend to accumulation,
then the granaries will be empty.
If such is the case and the ruler does not change,
then those who commit robbery, theft,
injury, and aggressive seizure will arise.
Internally, the court has no good ministers,
soldiers are not of use,
and granaries are empty;
and externally there is the worry of strong enemies,
then the country will reside in a state where it destroys itself.
Therefore it is said:
"Calculate the enemy’s allies,
measure the superior’s intentions,
examine the state’s foundation,
observe the surplus or deficiency of the people’s production,
and the survival or downfall of a state can be known."
Therefore, by using these eight factors to observe a ruler’s state,
the ruler will have nowhere to hide his true condition.
5.2 Fǎ Jìn, Number Fourteen, Wài Yán Five. When laws and systems are not debated,
then the people do not act out of private interest;
when punishments and executions are never pardoned,
then the people do not act perfunctorily in doing good;
when titles and stipends are not falsely bestowed,
then subordinates do not cause disorder for their superiors.
These three are preserved in the offices
as laws,
and when applied to the state, they become customs.
The rest will be governed without coercion.
Once the ruler establishes the standards,
then the hundred officials uphold the laws;
when the superior clearly displays the regulations,
then the subordinates all meet the requirements.
If the ruler is not consistent in establishing standards,
then the number of subordinates who violate the law
and establish private principles will certainly be many.
Thus, people use their private interests,
discard the superior’s regulations,
and follow what they have heard privately.
Thus, subordinates compete with officials over the laws,
and those above share authority with the ruler;
the danger to the state
must surely begin from this.
In the past, the way the Shèngwáng governed their people was not like this;
those who discarded the superior’s laws and regulations
were surely burdened with shame.
Providing thick wealth and broad favors
to privately endear oneself to the people
was corrected by the proper standards.
After the Shèngwáng passed away,
those who inherited from them declined.
When those who rule people cannot understand the way to establish a ruler
as the foundation of the state,
then the high ministers’ subverting of those below
and targeting the people’s hearts will certainly be many.
When a ruler cannot carefully establish his laws
to serve as regulations for those below,
then the common people’s establishing of private principles
and rushing toward personal gain will certainly be numerous.
In the past, when the Shèngwáng governed people,
they did not value people for being broad in learning;
they desired people to be harmonious and unified
so as to obey orders.
The Tài Shì says:
"Zhòu had hundreds of millions of subjects,
but they also had hundreds of millions of minds.
Wǔwáng had three thousand subjects, yet they had one mind."
Therefore, Zhòu perished because of the hundreds of millions of minds,
while Wǔwáng survived because of the one mind.
Therefore, a ruler who possesses a state,
if he cannot unify the people’s hearts,
unify the state’s authority,
standardize the righteousness of the scholars,
and transmit the superior’s governance
as the law for those below,
then even if he has extensive land and numerous people,
he still cannot achieve stability.
When the ruler loses the Way,
then the high ministers align their power and weight
to promote one another in the state,
and the lesser officials will surely follow profit to join them.
Therefore, they treat the state’s
scholars
as their own faction,
carrying out public duties as if they were private favors;
when advancing, they push one another before the ruler;
when withdrawing, they praise one another among the people;
each seeking convenience for themselves
while forgetting the Shèjì,
to expand their own residences,
gathering followers into groups,
above to obscure the ruler,
below to exploit the people—
these are all ways to weaken the ruler and bring disorder to the state.
Thus, the state falls into danger.
Ways that bring disorder to the state
and change the state’s constants,
such as granting rewards according to one’s own whims,
are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Usurping state power to deeply exploit the people
is a prohibition of the Shèngwáng.
Occupying a position without performing duties for the superior
is a prohibition of the Shèngwáng.
Advancing to receive a stipend from the ruler
but withdrawing to hide that wealth in one's house,
not attending to the duties of office,
but only exerting effort for one's subordinates,
treating the king’s officials as private,
treating the ruler’s affairs as private,
excluding those who are not of their kind
and acting for private ends—
these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Practicing conduct without making kinship the foundation,
managing affairs without making the office the primary focus,
promoting those without ability
and advancing those without merit—
these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Making connections with people as if it were one’s own gift,
recommending people as if it were one’s own labor,
and making people officials only to share in their stipends—
these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Networking for gain and profiting from the poor,
taking lightly from one’s own people
while offering heavily to the ruler,
stripping from those above to attach to those below,
or perverting the law to seek from the people—
these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Being employed in a way that does not match one's person,
having a family wealthier than others of one’s rank,
or having a very small stipend but very much wealth—
these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Opposing the world in one’s conduct,
criticizing the superior to gain a reputation,
and constantly going against the superior’s laws to form factions in the state—
these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Dressing up in poverty
and manifesting hard labor,
balancing on poverty and low status,
having no official duties,
having no established lineage in the family,
positioning oneself between the high and low,
and speaking as if for the people—
these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Treating traveling scholars as one’s own capital,
refining armor as one’s own foundation,
nourishing treacherous ministers and those who would surely die for private causes,
and then making bold demands to bargain deeply with the superior—
these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Carefully adorning minor details to show the people,
occasionally speaking of great matters to move the superior,
forming distant alliances to surpass the group,
and using false titles to preside over the court—
10 these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Humbling oneself and living among the common,
acting in secret and being biased,
entering through the side and welcoming from afar,
evading the superior and evading the people—
these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Contradicting customs and being eccentric in rituals,
speaking grandiosely and acting according to personal rules,
making what one does difficult
and loftily setting oneself apart—
these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Holding to one's post while living in leisure,
distributing broadly to attract the masses,
toiling personally to carry out actions,
persuading people with goods and wealth,
aiding people to buy a reputation,
being very quiet oneself
while making others seek one out—
these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Acting in a perverted way yet remaining firm,
speaking deceitfully yet being eloquent,
having wrong methods yet being extensive,
and following evil yet being polished—
these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Treating cliques as friends,
treating the concealment of evil as benevolence,
treating frequent changes as wisdom,
treating heavy taxation as loyalty,
and treating the venting of anger as courage—
these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
Strengthening the state’s foundation
while personally striving toward the superior,
and deeply attaching oneself to the feudal lords—
these are prohibitions of the Shèngwáng.
In the person of a *Shèng Wáng* and in a time of a well-ordered world,
there must be that which is approved in virtuous conduct,
and there must be that which is clarified in moral principles.
Therefore, the scholar-officials dare not deviate from custom or vary from ritual
to distinguish themselves in the state;
they dare not distribute favors or act with indulgence
to cultivate relationships between superiors and subordinates
and gain private intimacy with the people;
they dare not leap over ranks or exceed their offices,
nor fish for profit or claim unearned merit
to curry favor with their ruler.
In the *Shèng Wáng*’s governance of the people,
when they advance, he ensures they have no means to obtain unmerited profit;
when they retreat, he ensures they have no means to avoid deserved harm.
He must make them return to being secure in their positions,
happy in their groups,
diligent in their duties,
and find honor in their reputations,
and only then does he stop.
Therefore, those who exceed their office and separate from their group
must be made to suffer harm;
those who are incapable in their tasks and fail in their duties
must be made to feel shame.
For this reason, in the *Shèng Wáng*’s teaching of the people,
he establishes them in benevolence,
employs them through shame,
and cultivates their abilities
until they achieve accomplishment, and then he stops.
Therefore it is said:
"Being decisive and firm,
quiet and well-governed,
secure and honored,
taking actions without changing principles—
this is the Way of the *Shèng Wáng*."
5.3 *Zhòng Lìng*, Number Fifteen, *Wài Yán* Six. Among all the vital instruments for ruling a state,
none is more important than the order.
When orders are valued, the ruler is respected;
when the ruler is respected, the state is secure.
When orders are slighted, the ruler is base;
when the ruler is base, the state is in danger.
Therefore, securing the state lies in respecting the ruler;
respecting the ruler lies in carrying out orders;
carrying out orders lies in strict punishments.
If punishments are strict and orders are carried out,
then all officials will be in awe;
if punishments are not strict
and orders are not carried out,
then all officials will be joyful.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler examines the root of governing the people;
no root is more essential than the order.
Thus it is said:
"Those who diminish orders shall die;
those who add to orders shall die;
those who do not carry out orders shall die;
those who delay orders shall die;
those who do not follow orders shall die."
These five offenses lead to death without pardon;
focus is solely on the order.
Thus it is said:
"When orders are valued, those below are in awe."
If the one above is not enlightened,
although the order originates from the superior,
the discussion of its feasibility rests with those below.
To disregard the superior's order to establish one's own authority,
and then act willfully for private gain—
why would the various officials not be joyful?
Furthermore, if an order originates from the superior
but its feasibility is debated by those below,
then authority is tied to the people below.
If authority is tied to the people below,
yet one seeks for the superior to be out of danger,
it cannot be achieved.
If an order is issued but those who delay it go unpunished,
this is teaching the people to be disrespectful.
If an order is issued but those who do not carry it out go unpunished,
while those who do carry it out are penalized,
this is teaching the people not to obey.
If an order is issued but its feasibility is debated by the officials,
then authority is divided below.
If those who add to or subtract from orders go unpunished,
then this is teaching the people crooked paths.
In such a case,
then the cunning and sycophantic
will use this to form private cliques;
the partisan
will use this to favor their factions and trade favors;
the greedy
will use this to collect goods and amass wealth;
the weak
will use this to fawn upon the noble and wealthy
and serve the favorites; the boastful
will use this to buy reputation and achieve fame.
Therefore, once an order is issued,
if it shows the people five crooked paths,
yet one seeks for the superior to be out of danger
and the lower ranks to be without chaos,
it cannot be achieved.
When beans and grain are insufficient
and secondary industries are not restricted,
the people will surely have the look of hunger;
yet if artisans compete with one another in decorative carving and engraving,
this is called contrariness.
When cloth and silk are insufficient
and clothing has no regulation,
the people will surely suffer from freezing cold;
yet if women compete with one another in beautiful clothes of brocade and embroidery,
this is called contrariness.
A state of ten thousand chariots that stores weapons
but whose soldiers cannot fight in the field to meet the enemy
will surely face the disaster of peril and ruin for the *Shè Jì*;
yet if the scholar-officials compete with one another in avoiding labor service,
this is called contrariness.
If noble titles are granted without considering ability
and stipends are given without considering merit,
then the scholar-officials will have no reason to follow regulations or die for their integrity;
and the various ministers will surely communicate with outsiders to seek favors,
take the path of power,
act as sycophants,
and compete with one another in using nobility and wealth as glory—
this is called contrariness.
The court has constant ministers,
the state has constant customs,
and the people have constant livelihoods.
What are called the court's constant ministers?
Those who examine their own abilities before accepting office
and do not deceive their superiors;
who are prudent in following laws and regulations in their governance
and do not favor factions;
who exhaust their abilities and efforts
without prioritizing gain;
who face difficulties and calamities
without shrinking from death;
whose stipends do not exceed their merit
and whose positions do not surpass their abilities;
and who do not accept rewards without substance—
these are the court's constant ministers.
What are called the state's constant customs?
When likes and dislikes
do not contradict those of the superior;
when what is valued and what is despised
does not go against the orders;
when there are no actions that oppose the superior,
no talk of forming lower-level cliques,
no extravagant upbringing,
and no clothing that exceeds one's rank;
when one is prudent in conduct within the village
and does not go against the affairs of the court—
these are the state's constant customs.
What are called the people's constant livelihoods?
Raising livestock and planting crops,
following the seasons to grow grain,
laboring in farming to clear the wild grass,
and prohibiting secondary activities—
these are the people's constant livelihoods.
Therefore it is said:
"If the court does not value constant ministers,
then sycophants will advance,
taking rewards without merit;
the treacherous and wicked will act freely,
and those without ability will reach the top.
If the state does not follow constant customs,
then the ministers and subordinates will not be compliant,
and the orders of the superior will be difficult to carry out.
If the people do not apply themselves to constant livelihoods,
then the granaries will be empty
and resources will be insufficient."
If sycophants are able to advance
and rewards are taken without merit;
if the treacherous act freely
and those without ability reach the top,
then the high ministers will not be in harmony.
If subordinates are not obedient,
and the orders of the superior are difficult to implement,
then responding to difficulties will not be successful.
If granaries and storehouses are empty,
and financial resources are insufficient,
then the state has no means to defend itself firmly.
If one of these three situations appears,
then enemy states will control it.
Therefore, a state is not respected without cause,
an army does not win without cause,
the people are not employed without cause,
and orders are not executed without cause.
In general, for a state to be respected,
it must depend on the victory of the army,
and only then is the state respected.
In general, for an army to win,
it must depend on the employment of the people,
and only then does the army win.
In general, for the people to be employed,
it must depend on the execution of orders,
and only then are the people employed.
In general, for orders to be executed,
it must depend on authority prevailing over those close to the ruler,
and only then are orders executed.
Therefore, if prohibitions do not prevail over close relatives and the noble,
if punishments are not carried out against personal favorites,
if legal prohibitions do not execute those who are powerful and severe,
but instead harm those who are distant and estranged,
and if celebratory rewards are not bestowed upon the low and humble,
yet one seeks for orders to be certainly executed,
it cannot be attained.
If ability does not lead to official appointment,
if receiving salaries and rewards does not correspond to merit,
if commands and orders run contrary to the hearts of the people,
and if movement and stillness are deceptive regarding seasonal changes,
if those with merit are not necessarily rewarded,
if those with guilt are not necessarily executed,
if what is ordered is not necessarily carried out,
and if what is prohibited is not necessarily stopped;
when those in high positions have no means to employ subordinates,
yet seek for the people to be certainly employed,
it cannot be attained.
If generals and commanders do not have strict majesty,
if the hearts of the people are not singular and focused,
if soldiers in formation do not fight to the death for the regulations,
and if rank-and-file soldiers do not make light of the enemy,
yet one seeks for the army to be certainly victorious,
it cannot be attained.
If internal defense cannot be complete,
if external attack cannot cause submission,
if field battles cannot control the enemy,
and if invasions and expeditions cannot overawe the four neighbors,
yet one seeks for the state to be respected,
it cannot be attained.
If virtue is not extended to the weak and small,
if majesty is not trusted by the strong and great,
if punitive expeditions cannot subdue *Tiānxià*,
yet one seeks to become the *Bà* among the *Zhūhóu*,
it cannot be attained.
If one's majesty has a rival standing alongside it,
if one's army has a rival contending with it,
if virtue cannot cherish distant states,
and if orders cannot unify the *Zhūhóu*,
yet one seeks to become the *Wáng* of *Tiānxià*,
it cannot be attained.
Large land and a wealthy state,
a numerous population and a strong army—
these are the foundations of the *Bàwáng*,
however, they are also neighbors to peril and ruin.
The numbers of *Tiāndào*,
and the changes in the human heart:
the numbers of *Tiāndào*
are that once the extreme is reached, there is reversal,
and once prosperity is at its peak, there is decline;
the changes in the human heart
are that having an excess leads to arrogance,
and arrogance leads to laxity and indolence.
Now, those who are arrogant are arrogant toward the *Zhūhóu*;
for those who are arrogant toward the *Zhūhóu*,
the *Zhūhóu* are lost on the outside;
as for those who are lax and indolent,
the people become chaotic on the inside.
The *Zhūhóu* lost on the outside
and the people chaotic on the inside
is *Tiāndào*.
This is the time of peril and ruin.
As for those whose land is indeed large
but do not annex or merge,
and do not seize or plunder;
whose people are indeed numerous
but are not lax or indolent,
and do not treat subordinates with haughtiness;
whose state is indeed wealthy
but are not extravagant or excessive,
and do not indulge their desires;
whose army is indeed strong
but do not lightly insult the *Zhūhóu*,
and whose mobilization of the masses and use of the army
is necessarily for the political order of *Tiānxià*—
this is the foundation of correcting *Tiānxià*
and is the ruler of a *Bàwáng*.
Generally, the instruments with which the *Xiānwáng* governed the state are three,
and those that attack and destroy them are six.
An enlightened king is able to overcome these attacks;
therefore, without adding to the three instruments,
he naturally possesses the state and corrects *Tiānxià*.
A chaotic king is unable to overcome these attacks;
therefore, even though he does not diminish the three instruments,
he naturally loses *Tiānxià* and perishes.
"What are the three instruments?"
The answer is:
"Commands and orders,
axes and hatchets,
and salaries and rewards."
"What are the six attacks?"
The answer is:
"Relatives,
the noble,
wealth,
feminine beauty,
clever sycophancy,
and toys and favorites."
"What is the use of the three instruments?"
The answer is:
"Without commands and orders, there is no way to employ subordinates;
without axes and hatchets, there is no way to overawe the masses;
without salaries and rewards, there is no way to encourage the people."
"What is the failure caused by the six attacks?"
The answer is:
"Those who, although they do not listen, can still be preserved;
those who, although they violate prohibitions, can still be exempted;
those who, although they have no merit, can still be enriched.
Whenever a state has those who do not listen yet can be preserved,
then commands and orders are insufficient to employ subordinates;
if there are those who violate prohibitions yet can be exempted,
then axes and hatchets are insufficient to overawe the masses;
if there are those who have no merit yet can be enriched,
then salaries and rewards are insufficient to encourage the people.
When commands and orders are insufficient to employ subordinates,
axes and hatchets are insufficient to overawe the masses,
and salaries and rewards are insufficient to encourage the people,
in such a case, the people will have no reason to exert themselves.
When the people have no reason to exert themselves,
then battles are not won;
when battles are not won,
then defenses are not firm;
when defenses are not firm,
then enemy states will control it."
"In that case, what should the *Xiānwáng* do?"
The answer is:
"Do not allow the six to change or alter commands and orders;
do not allow the six to cause doubt or confusion regarding axes and hatchets;
do not allow the six to increase or decrease salaries and rewards.
If this is done,
then those far and near will be of one mind;
when those far and near are of one mind,
then the many and the few will work with the same strength;
when the many and the few work with the same strength,
then battles can certainly be won,
and defenses can certainly be firm.
This is not for the sake of annexing, merging, seizing, or plundering,
but for the sake of the political order of *Tiānxià*;
this is the Way to correct *Tiānxià*."
If one does not take the law as law, then affairs will have no constancy;
if the law is not lawful, then orders will not be carried out.
If orders are given but not carried out,
then the orders are not lawful;
if the law exists but is not carried out,
then those who cultivate the orders are not discerning;
if they are discerning but the orders are not carried out,
then rewards and punishments are light;
if they are heavy but not carried out,
then rewards and punishments are not trusted.
Being trusted but not acting
means one does not lead by example.
Therefore it is said:
“If prohibitions are mastered within oneself,
then orders will be carried out among the people.”
To hear of the xiánzhě but not promote them
is dangerous;
to hear of the good but not seek it out
is dangerous;
to see ability but not employ it
is dangerous;
to be close to people but not firm
is dangerous;
to join in a plan but then distance oneself
is dangerous;
to endanger people while being incapable
is dangerous;
to dismiss people and then reinstate them
is dangerous;
to see what is possible but not do it
is dangerous;
to have sufficiency but not bestow
is dangerous;
to have opportunity but not be discreet
is dangerous.
If the rénzhǔ is not circumspect and discreet,
then scholars of upright speech and straightforward conduct are in danger;
when scholars of upright speech and straightforward conduct are in danger,
the rénzhǔ becomes isolated and has no inner support;
when the rénzhǔ is isolated and has no inner support,
then the ministers form factions and groups.
To make the rénzhǔ isolated and without inner support
and for ministers to form factions and groups
is not the fault of the ministers,
but the error of the rénzhǔ.
If the people commit no heavy crimes,
it is because their errors are not great;
if the people have no great errors,
the superior should grant no pardons.
If the superior pardons small errors,
then the people will commit many heavy crimes;
this is what arises from accumulation.
Therefore it is said:
“If pardons are issued, the people will not be respectful;
if benevolence is practiced, errors will increase daily.”
When benevolence and pardons are bestowed upon the people,
even if the prisons are full
and executions are frequent,
wickedness will not be overcome.
Therefore it is said:
“Against evil, nothing is better than early prohibition.”
Generally, those who pardon
achieve small benefit but cause great harm;
thus over time they cannot overcome the resulting calamity.
Those who do not pardon
cause small harm but achieve great benefit;
thus over time they cannot overcome the resulting blessing.
Therefore, pardons
are the loosened reins of a galloping horse;
not pardoning
is the stone needle for an abscess.
Wén has three leniencies,
but Wǔ has not a single pardon.
One who is benevolent grants many pardons;
this is easy at first but difficult later,
and over time one cannot overcome its calamity;
law
is difficult at first but easy later,
and over time one cannot overcome its blessing.
Therefore, benevolence is the enemy of the people,
while law is the parent of the people.
Tàishàng establishes the systems;
the next best, when things are lost, can pursue and rectify them;
even if there are errors,
they will not be severe.
To pardon errors and neglect the good
means the people will not be encouraged.
Having errors and not pardoning them,
having good and not neglecting it;
the way to encourage the people
is applied here.
Therefore it is said:
“A míngjūn is one who is decisive in affairs.”
A ruler has three desires regarding the people;
if these three desires are not moderated,
the superior position is in danger.
What are the three desires?
The first is seeking,
the second is prohibiting,
the third is commanding.
Seeking must aim to obtain,
prohibiting must aim to stop,
commanding must aim to be carried out.
Those who seek much
obtain little;
those who prohibit much
stop little;
those who command much
have little carried out.
To seek and not obtain
means authority is daily diminished;
to prohibit and not stop
means punishments are mocked;
to command and not have it carried out
means the inferiors insult the superior.
Thus, there has never been one who could seek much and obtain much,
nor one who could prohibit much and stop much,
nor one who could command much and have it carried out much.
Therefore it is said:
“If the superior is harsh, the inferiors will not listen;
if the inferiors do not listen and are forced with punishments,
then the people will all plot against their superior.”
If one is a superior and the people plot against him,
even if he wishes not to be in danger,
it is impossible.
Once commands are issued
then to change them,
once rituals and righteousness are implemented
then to stop them,
once measures are established
then to alter them,
once laws are set
then to move them—
if it is like this,
then although rewards are heavy,
the people will not be encouraged;
although executions are frequent,
the people will not be afraid.
Therefore it is said:
“When the superior has no firm foundation,
the inferiors have doubting hearts;
the state has no constant principles,
and the strength of the people is not fully exerted;
this is the natural consequence.”
When a míngjūn is in the superior position,
the people dare not establish private opinions to value themselves;
the state has no strange severities,
no mixed customs,
no divergent rituals,
and scholars have no private opinions.
Those who are arrogant and disregard orders,
who set aside etiquette
and delineate their own systems,
and those who create private discourses
are all executed.
Thus the strong are broken,
the sharp are blunted,
and the hard are shattered.
Guiding them with the marking line,
correcting them with execution and death,
thus the hearts of the ten thousand people all submit and follow the superior;
push them and they go,
pull them and they come.
If inferiors establish private opinions to value themselves
and dissent and withdraw,
then orders will henceforth not be carried out.
Therefore it is said:
“When private opinions are established, the zhǔdào is debased;
how much more so if arrogance and disregard for orders,
setting aside etiquette and delineating private systems,
changing customs,
and wearing strange clothes or holding divergent views are still allowed to stand?”
Those who do not carry out the orders of the ruler,
who do not harmonize with their villages and neighborhoods,
who change things of their own accord
and alter the established customs of the state,
are called the bùmù zhī mín.
The bùmù zhī mín
are outside the marking line.
Those outside the marking line are executed.
Let the xiánzhě be sustained by their ability,
and the fighting men be sustained by their merit.
If the xiánzhě are sustained by their ability,
the superior is honored and the people follow;
if the fighting men are sustained by their merit,
then the soldiers treat trouble lightly and look down upon the enemy.
When the superior is honored and the people follow,
and the soldiers treat trouble lightly and look down upon the enemy,
if these two are established in the state,
then the world is governed and the ruler is at peace.
If rank is not honored
and stipends are not heavy,
one cannot plan for difficulties or face dangers with the people,
because they would consider that path as one by which they cannot seek them.
For this reason, the former kings established carriages and caps
sufficient to manifest nobility and baseness,
without seeking their beauty;
they established ranks and stipends
as a means to maintain their duties,
without seeking their appearance.
They caused the *Jūnzǐ* to be sustained by the Way,
and the *Xiǎorén* to be sustained by their labor.
When the *Jūnzǐ* are sustained by the Way,
then those above are honored and the people are submissive;
when the *Xiǎorén* are sustained by their labor,
then wealth is abundant and nourishment is sufficient.
When those above are honored and the people are submissive,
and wealth is abundant and nourishment is sufficient,
when these four things are complete in their substance,
then waiting for the right time to rule as *Wáng* will not be difficult.
A brilliant ruler establishes ancestral temples
sufficient to set out for guests and sacrifices,
without seeking their beauty;
he builds palaces, halls, terraces, and pavilions
sufficient to avoid dryness, dampness, cold, and heat,
without seeking their greatness;
he makes carvings and engravings
sufficient to distinguish nobility and baseness,
without seeking their appearance.
Therefore, the farmers do not lose their seasons,
the various craftsmen do not lose their work,
merchants do not lose their profits,
the people have no idle days,
and wealth does not stagnate.
Therefore it is said:
"Is frugality not the Way?"
If orders have not been proclaimed, yet the people happen to do something
and rewards follow them,
then the superior is giving recklessly.
When the superior gives recklessly,
then meritorious officials will be resentful;
when meritorious officials are resentful
and the ignorant people handle matters through reckless action,
and the ignorant people handle matters through lowly action,
then this is the root of great chaos.
If orders have not been proclaimed, yet punishment reaches them,
then the superior is executing recklessly.
When the superior executes recklessly, then the people think lightly of life;
when the people think lightly of life, then violent men arise,
and factions form while chaotic rebels appear.
If orders have been proclaimed, yet rewards do not follow,
then this causes the people not to be encouraged,
not to implement the systems,
and not to die for their integrity.
If the people are not encouraged,
do not implement the systems,
and do not die for their integrity, then they will not be victorious in battle and their defense will not be firm;
if they are not victorious in battle and their defense is not firm,
then the state will not be at peace.
If orders have been proclaimed, yet punishment does not reach violators,
then this is teaching the people not to listen.
If the people do not listen,
then the strong will establish themselves;
if the strong establish themselves,
then the ruler's position is endangered.
Therefore it is said:
"Constitutions, laws, and systems must model themselves on the Way;
commands and orders must be clear and bright;
rewards and punishments must be reliable and thorough;
these are the constant principles for correcting the people."
Generally, the ruler of a large state is honored,
and the ruler of a small state is humble.
Why is the ruler of a large state honored?
It is said:
"Those who can be used by him are many."
Why is the ruler of a small state humble?
It is said:
"Those who can be used by him are few."
Thus, if those who can be used are many, he is honored;
if those who can be used are few, he is humble.
How then can a ruler not wish for the people to be many and serve him?
How to make the people many and serve oneself?
It is said:
"When laws are established and orders are carried out,
then those of the people who can be used will be many;
when laws are not established
and orders are not carried out,
then those of the people who can be used will be few."
Therefore, when the things established by law
and the things carried out by order are many,
and the things discarded are few,
then the people will not slander or criticize;
when the people do not slander or criticize,
then they will listen and obey.
When the things established by law
and the things carried out by order
are equal to the things discarded,
then the state has no constant principles;
when the state has no constant principles,
then the people will act recklessly.
When the things established by law
and the things carried out by order are few,
and the things discarded are many,
then the people will not listen;
when the people do not listen,
then violent men arise and the treacherous and evil appear.
Considering the reason the superior loves the people,
it is for the sake of using them that he loves them.
If, for the sake of loving the people,
he does not hesitate to destroy the law and damage orders,
then he has lost what is called loving the people.
If one uses the people by means of love,
then it is clear that the people will not be used.
Those who are good at using the people:
they may kill them, endanger them,
exhaust them,
hunger them, and thirst them.
One who uses the people will push them to these extremes,
yet the people have no one with whom they could contemplate harming the ruler.
When a brilliant ruler is above
and the laws of the Way are carried out in the state,
the people all abandon what they like and perform what they hate.
Therefore, for one who is good at using the people,
carriages and caps are not imitated from below,
and axes and hatchets are not resorted to from above.
In this way,
the worthy are encouraged and the violent are stopped.
When the worthy are encouraged and the violent are stopped,
then merit and fame will be established thereafter.
They tread on sharp blades,
receive arrows and stones,
and enter water and fire
to obey the superior's orders.
When the superior's orders are fully carried out
and prohibitions are fully stopped,
when led and used,
the people do not dare to divert their strength;
when pushed and sent to battle,
the people do not dare to cherish their lives.
Only if they do not dare to divert their strength
will there be merit;
only if they do not dare to cherish their lives
will they be invincible.
To be invincible in advance
and have merit in retreat,
is how the masses of the three armies
can all preserve their heads and necks,
and their parents, wives, and children
can remain safe and secure within.
Therefore, the people can never be consulted at the beginning,
but they can share in the joy of success.
For this reason, the benevolent,
the wise, and those who possess the Way
do not consult with others at the beginning.
A state is never carved up or perishes because of being small or unlucky;
it must be that the ruler and high ministers have lost their virtuous conduct in their own persons,
that offices,
laws, and political education have been lost in the state,
and that the strategies regarding the *Zhūhóu* have failed externally;
thus the territory is carved up and the state is endangered.
A state never achieves merit and fame because of being large or lucky;
it must be that the ruler and high ministers have attained virtuous conduct in their own persons,
that offices,
laws, and political education have been attained in the state,
and that the strategies regarding the *Zhūhóu* have succeeded externally.
Only then is merit established and fame achieved.
That being so, how can a state be without the Way?
How can a person be without worthiness?
Attaining the Way and leading with it,
attaining the worthy and employing them,
will lead to great expectations in promoting benefits and eliminating harms.
In terms of expectations in promoting benefits and eliminating harms,
nothing is more urgent than one's own person.
But you alone are excessive. As for the harm,
one must first cause them to lose their orders.
When a ruler of men loses his orders, he is obscured;
once obscured, he is coerced;
once coerced, he is assassinated.
Generally, that by which a ruler of men is a ruler
is his power.
Therefore, if a ruler loses power,
then the ministers will control him.
If power resides below,
then the ruler is controlled by the ministers;
if power resides above,
then the ministers are controlled by the ruler.
Therefore, the swapping of positions between ruler and minister
is because power resides below.
If power stays with a minister for a full year,
even if the minister is disloyal,
the ruler cannot take it away;
if it stays with a son for a full year,
even if the son is unfilial,
the father cannot make him submit.
Thus, the records of the *Chūn Qiū*:
there are ministers who assassinate their rulers,
and sons who assassinate their fathers.
Thus it is said:
“The hall is farther than a hundred *lǐ*,
below the hall is farther than a thousand *lǐ*,
and the gates and courtyard are farther than ten thousand *lǐ*.”
Now, for one walking for a single day,
conditions over a hundred *lǐ* can be conveyed;
yet if something occurs in the hall,
and the ruler does not hear of it for ten days,
this is what is called being farther than a hundred *lǐ*;
for one walking for ten days,
conditions over a thousand *lǐ* can be conveyed;
yet if something occurs below the hall,
and the ruler does not hear of it for a month,
this is what is called being farther than a thousand *lǐ*;
for one walking for a hundred days,
conditions over ten thousand *lǐ* can be conveyed;
yet if something occurs in the gates and courtyard,
and the ruler does not hear of it for a full year,
this is what is called being farther than ten thousand *lǐ*.
Therefore, when requests enter but do not go out,
it is called extinction;
when orders go out but do not enter,
it is called severance;
when requests enter but do not reach the ruler,
it is called encroachment;
when orders go out but are stopped on the road,
it is called obstruction.
A ruler suffering from extinction, severance, encroachment, or obstruction
is not because someone blocked his gates or guarded his doors,
but because the administration is not functioning.
Thus it is said:
“Orders are weightier than treasures,
the *Shè Jì* come before relatives,
the law is weightier than the people,
and authority is more valuable than rank and emolument.”
Therefore, one does not treat commands lightly for the sake of heavy treasures,
does not put the *Shè Jì* last for the sake of relatives,
does not bend the law out of love for the people,
and does not divide authority for the sake of rank and emolument.
Thus it is said:
Power is not something to be given to others.
Governing
is rectification.
Rectification
is that which rectifies and fixes the fate of the myriad things.
For this reason, the Sage refines virtue and establishes the center to generate correctness,
and clarifies correctness to rule the state.
Thus, correctness is that which stops excess and reaches what is insufficient.
Both excess and insufficiency
are not correctness.
If things are not correct,
then the damage to the state is the same.
Bravery without righteousness
harms the military;
benevolence without correctness
harms the law.
Thus, the defeat of an army
arises from unrighteousness;
the encroachment upon the law
arises from incorrectness.
Thus, there are speeches that are eloquent but not pertinent to affairs;
there are actions that are difficult but not good.
Thus, speech must hit the mark of the affairs
and not be carelessly eloquent;
action must consider goodness
and not be carelessly difficult.
The compass and square
are the standards for circles and squares.
Even if one has skillful eyes and agile hands,
they are not as good as a clumsy compass and square in rectifying circles and squares.
Therefore, a skillful person can create a compass and square,
but cannot discard the compass and square to rectify circles and squares.
Even though a Sage can create the law,
he cannot discard the law to rule the state.
Thus, even if one has bright wisdom and high conduct,
if one rules by turning one's back on the law,
it is like discarding the compass and square to rectify circles and squares.
One version says:
Generally, the majesty of a ruler of men
is not because his virtue and conduct alone can completely surpass those of others.
He is called the ruler of men,
so people follow and honor him,
not daring to discuss whether his virtue and conduct are high or low,
because there is a reason.
Because his power over life and death
is more urgent than the *Sī Mìng*;
his making people rich or poor
causes people to care for one another;
his making people noble or base
causes people to serve one another as ministers.
The ruler of men wields these six powers to maintain his ministers;
the ministers also look toward these six to serve their ruler.
The assembly of ruler and minister
regards these six as their scheme.
If these six stay with a minister for a full year,
even if the minister is disloyal,
the ruler cannot take them away;
if they stay with a son for a full year,
even if the son is unfilial,
the father cannot take them away.
Thus, the records of the *Chūn Qiū*:
there are ministers who assassinate their rulers,
and sons who assassinate their fathers,
because they obtained these six powers
while the ruler or father was not wise.
If these six reside with the ministers,
then the ruler is obscured.
When the ruler is obscured,
he has lost his orders.
Thus it is said:
when orders enter but do not go out,
it is called obscuration;
when orders go out but do not enter,
it is called obstruction;
when orders go out but are not carried out,
it is called dragging;
when orders enter but do not reach the ruler,
it is called flaw.
A ruler suffering from dragging,
flaw,
obscuration,
or obstruction
is not because someone dared to block his gates or guard his doors,
but because his orders are not carried out in some way.
The reason why this is so
is that worthy men do not arrive and loyal ministers are not used.
Therefore, a ruler of men cannot but be careful with his orders.
Orders
are the great treasure of the ruler of men.
One version says:
When worthy men do not arrive,
it is called obscuration;
when loyal ministers are not used,
it is called blockage;
when orders are given but not carried out,
it is called barrier;
when prohibitions are made but do not stop,
it is called rebellion.
A ruler suffering from obscuration, blockage, barrier, or rebellion
is not because someone dared to block his gates or guard his doors,
but because worthy men do not arrive
and orders are not carried out.
Generally, the people follow their superiors;
they do not follow what the mouth speaks,
but follow what the heart loves.
If the superior loves bravery,
then the people will think little of death;
if the superior loves benevolence,
then the people will think little of wealth.
Therefore, whatever the superior loves,
the people will surely pursue to an extreme.
For this reason, the enlightened ruler knows that the people will inevitably take the superior's mind as their own;
therefore, he establishes laws to govern himself
and sets up standards to rectify himself.
Therefore, if those above do not act,
then the people will not follow;
if those people do not submit to the laws or respect the regulations unto death,
then the state will surely be in chaos.
For this reason, a ruler who possesses the Way
implements the laws and cultivates the regulations,
so that the people are the first to submit.
Generally, in evaluating people, there are essential points:
Of those who are boastful toward things,
there are no great scholars among them.
Those who are boastful
are full;
those who are full
are empty.
Fullness and emptiness lie in things;
being in things, they become constraints.
Those who are boastful
belong to the category of the trivial.
Generally, in evaluating people, among those who go against antiquity,
there are no lofty scholars.
Among those who do not know antiquity yet change its achievements,
there are no wise scholars.
Those whose virtuous conduct is not yet established in themselves and who distance themselves from antiquity
are lowly people.
Those who have no resources for their affairs,
yet who neglect their profession when encountering opportunity,
are foolish scholars.
Among those who fish for fame,
there are no worthy scholars;
among rulers who fish for profit,
there are no kingly lords.
When a worthy person conducts himself,
he forgets that he has fame;
when a kingly lord practices his Way,
he forgets his success.
The conduct of a worthy person
and the Way of a kingly lord
are things they cannot stop.
An enlightened ruler treats the state as public and unifies the people to be heard by the world,
and a loyal minister advances directly to discuss his ability.
An enlightened ruler does not use emoluments or ranks to favor those he loves,
and a loyal minister does not feign ability to seek ranks and emoluments.
When the ruler does not treat the state as private
and the minister does not feign ability,
for those who follow this Way,
even if there is not yet great order,
it is the constant standard for rectifying the people.
Nowadays, using ministers who feign ability
to serve a ruler who treats the state as private,
yet being able to achieve success and fame,
has never occurred from ancient times to the present.
People who feign ability are easy to recognize.
I have measured it by the former kings:
When Shùn possessed the world,
Yǔ was the Sīkōng,
Xiè was the Sītú,
Gāoyáo was the Lǐ,
and Hòujì was the Tián;
these four scholars
were the worthy people of the world,
yet they still concentrated on a single virtue
to serve their ruler.
Nowadays, those who feign ability,
in their service and official posts,
all claim to possess the abilities of these four worthies.
Looking at it from this perspective,
that success and fame are not established
is also easy to understand.
Therefore, when ranks are honorable and emoluments are heavy,
there is nothing they will not accept;
when power and profit are great and offices are high,
there is nothing they will not follow;
using this to serve a ruler,
these are what are called ministers who feign ability and usurp profit.
If the world has no ruler who treats the state as public,
then there will be no scholars who advance directly;
if there is no lord who evaluates ability,
then there will be no ministers who achieve success.
In the past, when the Sāndài transmitted power to one another,
how could they have had two worlds to treat as private?
Nothing impoverishes the people and harms wealth
more than military conflict;
nothing endangers the state and causes anxiety to the lord
more swiftly than military conflict.
These four disasters are clear,
and from ancient times to the present, no one has been able to abolish them.
If military conflict should be abolished but is not,
then it is a delusion;
if it should not be abolished
yet one desires to abolish it,
then it is also a delusion.
These two
harm the state equally.
Huángdì, Táng, and Yú
were the peak of emperors,
possessing the resources of the world,
with regulation lying in one person;
at that time,
military conflict was not abolished.
Now, when virtue does not reach that of the three emperors,
and the world is not submissive,
yet one seeks to abolish military conflict,
is that not difficult?
Therefore, that which an enlightened ruler masters
is knowing what to worry about.
That the state is well-ordered and the people devote themselves to accumulation,
this is what is called mastery.
Movement and stillness,
these are what are worried about.
For this reason, the enlightened ruler examines what he masters
in order to prepare for what he worries about.
A fierce and resolute ruler
cannot avoid external difficulties;
a cowardly and weak ruler
cannot avoid internal disorder.
A fierce and resolute ruler executes people readily;
when the practice of executing people readily flows,
those who are correct in their way are not at peace;
if those who are correct in their way are not at peace,
then ministers of talent and ability will leave and vanish.
Those wise ones will know our true and false conditions
and will plot against us for the enemy,
so external difficulties will arrive of their own accord.
Therefore it is said:
"A fierce and resolute ruler
cannot avoid external difficulties."
A cowardly and weak ruler is reluctant to execute;
the fault of being reluctant to execute
is that those who act wickedly are not reformed;
if those who act wickedly go long without reform,
then the various ministers will form cliques;
if the ministers form cliques,
then they will obscure the good and promote the bad;
if they obscure the good and promote the bad,
then internal disorder will arise of its own accord.
Therefore it is said:
"A cowardly and weak ruler
cannot avoid internal disorder."
An enlightened ruler does not endanger his altars of soil and grain for the sake of relatives,
for the altars are closer than relatives;
he does not change his orders for the sake of the ruler's desires,
for the orders are more venerable than the ruler;
he does not divide his majesty for the sake of heavy treasures,
for majesty is more precious than treasure;
he does not undermine his laws for the sake of loving the people,
for the law is more beloved than the people.
6.2 Bīngfǎ, Number Seventeen, Wàiyán Bā. One who is enlightened regarding the One is a Huáng;
one who examines the Way is a Dì;
one who is pervasive in virtue is a Wáng;
one who plans effectively and wins with the military is a Bà.
Therefore, as for the military,
although it is not the complete Way or the ultimate virtue,
nevertheless, it is that by which one assists kings and achieves hegemony.
Those of the present age who use the military are not like this;
they are ones who do not understand the weighing of military matters.
Therefore, on the day the army is raised, the interior of the borders becomes impoverished,
battles are not necessarily won,
and if won, many die;
land is gained but the state is ruined.
These four things
are the calamities of using the military.
If these four calamities affect the state,
then there is nothing that is not endangered.
The Dàdù zhī Shū says:
On the day the army is raised,
the interior of the borders is not impoverished;
when fighting, one surely wins;
when winning, people do not die;
land is gained and the state is not ruined.
How does one achieve these four things?
On the day the army is raised,
that the interior of the borders is not impoverished
is because calculations and numbers are correct.
Those who fight and are certain to win
have carefully examined laws and regulations.
Those who win and do not perish
have training and equipment that are fully prepared and sharp,
so that the enemy dares not challenge them.
Those who gain territory and whose state is not defeated
rely on their people.
By relying on their people,
then commands and systems have an effect when issued.
When training and equipment are fully prepared and sharp,
then there is discipline.
When laws and regulations are carefully examined,
then there is steadfastness.
When calculations and numbers are correct,
then there is clarity.
Governing the masses requires methods;
defeating the enemy requires principles.
By examining methods, one knows the principles;
by examining equipment, one recognizes victory;
by clarifying principles, one defeats the enemy.
Settling the ancestral shrines,
fulfilling the needs of men and women,
and dividing the officials into four sections,
then one can establish majesty and virtue;
establishing legal standards,
and issuing commands,
then one can unify the masses and govern the people.
If an army has no leader,
then it will not know the enemy early.
If the countryside has no officials,
then there will be no stored resources.
If official positions have no constancy,
then the subordinates will resent the superiors,
and equipment will not be effective.
If the court has no administration
and rewards and punishments are not clear,
then the people will treat their property lightly.
Therefore it is said:
knowing the enemy early
allows for independent action;
having stored resources
allows for long endurance without depletion;
having skillful equipment
allows for attacking without waste;
having clear rewards and punishments
encourages brave warriors.
If the Sān Guān do not err,
the Wǔ Jiào are not in chaos,
and the Jiǔ Zhāng are clearly displayed,
then even in extreme danger there is no harm,
and in extreme straits there are no difficulties.
Thus, one can reach far distances using methods
and unleash strength using control.
The Sān Guān:
the first is called the Gǔ,
the Gǔ is used for assigning tasks,
for starting movement,
and for advancing;
the second is called the Jīn,
the Jīn is used for halting,
for retreating,
and for dismissal;
the third is called the Qí,
the Qí is used for positioning troops,
for controlling troops,
and for resting troops.
These are what are called the Sān Guān.
With these three commands, the art of war is governed.
The Wǔ Jiào:
first, teach their eyes with flags of different forms and colors;
second, teach their ears with the signals of commands;
third, teach their feet with the measures of advancing and retreating;
fourth, teach their hands with the utility of long and short weapons;
fifth, teach their hearts with the sincerity of rewards and punishments.
When the Wǔ Jiào are each practiced,
then the soldiers will rely on their bravery.
The Jiǔ Zhāng:
first, raising the Rì Zhāng
means day travel;
second, raising the Yuè Zhāng
means night travel;
third, raising the Lóng Zhāng
means traveling by water;
fourth, raising the Hǔ Zhāng
means traveling through forests;
fifth, raising the Wū Zhāng
means traveling on slopes;
sixth, raising the Shé Zhāng
means traveling through marshes;
seventh, raising the Què Zhāng
means traveling on plains;
eighth, raising the Láng Zhāng
means traveling through mountains;
ninth, raising the Gāo Zhāng
means carrying food and hitching up the chariots.
When the Jiǔ Zhāng are established,
then movement and stillness will not err.
The Sān Guān,
Wǔ Jiào, and Jiǔ Zhāng
begin from no origin
and end in no limit.
Beginning from no origin
is the Dào;
ending in no limit
is Dé.
The Dào cannot be measured,
and Dé cannot be counted.
Because it cannot be measured,
the strong masses cannot plot against it;
because it cannot be counted,
the deceitful dare not approach it.
When both are applied,
movement and stillness will be successful.
Passing through where they are unknown,
emerging where they are unexpected.
Because they pass where unknown,
none can resist them;
because they emerge where unexpected,
none can respond to them.
Thus they achieve total victory without harm.
Teach according to convenience,
and act based on advantage.
Teaching has no constant form,
and action has no constant form.
When both are applied,
action will be successful.
When equipment is ready and teaching applied,
pursuing the fleeing is like a gusting wind,
and striking and stabbing are like thunder and lightning.
Isolated territory cannot be held against them,
and fortifications cannot withstand them.
Occupying the center without rivals,
commands are executed without delay.
When equipment is ready and teaching applied,
scattering them is without fixed direction,
and gathering them is beyond counting.
When training and equipment are fully prepared and sharp,
advancing and retreating are like thunder and lightning,
without doubt or depletion.
When the spirit is singular and focused,
then one communicates everywhere without doubt;
by sharpening the soldiers and refining equipment,
one crosses difficulties without depletion.
Advancing without doubt
and retreating without depletion,
the enemy is then made use of.
Ascending mountains and pits
without waiting for hooks or ladders;
crossing rivers and valleys
without needing boats or oars.
Passing through isolated terrain,
attacking fortified positions,
going out and coming in alone,
and none can stop them.
In reality, they do not enter alone,
yet none can stop them;
in reality, they do not go out alone,
so none can restrain them.
The ultimate namelessness is complete;
being complete and unexpected,
even the spirits cannot doubt it.
Nurturing them with the Dào,
then the people are harmonious;
sustaining them with Dé,
then the people are unified.
Harmony and unity bring accord;
accord brings cohesion.
With complete harmony and cohesion,
nothing can harm them.
Establish the One Utmost,
practice the Two Essentials,
unleash the Three Powers,
apply the Wǔ Jiào,
activate the Four Mechanisms,
set the Six Actions,
discuss the Seven Calculations,
and maintain the Eight Responses.
Carefully examine the Nine Chapters;
each chapter has ten designations.
Thus one can achieve complete victory and great victory.
There is nothing that cannot be defended,
so one can maintain victory through defense.
Frequent battles exhaust the soldiers;
frequent victories make the ruler arrogant.
If an arrogant ruler employs exhausted people,
how can the state not be in danger?
Therefore, the highest excellence is not to fight;
the next best is to unify them.
Breaking the great and defeating the strong
is the pinnacle of unification.
Disrupting them without using variations,
taking advantage of them without using deceit,
defeating them without using trickery,
is the reality of unification.
When near, use substance;
when far, issue commands.
Power that cannot be measured,
strength that cannot be estimated,
spirit that cannot be exhausted,
virtue that cannot be fathomed,
is the source of unification.
The many are like timely rain;
the few are like a whirlwind;
this is the end of unification.
Fabricating equipment appropriately
is the height of weaponry;
using it appropriately
is the perfection of training.
Those who cannot perfect weaponry
cannot utilize suitability;
those who cannot perfect training
cannot use suitability.
Those who cannot employ the enemy are exhausted;
those who cannot perfect weaponry are distressed.
By moving the army swiftly,
one can surely win.
Entering and exiting by different routes
will harm the enemy.
Deeply penetrating into dangerous territory
will cause soldiers to discipline themselves;
when soldiers discipline themselves,
they will be of one heart and one strength.
When a master of warfare leads,
he makes the enemy feel as if occupying a void
or striking a shadow.
Establishing nothing and having no form,
there is nothing that cannot be accomplished;
having no form and taking no action,
there is nothing that cannot be transformed.
This is what is called the Way.
As if lost yet existing,
as if behind yet in front,
power is insufficient to name it.
Qí Xī Gōng produced Prince Zhū Ér,
Prince Jiǔ,
and Prince Xiǎo Bái.
He ordered Bào Shū to be the tutor for Xiǎo Bái.
Bào Shū declined,
claiming illness and not coming out.
Guǎn Zhòng and Zhào Hū went to see him and said,
“For what reason do you not come out?”
Bào Shū said,
“The ancients had a saying:
‘No one knows a son better than his father;
no one knows a minister better than his ruler.’
Now the ruler knows I am unworthy,
and so he has ordered this humble servant to tutor Xiǎo Bái.
This humble servant knows he has been cast aside.”
Zhào Hū said,
“You should firmly decline and not come out.
I will take responsibility for your risks, even unto death,
and will surely see you exempted.”
Bào Shū said,
“If you do this,
what exemption would there be?”
Guǎn Zhòng said,
“This will not do.
Those who uphold the altars of state and the ancestral temple
do not decline duties
or seek expanded leisure.
Who will possess the state
is not yet known.
You should come out.”
Zhào Hū said,
“This will not do.
The three of us in the state of Qí
are like the legs of a tripod;
if one is removed,
it surely will not stand.
I observe that Xiǎo Bái
will surely not be the successor.”
Guǎn Zhòng said,
“That is not so.
The people of the state detest the mother of Jiǔ
and by extension Jiǔ himself,
while they pity Xiǎo Bái for having no mother.
Zhū Ér is the eldest but of lowly status;
the matter is not yet certain.
The one who will stabilize the state of Qí,
if it is not one of these two princes,
there will be no end to the trouble.
Xiǎo Bái’s character
is without petty cleverness; he is cautious
and possesses great foresight.
None but Yí Wú can tolerate Xiǎo Bái.
If Heaven unfortunately brings disaster and calamity upon Qí,
even if Jiǔ should be established,
affairs will not be successful.
If you do not stabilize the state,
who else will it be?”
Zhào Hū said,
“After a hundred years,
when our ruler departs this world,
if anyone violates our ruler’s command
and deposes the one I have established,
taking my Jiǔ away,
even if I were given the whole world, I would not live.
You and I share the administration of the state of Qí;
to receive the ruler’s command and not change it,
to support the one established even if not successful,
this is my duty.”
Guǎn Zhòng said,
“As for Yí Wú’s conduct as a minister,
I will carry out the ruler’s commands,
support the altars of state,
and maintain the ancestral temple;
how could I die for the sake of one Prince Jiǔ?
That for which Yí Wú would die
is the ruin of the state,
the destruction of the ancestral temple,
and the termination of sacrifices;
only then would Yí Wú die for it.
If it is not these three things,
then Yí Wú will live.
If Yí Wú lives,
then the state of Qí will benefit;
if Yí Wú dies,
then the state of Qí will not benefit.”
Bào Shū said,
“If that is so, then what should be done?”
Guǎn Zǐ said,
“It is best for you to come out and follow the command.”
Bào Shū agreed,
so he came out to follow the command,
and thus became the tutor for Xiǎo Bái.
Bào Shū said to Guǎn Zhòng,
“How shall we act?”
Guǎn Zhòng said,
“As a minister,
if one does not exert all effort for the ruler,
one will not be trusted;
if one is not trusted,
one’s words will not be heard;
if one’s words are not heard,
the state will not be stabilized.
He who serves a ruler should have no divided heart.”
Bào Shū agreed.
The younger brother of Xī Gōng by the same mother, Yí Zhòng Nián,
produced Gōng Sūn Wú Zhī,
who was favored by Xī Gōng;
his clothing and ritual status were like those of a legitimate heir.
When Xī Gōng died,
because Zhū Ér was the eldest, he became the ruler;
this was Xiāng Gōng.
After Xiāng Gōng was established,
he demoted Wú Zhī.
Wú Zhī was angry.
The Duke ordered Lián Chēng and Guǎn Zhìfù to garrison Kuíqiū,
saying:
"Depart when the melons are in season,
and return when the melons are in season again."
When the term of the garrison ended,
no message arrived from the Duke.
They requested to be replaced, but he would not permit it.
Therefore, the two men relied on Gōngsūn Wúzhī to stage a rebellion.
Lady Wénjiāng, the wife of Lǔ Huán Gōng,
was a woman of Qí.
When the Duke was about to go to Qí,
he traveled together with his wife.
Shēn Yú remonstrated, saying:
"This is not permissible.
A woman has her husband's family,
and a man has his wife's household;
they must not defile one another.
This is what is called having propriety."
The Duke did not listen,
and subsequently met with the Qí Hóu at Luò together with Wénjiāng.
Wénjiāng had an illicit affair with the Qí Hóu.
Lǔ Huán Gōng heard of it
and rebuked Wénjiāng.
Wénjiāng told the Qí Hóu.
The Qí Hóu was angry.
He feasted the Duke,
and ordered Gōngzǐ Péngshēng to assist the Lǔ Hóu into his carriage
and crush his ribs.
The Duke died in the carriage.
Shù Màn said:
"A worthy man dies for loyalty to resolve doubts,
and the common people rely on him;
a wise man investigates principles and thinks long-term,
and so his person escapes harm.
Now Péngshēng was double-minded toward the ruler;
he did not speak frankly
but acted with flattery to delude our ruler,
causing our ruler to lose the propriety due to relatives. Now
he has furthermore exerted himself to complete our ruler's calamity,
thereby inciting resentment between the two states.
Can Péngshēng possibly escape punishment?
The logic of calamity is attached to him.
The ruler followed through with calamity because of anger,
not fearing the hatred of relatives, and giving way
to the arising of confusion; he felt no shame.
How could it have reached Péngshēng and he be able to stop it?
If Lǔ seeks an execution,
they will surely use Péngshēng as the explanation."
In the second month,
the people of Lǔ told Qí, saying:
"Our late ruler stood in awe of your majesty's power
and did not dare to dwell at ease,
so he came to renew our old friendship.
The ritual was completed but he did not return.
Having nowhere to place the blame,
we request that Péngshēng be used to remove it."
The people of Qí killed Péngshēng for them
in order to apologize to Lǔ.
In the fifth month,
Duke Xiāng hunted at Bèiqiū
and saw a boar.
An attendant said:
"It is Gōngzǐ Péngshēng!"
The Duke said angrily:
"How does Gōngzǐ Péngshēng dare to appear!"
He shot at it;
the boar stood up like a human and cried out.
The Duke was terrified
and fell from his carriage,
injuring his foot and losing his sandal.
Upon returning,
he demanded the sandal from the attendant Fèi.
It could not be found,
so he whipped him until blood appeared.
Fèi ran out
and met the rebels at the gate.
They threatened and bound him.
Fèi bared and showed them his back.
The rebels believed him
and sent Fèi in first.
He hid the Duke and came back out, fighting
until he died in the doorway.
Shí Zhīfēnrú died at the foot of the throne.
Mèng Yáng took the ruler's place and lay on the bed.
The rebels killed him,
saying:
"This is not the ruler;
he does not resemble him."
They saw the Duke's feet beneath the door,
subsequently killed the Duke
and established Gōngsūn Wúzhī.
Bào Shūyá escorted Gōngzǐ Xiǎobái as he fled to Jǔ.
Guǎn Yíwú and Zhào Hū escorted Gōngzǐ Jiū as he fled to Lǔ.
In the ninth year,
Gōngsūn Wúzhī acted tyrannically toward Yōng Lǐn,
and Yōng Lǐn killed Wúzhī.
Duke Huán entered first from Jǔ.
The people of Lǔ attacked Qí
to install Gōngzǐ Jiū.
They fought at Gānshí;
Guǎn Zhòng shot at Duke Huán
and hit his belt buckle.
The Lǔ army was utterly defeated,
and Duke Huán ascended the throne.
Thereupon he pressured Lǔ,
forcing Lǔ to kill Gōngzǐ Jiū.
Duke Huán asked Bào Shū, saying:
"How shall I stabilize the state?"
Bào Shū said:
"If you obtain Guǎn Zhòng and Zhào Hū,
then the state will be stabilized."
The Duke said:
"Yíwú and Zhào Hū
are my enemies."
Bào Shū then informed the Duke of their former plans.
The Duke said:
"In that case, can they be obtained?"
Bào Shū said:
"If you summon them quickly,
then they can be obtained.
If not quickly,
they cannot be obtained.
Now Shī Bó of Lǔ knows that Yíwú is a man of great wisdom.
His plan will surely be to have Lǔ entrust the government to Yíwú.
If Yíwú accepts it,
then they will know they can weaken Qí.
If Yíwú does not accept,
they will know he intends to return to Qí
and they will surely kill him."
The Duke said:
"Then will Yíwú accept the government of Lǔ?
Or will he not?"
Bào Shū replied:
"He will not accept.
That Yíwú did not die with Jiū
was because he wished to stabilize the state of Qí.
If he were now to accept the government of Lǔ,
that would be to weaken Qí.
In Yíwú’s service to a ruler, he has no double-mindedness.
Even if he knows he will die,
he will surely not accept."
The Duke said:
"As for his attitude toward me,
could it really be like this?"
Bào Shū replied:
"It is not for your sake;
it is for the sake of the late rulers.
His relationship with you was not as close as it was with Jiū,
yet he did not die for Jiū;
how much less then would he for you?
If you wish to stabilize the state of Qí,
then quickly welcome him back."
The Duke said:
"I fear I will not be in time.
What should be done?"
Bào Shū said:
"As for Shī Bó's character,
he is clever but very cautious.
If your request arrives first,
he will fear drawing your resentment upon himself
and will surely not kill him."
The Duke said:
"Very well."
Shī Bó went forward and spoke to the ruler of Lǔ:
"Guǎn Zhòng has wisdom,
but his undertaking was not successful.
Now that he is in Lǔ,
you should entrust the government of Lǔ to him.
If he accepts it,
then Qí can be weakened.
If he does not accept,
then kill him.
Kill him
to please Qí
and share their anger;
this would still be better than letting the matter end without action."
The Lord said: "Agreed."
Before Lǔ could hand over the administration,
an envoy from Qí arrived,
saying:
"Yí Wú and Shào Hū
are my enemies.
Now they are in Lǔ,
and I wish to capture them alive.
If I do not get them,
then you, Lord, are siding with my enemies."
The Lord of Lǔ asked Shī Bó,
and Shī Bó said:
"You should give them to him.
I have heard that the Lord of Qí is cautious but prone to arrogance;
even if he gets worthy men,
how can he be sure to employ them?
By the time the Lord of Qí is able to employ them,
the work of Guǎn Zǐ will be accomplished.
Indeed, Guǎn Zhòng is a great sage of the world.
Now if he returns to Qí,
the whole world will turn toward him;
how could it be only Lǔ!
If we kill him now,
since he is a friend of Bào Shū,
Bào Shū would use this to cause trouble;
you, Lord, will certainly not be able to withstand it.
It is better to give them to him."
The Lord of Lǔ then bound Guǎn Zhòng and Shào Hū.
Guǎn Zhòng said to Shào Hū:
"Are you afraid?"
Shào Hū said:
"What is there to fear?
I did not die early
because I was waiting for things to be settled.
Now that the order is settled,
if you are ordered to assist the left side of Qí,
I, Hū, will surely be ordered to assist the right side of Qí.
However,
to kill my lord and then employ my person
would be a double disgrace to me.
You shall be the minister who lives,
while I, Hū, shall be the minister who dies.
I, Hū, know that I shall die after the administration of a state of ten thousand chariots is obtained;
Gōngzǐ Jiǔ can be said to have a minister who dies for him.
You shall live and make the feudal lords hegemon;
Gōngzǐ Jiǔ can be said to have a minister who lives for him.
The one who dies fulfills his conduct,
and the one who lives fulfills his name.
Name and conduct do not stand together;
conduct does not arrive in vain.
May you exert yourself;
there is a distinction between death and life."
They then set out, and upon entering the border of Qí,
he cut his own throat and died.
Guǎn Zhòng then entered.
When the superior man heard of this, he said:
"Shào Hū's death
was more worthy than his living;
Guǎn Zhòng's living
was more worthy than his dying."
Someone said:
The following year,
Xiāng Gōng pursued Xiǎo Bái,
and Xiǎo Bái fled to Jǔ.
In the twelfth year,
Xiāng Gōng passed away,
and Gōngzǐ Jiǔ ascended the throne.
The people of the state summoned Xiǎo Bái.
Bào Shū said:
"Why not go?"
Xiǎo Bái said:
"It is not possible.
Guǎn Zhòng is wise,
and Shào Hū is strong and brave.
Although the people of the state summon me,
I still cannot enter."
Bào Shū said:
"If Guǎn Zhòng is able to exercise his wisdom in the state,
can the state be called chaotic?
Shào Hū is strong and brave,
but how can he plot against us alone?"
Xiǎo Bái said:
"Even if he cannot exercise his wisdom,
how can it be that he is not there?
Even if Shào Hū does not have the masses,
are his associates not enough to plot against me?"
Bào Shū replied:
"When a state is in chaos,
wise men cannot manage internal affairs,
and friends cannot unite and cooperate,
and only then can the state be plotted for."
He then ordered the carriage to be prepared;
Bào Shū drove, Xiǎo Bái rode, and they set out from Jǔ.
Xiǎo Bái said:
"Those two men
follow the lord's commands;
I cannot take a risk."
He was about to step down.
Bào Shū stepped on his foot and said:
"The success of the matter
is at this very moment.
If the matter does not succeed,
this old servant will die for it,
and the Prince will still
escape."
They then proceeded.
Arriving at the outskirts of the capital,
Bào Shū ordered twenty chariots to go ahead
and ten chariots to follow behind.
Bào Shū then told Xiǎo Bái:
"As for the state's doubt,
among these few gentlemen, none can withstand this old servant.
