Since the matter has not yet succeeded,
I, this old servant, shall block the way."
Bào Shū then swore an oath, saying:
"If the matter succeeds,
follow my orders;
if the matter does not succeed,
those who save the Prince shall be of the highest merit,
those who die shall be lower;
I will use the strength of five chariots to block the road."
Bào Shū then acted as the vanguard,
and finally entered the capital,
driving out Gōngzǐ Jiǔ.
Guǎn Zhòng shot an arrow at Xiǎo Bái
and hit his belt buckle.
Guǎn Zhòng, together with Gōngzǐ Jiǔ and Shào Hū, then fled to Lǔ.
Huán Gōng ascended the throne.
Lǔ attacked Qí,
attempting to install Gōngzǐ Jiǔ but failing.
In the first year of Huán Gōng,
he summoned Guǎn Zhòng.
Guǎn Zhòng arrived,
and the Lord asked:
"Can the state be stabilized?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"If the Lord becomes a hegemon,
the state will be stable;
if the Lord does not become a hegemon,
the state will not be stable."
The Lord said:
"I do not dare to aim for something so great;
I only wish to stabilize the state."
Guǎn Zhòng requested again,
but the Lord said:
"I cannot."
Guǎn Zhòng took his leave of the Lord, saying:
"The Lord has spared me from death,
which is my good fortune.
However, the reason I did not die for Jiǔ
was because I wished to stabilize the state.
If the state is not stabilized,
and I receive the emoluments of the administration of Qí
while having not died for Jiǔ,
I do not dare to accept it."
He then walked out,
and reaching the gate,
the Lord summoned Guǎn Zhòng back.
Guǎn Zhòng returned;
the Lord, breaking into a sweat, said:
"Do not stop;
let us strive for hegemony!"
Guǎn Zhòng bowed twice, touching his head to the ground, and then rose, saying:
"Today the Lord establishes hegemony,
and I, in my greed, accept your command
to hasten to take my place in the position of Prime Minister."
He then ordered the five officials to carry out their duties.
Another day,
the Lord said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"I wish for there to be no conflict among the feudal lords,
and so I shall slightly repair our weapons and armor."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It is not possible.
The common people are suffering;
My Lord should first favor the common people
rather than storing up weapons.
Rather than being generous toward the military,
it is better to be generous toward the people.
The state altars of Qí are not yet stable.
You, My Lord, have not yet begun with the people
but have begun with the military;
abroad, you are not close to the feudal lords,
and internally, you are not close to the people."
The Duke said:
"Very well."
But the policies were not yet put into practice.
In the second year,
Huán Gōng was increasingly troubled by disorder,
and he again told Guǎn Zhòng:
"I wish to repair the weapons."
Guǎn Zhòng again said:
"It is not possible."
The Duke did not listen
and indeed prepared the weapons.
Huán Gōng was drinking on a boat with the Lady of Sòng;
the lady rocked the boat and frightened the Duke.
The Duke was enraged
and sent her away;
Sòng received her and married her to the Cài Hóu.
The following year,
the Duke was enraged
and told Guǎn Zhòng:
"I wish to attack Sòng."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It is not possible;
I have heard that if internal affairs are not cultivated,
external ventures will not succeed."
The Duke did not listen
and indeed attacked Sòng.
The feudal lords raised troops to rescue Sòng
and greatly defeated the Qí army.
The Duke was enraged;
upon returning, he told Guǎn Zhòng:
"I request to repair the weapons and armor.
My soldiers are not trained,
and my weaponry is not substantial;
therefore, the feudal lords dared to rescue my enemy.
Let us repair the weapons and armor internally!"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It is not possible;
the state of Qí is in danger.
Internally, you seize the resources used by the people;
if the soldiers are encouraged only by bravery,
it is the root of disorder.
Externally, you offend the feudal lords,
and the people have much resentment.
Men of righteousness
will not enter the state of Qí;
how can it be without danger?"
Bào Shū said:
"My Lord must use the words of Yí Wú."
The Duke did not listen
and ordered the repair of weapons within the four borders.
He increased the levies on the passes and markets,
and the Duke then proceeded to use bravery as the basis for granting emoluments.
Bào Shū said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"In the past,
the Duke promised you hegemony,
but now the state is increasingly in disorder;
what will you do?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Our ruler is apprehensive;
his wisdom will receive much instruction.
For the time being, let us wait a little for him to realize it himself."
Bào Shū said:
"By the time he realizes it himself,
will the state not be lost or destroyed?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Not yet.
Regarding the governance within the state,
I, Yí Wú, am still subtly managing it;
as for the disorder, we can still wait.
Among the advisors of the external feudal lords, since there are none
like the two of us,
none will dare to offend us."
The following year,
those in court quarreled over emoluments and stabbed each other;
those who tore their clothes and cut their own throats were incessant.
Bào Shū said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"The deaths in the state are many;
will this not be harmful?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"How could it be otherwise?
These are all greedy people.
What I, Yí Wú, worry about
is that among the feudal lords, those who are righteous are unwilling to enter Qí,
and among the people of Qí, those who are righteous are unwilling to serve.
This is what I, Yí Wú, worry about. As for those who die,
why should I care for them?"
The Duke again internally repaired the weapons.
In the third year,
Huán Gōng was about to attack Lǔ,
saying:
"Lǔ is near to us,
and yet their rescue of Sòng was swift;
I shall punish them."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It is not possible.
I have heard that for a ruler who possesses land,
if he does not toil with the military,
is not resentful of disgrace,
and does not reinforce his errors,
then the state altars will be secure.
If he toils with the military,
is resentful of disgrace,
and reinforces his errors,
then the state altars will be in danger."
The Duke did not listen,
raised an army to attack Lǔ,
and arrived at Zhāngsháo.
Lǔ Zhuāng Gōng raised an army to meet him
and greatly defeated him.
Huán Gōng said:
"My weapons are still too few;
if I surround them from three sides,
how can they resist me?"
In the fourth year,
he repaired the weapons;
with one hundred thousand armored troops
and five thousand chariots,
he said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"My soldiers are now trained
and my weapons are now many;
I wish to make Lǔ submit."
Guǎn Zhòng sighed deeply and said:
"The state of Qí is in danger!
You, My Lord, do not compete in virtue but compete in weapons.
Among the states of the world,
those with one hundred thousand armored troops are not few.
If we wish to use a small force to make a large force submit,
internally we lose our masses,
the feudal lords set up defenses,
and our people set up deceptions.
If the state wishes to be without danger,
how can that be possible?"
The Duke did not listen
and indeed attacked Lǔ.
Lǔ did not dare to fight
and withdrew fifty lǐ from the capital to establish a pass.
Lǔ requested to be aligned within the pass
to follow Qí,
provided that Qí would no longer invade Lǔ.
Huán Gōng agreed.
The people of Lǔ requested a covenant, saying:
"Lǔ
is a small state;
originally we did not carry swords.
Now that we carry swords,
it is because the news of clashing weapons has reached the feudal lords.
It would be better for you, My Lord, to stop.
Please put away the weapons."
Huán Gōng said:
"Very well."
He then ordered his followers not to carry weapons.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It is not possible.
The feudal lords have become more wary of you;
if you, My Lord, withdraw like this, it would be acceptable.
But if you truly weaken the ruler of Lǔ,
the feudal lords will also become more greedy toward you.
If there are matters in the future,
small states will become firmer
and large states will set up defenses.
This is not to the advantage of the state of Qí."
Huán Gōng did not listen.
Guǎn Zhòng again remonstrated, saying:
“Your Lordship must not go. Why would Lǔ
not use its troops?
Cáo Guì’s character
is firm, strong, and resentful;
he cannot be dealt with through a covenant.”
Huán Gōng did not listen
and ultimately met with him.
Zhuāng Gōng personally concealed a sword in his robes,
and Cáo Guì also concealed a sword.
As they ascended the altar,
Zhuāng Gōng drew the sword from his robes and said:
“The borders of Lǔ are only fifty li from the capital;
there is nothing left for us but to die.”
Cáo Guì seized Huán Gōng with his left hand
while supporting himself with his right,
saying:
“Since death is the same in any case,
I shall die having been executed before my lord.”
Guǎn Zhòng ran toward his lord,
but Cáo Guì drew his sword and stood between the two flights of stairs, saying:
“The two lords are about to change their plans;
let no one advance!”
Guǎn Zhòng said:
“My lord will grant the land,
using the Wèn River as the border.”
Huán Gōng agreed
and returned after establishing the Wèn River as the border.
After Huán Gōng returned, he refined the administration
and did not focus on military armaments.
He confined himself and avoided people;
because of his error, he halted the army.
In the fifth year,
Sòng attacked Qǐ.
Huán Gōng said to Guǎn Zhòng and Bǎo Shū:
“As for Sòng,
I have long wanted to attack them,
but what about the other feudal lords?
As for Qǐ,
they are the descendants of the enlightened kings.
Now that Sòng is attacking them,
I wish to save them;
is that possible?”
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
“It is not possible.
I have heard that if internal administration is not refined,
external righteous actions will not be trusted.
If Your Lordship wishes to perform righteous deeds externally
and precedes them with your own conduct,
then the feudal lords can be made to submit.”
Huán Gōng said:
“If I do not save them now,
later I will have no grounds to attack Sòng.”
Guǎn Zhòng said:
“The rulers of the feudal states
are not greedy for land.
Being greedy for land
inevitably leads to exhausting the military;
exhausting the military
inevitably burdens the people;
and when the people are burdened, they become deceitful.
Those who act after their deceit is well-concealed will win,
but being deceitful leads to a lack of trust among the people.
A lack of trust among the people leads to chaos;
internal instability endangers one's own person.
Therefore, those of old who heard the Way of the Former Kings
did not compete in military force.”
Huán Gōng said:
“Then what should be done?”
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
“In my opinion, do not attack,
but send someone with heavy gifts.
If sending an envoy does not work,
Your Lordship should receive them and enfeoff them.”
Huán Gōng asked Bǎo Shū:
“What do you think?”
Bǎo Shū said:
“Your Highness should follow Yí Wú’s words.”
The Duke then ordered Cáo Sūn Sù to go as an envoy to Sòng.
Sòng did not listen
and ultimately attacked Qǐ.
Huán Gōng built Yuán Líng to enfeoff them,
giving them one hundred chariots
and one thousand suits of armor.
The next year,
the Dí people attacked Xíng.
The ruler of Xíng fled
and arrived in Qí.
Huán Gōng built Yí Yí to enfeoff him,
giving one hundred chariots
and one thousand soldiers.
The next year,
the Dí people attacked Wèi. The ruler of Wèi fled and arrived
at Xū.
Huán Gōng was about to enfeoff him.
Xí Péng and Bīn Xū Wú remonstrated, saying:
“This is not possible.
The reason these three states perished was that they were small.
Now if Your Lordship insists on enfeoffing perished states,
what will happen when the land is exhausted?”
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zhòng:
“What do you think?”
Guǎn Zhòng said:
“Your Lordship has the reputation for these deeds;
how can you not provide the reality?
Your Lordship should carry it out.”
The Duke also asked Bǎo Shū.
Bǎo Shū said:
“Your Highness should follow Yí Wú’s words.”
Huán Gōng built Chǔ Qiū to enfeoff them,
giving five hundred chariots
and five thousand suits of armor.
Having enfeoffed Wèi,
the next year, Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zhòng what should be done next.
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
“If Your Highness refines the administration internally and encourages the people,
you can be trusted by the feudal lords.”
The Lord agreed.
He then lightened taxes,
relaxed the levies on passes and markets,
and established a system for taxes and salaries.
Once this was done,
Guǎn Zhòng again requested:
“Inquire after the sick.
I wish for rewards without punishments;
in five years,
the feudal lords can be made to submit.”
The Duke said:
“Agreed.”
After carrying this out,
Guǎn Zhòng again requested:
“As for the rituals of the feudal lords,
let Qí go with leopard skins
and the smaller lords respond with deer skins;
let Qí go with horses
and the smaller lords respond with dogs.”
Huán Gōng agreed and carried it out.
Guǎn Zhòng again requested to grant rewards within the state and to the feudal lords.
The Lord said:
“Agreed.”
He carried it out.
Guǎn Zhòng distributed rewards within the state,
and the Lord distributed rewards among the feudal lords.
If the rulers of the feudal lords had performed good deeds,
he would congratulate them with heavy gifts.
For those from the rank of scholar downward who had done good,
he would congratulate them with clothing.
Whenever a minister of a feudal lord
remonstrated with his ruler effectively,
he would send a seal to inquire after him
to validate his words.
Once the Duke had carried this out,
he again asked Guǎn Zhòng:
“What should be done now?”
Guǎn Zhòng said:
“Xí Péng is intelligent and quick-witted;
he can be put in charge of the eastern states.
Bīn Xū Wú is firm, strong, and virtuous;
he can be put in charge of the western lands.
The customs of the state of Wèi
are precarious yet focused on profit.
Gōngzǐ Kāifāng's character
is clever and quick,
but he cannot endure long and only enjoys the beginning;
he can be sent to travel in Wèi.
The customs of the settlements of Lǔ
favor intimacy and are instructed in ritual.
Jì Yǒu's character
is respectful and refined,
broad in ritual,
and possesses much minor trustworthiness;
he can be sent to travel in Lǔ.
The customs of the state of Chǔ
are cleverly ornate yet focused on profit;
they do not like to establish great righteousness,
but like to establish minor trustworthiness.”
Měng Sūn is extensive in teaching,
and Wén is clever in rhetoric;
they do not like to establish grand principles
but prefer to build small trusts;
they may travel to Chǔ.
When the small lords have submitted
and the great lords have become attached,
only when it is thus
can administration begin to be implemented."
The Ruler said:
"Agreed."
He then sent Gōngzǐ Kāifāng to Wèi,
Jì Yǒu to Lǔ,
and Měng Sūn to Chǔ.
After five years, the feudal lords became attached.
When the Dí people attacked,
Huán Gōng announced to the feudal lords:
"I request to rescue those attacked."
The feudal lords agreed:
the great lords provided two hundred chariots
and two thousand troops;
the small lords provided one hundred chariots
and one thousand troops.
The feudal lords all agreed.
Qí sent a thousand chariots,
and the troops reached Yuánlíng,
fighting from the rear.
Thus they defeated the Dí.
As for their chariots, armor, and goods,
the small lords received them.
As for the great lords nearby,
they were given portions from the counties,
without their own states being trampled.
When the lords of the northern region did not come,
Huán Gōng met the lords of the southern region at Zhàolíng
and said:
"The Dí have been unprincipled,
violating the Tiānzǐ's orders
to attack small states.
For the sake of the Tiānzǐ,
and respecting Heaven's command, I ordered
a rescue for the attacked.
The lords of the northern region did not arrive;
above, they do not listen to the Tiānzǐ's orders,
and below, they are disrespectful to the feudal lords.
I request
to punish the lords of the northern region."
The feudal lords agreed.
Huán Gōng then went north to attack Lìngzhī,
descended from Mount Fú,
cut down Gūzhú,
and encountered and blocked the Shānróng.
He looked back and asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What shall we do next?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"You should teach the feudal lords to gather food for the people.
If the feudal lords' troops are insufficient,
you should help them mobilize.
Only after this
can administration begin to be expanded."
Huán Gōng then told the feudal lords
that they must have food sufficient for three years
and then use the remainder to repair their weaponry.
If weaponry is insufficient,
they should report the matter to Qí,
and Qí would help them mobilize.
After this was implemented,
the Duke again asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What should be done?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"When you have unified their rulers and ministers, fathers and sons,
then you can expand administration."
The Duke said:
"What is the way to unify them?"
He said:
"The feudal lords shall not arbitrarily elevate concubines to be wives,
nor shall they arbitrarily execute high ministers;
for those with national merit,
they shall not arbitrarily grant stipends.
Officers and commoners shall not arbitrarily discard their wives;
they shall not divert dikes,
nor hoard grain,
nor prohibit the use of materials.
If this is practiced for a full year,
only then can punishments begin."
The Ruler then proclaimed this to the feudal lords,
and the feudal lords agreed,
receiving and implementing it.
After a full year,
the people of Wú attacked Gǔ.
Before Huán Gōng had finished notifying all the feudal lords,
the armies of the feudal lords all arrived
to await Huán Gōng.
Huán Gōng with a thousand chariots met the feudal lords at the border;
before the capital army arrived,
the Wú people fled.
The feudal lords all dispersed.
Huán Gōng returned
and asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What shall we do next?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"You can now expand administration."
He said:
"From now on for two years,
if a legitimate son is not heard to be filial,
is not heard to love his younger brother,
or is not heard to respect the elders and the state's virtuous men—
if he lacks even one of these three,
he may be executed.
If the ministers of the feudal lords and those in state affairs
are not heard to do good for three years,
they may be punished.
If the ruler has faults
and the grandees do not remonstrate,
or if officers and commoners have merit
and the grandees do not promote them,
they may be punished.
If officers and commoners are heard by the officials to be worthy, filial, or brotherly,
they may be rewarded."
Huán Gōng received and implemented this.
None of the nearby lords failed to request instructions.
There were six assemblies with war chariots
and three assemblies with passenger chariots.
He ruled the state for forty-two years.
Huán Gōng had been on the throne for nineteen years
when he relaxed the taxes on passes and markets,
taking one part in fifty.
He distributed stipends in grain
and taxed based on the land survey.
Every two years he taxed once:
in a superior harvest year, he took three-tenths;
in a medium harvest year, he took two-tenths;
in a poor harvest year, he took one-tenth.
In years of famine, no tax was collected; in years of famine, taxes were relaxed.
Huán Gōng had Bǎo Shū identify those among the ministers who were virtuous,
Yàn Zǐ identify those among the non-officials and farmers who were virtuous,
Gāo Zǐ identify those among the craftsmen and merchants who were virtuous.
Guó Zǐ served as Lǐ,
Xí Péng managed the eastern states,
Bīn Xūwú managed the western lands,
and Fú Zhèng managed the households.
Generally, those who served as officials were stationed near the Duke,
those who did not serve and the farmers were near the gates,
and the craftsmen and merchants were near the markets.
Every thirty lǐ a post station was established and supplied,
with officials in charge.
Whenever feudal lords wished to pass through,
for the officials in their retinue,
one person was assigned to carry loads with a cart;
if they stayed overnight,
people were ordered to tend their horses
and feed them from the stores.
The guests and the officials exchanged tallies;
upon reaching the capital, they submitted the tallies for expenses.
If the accounting was improper,
it was a crime.
Whenever a commoner wished to pass through a township,
if the official did not let him pass
within seven days, the official was imprisoned.
If an officer wished to pass,
and the official did not let him pass
within five days, the official was imprisoned.
If the son of a noble wished to pass,
and the official did not let him pass
within three days, the official was imprisoned.
Whenever a county official promoted an officer of the feudal lords who was virtuous,
his reward was determined by the magnitude of that officer's ability;
if there were faults but no crimes, he was spared.
He ordered Bǎo Shū to promote grandees and encourage the state;
to achieve success without regret
was regarded as the highest conduct.
In the conduct of administration, governance was second;
treating the wilderness as the foundation,
and many things remained unpublicized;
raising litigation without arrogance
was next to that.
To exhort the state
and achieve success but then regret it;
to conduct administration and bring order yet lack capability, while the fields
are frequently overgrown,
and arrogant lawsuits arise—
to perform these three is to be of the lowest rank.
Order Yàn Zǐ to recommend the sons of the nobility:
those who are not wild when going out,
are not extravagant at home,
and whose friends include both the young and the old
are to be recommended as the highest;
those who achieve two are the next tier;
those who achieve one are the lowest.
Regarding scholar-officials: those who dwell in tranquility,
respect the elderly and the noble,
and do not lose decorum in social interactions—
to perform these three
is the highest recommendation;
to achieve two is the next tier;
to achieve one is the lowest.
Regarding farmers: those who
diligently apply their strength to agriculture,
respond appropriately to their fathers and elder brothers,
and frequently serve the worthy—
to perform these three
is the highest recommendation;
to achieve two is the next tier;
to achieve one is the lowest.
Order Gāo Zǐ to recommend artisans and merchants:
those who respond appropriately to their fathers and elder brothers,
serve their elders and provide for the aged,
and are respectful in carrying out their duties—
to perform these three
is the highest recommendation;
those who achieve two are the next tier;
those who achieve one are the lowest.
Order Guó Zǐ to judge legal cases according to the circumstances.
Once the three Grand Masters have completed their selections and recommendations,
have the districts implement them.
Guǎn Zhòng came forward and presented his words; he went up
to see the Lord,
and at the end of the year, the Lord made the appointments.
Guǎn Zhòng said to Bào Shū:
"To exhort the state, yet fail to achieve success and then regret it;
to conduct administration without order and
lacking capability, while the fields
are frequently overgrown;
or to have arrogant lawsuits—
in all these three cases,
there is guilt and no pardon."
He said to Yàn Zǐ:
"If the sons of the nobility
live extravagantly,
associate with those of lower status,
and love eating and drinking—
if they perform these three,
there is guilt and no pardon.
If scholar-officials go in and out without regularity,
do not respect the elderly, and seek after wealth—
if they perform these three,
there is guilt and no pardon.
If farmers do not respond to their fathers and elder brothers when going in and out,
do not apply their strength to agriculture,
and do not serve the worthy—
if they perform these three,
there is guilt and no pardon."
He said to Gāo Zǐ:
"If artisans and merchants do not respond to their fathers and elder brothers when going in and out,
are not respectful in carrying out their duties,
and disobey the elderly or manage affairs dangerously—
if they perform these three,
there is guilt and no pardon.
Generally, if one has no faults toward fathers and elder brothers,
and is praised by the neighborhood,
the officials shall recommend him,
and the Lord shall employ him.
If there is good but no reward,
or if there is a fault but no punishment.
If an official does not recommend such a person, he shall be dismissed.
If one has no faults toward fathers and elder brothers
but is not praised by the neighborhood,
yet the official recommends him
and the Lord employs him,
if he turns out to be good,
it shall be the official's highest reward;
if he is not good,
the official shall be punished."
The Lord said to Guó Zǐ:
"Regarding the principle of the noble and the humble:
when at home, be with the father;
when abroad, be with the teacher;
when above, be with the Lord.
In any of these three cases, if one encounters a rebel
and does not die,
or does not recognize the rebel,
then there is no pardon.
In judging legal cases,
if facts and justice are traded,
or if justice and salary are traded,
or if salary is collected without restraint,
there is guilt and no pardon.
Guǎn Zhòng calculated the state's expenditures:
two-thirds were spent on guests
and one-third remained in the state.
Guǎn Zhòng was afraid and reported this.
Huán Gōng said:
'My master, are you still concerned like this?
When the guests from the four neighbors
arrive, they are pleased;
when they leave, they give praise;
and brilliant fame fills the world.
If those who enter are not pleased
and those who leave do not praise,
a foul reputation would fill the world.
Soil can be made into grain,
and wood can be made into goods.
When grain is exhausted, there is new growth;
when wealth is dispersed, it can be re-accumulated.
For one who rules people,
reputation is what is precious;
why should one possess wealth?'
Guǎn Zhòng said:
'This is the brilliance of the Lord.'
Huán Gōng said:
'The people have prepared for military affairs;
I wish to punish those of the large states who are unprincipled—is this possible?'
He replied:
'It is not possible.
Armor and weapons are not yet sufficient.
I request that you lighten punishments and penalties in order to increase armor and weapons.'
Thereupon, those guilty of capital crimes were not killed,
and those guilty of corporal crimes were not punished;
they were made to redeem themselves with armor and weapons.
A capital crime was redeemed with a set of rhinoceros-hide armor and one halberd;
a corporal crime with a flank shield and one halberd;
a minor offense with a weight of metal;
and those who litigated without restraint
were settled with a bundle of arrows.
Huán Gōng said:
'Armor and weapons are now sufficient;
I wish to punish those of the large states who are unprincipled—
is this possible?'
He replied:
'Show love within the four borders,
and only then can you detest the unvirtuous outside the borders.
Bring peace to the houses of the Qīng Dàfū,
and only then can you endanger or save enemy states.
Grant land to small states,
and only then can you punish those of the large states who are unprincipled.
Elevate the worthy and good, and only then can you dismiss those people who are negligent of the law and are vulgar or lowly.
Therefore, the former kings certainly had those they established
before they had those they dismissed;
they certainly had those they benefited
before they had those they harmed.'
Huán Gōng said:
'As for the Sān Wáng of old,
they killed their rulers;
yet now when we speak of benevolence and righteousness,
we must take the Sān Wáng as the standard—
I do not know what the reason for this is?'
He replied:
'In the past, Yǔ brought peace and order to the world,
but by the time of Jié, it was brought to chaos;
Tāng exiled Jié
to stabilize the achievements of Yǔ.
Tāng brought peace and order to the world,
but by the time of Zhòu, it was brought to chaos;
Wǔ Wáng attacked Zhòu
to stabilize the achievements of Tāng.
Moreover, for the good to attack the not-good—
from ancient times until now,
this has never changed.
Why should the Lord doubt it?'
Huán Gōng asked again:
'As for the fallen states of old,
what did they lose?'
He replied:
"To calculate the gain of land and treasures,
but not calculate the loss of the feudal lords;
to calculate the gain of accumulated wealth,
but not calculate the loss of the common people;
to calculate being favored but not calculate being abandoned.
If one of these three belongs to a ruler,
it is enough to diminish the state;
if they have all of them, the state will perish.
Those of old who destroyed states and ruined the altars of earth and grain
did not do so intentionally;
they surely found some small pleasure in it
and did not realize they were falling into evil."
Huán Gōng said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"I request to bring Zhòngfù
his joy." The Duke gave an office to Zhòngfù and was about to drink with him;
he dug a new well and fenced it with brushwood.
After ten days of fasting,
he summoned Guǎn Zhòng.
Guǎn Zhòng arrived,
the Duke held the wine cup,
the lady held the wine vessel,
and after three rounds of drinks,
Guǎn Zhòng hurried out.
The Duke said angrily:
"I fasted for ten days to drink with Zhòngfù,
and I considered myself to have shown cultivation.
Zhòngfù left without informing me;
what is the reason for this?"
Bào Shū and Xí Péng hurried out,
catching up with Guǎn Zhòng on the road,
and said:
"The Duke is angry."
Guǎn Zhòng returned,
entered,
and stood with his back to the screen;
the Duke did not speak with him.
He advanced slightly into the courtyard,
but the Duke did not speak with him.
He advanced slightly to reach the hall,
and the Duke said:
"I fasted for ten days to drink with Zhòngfù,
and I considered myself free from fault.
Zhòngfù left without informing me;
I do not know the reason."
He replied:
"I have heard that
those who are immersed in pleasure will meet with sorrow;
those who are excessive in flavors will be deficient in conduct;
those who are negligent at court will be sluggish in administration;
those who harm the state will endanger the altars of earth and grain.
This is why I dared to leave."
The Duke hurriedly descended from the hall and said:
"I did not dare to be indulgent for my own sake;
Zhòngfù is of great age,
and even I am declining.
I wished for one morning to bring comfort to Zhòngfù."
He replied:
"I have heard that the strong should not be idle,
and the old should not be indulgent.
To follow the way of Heaven,
one must conclude well.
The Three Kings lost it
not through the accumulation of a single morning.
How can my lord be indulgent?"
Guǎn Zhòng walked out,
and the Lord, using the etiquette for a guest, bowed twice to see him off.
The next day,
Guǎn Zhòng attended court,
and the Duke said:
"I wish to hear about the trustworthiness of a ruler."
He replied:
"The people love him,
neighboring states are close to him,
and all under Heaven trust him.
This is the trustworthiness of a ruler."
The Duke said:
"Excellent.
May I ask where trustworthiness begins?"
He replied:
"It begins with cultivating oneself,
continues with managing the state,
and is completed with serving all under Heaven."
The Duke said:
"May I ask about cultivating oneself."
He replied:
"Guide one's vital energy
to seek longevity,
a lasting mind, and enduring virtue.
This is cultivating oneself."
The Duke said:
"May I ask about managing the state."
He replied:
"Seek out and promote worthy men from afar,
show compassion and love for the common people,
preserve states that are perishing abroad,
continue lineages that have been cut off,
and raise up the orphans;
lighten taxes and levies,
and mitigate punishments.
This is the great ritual of managing a state."
The Duke said:
"May I ask about serving all under Heaven."
He replied: "Laws are implemented without being harsh,
punishments are moderate but not pardoned without cause,
officials are lenient and do not oppress;
for those who are obstructed, muddied, or in distress, the regulations are not lost;
those who depart do not return in resentment,
and the people travel through the world freely.
This is serving all under Heaven."
Huán Gōng returned to Qí from Jǔ
and made Bào Shūyá the Prime Minister.
Bào Shū declined, saying:
"I
am my lord's mediocre servant.
If my lord grants favor to his servant
so that I do not suffer from cold or hunger,
then that is my lord's gift.
If you must govern the state and its altars,
then that is not what I am capable of;
for that, there is only Guǎn Yíwú.
There are five ways in which I am not as good as Guǎn Yíwú:
In being generous and kind and loving the people,
I am not his equal;
in governing the state without losing hold of the essentials,
I am not his equal;
in loyalty and trustworthiness that can bind the feudal lords,
I am not his equal;
in establishing rituals and righteousness that can be modeled in all directions,
I am not his equal;
in wearing armor and holding the drumstick
while standing at the gate of the army,
causing the common people to all increase in courage,
I am not his equal.
Guǎn Zhòng is the father and mother of the people;
if you wish to govern their children,
you cannot cast aside their father and mother."
The Duke said:
"Guǎn Yíwú personally shot at me,
hitting my belt buckle,
and I nearly died.
Now you would use him; is that possible?"
Bào Shū said:
"He acted on behalf of his lord.
If my lord pardons him and brings him back,
he will do the same for my lord."
The Duke said:
"In that case, how should we proceed?"
Bào Shū said:
"My lord should send someone to request him from Lǔ."
The Duke said:
"Shī Bó
is a scheming minister of Lǔ.
If he knows I intend to use him,
he will certainly not give him to me."
Bào Shū said:
"My lord should command the messenger to say:
'My lord has a disobedient servant in your state,
and wishes to request him so as to execute him before all the ministers.'
The Lord of Lǔ will surely agree.
Furthermore, since Shī Bó knows
Yíwú's talent,
he would certainly entrust him with the government of Lǔ.
If Yíwú accepts it,
then Lǔ would be able to weaken Qí.
If Yíwú does not accept,
and Shī Bó knows he will return to Qí,
he will certainly kill him."
The Duke said:
"In that case, will Yíwú accept?"
Bào Shū said:
"He will not accept.
Yíwú serves his lord with no second heart."
The Duke said:
"Is he still like this toward me?"
He replied:
"It is not for your sake,
but for the sake of the late lord and the altars of soil and grain.
If you wish to stabilize the ancestral temple,
then urgently request him;
otherwise,
it will be too late."
The Duke then sent Bào Shū to negotiate peace,
saying:
"Gōngzǐ Jiǔ is my kin.
I request that you, Lord, execute him."
The people of Lǔ killed Gōngzǐ Jiǔ for him.
He further said:
"Guǎn Zhòng is an enemy.
I request to receive him to satisfy my heart."
The Lord of Lǔ agreed.
Shī Bó said to the Marquis of Lǔ:
"Do not give him up.
They do not intend to execute him,
but intend to use him in their government.
As for Guǎn Zhòng,
he is a worthy man of the realm
and a man of great capacity.
If he is in Chǔ,
then Chǔ will have its way in the realm;
if he is in Jìn,
then Jìn will have its way in the realm;
if he is among the Dí,
then the Dí will have their way in the realm.
Now if Qí seeks and obtains him,
then he will surely be a long-term worry for the state of Lǔ.
Why does the Lord not kill him and hand over his corpse instead?"
The Lord of Lǔ said:
"Very well."
He was about to kill Guǎn Zhòng.
Bào Shū stepped forward and said:
"To kill him in Qí
is an execution by Qí.
To kill him in Lǔ
is an execution by Lǔ.
My humble ruler
wishes to obtain him alive
to parade him through the state
and have him executed by the ministers;
if he is not obtained alive,
then you, Lord, would be as if siding with my ruler's enemy.
This was not what my humble ruler requested,
and it would make it impossible for me, your servant, to accept the order."
Thereupon, the Lord of Lǔ did not kill him,
but bound him alive and put him in a cage to hand over to Qí.
Bào Shū received him and wailed for him, raising his voice three times.
Shī Bó looked on and laughed,
saying to the high officials:
"Guǎn Zhòng will certainly not die.
As for Bào Shū's benevolence,
he will not execute a worthy man;
his wisdom lies in praising the worthy to establish his own success.
Bào Shū assisted Gōngzǐ Xiǎobái,
who entered first and gained the state,
while Guǎn Zhòng and Zhào Hū supported Gōngzǐ Jiǔ and entered later;
they fought alongside Lǔ
and were able to cause Lǔ's defeat;
their merit was sufficient. Whether one gains Heaven's favor or loses it,
human effort is the same.
Now Lǔ is afraid
and has killed Gōngzǐ Jiǔ and Zhào Hū
and imprisoned Guǎn Zhòng to give him to Qí.
Bào Shū knows there are no further troubles,
so he will surely exert himself for Guǎn Zhòng to show diligence to his lord's favor
and make his own merit known.
The multitude will surely agree that he has gained something.
The merit of striving to the death
can still be surpassed,
but the merit of making the living illustrious,
what can compare to that?
This is to illuminate virtue to assist the ruler;
the wisdom of Bào Shū
is not lacking."
When they arrived at Táng Fù,
Bào Shū purified and bathed him three times.
Huán Gōng personally welcomed him in the outskirts.
Guǎn Zhòng bent his cap-strings and tucked in his lapels,
and had someone hold an axe standing behind him.
The Duke declined the axe three times and then had the person withdraw it.
The Duke said:
"Lower your cap-strings and let down your lapels,
for I wish to see you."
Guǎn Zhòng bowed twice, touching his head to the ground, and said:
"In response to your Grace's kindness,
even if I were killed and sent to the Yellow Springs,
my death would be immortal."
The Duke then returned with him,
honored him in the ancestral temple,
poured three libations and asked him about governing,
saying:
"In the past, the late lord Xiāng Gōng
built high towers and broad ponds,
indulged in music and drinking wine,
hunted and fowled with nets and arrows,
and did not attend to the state's government.
He debased the sagely and insulted scholars,
exalting only women,
with nine high consorts and six lower ones,
and thousands of concubines arrayed.
For food, they had to have fine grain and meat;
for clothing, they had to have patterns and embroidery;
yet the soldiers were freezing and hungry.
The war horses waited for the worn-out parts of pleasure carriages,
and the soldiers waited for the leftovers of the concubines.
Singers, entertainers, and dwarves were in front,
while worthy high officials were behind.
Because of this, the state did not improve daily
nor grow monthly.
I fear the ancestral temple will not be swept,
and the altars of soil and grain will not receive blood sacrifices.
I venture to ask, what should be done about this?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"In the past, our former kings,
Zhōu Zhāo Wáng and Mù Wáng,
followed the distant traces of Wén and Wǔ for generations
to establish their fame.
They gathered the elders,
compared and examined those among the people who possessed the Way,
and established models to serve as the people's discipline.
They used tallies and contracts to correspond with each other,
compiled and recorded them in writing,
tracing the roots and exhausting the branches.
They encouraged them with rewards and honors,
corrected them with punishments,
swept away their confusion,
and granted gifts to soothe them,
serving as the beginning and end for the people."
The Duke said:
"How shall I do this?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"In antiquity, when the sage kings governed their people,
they divided the capital into three and the countryside into five,
settled the people's dwellings,
established the people's occupations,
to serve as the people's discipline.
They carefully used the six handles;
in this way, the people's true circumstances could be grasped
and the hundred surnames could be managed."
Huán Gōng asked:
"What are the six handles?"
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"Death, life, nobility, meanness, poverty, and wealth—
these are the six handles."
Huán Gōng asked:
"What of dividing the capital into three?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Organize the capital into twenty-one districts:
six districts for merchants and artisans,
and fifteen districts for scholars and farmers.
The Duke shall lead eleven districts,
Gāo Zǐ shall lead five districts,
and Guó Zǐ shall lead five districts;
by dividing the capital into three, three armies are formed.
The Duke shall establish three types of officials:
three districts for the markets,
three clans for the artisans,
three wardens for the marshes,
and three supervisors for the mountains.
Establish five families as a guǐ,
and each guǐ has a head.
Ten guǐ make a lǐ,
and each lǐ has an overseer.
Four lǐ make a lián,
and each lián has a head.
Ten lián make a xiāng,
and each xiāng has a magistrate.
Every five xiāng shall have one commander."
Huán Gōng said:
"What about the five border districts?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Regulate five households to be a *guǐ*,"
"and the *guǐ* shall have a head."
"Six *guǐ* make a *yì*,"
"and the *yì* shall have an official."
"Ten *yì* make a *zú*,"
"and the *zú* shall have a head."
"Ten *zú* make a *xiāng*,"
"and the *xiāng* shall have a *liáng rén*."
"Three *xiāng* make a *shǔ*,"
"and the *shǔ* shall have a *dà fū*."
"There are five *shǔ* and five *dà fū*."
"Military administration is heard by the *shǔ*,"
"civil administration is heard by the *xiāng*."
"Each maintains their position and attends to their duties,"
"ensuring there are no profligate or dissolute people."
Huán Gōng said:
"To fix the people's dwellings"
"and bring the people's work to fruition,"
"how is this done?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"The four classes of people—scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants—"
"are the bedrock people of the state."
"They must not be allowed to live in a jumble."
"If they live in a jumble, their speech will be confused,"
"and their work will be disordered."
"Therefore, when the sage kings settled the scholars,"
"they were necessarily in quiet and leisurely places."
"When settling the farmers, they were necessarily near the fields and wilds."
"When settling the artisans, they were necessarily near the government offices."
"When settling the merchants, they were necessarily near the marketplaces."
"As for those scholars, let them gather in groups and live in their own districts."
"In their leisure, fathers talk with fathers about righteousness,"
"and sons talk with sons about filial piety."
"Those serving the ruler talk of reverence,"
"the elders talk of love,"
"and the young talk of fraternal respect."
"From dawn until dusk, they engage in these matters,"
"using them to teach their sons and younger brothers."
"Having practiced this since youth,"
"their minds find peace in it,"
"and they do not change even if they see different things."
"For this reason,"
"the teaching of their fathers and elder brothers is completed without sternness;"
"the learning of their sons and younger brothers is mastered without toil."
"Thus, the sons of scholars always become scholars."
"As for those farmers, let them gather in groups and live in their own districts."
"They carefully observe the four seasons,"
"measure and regulate the use of resources,"
"and prepare their implements and tools."
"They line up their plows and shares"
"flails and sickles. When the cold arrives,"
"they beat the straw and clear the fields,"
"to wait
for the time to plow."
"They plow deeply, sow seeds uniformly, and harrow swiftly."
"They weed and hoe before the rain, waiting for the timely rains."
"Once the timely rains have arrived,"
"grasping their spades, sickles, hoes, and weeders,"
"they work in the fields and wilds from morning until night."
"They shed their outer garments to apply themselves to the work,"
"separating the sprouts from the weeds,"
"and arranging them in sparse or dense rows."
"On their heads, they wear hats of ramie or rushes,"
"and on their bodies, they wear coarse rain-capes."
"Drenching their bodies and muddying their feet,"
"exposing their hair and skin to the sun,"
"they exhaust the strength of their four limbs"
"to work diligently in the fields and wilds."
"Having practiced this since youth,"
"their minds find peace in it,"
"and they do not change even if they see different things."
"For this reason, the teaching of their fathers and elder brothers is completed without sternness;"
"the learning of their sons and younger brothers is mastered without toil."
"Thus, the sons of farmers always become farmers."
"Simple and rustic, they are without wickedness."
"Those among them whose outstanding talents enable them to become scholars"
"are sufficient to be relied upon."
"Therefore, using them for farming results in much grain;"
"using them for service results in many worthies."
"Thus, the sage kings respected and cared for the farmers."
"(And if they did not report it), (their crimes were five)."
"As for those artisans, let them gather in groups and live in their own districts."
"They examine fine materials,"
"carefully observe the four seasons,"
"and distinguish between good and bad workmanship."
"They measure and regulate their usage,"
"discussing, comparing, and calculating"
"the designs and the cutting of vessels,"
"valuing completeness and sharpness."
"They talk with one another about their work,"
"show one another their achievements,"
"display their skills to one another,"
"and vie with one another in wisdom."
"From dawn until dusk, they engage in these matters,"
"using them to teach their sons and younger brothers."
"Having practiced this since youth,"
"their minds find peace in it,"
"and they do not change even if they see different things."
"For this reason, the teaching of their fathers and elder brothers is completed without sternness;"
"the learning of their sons and younger brothers is mastered without toil."
"Thus, the sons of artisans always become artisans."
"As for those merchants, let them gather in groups and live in their own districts."
"They observe poor harvests and famines,"
"examine the changes in the state,"
"carefully observe the four seasons,"
"and monitor the goods of their districts,"
"so as to know the prices in the market."
"Carrying loads on their backs and shoulders,"
"using oxen and horses with carriages to travel to the four directions;"
"they calculate quantities,"
"estimate high and low prices,"
"using what they have"
"to exchange for what they lack,"
"buying low and selling high."
"Thus, feathers and banners arrive without being sought,"
"bamboo and arrows are in surplus in the state,"
"strange and unusual things arrive from time to time,"
"and rare and precious objects gather there."
"From dawn until dusk, they engage in these matters,"
"using them to teach their sons and younger brothers."
"They talk with one another about profit,"
"show one another the right timing,"
"and display to one another their knowledge of prices."
"Having practiced this since youth,"
"their minds find peace in it,"
"and they do not change even if they see different things."
"For this reason, the teaching of their fathers and elder brothers is completed without sternness;"
"the learning of their sons and younger brothers is mastered without toil."
"Thus, the sons of merchants always become merchants."
"Observe the land and grade the taxes accordingly,"
"then the people will not move"
"away."
"Regulate the travel lodges and old stations,"
"then the people will not be lazy."
"Access the mountains and marshes according to their proper seasons,"
"then the people will not be reckless."
"Balance the highlands, plains, hills, mounds, and fields,"
"then the people will not be confused."
"Do not usurp the people's time,"
"and then the hundred surnames will be wealthy."
"When the sacrificial animals are not overworked,"
"then the cattle and horses will be well-bred."
Huán Gōng asked again:
"I wish to cultivate the administration to achieve my aims in the world;"
"is this possible?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"It is possible."
The Duke said:
"Where can I begin so it may be possible?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Begin with loving the people."
The Duke said:
"What is the way to love the people?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Let your lordship cultivate the ducal clan,"
"let the great families cultivate their own clans,"
"making them connected through shared tasks,"
"and linked by their stipends,"
"then the people will become close to one another."
"Pardon old crimes,"
"restore old lineages,"
"and establish heirs for those without descendants,"
"then the people will multiply."
"Lessen punishments and penalties,"
"and lighten taxes and levies,"
"then the people will be wealthy."
"Appoint worthy scholars in the districts,"
"and have them teach throughout the state,"
"then the people will possess ritual propriety."
"Issue commands and do not change them,"
"then the people will be upright."
"This is the way to love the people."
The Duke said:
"If the people are wealthy and close to one another,"
"then can I employ them?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Amass wealth and encourage craftsmanship,
so as to satisfy the needs of the people;
deploy strength and honor the worthy,
so as to encourage the wisdom of the people;
apply punishments without harshness,
so as to assist the common people.
If these are practiced without selfishness,
then it will be sufficient to accommodate the masses;
if words spoken are always trustworthy,
then orders will never be exhausted.
This is the way to employ the people."
Huán Gōng said:
"The people's dwellings are settled,
and affairs are already completed;
I wish to engage with the feudal lords of the realm—
is it possible?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Not yet.
The hearts of the people are not yet at ease with us."
The Gōng said:
"How shall I put them at ease?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Revise the old laws,
select those that are good,
and strictly implement them;
be compassionate to the people,
and give to them without regard for wealth;
relax government labor services,
and respect the common people;
then the state will be wealthy and the people will be at ease."
The Gōng said:
"The people are at ease;
is it possible now?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Not yet.
If you, my lord, wish to organize the ranks and files
and repair armor and weapons,
then the large states will also organize their ranks and files
and repair their armor and weapons.
When you have matters of military expeditions,
then the ministers of the feudal lords of small states will have preparations for defense.
In that case, it will be difficult to quickly achieve your will in the realm.
If you wish to quickly achieve your will among the feudal lords of the realm,
then matters must be concealed
and administration must have a hidden purpose."
The Gōng said:
"How is this to be done?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Organize the internal administration and lodge the military commands within it.
Establish the neighborhoods of Gāo Zǐ,
establish the neighborhoods of Guó Zǐ,
and establish the Gōng's neighborhoods;
divide the state of Qí into three
to form the three armies.
Select the worthy among the people
and make them the neighborhood heads.
The xiāng will have ranks and files, and the heads of the soldiers
will establish their regulations and orders;
then through hunting,
and applying rewards and punishments accordingly,
the common people will become well-versed in military affairs."
Huán Gōng said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon Guǎn Zǐ established five households as a guǐ,
with a head for the guǐ.
Ten guǐ made a lǐ,
and the lǐ had an official.
Four lǐ made a lián,
and the lián had a head.
Ten lián made a xiāng,
and the xiāng had a liángrén.
These were used for military organization.
Therefore, five households made a guǐ,
and five men made a wǔ,
led by the guǐ head.
Ten guǐ made a lǐ,
therefore fifty men made a xiǎoróng,
led by the lǐ official.
Four lǐ made a lián,
therefore two hundred men made a zú,
led by the lián head.
Ten lián made a xiāng,
therefore two thousand men made a lǚ, and the xiāng
liángrén led them.
Five xiāng had one commander,
therefore ten thousand men made one army,
led by the commander of the five xiāng.
For the three armies,
there were the drums of the Central Army,
the drums of Gāo Zǐ,
and the drums of Guó Zǐ.
In spring they went hunting, called sōu,
to drill the troops.
In autumn they went hunting, called xiǎn,
to exercise the soldiers.
Thus, the administration of the ranks and files was settled in the lǐ.
The administration of the army and the lǚ was settled in the suburbs.
Once the internal instruction was completed,
it was ordered that no one move away.
Thus, among the people of the ranks and files,
people protected one another,
families loved one another,
in youth they lived together,
as adults they associated together,
in sacrifices they shared blessings,
in death and mourning they comforted one another,
in misfortune and fortune they shared concerns,
in their dwellings they shared joy,
in work they were in harmony,
and in weeping they shared grief.
For this reason, in night battles their voices could be heard by one another,
which was sufficient to prevent disorder;
in day battles their eyes could see one another,
which was sufficient for recognition.
Their mutual joy was sufficient to make them die for one another.
Therefore, in defense they were firm,
and in battle they were victorious.
If you, my lord, have thirty thousand such trained soldiers
to range freely across the realm,
punishing those without the Dào and stabilizing the House of Zhōu,
no ruler of the large states in the realm will be able to resist you."
At the audience of the first month,
the xiāng heads reported on their affairs,
and the Gōng personally questioned them,
saying:
"In your xiāng,
are there any who in their daily life are righteous, who love learning,
who are intelligent and inherently benevolent,
who are compassionate and filial to their parents,
and whose respect for elders and brothers is known in the xiāng and lǐ?
If there are, then report them.
If there are such men and you do not report them,
it is called 'concealing the worthy,'
and the punishment is fivefold."
The officials finished their tasks and withdrew.
The Gōng questioned them again,
saying:
"In your xiāng,
are there any with physical courage and great strength of limb,
whose sinews and bones stand out from the crowd?
If there are, then report them.
If there are such men and you do not report them,
it is called 'concealing talent,'
and the punishment is fivefold."
The officials finished their tasks and withdrew.
The Gōng questioned them again,
saying:
"In your xiāng,
are there any who are not compassionate or filial to their parents,
who do not respect elders and brothers in the xiāng and lǐ,
who are arrogant, restless, licentious, or violent,
and who do not obey the orders of superiors?
If there are, then report them.
If there are such men and you do not report them,
it is called 'colluding with the lowly,'
and the punishment is fivefold."
The officials finished their tasks and withdrew.
Thereupon the xiāng heads retired to cultivate virtue and recommend the worthy.
Huán Gōng personally interviewed them
and subsequently employed them in official positions.
The Gōng ordered the heads of the departments to report on achievements at fixed intervals,
and also ordered them to select the worthy among the officials and report back on them.
He said:
"If there are men serving in my administration
who have merit, whose excellent virtue
is compliant, who are upright and sincere
while awaiting the time for service,
who cause the people to be respectful and encouraged,
and whose words of praise or censure
are sufficient to remedy the failings of the administration."
The Duke publicly inquired in their home districts,
and conducted examinations.
Then he summoned them to sit with him,
scrutinizing their character to compare it with their accomplishments and deeds.
If they were fit to be established, he would appoint them at the appropriate time.
He posed questions about the troubles of the state without failing to investigate;
afterward, he investigated and inquired in their home districts
to observe what they were capable of.
If there were no major faults,
he promoted them to be assistants to the Shàng Qīng.
This was called the "Three Selections."
Gāo Zǐ and Guó Zǐ retired to regulate their Xiāng,
the Xiāng heads retired to regulate the Lián,
the Lián heads retired to regulate the Lǐ,
the Lǐ heads retired to regulate the Guǐ,
the Guǐ heads retired to regulate the households (Jiā).
Therefore, if a common man did good,
it could be known and he could be promoted;
if a common man did wrong,
it could be known and he could be punished.
Once the administration was established,
in the districts, one did not bypass the elders,
and at court, one did not bypass rank.
Inept scholars had no place in the ranks,
and inept women had no home.
If a scholar divorced three wives,
he was expelled beyond the borders.
If a woman married three times,
she was sent to pound grain.
Therefore, the people all strove to do good;
for a scholar, rather than doing good in the Xiāng,
it was better to do good in the Lǐ;
rather than doing good in the Lǐ,
it was better to do good in the household.
Therefore, scholars did not dare to speak of temporary convenience;
they all had plans for the whole year;
they did not dare to discuss only the whole year;
they all sought merit for their whole lives.
At the court of the first month,
the Dàfū of the five departments reported their affairs
to the Duke, who selected those with few accomplishments and rebuked them, saying:
"The lands and people assigned to you are equal;
why is it that you alone have few accomplishments?
Why do you not match others?
If your instruction is not good
and administrative affairs are not managed,
the first and second times I will pardon you,
but the third time there will be no mercy."
The Duke further inquired of them,
saying:
"Among your subordinates,
are there any who live righteously, love learning,
are intelligent, worthy and benevolent,
kind and filial to their parents,
and known in their home districts for being respectful to elders and brothers?
If there are such, report them.
If they exist and you do not report them,
it is called 'concealing the worthy';
the punishment is fivefold."
The officials finished their business and withdrew.
The Duke further inquired of them,
saying:
"Among your subordinates,
are there any with physical courage or strength of limb and torso that stands out from the crowd?
If there are such, report them.
If they exist and you do not report them,
it is called 'concealing talent';
its punishment is fivefold."
The officials finished their business and withdrew.
The Duke further inquired of them,
saying:
"Among your subordinates,
are there any who are not kind or filial to parents,
not respectful to elders and brothers in the home districts,
arrogant, impetuous, licentious, or violent,
or who do not follow the orders of superiors?
If there are such, report them.
If they exist and you do not report them,
it is called 'colluding with inferiors';
its punishment is fivefold."
The officials finished their business and withdrew.
Thereupon, the Dàfū of the five departments retired to regulate their departments,
the departments retired to regulate the Lián,
the Lián retired to regulate the Xiāng,
the Xiāng retired to regulate the Zú,
the Zú retired to regulate the Yì,
the Yì retired to regulate the households (Jiā).
Therefore, if a common man did good,
it could be known and he could be promoted;
if a common man did wrong,
it could be known and he could be punished.
The administration was established and the state was secure;
defense was firm,
and warfare was strong.
The territory within the borders was well-governed,
the common people were close to the ruler,
and they could go on expeditions in all four directions,
establishing a Bà Wáng.
Huán Gōng said:
"The military ranks are settled,
and affairs are established.
I wish to take action among the Zhūhóu;
is it possible?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Not yet.
As for military orders,
I have already integrated them into domestic administration,
but the state of Qí has few armors and weapons.
I wish to adjust the gravity of crimes and divert them into armors and weapons."
The Duke said:
"How shall we do this?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Establish that for heavy crimes, one pays with rhinoceros-hide armor and two Jǐ;
for light crimes, one pays with quivers, shields, leather armguards, and two Jǐ;
for minor crimes, one pays with a certain weight of bronze;
for pardoning petty crimes,
one pays with half a Jūn;
for those who are not guilty but are oppressed and bring lawsuits,
if judged three times
and they are forbidden but still do not act rightly,
then they pay a bundle of arrows as a penalty.
Fine metal is used to cast Gē, swords, spears, and Jǐ,
testing them on dogs and horses;
inferior metal is used to cast adzes, axes, hoes, scythes, saws, and picks,
testing them on wood and earth."
Huán Gōng said:
"Armor and weapons are now quite sufficient.
I wish to take action among the Zhūhóu;
is it possible?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Not yet.
Internal governance is not yet complete,
and external affairs are not yet prepared."
Therefore, he made Bào Shū Yá the Dà Jiàn,
Wáng Zǐ Chéng Fù the General,
Xián Zǐ Qí the Lǐ,
Nìng Qī in charge of Tián,
Xí Péng in charge of Xíng.
Cáo Sù Sūn was stationed in Chǔ,
Shāng Róng was stationed in Sòng,
Jì Yǒu was stationed in Lǔ,
Wèi Kāi Fāng was stationed in Wèi,
Yàn Shàng was stationed in Yān,
Shěn Yǒu was stationed in Jìn.
Also, eighty traveling scholars
were provided with carriages, horses, clothing, and furs,
given abundant provisions,
and supplied with sufficient wealth and currency,
sent out to travel in all directions
to summon and recruit the worthy scholars of the world.
Decorated curios and luxuries were prepared,
and sent to travel in all directions,
to be sold to the Zhūhóu,
to observe what those above and below valued and desired,
choosing those states in decadence and disorder to be the first targets of action.
The Duke said:
"Foreign and domestic matters are settled;
is it possible?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Not yet.
Neighboring states are not yet close to us."
The Duke asked:
"How do we make them close?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Examine our borders,
return any land that was seized,
and rectify the boundaries;
do not accept their bribes,
but prepare fine skins and silks
to perform the utmost courtesies in missions and visits to the Zhūhóu,
so as to put the neighbors at ease;
then neighboring states will become close to us."
Huán Gōng said:
"Armor and weapons are fully sufficient.
I wish to campaign to the south.
On whom should I rely as a host?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Take Lǔ as the host.
Return its encroached lands, Cháng and Qián.
Let it have the sea as a screen,
the Qú Mí River with its islands,
and the surrounding mountains as a stronghold."
Huán Gōng said:
"I wish to campaign to the west.
On whom should I rely as a host?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Take Wèi as the host.
Return its encroached lands, Tái Yuán, Gū, and Qī Lǐ.
Let it have the sea as a screen,
the Qú Mí River with its islands,
and the surrounding mountains as a stronghold."
Huán Gōng said:
"I wish to campaign to the north.
On whom should I rely as a host?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Take Yān as the host.
Return its encroached lands, Chái Fū and Fèi Gǒu.
Let it have the sea as a screen,
the Qú Mí River with its islands,
and the surrounding mountains as a stronghold."
The four neighbors became very close.
After returning their encroached lands
and rectifying their boundaries,
the territory reached south to the northern side of Dài,
west to the Jì River,
north to the sea,
and east to Jì and Suí.
The land area was three hundred and sixty lǐ.
In three years, the administration was settled;
in four years, the education was complete;
in five years, the troops set out.
There were thirty thousand trained soldiers
and eight hundred leather-covered chariots.
Many of the feudal lords were sunken in disorder
and did not submit to the Tiān Zǐ.
Thereupon, Huán Gōng rescued Xú Zhōu in the east,
dividing Wú by half;
he preserved Lǔ and pressured Cài,
and carved off territory from Yuè.
To the south, he relied on Sòng and Zhèng
to campaign against Chǔ,
crossing the Rǔ River,
passing over Fāng Chéng,
and viewing Wén Shān,
making them present silk as tribute to the Zhōu royal house.
Chéng Zhōu returned the sacrificial meat at Lóng Yuè,
and among the feudal lords of Jīng Zhōu,
none failed to come and submit.
In the center, he rescued Jìn Gōng,
captured the Dǐ King,
defeated the Hú and Mò,
and crushed the Tú Hé,
so that the mounted invaders first submitted.
In the north, he campaigned against the Shān Róng,
controlled Lǐng Zhī,
and cut down Gū Zhú,
so that the Jiǔ Yí first obeyed.
Among the feudal lords along the seacoast,
none failed to come and submit.
In the western expedition,
he expelled the Bái Dǐ from their lands,
reached as far as the Xī Hé,
lashed boats together into rafts,
and crossed the river on floats,
reaching Shí Zhěn.
They suspended the chariots and tied up the horses
to cross the valleys of Dà Háng and Bēi Ěr,
and restrained Tài Xià.
In the west, they subdued Liú Shā and Xī Yú,
so that the Qín Róng first followed.
Thus, with one deployment of troops, twelve great achievements were made.
Therefore, the Dōng Yí, Xī Róng, Nán Mán, and Běi Dǐ,
as well as the feudal lords of Zhōng Guó,
none failed to submit as guests.
Together with the feudal lords, he decorated sacrificial animals for the covenant documents to swear
and make oaths to the various gods above and below.
Then he led the world to stabilize the Zhōu royal house
and held a great assembly of the feudal lords at Yáng Gǔ.
Thus, there were six assemblies with war chariots,
three assemblies with civilian carriages,
nine times uniting the feudal lords,
and once rectifying the world.
Armor was not unfastened in the camps,
weapons were not removed from their covers;
the cases contained no bows,
the quivers contained no arrows.
Military affairs were put to rest,
and civil ways were practiced
to pay court to the Tiān Zǐ.
At the assembly of Kuí Qiū,
the Tiān Zǐ sent the Grand Official Zǎi Kǒng
to deliver sacrificial meat to Huán Gōng, saying:
"I, the Lone One, have performed sacrifices for Wén and Wǔ.
I have sent Zǎi Kǒng to deliver the meat."
There was further a subsequent command
saying:
"Because you have aged and worked hard,
I truly tell you, my Elder Uncle, not to bow down in thanks."
Huán Gōng summoned Guǎn Zhòng to deliberate,
and Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"For a ruler not to act like a ruler,
and for a minister not to act like a minister,
is the root of disorder."
Huán Gōng said:
"I have had three assemblies with civilian carriages,
six assemblies with war chariots,
nine times uniting the feudal lords,
and once rectifying the world.
To the north, I reached Gū Zhú, Shān Róng, and Wèi Mò,
and restrained Tài Xià.
To the west, I reached Liú Shā and Xī Yú.
To the south, I reached Wú,
Yuè, Bā,
Zāng Kē, Gē,
Bù Yǔ,
Diāo Tí, and Hēi Chǐ.
Among the states of the Jīng and Yí,
none disobey my commands.
Yet Zhōng Guó treats me as lowly.
Of those who received the mandate in the three dynasties of old,
was it any different from this?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"The Fèng Huáng and Luán birds
do not descend,
while hawks, falcons, owls, and kites are numerous.
The various gods do not arrive,
the sacred tortoises do not show omens,
and those who hold grain to divine frequently hit the mark.
Timely rains and sweet dew do not descend,
while whirlwinds and torrential rains frequently arrive.
The five grains do not flourish,
the six domestic animals do not breed,
while weeds, mugwort, and pigweed all spring up.
The pattern of the Fèng Huáng,
with virtue and righteousness in front
and daily prosperity behind.
Of those who received the mandate in the past,
the dragon and tortoise appeared,
the River produced the Chart,
the Luò produced the Script,
and the earth produced the Chéng Huáng horse.
Now these three auspicious signs have not been seen;
even if one claims to have received the mandate,
would that not be a loss of it?"
Huán Gōng was afraid,
went out to see the guest, and said:
"The majesty of Heaven is not even a foot away from my face.
I, Xiǎo Bái, receive the command of the Tiān Zǐ
and shall not fail to bow.
I fear falling prostrate below
and thus bringing shame to the Tiān Zǐ."
He then bowed down,
went up to receive the awarded garments, the Grand Carriage,
the dragon banner with nine streamers,
and the red flag of the Qú gate.
The Tiān Zǐ gave commands to Huán Gōng which he did not accept,
and the feudal lords of the world praised his compliance.
Huán Gōng was concerned about the feudal lords of the world.
In Lǔ, there was the rebellion of Qìng Fù,
and two rulers were assassinated,
leaving the state without an heir.
Huán Gōng heard of this
and sent Gāo Zǐ to preserve it.
Men and women did not act licentiously,
and horses and oxen were selected and provided.
They held jade to see him,
requesting to be a lord within the passes,
but Huán Gōng did not allow it.
The Dí people attacked Xíng,
and Huán Gōng built Yíyí to enfeoff them.
Men and women were not licentious,
and horses and oxen were selected and provided.
Holding jade for an audience,
they asked to become Marquises within the passes,
but Huán Gōng did not permit it.
The Dí people attacked Wèi,
and the people of Wèi fled to Cáo;
Huán Gōng walled Chǔqiū to enfeoff them.
Their livestock had been scattered and lost,
so Huán Gōng gave them three hundred harnessed horses;
the feudal lords of the world praised his benevolence.
Thereupon, the feudal lords of the world knew that Huán Gōng worked diligently for them;
thus, the way the feudal lords turned to him
was like people flocking to a market.
Huán Gōng knew the feudal lords were turning to him,
so he caused their tribute to be light and their rituals to be weighty.
Therefore, he allowed the feudal lords of the world to use exhausted horses, dogs, and sheep as tribute,
while Qí reciprocated with fine horses.
The feudal lords used plain silk and four sets of deer hides as tribute,
while Qí reciprocated with patterned brocade and tiger and leopard skins.
The envoys of the feudal lords
entered with hanging bags
and returned with heavy loads.
Thus, he lured them with love,
attracted them with profit,
bound them with trust,
and demonstrated to them with military might.
For this reason, the feudal lords of small states
already submitted to Huán Gōng;
none dared to betray him, and all turned to him.
They rejoiced in his love and craved his benefits;
they trusted his benevolence and feared his might.
Huán Gōng knew that many feudal lords of small states sided with him,
so he then bestowed great favors upon them.
What could be a cause for worry, he worried about for them;
what could be planned, he planned for them;
what could be acted upon, he acted upon for them.
He attacked Tán and Lái but did not take possession of them;
the feudal lords praised his benevolence.
He circulated the fish and salt of Qí to Dōnglái,
caused the custom houses and markets to inspect but not to levy duties,
and registered goods but did not tax them,
all for the benefit of the feudal lords;
the feudal lords praised his leniency.
He built up Cài, Yānlíng, Péixià, and Língfùqiū
to defend the lands from the Róng and Dí,
in order to prohibit violence against the feudal lords.
In Zhōngmóu, he built Wǔlù, Yè, Gài, and Mǔqiū
to protect the lands of the Zhūxià,
in order to demonstrate authority in the Central States.
His instruction was a great success.
Therefore, the world’s regard for Huán Gōng was such that
the people of distant states
looked up to him like parents,
and the people of nearby states
followed him like flowing water.
Thus, as the lands he reached became more distant,
the people he gained became more numerous.
Why was this?
They cherished his civility and feared his might.
Therefore, he killed those who lacked the Way
and stabilized the Zhōu House;
no one in the world could resist him,
for military matters were established.
He settled the three types of armor
and laid down the five types of weapons;
he crossed the Yellow River in court robes without any fear,
for civil matters triumphed.
Therefore, the rulers of large states felt ashamed,
and the lords of small states grew close to him.
Therefore, the rulers of large states
served him like servants,
and the lords of small states
rejoiced in him like parents.
Since it was so,
the rulers of large states were not arrogant,
and the lords of small states were not lowly.
Therefore, the rulers of large states were not prideful,
and the lords of small states were not terrified.
Thereupon, he arranged wide lands to benefit narrow lands
and reduced those with wealth to give to those without wealth.
Providing for the gentlemen,
he did not lose successful achievements;
providing for the common people,
he did not lose the established mandates.
If it is like this,
dwelling at home is harmonious,
and going out results in success.
He did not boast of mobilizing armor and weapons
to fulfill the traces of civility and might throughout the world.
Huán Gōng was able to utilize the plans of his ministers
to enhance his own wisdom.
His chancellor was named Yíwú;
his grand officers were Níng Qī, Xí Péng, Bīn Xūwú, and Bào Shūyá.
Using these five men, what were the achievements?
Deliberating on righteousness, shining with virtue,
continuing the laws, and carrying them on to
the world to leave for descendants;
bequeathing filial piety to the Zhāomù ancestral sequence,
greatly dominating the world,
his reputation was wide and abundant,
and could not be obscured.
This was only because there was an enlightened ruler above
and perceptive ministers below.
Initially,
Huán Gōng met Guǎnzǐ in the suburbs and questioned him.
Guǎn Zhòng declined,
and then replied with the system of three divisions for the capital and five for the countryside;
establishing five townships to promote culture,
establishing five districts to encourage military prowess,
integrating the military with the administration,
regularizing punishments, and preparing weapons,
applying military force to those lords who lacked the Way
in order to serve the Zhōu House.
Huán Gōng was greatly pleased.
Thereupon, he fasted for ten days,
intending to make Guǎn Zhòng his chancellor.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I am a man destined for the executioner's axe,
fortunately spared
to keep my waist and neck together;
this is my fortune.
As for managing state affairs,
it is not my responsibility."
The Duke said:
"If you, grand officer, accept the administration,
I will be equal to the task;
if you, grand officer, do not accept the administration,
I fear I will collapse."
Guǎn Zhòng consented,
bowed twice, and accepted the chancellorship.
Three days later,
the Duke said:
"I have three great vices;
can I still rule the state?"
He replied:
"I have not yet heard them."
The Duke said:
"I unfortunately love hunting,
staying out until dark by the animals,
never returning from the field until the animals are sighted;
envoys from the lords have no one to receive them,
and the various officials have no one to whom to report."
He replied:
"Bad as it may be,
it is not the most urgent matter."
The Duke said:
"I unfortunately love wine,
following day with night,
envoys from the lords have no one to receive them,
and the various officials have no one to whom to report."
He replied:
"Bad as it may be,
it is not the most urgent matter."
The Duke said:
"I have impure conduct;
I unfortunately love lust,
and there are paternal aunts and sisters who are unmarried."
He replied:
"Bad as it may be,
it is not the most urgent matter."
The Duke changed his expression and said:
"If these three are acceptable,
then what could possibly be unacceptable?"
He replied:
"For a ruler, only being unloving and being slow are unacceptable.
Being unloving means losing the masses;
being slow means failing to keep up with affairs."
The Duke said:
"Excellent.
Sir, please go to your quarters;
another day, I shall consult with you on this matter."
He replied:
“The time is right
to grant it to Yíwú;
why wait for another day?”
The Duke said:
“What should be done?”
He replied:
“Gōngzǐ Jǔ is a man of broad learning who knows the rites,
he loves learning and is modest in speech;
please send him to travel to Lǔ
to establish relations there.
Gōngzǐ Kāifāng is a man of clever adaptability and keen profit-seeking;
please send him to travel to Wèi
to establish relations there.
As for Cáo Sūn Sù's character,
he is slightly frugal and bears a sense of caution,
excessively respectful and fluent in speech;
he is the model for dealing with Jīng;
please send him to travel there
to establish relations there.”
Thereupon, the three envoys were immediately dispatched, and he withdrew.
After serving as Chancellor for three months,
he requested to discuss the various officials.
The Duke said:
“Agreed.”
Guǎn Zhòng said:
“In matters of ascending and descending, bowing and yielding,
being well-practiced in advancing and retreating,
and distinguishing the hardness and softness of rhetoric,
I am not as good as Xí Péng;
please appoint him as Dàxíng.
In clearing the wilderness and establishing settlements, opening up the land,
gathering grain and increasing the population,
and exhausting the profits of the earth,
I am not as good as Nìng Qī;
please appoint him as Dàsītián.
On the flat plains and wide pastures,
where chariots do not get stuck in ruts,
and soldiers do not turn their heels to flee,
where at the beat of the drum the soldiers of the three armies view death as returning home,
I am not as good as Wángzǐ Chéngfù;
please appoint him as Dàsīmǎ.
In deciding lawsuits and being impartial,
not killing the innocent,
and not falsely accusing the guiltless,
I am not as good as Bīn Xūwú;
please appoint him as Dàsīlǐ.
In confronting the Ruler’s expression,
offering remonstrance with absolute loyalty,
not avoiding death,
and not being swayed by wealth or status,
I am not as good as Dōngguō Yá;
please appoint him as the official of Dàjiàn.
In these five gentlemen,
Yíwú is not as good in even one aspect;
yet if you were to exchange them for Yíwú,
Yíwú would not do it.
If the Lord wishes to govern the state and strengthen the military,
then these five gentlemen are sufficient;
if you wish to become a Hegemon or King,
Yíwú is here.”
Huán Gōng said:
“Excellent.”
[The chapter is missing.]
While Huán Gōng was on the throne,
Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng had an audience.
After they had been standing for a while,
a pair of wild geese flew past them.
Huán Gōng sighed and said:
“Zhòngfù,
now those wild geese
sometimes go south,
sometimes go north,
sometimes go forth,
and sometimes return;
the four directions are not too far for them,
and they arrive wherever they wish to go.
Is it not only because they have wings
that they can communicate their will throughout the world?”
Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng did not answer.
Huán Gōng said:
“Why did you two not answer?”
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
“The Lord has the heart of a Hegemon or King,
but Yíwú is not the minister of a Hegemon or King;
therefore I did not dare to answer.”
Huán Gōng said:
“Zhòngfù, why is that so?
Why not say what is appropriate?
Do I not have a direction?
My having Zhòngfù
is like the flying goose having wings,
or like crossing a great water having a boat and oars.
If Zhòngfù does not teach me with a single word,
even though I have ears,
how will I hear the Way and obtain the standards?”
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
“If the Lord wishes to be a Hegemon or King and undertake great matters,
then he must begin from the fundamental tasks.”
Huán Gōng straightened his posture and moved his mat,
cupped his hands in respect and asked:
“I venture to ask, what is meant by the fundamental?”
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
“The common people of Qí Guó
are your fundamental, my Lord.
The people worry greatly about hunger,
yet taxes and levies are heavy;
the people fear death greatly,
yet punishments and administration are harsh;
the people are exhausted by labor,
yet the superiors undertake projects at the wrong times.
If the Lord lightens their taxes and levies,
