then the people will not worry about hunger;
if you relax your punishments and administration,
then the people will not fear death;
if you undertake projects at the right times,
then the people will not be exhausted by labor.”
Huán Gōng said:
“I have heard Zhòngfù’s words on these three matters;
I have received the instruction.
I do not dare to act on my own authority,
I shall present them to the former lords.”
Thereupon he ordered the various officials and functionaries
to shave the wooden tablets
and prepare ink and brushes.
The next day,
all attended the court at the gate of the Tàimiào,
and established orders for the various officials.
He made the tax one zhōng out of a hundred,
orphans and the young were not punished,
marshes and bridges were opened at the proper times,
customs posts inspected but did not collect tolls,
marketplaces recorded but did not levy taxes,
those nearby were shown loyalty and trustworthiness,
those afar were shown ritual and righteousness.
After practicing this for several years,
the people flocked to him like flowing water.
After this,
Sòng attacked Qǐ,
the Dí attacked Xíng and Wèi;
Huán Gōng did not go to their aid,
but bared his body, bound his chest, and claimed illness.
He summoned Guǎn Zhòng and said:
“I have food for a thousand years,
but not a lifespan of a hundred years;
now that I am ill,
let us enjoy ourselves for a while!”
Guǎn Zǐ said:
“Agreed.”
Thereupon he ordered the frames for bells and chimes to be hung,
arranged the music of songs, dances, reed pipes, and zithers,
and killed dozens of oxen every day for several weeks.
The gathered ministers came forward to remonstrate, saying:
“Sòng is attacking Qǐ,
and the Dí are attacking Xíng and Wèi;
the Lord cannot fail to save them.”
Huán Gōng said:
“I have food for a thousand years,
but not a lifespan of a hundred years;
now I am ill besides,
let us enjoy ourselves for a while!
Moreover, they are not attacking my state;
they are attacking neighboring states;
you have no business with this.”
Sòng had already taken Qǐ,
and the Dí had already captured Xíng and Wèi.
Huán Gōng rose
and walked between the sǔnjù stands.
Guǎn Zǐ followed him,
and when they reached the west of the great bell,
Huán Gōng stood facing south,
and Guǎn Zhòng stood facing north opposite him.
The great bell sounded.
Huán Gōng leaned toward Guǎn Zǐ and said:
“Is it not joyful,
Zhòngfù?”
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"This is what your servant calls sorrow,
not joy.
Your servant has heard
that when the ancients spoke of joy among the bells and chimes, it was not like this.
When words left their mouths,
their orders were carried out throughout the world;
they enjoyed themselves among the bells and chimes
without the worry of military conflict on all sides.
Now, in your Highness's case,
when words leave your mouth,
your orders cannot be carried out throughout the world;
while among the bells and chimes,
you have the worry of military conflict on all sides.
This is what your servant calls sorrow,
not joy."
Lord Huán said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, he dismantled the racks for bells and chimes
and dismissed the musical performances of song and dance.
The palace became empty and silent.
Lord Huán said:
"I have dismantled the racks for bells and chimes
and dismissed the musical performances of song and dance;
may I ask, starting with the state,
what course of action should be taken?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Sòng has attacked Qǐ,
and the Dí have attacked Xíng and Wèi,
yet your Highness does not rescue them.
Your servant asks to offer congratulations on this.
Your servant has heard
that when the feudal lords struggle for power,
do not share in their struggle for power.
Now, why does your Highness not settle the residences of the three lords?"
At this, Lord Huán said:
"Agreed."
He then ordered one hundred chariots
and one thousand soldiers
to enfeoff Qǐ at Yuánlíng;
one hundred chariots
and one thousand soldiers
to enfeoff Xíng at Yíyí;
five hundred chariots
and five thousand soldiers
to enfeoff Wèi at Chǔqiū.
Lord Huán said:
"I have settled the residences of the three lords;
now, what should be done next?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Your servant has heard that if the feudal lords are greedy for profit,
do not share in their pursuit of profit.
Why does your Highness not dispatch tiger and leopard skins and patterned silks to the feudal lords
and order them to reciprocate with plain silk and deerskins?"
Lord Huán said:
"Agreed."
Thereupon, he sent tiger and leopard skins and patterned silks to the feudal lords,
and the feudal lords reciprocated with plain silk and deerskins.
Thus, his orders began to be firmly carried out throughout the world.
After this, the people of Chǔ attacked Sòng and Zhèng.
They burned and scorched
the lands of Zhèng,
so that the destroyed city walls could not be rebuilt,
and the burned houses could not be repaired;
they caused the people to lose their mates,
living in dwellings like birds and rats in holes.
They seized the fields of Sòng
and dammed up the two rivers,
preventing the water from flowing eastward.
To the west of Dōngshān,
the water was so deep it submerged the hills;
it was only after four hundred lǐ that farming was possible.
Chǔ wished to swallow Sòng and Zhèng but feared Qí,
thinking that if there were many people and strong soldiers who could harm them,
it must be Qí.
Thereupon, the King of Chǔ issued an order within his state, saying:
"Among the rulers of men known to me,
none is like Lord Huán;
among the servants of men who are worthy,
none is like Guǎn Zhòng.
Enlightened is their ruler and worthy is their minister;
I wish to serve them.
Whoever can establish relations with Qí for me,
I will not begrudge them a title of marquis."
Thereupon, the worthy scholars of the state of Chǔ all carried their heavy treasures and silks to serve Qí.
Among the attendants of Lord Huán,
there was none who did not receive heavy treasures and silks.
Then Lord Huán summoned Guǎn Zhòng and said:
"I have heard
that for those who are good to others,
others will also be good to them.
Now the King of Chǔ's goodness toward me is extreme;
if I am not good in return,
I will be straying from the Way.
Why does Zhòngfù not proceed to establish relations with Chǔ?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"You must not.
The people of Chǔ attacked Sòng and Zhèng:
they burned and scorched the lands of Zhèng,
so that the destroyed city walls could not be rebuilt,
and the burned houses could not be repaired;
they caused the people to lose their mates,
living in dwellings like birds and rats in holes.
They seized the fields of Sòng
and dammed up the two rivers,
preventing the water from flowing eastward.
To the west of Dōngshān,
the water was so deep it submerged the hills;
it was only after four hundred lǐ that farming was possible.
Chǔ wishes to swallow Sòng and Zhèng,
and thinking of those with many people and strong soldiers
who can harm them,
it must be Qí.
This is a desire to overcome Qí through diplomatic means
while taking Sòng and Zhèng through military force.
If Chǔ takes Sòng and Zhèng
and we do not stop them,
then we lose Sòng and Zhèng;
if we forbid it,
then we are unfaithful to Chǔ.
To have our wisdom fail internally
and our soldiers exhausted externally
is not a good course of action."
Lord Huán said:
"Excellent.
If that is so, then what should be done?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"I request that we raise troops and go south to preserve Sòng and Zhèng,
and issue an order saying: 'Do not attack Chǔ;
we wish to meet with the King of Chǔ.'
When we reach the meeting,
we shall make requests regarding the walls of Zhèng and the waters of Sòng.
If Chǔ agrees,
then we have commanded them through diplomatic means;
if Chǔ does not agree,
then we shall proceed to command them through military force."
Lord Huán said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, he raised troops and went south to preserve Sòng and Zhèng,
meeting the King of Chǔ at Zhàolíng,
and at the meeting he issued an order saying:
"Do not hoard grain,
do not build crooked dikes,
do not arbitrarily depose rightful heirs,
and do not make concubines into wives."
He then made requests to Chǔ regarding the walls of Zhèng and the waters of Sòng.
The people of Chǔ did not agree.
He then withdrew seventy lǐ and encamped.
He ordered his soldiers to wall the southern lands of Zhèng,
establishing the Bǎidài City there.
He said:
"From here northward
to the Hé,
let Zhèng build its own walls,
and Chǔ shall not dare to destroy them."
In the east, they cleared the fields of Sòng,
opened the two rivers,
and made the water flow eastward again,
and Chǔ did not dare to dam them up.
Then he attacked Chǔ in the south,
crossed Fāngchéng,
crossed the Rǔ River,
gazed at Wènshān,
and summoned the rulers of Wú and Yuè in the south.
He attacked Qín in the west,
attacked the Dí in the north,
and preserved the Lord of Jìn in the east and south,
attacked Gūzhú in the north,
and on his return preserved the Lord of Yān.
He held six assemblies of war chariots,
three assemblies of peace chariots;
nine times he unified the feudal lords
and returned to his position having achieved hegemony;
he restored the bells and chimes and resumed the music.
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"This is what your servant calls joy."
The form of a Bà Wáng,
models itself after Tiān and takes Dì as its law;
he transforms the people and changes the era,
establishes institutions for the world,
ranks the Zhūhóu,
makes those within the four seas his guests and subjects,
and periodically rectifies the world;
he diminishes large states,
rectifies crooked states,
weakens strong states,
and lightens heavy states;
he annexes chaotic states,
and destroys tyrannical Wáng:
he punishes their crimes,
lowers their rank,
secures their people,
and only then rules over them as Wáng.
One who enriches the state is called a Bà,
and one who integrates and rectifies states is called a Wáng.
A Wáng possesses a unique brilliance.
He does not take from those whose virtue is equal to his,
and he does not rule as Wáng over those whose Dào is the same as his.
One who contends for the world
uses prestige to replace danger and tyranny;
this is the constant practice of a Wáng.
There is a Dào for those who rule people,
and there is a proper time for Bà and Wáng.
When one's own state is cultivated while neighboring states are without the Dào,
this is the capital of a Bà or Wáng.
The preservation of a state
depends on neighboring states;
the downfall of a state
also depends on neighboring states.
When a neighboring state has troubles,
its neighbor gains from it;
when a neighboring state has troubles,
its neighbor may perish because of it.
When the world has troubles,
then a Shèngwáng benefits.
When a state is in danger,
then a Shèngrén knows it.
The reason Xiānwáng were able to rule as Wáng
was by capitalizing on the improper actions of neighboring states.
If actions are improper,
this is how neighboring enemies achieve their aims.
One who wishes to exercise the power of the world
must first distribute virtue among the Zhūhóu.
Therefore, the Xiānwáng had things they took and things they gave,
things they yielded and things they asserted,
and only then could they exercise the power of the world.
Military force relies on power,
and power relies on the land.
Thus, among the Zhūhóu, those who gain the advantages of the land
will have power follow them;
those who lose the advantages of the land
will have power leave them.
One who contends for the world
must first contend for people.
One who understands the great principles gains people;
one who scrutinizes small schemes loses people.
One who gains the masses of the world becomes a Wáng;
one who gains half of them becomes a Bà.
Therefore, the Shèngwáng uses humble rituals to lower himself before the world's worthies and appoints them,
and uses fair distribution to attract the world's masses and make them his subjects.
Thus, though his rank is as noble as the Tiānzǐ,
and his wealth encompasses the world,
the world does not call him greedy
because his great plan is preserved.
Using the wealth of the world
to benefit the people of the world;
using the display of brilliant prestige
to unite the power of the world;
using the practice of perfect virtue
to forge ties of kinship with the Zhūhóu;
using the punishment of the wicked and flatterers
to discipline the hearts of the world;
relying on the prestige of the world
to expand the military expeditions of a brilliant Wáng;
attacking rebellious and chaotic states,
rewarding the labor of those with merit;
enfeoffing the virtue of the worthy and sagely,
and making the conduct of the One Man clear—then the Bǎixìng will be settled.
When the Xiānwáng took the world,
how skillfully they used great virtue!
It was what is called benefiting all things.
One who makes the state constantly free of trouble
so that fame and benefit arrive together
is a Shénshèng;
when a state is on the brink of ruin,
one who can make it endure
is a Míngshèng.
Therefore, those whom the Xiānwáng took as their teachers
were the Shénshèng;
those whom they rewarded
were the Míngshèng.
A single word that makes a state endure,
or the refusal to listen which leads to a state's ruin—
such are the words of a Dàshèng.
What a brilliant Wáng lightly regards are horses and jade;
what he highly regards are governance and the military.
If a failing ruler is not like this,
he lightly gives others governance
but is heavy-handed in giving others horses;
he lightly gives others the military
but is heavy-handed in giving others jade;
he values the construction of palace gates
but lightly regards the defense of the four borders;
this is why his territory is carved away.
Power
is that which the Shénshèng relies upon.
Unique brilliance
is the world's sharpest tool;
unique decisiveness
is a subtle and dense fortress.
These two are what the Shèngrén takes as his model.
The Shèngrén fears the subtle
while the fool fears the obvious.
The hatred of the Shèngrén is internal,
while the hatred of the fool is external.
When the Shèngrén is about to act,
he is certain to know;
the fool, even when extreme danger arrives, does not withdraw.
The Shèngrén can assist the times
but cannot go against the times.
The wise are good at planning,
but that is not as good as meeting the right time.
One who is expert in the times achieves much success in few days.
Plans without a master lead to distress,
and affairs without preparation lead to failure.
Therefore, the Shèngwáng makes it his business to complete his preparations
and cautiously observes the proper time.
Using preparation to wait for the time,
using the time to initiate affairs,
and when the time arrives, he raises his troops.
He overcomes the strong to attack states,
shatters the large to control the land,
making the root great and the branches small,
and with a nearby base, he attacks the distant.
Using the large to pull the small,
using the strong to employ the weak,
using the many to overcome the few,
his virtue benefits the Bǎixìng,
and his prestige shakes the world;
his orders are carried out among the Zhūhóu without opposition;
those near all submit,
and those far away all obey.
That a brilliant Wáng serves as the standard for the world is a matter of principle.
He restrains the strong and aids the weak,
fends off the tyrannical and stops the greedy,
preserves those perishing and stabilizes those in danger,
and continues lineages that have been cut off;
this is what the world supports,
what the Zhūhóu join with,
and what the Bǎixìng benefit from;
therefore, the world makes him Wáng.
One whose wisdom covers the world,
whose decisiveness is the greatest of the age,
and whose talent shakes the four seas
is an assistant to a Wáng.
If a state of a thousand chariots attains its proper defense,
the Zhūhóu can be made its subjects
and the world can be possessed.
If a state of ten thousand chariots loses its proper defense,
the state is no longer one's own state.
If the world is all well-ordered
while one's own state alone is in chaos,
the state is no longer one's own state;
if the Zhūhóu are all allied
while one is alone and isolated,
the state is no longer one's own state;
if neighboring states are all strategic and difficult
while one's own state alone is easy to invade,
the state is no longer one's own state.
These three
are the omens of a falling state.
Now, when a state is large
but its governance is petty,
the state will follow its governance.
When a state is small but its governance is grand,
the state will grow ever larger.
To be large but not to act
leads back to being small.
To be strong but not to maintain order
leads back to being weak.
To be populous but not to maintain order
leads back to being few.
To be noble but without ritual propriety
leads back to being base.
To be significant but to overstep constraints
leads back to being insignificant.
To be wealthy but arrogant and unrestrained
leads back to being poor.
Therefore, those who observe a state observe its ruler.
Those who observe an army observe its general.
Those who observe preparedness observe the countryside.
If the ruler appears enlightened
but is not actually enlightened,
if the general appears worthy
but is not actually worthy,
if the people appear to be farmers
but are not actually farming,
once these three defenses are lost,
the state is no longer its state.
When the land is vast but not utilized,
it is called "excess of soil."
When the people are numerous but not governed,
it is called "excess of people."
When the military has prestige but is not righteous,
it is called "excess of martiality."
If these three excesses are not halted,
the state is no longer its state.
If the land is vast but not tilled,
it is not one's own land.
If a high official is noble but does not act as a subject,
he is not one's own official.
If the people are numerous but not loyal,
they are not one's own people.
One who lacks land but desires wealth will have sorrow.
One who lacks virtue but desires to be a king will face danger.
One who bestows little but seeks much will be isolated.
When those above are restrictive and those below are treacherous,
or when the state is small but the capital is large, there will be assassinations.
When the ruler is honored and the subjects are humble,
when those above have authority and those below are respectful,
when orders are carried out and the people are submissive,
it is the height of governance.
If the world were to have two Sons of Heaven,
the world could not be governed.
If a state has two rulers,
the state cannot be governed.
If a household has two fathers,
the household cannot be governed.
As for orders, if they are not elevated, they will not be carried out;
if they are not focused, they will not be heard.
The people of Yáo and Shùn
were not born orderly.
The people of Jié and Zhòu
were not born disorderly.
Therefore, order or disorder depends on those above.
In the beginning of Hegemony or Kingship,
one takes the people as the foundation.
When the foundation is orderly, the state is solid.
When the foundation is disorderly, the state is in danger.
Therefore, when those above are enlightened, those below are respectful.
When governance is fair, the people are at peace.
When the officers are taught harmony,
then the army will overcome the enemy.
Employing the capable
leads to the management of all affairs.
Being close to the benevolent
prevents danger to the one above.
Appointing the worthy
results in the submission of the feudal lords.
In the manifestation of Hegemony or Kingship:
virtue and righteousness overcome others;
wisdom and strategy overcome others;
military battle overcomes others;
geographical terrain overcomes others;
actions and movements overcome others.
Thus, one reigns as a king.
Those who are good at employing the state
take advantage of the weight of a large state
to use its own momentum to diminish it.
They take advantage of the authority of a strong state
to use its own momentum to weaken it.
They take advantage of the form of a significant state
to use its own momentum to slight it.
If strong states are many,
unite with the strong to attack the weak
to seek Hegemony.
If strong states are few,
unite with the small to attack the large
to seek Kingship.
If strong states are many,
yet one speaks of the potential for Kingship,
that is the wisdom of a fool.
If strong states are few,
yet one implements the Way of Hegemony,
that is a plan that ruins affairs.
The divinely sagacious observe the situation of the world
and know the timing of movement and stillness.
They observe the balance of priority
and know the gates of calamity and fortune.
When strong states are many,
the one who acts first is in danger,
and the one who acts later profits.
When strong states are few,
the one who acts first becomes King,
and the one who acts later perishes.
When warring states are many,
acting later can lead to Hegemony.
When warring states are few,
acting first can lead to Kingship.
The heart of a King
is upright but not extreme.
In rank, he does not yield to the worthy;
the worthy do not rank themselves as subordinates choosing from a crowd;
this is to be ambitious for great matters.
In this way, the form of Kingship is great.
When the former kings contended for the world,
they did so with uprightness.
When they established it,
they did so with order and uniformity.
When they managed it,
they did so with fairness and simplicity.
Establishing governance and issuing orders
utilize the Way of Man.
Distributing ranks and emoluments
utilizes the Way of Earth.
Undertaking great affairs
utilizes the Way of Heaven.
Therefore, when the former kings campaigned,
they attacked the rebellious and not the submissive.
They attacked the treacherous and not the easy.
They attacked those who overreached and not those who had attained their place.
Within the four borders,
they employed the people with uprightness.
At the assembly of feudal lords,
they brought them together with power.
Those who were near but did not submit
were troubled through territorial matters.
Those who were far but did not listen
were endangered through strategic situation.
To be duplicitous
and then be attacked
is the martial way.
To submit
and then be spared
is the civil way.
When both the civil and martial are fulfilled,
it is virtue.
In the situation of weight, insignificance, strength, and weakness,
when the feudal lords unite, they are strong;
when they are isolated, they are weak.
Even with the talent of a Jì horse,
if a hundred horses take its place in turns,
the Jì horse will surely be exhausted.
Even if one is the strongest of a generation,
if the world attacks them,
the state will surely be weakened.
A strong state gains its position by gathering the small;
it loses it by relying on its own strength.
A small state gains its position by maintaining constraints;
it loses it by alienating the strong.
Whether a state is small or large, there are strategies;
whether it is strong or weak, there is a situation.
To make those near submit and to be stronger than those far
is the form of a King’s state.
Combining small states to attack a large one is the configuration for rival states;
attacking one coastal region from another coastal region is the configuration for the
Zhōngguó;
humbling oneself to serve a strong power to avoid punishment is the
configuration for small states.
From antiquity until today,
there has never been
one who could initiate a conflict first,
defying the times and changing the configuration,
and yet succeed in establishing merit and fame;
nor has there ever been a case where one habitually
initiates conflict first,
defies the times, and changes the configuration,
without meeting defeat.
Now, one who desires to have a minister strike a ruler and
rectify the world within the four seas
cannot take it by military force alone
to achieve the goal.
One must first settle plans and considerations,
take advantage of the terrain,
utilize the balance of power,
befriend allied states,
and act according to the timing; this is the technique of a
Wáng.
In the expeditions of the former kings,
their mobilization was surely righteous,
their application was surely swift and fierce;
they assessed the configuration to know what was possible,
measured their strength to know when to attack,
and examined gains to know the timing.
Therefore, in the expeditions of the former kings,
they would surely first battle and then attack,
and first attack and then take territory.
Thus, one who is good at attacking
estimates the numbers to attack numbers,
estimates provisions to attack provisions,
and estimates defenses to attack defenses.
Attacking numbers with numbers,
if their numbers remain, do not attack;
attacking provisions with provisions,
if their provisions remain, do not attack;
attacking defenses with defenses,
if their defenses remain, do not attack.
Abandon the substantial and attack the hollow;
abandon the hard and attack the soft;
abandon the difficult and attack the easy.
Consolidation of a state does not lie in venerating antiquity;
governing an era does not lie in following old ways;
becoming a Bà or a Wáng does not lie in established codes.
If actions fail, the state is endangered;
if punishments are excessive, authority is overturned;
if plans are changed lightly, disaster follows;
if calculations are sound, strength is trusted;
if merit is achieved, fame follows;
if power is weighty, orders are carried out—
this is certainly the natural course.
A state contending for strength
must first contend in planning, contend in strategic configuration, and contend in power.
That which causes a ruler to be now pleased and now angry is
planning;
that which makes a state now light and now heavy is
strategic configuration;
that which makes an army now advance and now retreat is
power.
Therefore, if one is refined in planning,
the ruler's wishes can be fulfilled
and orders can be implemented;
if one is refined in strategic configuration,
the territory of large states can be seized
and the armies of strong states can be repelled;
if one is refined in power,
the armies of the world can be unified
and the lords of the Zhūhóu can be made to pay court.
A divinely wise person observes the configuration of the world,
knows what the age plans,
knows what the army attacks,
knows to whom the land will return,
and knows where the orders will be applied.
If the army attacks what it hates
and benefits from it,
neighboring states will not be close.
If power is moved against what is disliked,
and reality has few to return to, that state is strong.
If one breaks a state by one's own authority
and the strength lasts for future generations, one is a Wáng.
If one breaks a state by one's own authority
and the strength benefits neighboring states, one will perish.
Whenever establishing a court,
there are fundamental records for inquiry.
If ranks are granted to the virtuous,
then high officials will promote righteousness;
if stipends are given to those with merit,
then Shì will think lightly of death for their principles;
if the superior leads the Shì with what the people support,
then those above and below will be in harmony;
if tasks are assigned based on ability,
then people will prioritize merit.
If punishments are scrutinized to fit the crimes,
then people will not lightly engage in litigation;
if the Shèjì and ancestral temples are not disturbed,
then the people will have something to revere.
If the elderly are not neglected and kin are not forgotten,
then high officials will not feel resentment;
if actions show awareness of the people's emergencies,
then the masses will not fall into disorder.
By practicing this way,
the state has constant principles,
and the people know the beginning and the end;
this is the technique of Bà and Wáng.
Thereafter, inquire into affairs:
prioritize great achievements in affairs,
but begin governance from small things.
Inquire about the orphans of those who died in service:
are there any who do not yet have fields or houses?
How many households have young and able-bodied men who are not yet capable of bearing armor and weapons?
Inquire about the widows of those who died in service:
how are their grain rations?
Inquire about those in the state with great merit:
of what office are they Lì?
Inquire about the Dàfū of the Zhōu:
from which Lǐ are these Shì?
For the current Lì, how are they distinguished?
Inquire about the application of punishments and judgments: they should be constant and
unchangeable.
How is it now regarding cases that have been delayed for a long time?
Inquire whether the five offices have regulations and systems,
and whether the capital offices have constant decisions.
What is the reason for the current delays in affairs?
Inquire how many people are solitary men, widows, orphans, destitute, or diseased.
Inquire which clans the outcasts of the state belong to.
Inquire how many people
are being cared for by the respectable families of the Xiāng.
Inquire how many households of the poor in the Yì
eat by borrowing.
How many households eat by managing gardens and orchards?
How many households of the people open fields and plow them?
How many households of Shì plow the fields themselves?
Inquire into the poor people of the Xiāng:
from which branch of which clan do they come?
Inquire about Zōngzǐ who take in their brothers:
how many households follow their brothers due to poverty?
Among the Yúzǐ who serve and have fields and Yì,
how many have come in now?
How many young men are known for their filial piety in their Xiāng and Lǐ?
How many Yúzǐ have living parents
but do not support them and have left home?
How many Shì have fields but do not make use of them?
What affairs do the Lì dislike?
How many Shì have fields but do not plow them?
What do they do personally?
Among the various ministers, how many have positions but not yet fields?
How many households of outsiders have come to follow us but do not yet have fields or houses?
How many of the state's young men are traveling abroad?
How many poor Shì are in debt to the Dàfū?
Among low-ranking officials who engage in trade,
how many go out themselves and use household retainers as their substitutes?
How many assistant officials and Lì have no fields or grain rations but manage affairs for nothing?
How many of the various ministers with rank serve the Dàfū of the offices?
Among outsiders who come to visit,
how many are in the houses of the Dàfū?
How many of the young men of the Xiāng work hard in the fields and serve as models for others?
Among the young men of the state who have no superior service,
lack moderation in food and clothing,
and lead other young men away from farming to hunt with bow and arrow, how many are there?
Are there any men and women who are not orderly
and corrupt the young people of the Xiāng?
Inquire how many households
have separate tallies for borrowing grain.
Inquire about the hidden resources of the state:
in how many places can they meet the people's emergencies?
What things cause harm to the people
in the Xiāng and Lǐ?
Inquire how many Shì who have fields and houses
are personally in the military ranks.
How many Yúzǐ are capable of bearing armor and weapons and are in the ranks of the army?
Ask how many men and women have clever skills
and are capable of providing for necessary use?
How many unmarried women perform craftwork?
Ask how many people in the state depend on others for food?
Ask how many people's worth of food a single citizen has?
Ask how many military chariots are in the calculation?
How many family horses and family chariots are yoked together?
How many scholars living in retirement practice self-cultivation,
sufficient to teach others,
and can be made to lead the masses and oversee the common people?
How many men of service can be employed during urgent crises?
Regarding the skill of artisans,
how many
are sufficient to benefit the military when sent out,
and
can repair city walls and supplement defensive preparations when staying at home?
For how many years can the grain in the city and the military rations last?
How many officials can be employed during urgent crises?
Regarding the equipment of the *Dàfū*:
How many sets of armor, weapons, chariots, banners, drums, gongs, curtains, and commander's supply wagons are there?
Regarding the equipment in storage:
The stringing of bows and crossbows, the sheaths for blades and swords, the manufacture of strings and hooks, the covers for spears and halberds—
how sharp and ready are they?
For those that should be repaired but are not,
what is the reason for this oversight?
As for the officials in charge of manufacturing and repair,
and the tools for issuing and storing equipment,
what is being waited for regarding those that should be activated but have not been?
For the local districts, the tools for manufacturing and repairing the commander's supply wagons,
how well-maintained are they?
The *Gōngyǐn* harvests materials for use,
but not during the three growing seasons.
When the various materials are harvested,
the manufacture of equipment is determined. In winter,
high-quality and complete supplies must be sufficient.
If the people have surplus weapons,
practice deceptive formations
to safeguard the state's constant order.
Regularly inspect and calculate the fatness or thinness of the lead horses and oxen;
for those that are old or dying, record them all;
how many go to the mountains, thickets, forests, and marshes to graze?
How many are the instances of entry and exit, death and birth?
Regarding the thickness of the city walls,
the depth of the moats,
the height of the gates and village entrances—
for those that should be repaired but are not,
the superiors must investigate
the units responsible for defense.
Ensure that equipment and goods do not lose their completeness,
and that each has a place for storage during heavy rains.
Ask how many officials of the military department
and heroic men of the state
are sufficient to take the lead or follow during urgent crises?
Military matters are dangerous things;
winning at the wrong time
or gaining through injustice
is not a blessing.
Failure through loss of strategy
is a danger to the state;
only by being cautious in strategy can the state be preserved.
Ask what matters are used to teach and select people?
Ask those who hold office in the capital
how many years they have held their positions and tasks?
How much wasteland has been cleared,
and how much benefit has been brought to the families and towns?
What things have been demarcated
to increase the people's livelihoods?
Where are the city walls built, the walls and gates repaired, the thoroughfares cut off, the narrow passes and gate-towers deepened, and the moats and dikes constructed
to increase the land's defense for the people
How many thieves and robbers have been captured, and how many harms to the people removed?
Regulating the Land.
The Sovereign says:
In the way of governing a state,
the virtue of the land is primary.
The rites of ruler and minister,
the affection between father and son,
the nurturing of the myriad people,
the storehouses of the government offices,
the strengthening of the army to preserve the state,
the strategic advantages of city walls,
and responding externally to the four cardinal directions—
all these are obtained from the land.
The market is where the wealth and goods of heaven and earth gather.
It is what the myriad people harmonize and profit from;
this is the proper way.
When the people's fields are neglected, do not be harsh;
when people fulfill the duties of the land,
they uniquely preserve their state.
Let each be master of their different positions,
and do not let slanderers disrupt the social order,
so that virtue may manage the affection of the nine armies.
Customs passes
are the corner paths for the Feudal Lords
and the gateways for external wealth,
through which the myriad people travel.
Make the way clear and repeat the instructions:
Those taxed at the customs passes
should not be taxed at the market;
those taxed at the market
should not be taxed at the customs passes.
Do not demand taxes from empty carts,
and do not tax those carrying loads on foot,
in order to attract people from afar.
Then the sixteen roads will act as one body.
When external affairs are handled with care,
then listen
to their reputations, ,
observe their countenances,
verify their deeds,
and examine their virtue
to observe their external conduct.
Then do not be oppressive toward those in power,
so as not to distress those of appearance and virtue.
The state will then not be confused;
this is the duty of conduct.
Ask the border officials, saying:
Small gains harm trust,
small anger harms righteousness,
and a lack of trust at the borders harms virtue.
Cultivate deep harmony with the four surrounding states
to follow and complete virtue,
and then face toward the four cardinal directions.
Command the officials who uphold the law, saying:
The standards of conduct must be clear,
and do not lose the constant norms.
(Text missing).
The Duke was about to travel to the east.
He asked *Guǎn Zhòng*, saying:
"My travel to the east will be like a grain measure rolling along,
reaching *Lángyé* in the south.
The *Sīmǎ* says,
'This is simply the travel of the former kings.'
What does this mean?"
*Guǎn Zhòng* replied:
"In the travel of the former kings,
going out in spring
to examine those whose agricultural matters were not fundamental
was called an excursion;
going out in autumn
to supplement what the people lacked
was called a sunset inspection.
When an army marches and consumes the people's food,
it is called a drain;
following pleasure without returning
is called dissipation.
The former kings had the work of excursions and sunset inspections for the people,
but they did not have the conduct of dissipation or drain for themselves."
*Huángōng* withdrew, bowed twice, and gave the command, saying:
"This is a precious law!"
*Guǎn Zhòng* further said to *Huángōng*:
"That which flies without wings is reputation;
that which is firm without roots is sentiment;
that which is noble without being established is life.
May Your Grace solidify sentiment and be careful with reputation,
in order to strictly honor life;
this is called the glory of the *Dào*."
*Huángōng* withdrew
and bowed twice:
"I request to follow these words."
*Guǎn Zhòng* further said to *Huángōng*:
"Of heavy responsibilities, none is greater than one's person;
of fearsome paths, none is greater than the mouth;
of long-term goals that are distant, none is greater than the year.
To walk a fearsome path with a heavy responsibility and reach a distant goal,
only a *jūnzi* is capable of this."
Huán Gōng retired,
bowed twice to him and said:
“You have taught me with these words many times.”
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
“Flavors, movement, and stillness
are the nourishment of life;
likes and dislikes, joy and anger, sorrow and happiness,
are the variations of life;
keenness of hearing and sight in accord with things
is the virtue of life.
Therefore, the Sage balances flavors and times movement and stillness,
governs the changes of the six qi correctly,
prohibits the excesses of sounds and colors,
so that corrupt behavior is absent from the body,
and perverse words do not remain in the mouth;
being tranquil and stabilizing life,
this is being a Sage.
Benevolence comes from within;
Righteousness acts from without.
Because of Benevolence, one does not use the world for personal profit;
because of Righteousness, one does not use the world for personal fame.
Because of Benevolence, one does not replace the King;
because of Righteousness, one returns the government at seventy.
Therefore, the Sage values virtue above achievement
and honors the Way while making light of material things.
When Way and Virtue are present in the person,
one is not deluded by things.
For this reason,
even when living among the grass and reeds,
there is no feeling of fear;
when facing south and ruling the world,
there is no look of pride.
Only in this way
can one become the King of the world.
That which is called Virtue
moves swiftly without moving,
is known without being told,
is completed without being made,
and arrives without being summoned;
this is Virtue.
Thus, Heaven does not move,
yet the four seasons rotate below,
and the myriad things are transformed;
the ruler does not move,
yet administrative orders are set forth below,
and the myriad achievements are completed;
the heart does not move,
yet the four limbs, ears, and eyes are employed,
and the essence of the myriad things is reached.
Having few interactions but many intimates
is called knowing people.
Undertaking few affairs but achieving success
is called knowing how to use things.
Hearing one word and using it to thread through the myriad things
is called knowing the Way.
To speak much but inappropriately
is not as good as speaking little;
to be broadly learned but not self-reflective
will surely lead to deviance.
Filial piety and fraternal love are
the ancestors of Benevolence;
loyalty and trustworthiness
are the standards of social interaction.
If internally one does not practice filial piety and fraternal love,
and externally one does not rectify loyalty and trustworthiness,
yet polishes the four classics and recites studies,
this is someone who will bring ruin to their own person.
The next day, Huán Gōng was hunting with arrows in the granary area;
Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng came to court.
The Duke saw the two gentlemen,
unstrung his bow, removed his arm guard,
and welcomed them, saying:
“Now, as for the swan geese, they go north in spring and south in autumn
without missing their time.
Is it not because they have wings to communicate their intent throughout the world?
Now, that I have not achieved my intent in the world,
is this not the concern of you two?”
Huán Gōng spoke twice,
but the two gentlemen did not reply.
Huán Gōng said:
“I have already spoken;
why do you two not reply?”
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
“Now, the people suffer from toil,
yet those above employ them out of season;
the people suffer from hunger,
yet those above tax them heavily;
the people suffer from death,
yet those above are hasty with punishments.
Under such conditions,
and if you furthermore stay close to sensual beauty
and remain distant from virtue,
even if you had the wings of a swan goose
or the boat and oars to cross great waters,
what could they do for you, my Lord?”
Huán Gōng looked uneasy and stepped back.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
“Formerly, when the ancient kings governed the people,
because the people suffered from toil,
those above employed them according to the seasons,
and so the people did not suffer from toil;
the people suffered from hunger,
and those above made taxes light,
and so the people did not suffer from hunger;
the people suffered from death,
and those above were lenient with punishments,
and so the people did not suffer from death.
In this way,
being close to virtue
and distant from sensual beauty,
those within the four borders
will look upon their ruler as their father and mother!
And those outside the four directions
will flock to the ruler like flowing water!”
The Duke stopped shooting, took the mounting strap, and boarded his carriage.
He drove it himself,
with Guǎn Zhòng on the left,
and Xí Péng as the third passenger.
After fasting for three days,
he presented the two gentlemen at the ancestral temple,
bowed twice, touched his head to the ground, and said:
“Since I have heard the words of these two gentlemen,
my ears have become keener and my sight clearer;
I do not dare to listen to them alone,
so I present them to my ancestors.”
Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng bowed twice, touched their heads to the ground, and said:
“That your Lordship will rule as King
is not due to our words,
but due to your Lordship’s own instruction.”
Thereupon Guǎn Zhòng and Huán Gōng made a covenant and issued an order saying:
“Do not punish the old and the weak;
grant three amnesties before executing any punishment;
inspect the passes but do not tax them;
regulate the markets but do not tax goods.
Regarding mountains, forests, weirs, and marshes,
open and close them according to the seasons
without taxing them.”
Those from the wilderness and salt marshes who flocked to him
were as numerous as people in a marketplace.
For three years he educated the people;
in the fourth year he selected the worthy to be leaders;
in the fifth year he began to mobilize the chariots and teams.
Then he attacked Chǔ in the south,
reaching the city of Shī.
He attacked the Shān Róng in the north,
bringing back winter onions and Róng beans,
and distributed them throughout the world.
Consequently, he thrice set the Son of Heaven right and nine times assembled the feudal lords.
Huán Gōng stayed in an outer residence
and did not have his meals served from the tripod;
Zhōngfù Zhūzǐ said to the palace attendants:
“Why do you not go out and follow him?
The Lord is about to go on a journey.”
The palace attendants all went out to follow him.
The Duke said angrily:
“Who said that I am going on a journey?”
The palace attendants said:
“Your humble servants heard it from Zhōngfù Zhūzǐ.”
The Duke summoned Zhōngfù Zhūzǐ and asked:
“How did you hear that I am going on a journey?”
She replied:
“I heard that
when a ruler stays in an outer residence and does not have meals served from the tripod,
if he does not have internal worries,
he must have external concerns.
Now you stay in an outer residence and do not have meals served from the tripod,
and you do not have internal worries,
so I knew that you were about to go on a journey.”
The Duke said:
“Good.
This was not something I intended to discuss with you,
but since your words have reached this point,
I will tell you.
I wish to assemble the feudal lords, but they do not come.
What should I do about it?”
Zhōngfù Zhūzǐ said:
"Since I have not allowed my person to be handled or touched by others,
nor have I ever received cloth woven by others,
is it possible that my appearance is not properly cared for?"
The next day,
Guǎn Zhòng attended court,
and the Duke told him of this.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"These are the words of a sage;
Your Lordship must put them into practice."
Guǎn Zhòng was ill in bed,
and Huán Gōng went to inquire of him, saying:
"Zhòngfù’s illness is severe.
If what cannot be spoken of should happen,
and you unfortunately do not recover from this illness,
to whom shall I transfer the government?"
Guǎn Zhòng did not yet respond.
Huán Gōng said:
"What is Bǎo Shū’s character like?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Bǎo Shū is a superior man.
Even a state of a thousand chariots,
if not given through the proper Way,
he would not
accept it.
Although this is so, he cannot be put in charge of the government.
As a man,
he loves good and hates evil excessively;
if he sees one evil deed, he never forgets it for the rest of his life."
Huán Gōng asked:
"If so, then who will do?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Xí Péng will do.
As for Péng’s character,
he values the knowledge of those above him and inquires of those below him.
I have heard that
one who gives to people through virtue
is called benevolent;
one who gives to people through wealth
is called good.
One who overcomes people with goodness
has never been able to make them submit;
one who nurtures people with goodness
has never failed to make them submit.
Regarding the state, there are matters of administration he does not know;
regarding the family, there are matters of affairs he does not know—
surely he must be enlightened!
Furthermore, as for Péng’s character,
while staying at home, he does not forget the public gates;
while at the public gates, he does not forget his home;
in serving his lord, he is not of two minds,
yet he does not forget his own person.
Even if he were to raise the currency of the entire state of Qí
and control fifty households of the powerful houses,
the people would not know of it.
How great is his benevolence!
That is Péng!
The Duke asked again:
"If I unfortunately lose Zhòngfù,
will the two or three ministers
still be able to keep the state peaceful?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Will Your Lordship please observe them?
Bǎo Shūyá’s character is to love uprightness;
Bīn Xūwú’s character is to love goodness;
Nìng Qī’s character is to be capable in affairs;
Sūn Sù’s character is to be good at speaking."
The Duke said:
"Among these four men,
who can be the foremost among men?
If I employ them all together as ministers,
why would they not be able to keep the state peaceful?
Why is that?"
He replied:
"Bǎo Shū’s character is to love uprightness,
but he cannot bend for the sake of the state;
Bīn Xūwú’s character is to love goodness,
but he cannot bend for the sake of the state;
Nìng Qī’s character is to be capable in affairs,
but he cannot rest when satisfied;
Sūn Sù’s character is to be good at speaking,
but he cannot remain silent despite being trustworthy.
I have heard that
only by following the ebb and flow, the waxing and waning,
and bending or stretching along with the common people,
can one bring peace to the state.
For one who does not cease,
could it be Péng?
As for Péng’s character,
his movements always measure his strength,
and his actions always measure his skill."
When he finished speaking,
he sighed deeply and said:
"When Heaven gave birth to Péng,
it was to serve as Yíwú’s tongue;
if the body dies,
how can the tongue survive?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"The states of Jiāng and Huáng are close to Chǔ.
If I, your servant, die,
Your Lordship must return them to Chǔ and entrust them there;
if Your Lordship does not return them,
Chǔ will surely take them for itself.
If they take them and you do not rescue them,
that would not do;
if you do rescue them,
then disorder will begin from this."
Huán Gōng said:
"Agreed."
Guǎn Zhòng further said:
"In the eastern outskirts, there is a snarling dog;
day and night it wishes to bite me,
but I restrain it and do not allow it.
Now as for Yì Yá,
he could not love his own son;
how could he love his lord?
Your Lordship must remove him."
The Duke said:
"Agreed."
Guǎnzǐ further said:
"In the northern outskirts, there is a snarling dog;
day and night it wishes to bite me,
but I restrain it and do not allow it.
Now as for Shù Diāo,
he did not love his own body;
how could he love his lord?
Your Lordship must remove him."
The Duke said:
"Agreed."
Guǎnzǐ further said:
"In the western outskirts, there is a snarling dog;
day and night it wishes to bite me,
but I restrain it and do not allow it.
Now as for Prince Kāifāng of Wèi,
he left his position as the crown prince of a state of a thousand chariots
to serve Your Lordship as a subject;
this is what he desired.
What he obtains from Your Lordship will be that which he desires even more than his thousand-chariot state.
Your Lordship must remove him."
Huán Gōng said:
"Agreed."
Guǎnzǐ then died.
Ten months after his death,
Xí Péng also died.
Huán Gōng removed Yì Yá, Shù Diāo, and Prince Kāifāng of Wèi.
But since the five flavors did not arrive,
he then brought back Yì Yá;
the inner palace fell into disorder,
so he brought back Shù Diāo;
when profitable words and humble speech were not by his side,
he brought back Prince Kāifāng of Wèi.
Internally, Huán Gōng did not measure his own strength,
and externally, he did not measure his alliances,
but forcefully attacked his four neighbors.
The Duke passed away.
His six sons all sought to be established.
Yì Yá and the Prince of Wèi
conspired within with Shù Diāo;
consequently, they together killed the various officials
and established Prince Wúkuī.
Thus, the Duke was not coffined for sixty-seven days after his death
and was not buried for nine months.
Xiào Gōng fled to Sòng,
and Xiāng Gōng of Sòng led the feudal lords to attack Qí;
they fought at Yǎn,
greatly defeating the Qí army,
killing Prince Wúkuī,
and returned after establishing Xiào Gōng.
Xiāng Gōng reigned for thirteen years;
Huán Gōng reigned for forty-two years.
In all matters of being a commander of the military,
one must first carefully examine and know the maps.
The narrows of Huànyuán,
the waters of Lànchē,
the locations of famous mountains, traversable valleys, major rivers, ridges, plains, and hills;
where thick grass, forests, and reeds flourish;
the distances of the routes;
the size of the inner and outer city walls;
and the locations of famous cities, abandoned cities, and fertile or barren lands;
all of these must be fully known.
The interlocking intricacies of the terrain's layout
must all be kept in mind.
Only then can one move the army and attack cities,
knowing the proper order of priorities in every action,
and not losing the advantages of the terrain.
This is the constant rule of the map.
The number of people,
the quality of the soldiers,
and the craftsmanship of the equipment—knowing all these fully
constitutes knowing the "form."
Knowing the form is not as good as knowing the capability;
knowing the capability is not as good as knowing the intent.
Therefore, the commander of the military must possess the "three components."
A wise ruler, an understanding chancellor, and a capable general are what are called the three components.
Thus, when the general issues orders and dispatches soldiers,
the timeframe is already set;
once the country to be campaigned against is determined,
ensuring that the various ministers, high officials, elders, and close attendants cannot debate success or failure
is the responsibility of the sovereign.
Evaluating merit and labor,
executing rewards and punishments,
not daring to obscure the worthy out of personal bias;
managing wealth and resources to provide for the army's requirements,
ensuring all officials are solemn and respectful,
and not daring to be idle or act wickedly
while awaiting the ruler's commands—
this is the responsibility of the Prime Minister.
Repairing weapons and equipment,
selecting and training soldiers,
establishing drills and discipline,
organizing the units of five and ten,
having comprehensive knowledge of the world,
and carefully managing the turning points of strategy—
these are the duties of the military commander.
For any sovereign,
being too fierce leads to being attacked,
and being too weak leads to being killed.
What is meant by being "fierce"?
Making light of punishing and killing people is called being fierce.
What is meant by being "weak"?
Hesitating too much to punish or kill is called being weak.
Both of these involve a failure of balance.
Generally, those who make light of punishment kill the innocent,
and those who hesitate to punish lose hold of the guilty.
Therefore, if those above kill the innocent,
then those on the upright path will feel insecure;
if those above lose hold of the guilty,
then those who act wickedly will not change.
If those on the upright path are insecure,
then talented people will flee;
if those who act wickedly do not change,
then the officials will form factions.
If talented people flee,
then there will surely be external difficulties;
if officials form factions,
then there will surely be internal chaos.
Therefore it is said: the fierce are attacked,
and the weak are killed.
The means by which a ruler is humbled or honored,
and the means by which a state is secured or endangered,
nothing is more critical than the military.
Thus, punishing a tyrannical state must be done with the military,
and restraining deviant people must be done with punishments.
Consequently, the military is used externally to punish the tyrannical,
and internally to restrain the wicked.
Therefore, the military is the fundamental principle for honoring the ruler and securing the state;
it cannot be discarded.
As for the common rulers of the age, they do not act this way.
Externally, they do not use the military
yet wish to punish the tyrannical,
so their territory will certainly be diminished;
internally, they do not use punishments
yet wish to restrain the wicked,
so their state will certainly fall into chaos.
Therefore, in all calculations of military deployment,
three "alarms" are equal to one "arrival,"
three arrivals are equal to one "army,"
and three armies are equal to one "battle."
Thus, one year of military campaigning
exhausts ten years of accumulated savings;
the cost of a single battle
consumes the achievements of several generations.
If one only seeks advantage after the blades have crossed and the soldiers have engaged,
then one has already defeated oneself in battle.
When attacking a city and surrounding a town,
if the inhabitants exchange children to eat them
and split bones for firewood,
then the attack has achieved its own conquest.
Therefore, the Sages conduct small expeditions for great rectifications;
they do not lose the timing of Heaven,
nor do they waste the advantages of the Earth;
they choose their days as if interpreting dreams;
their methods do not go beyond calculation.
Therefore, the plan must be fixed first before the army crosses the border.
If the plan is not fixed and the army crosses the border,
then one's own battle will fail,
and one's own attack will be ruined.
To gain the multitude but not their hearts
is the same as walking alone;
if weapons are not sharp and complete,
it is the same as having none to wield;
if armor is not strong and tight,
it is the same as being unarmored;
if crossbows cannot reach far,
it is the same as short-range weapons;
to shoot but not hit the mark
is the same as having no arrows;
to hit but not penetrate
is the same as having no arrowheads;
a general who only commands commoners
is the same as one who is crippled;
to face long-range arrows with short-range weapons
is the same as sitting and waiting for death.
Therefore, in all military matters, there are major considerations:
one must first consider the equipment,
consider the soldiers,
consider the general,
and consider the ruler.
Thus it is said:
"If equipment is poor and blunt,
one is handing over one's soldiers to others;
if soldiers cannot be used,
one is handing over one's general to others;
if the general does not understand military affairs,
one is handing over one's ruler to others;
if the ruler does not devote effort to military matters,
one is handing over one's state to others."
Thus, when the first instrument is complete,
the means of advancing are ready,
and the world loses the will to fight;
when the second instrument is complete,
the means of striking awe are ready,
and the world loses the will to defend cities;
when the third instrument is complete,
the means of mobility are ready,
and the world loses the will to gather forces.
What is meant by "no will to fight"
is knowing that if they fight, they will surely lose;
therefore it is said they have no will to fight.
What is meant by "no will to defend cities"
therefore it is said they have no will to defend cities.
What is meant by "no will to gather forces"
is knowing that the forces will surely be scattered;
therefore it is said they have no will to gather forces.
In all matters of military priority,
Sages and worthy men
do not act for the love of noble titles;
those with methods and skills
do not act for the love of official positions;
those with clever techniques and brave strength
do not act for the love of heavy salaries;
those with keen ears and sharp eyes
do not act for the love of gold and wealth.
Thus, Bóyí and Shūqí
did not only become famous on the day they died;
their previous conduct was highly cultivated.
Wǔwáng did not only achieve victory on the morning of Jiǎzǐ;
his previous governance was filled with much goodness.
Therefore, in a small expedition, everything within a thousand lǐ is known.
A wall being built,
or a gathering of ten people,
is checked five times a day through spies.
In a large expedition,
one has comprehensive knowledge of the whole world.
Every day, five types of spies are utilized,
distributing gold and wealth
to make use of intelligence.
Therefore, those skilled in employing troops
have no need for moats or ramparts but possess ears and eyes.
Their troops do not shout warnings,
do not gather haphazardly,
do not march recklessly,
and do not advance by force.
If warnings are shouted, the enemy becomes cautious;
if they gather haphazardly, the masses cannot be utilized;
if they march recklessly, the soldiers become exhausted;
if they advance by force, the elite warriors are thwarted.
Generally, in employing troops,
attacking strength results in resistance, while attacking flaws results in divine success.
Attacking strength makes the flawed points strong;
attacking flaws makes the strong points flawed.
Therefore, strengthen their strengths,
and exploit their flaws.
When Butcher Tǎn morning-dismantled nine oxen,
his blade could be harder than iron
because the edge traveled through the gaps.
Therefore, when the Way of Heaven is not followed,
even being bent is not enough to follow;
when human affairs are in chaos,
ten can destroy a hundred;
when equipment and preparations are not maintained,
half can strike double the number.
Thus, military competition
does not depend on the completion of city walls and moats;
those who possess the Way do not operate where there is no ruler.
Therefore, let none know when they will arrive,
so that upon arrival, they cannot be resisted;
let none know when they will depart,
so that upon departure, they cannot be stopped.
Even if the enemy is numerous,
they cannot stop or wait.
Order is the path to wealth,
but order does not necessarily mean wealth;
one must know the affairs of wealth,
and only then can one become wealthy.
Wealth is the path to strength,
but wealth does not necessarily mean strength;
one must know the calculations of strength,
and only then can one become strong.
Strength is the path to victory,
but strength does not necessarily mean victory;
one must know the principles of victory,
and only then can one be victorious.
Victory is the path to control,
but victory does not necessarily mean control;
one must know the divisions of control,
and only then can one exercise control.
For this reason, for governing a state there are instruments,
for enriching a state there are affairs,
for strengthening a state there are calculations,
for a victorious state there are principles,
and for controlling the world there are divisions.
He who is a ruler of men
cultivates the way of higher officials
and does not interfere in their internal matters;
he who is a minister
attends to the matters within his office
and does not speak of matters outside it.
If the ruler's way is not clear,
those who receive orders will doubt;
if the standards and measures are not unified,
those who follow righteousness will be confused.
When the people have hearts of doubt and vacillation
and those above cannot correct them,
then the gaps among the common people
are like raising a signal and ordering them to stop.
Therefore, one who can model the Way in the state,
apply it to the common people,
and is sufficient to organize officials and transform those below,
is an enlightened ruler.
One who can speak truthfully to the sovereign above,
devote effort to the people below,
and is sufficient to cultivate righteousness and follow orders,
is a loyal minister.
If those above are kind in their way,
and those below are diligent in their tasks,
and those above and below look to each other
as if looking at a reference marker,
then the wicked can be recognized.
The Lì Sè Fū are responsible for administrative affairs,
while the Mín Sè Fū are responsible for instruction.
Instruction lies with the common people,
discourse lies in remaining unyielding,
rewards lie in faithfulness and sincerity,
embodying it through the relationship of ruler and minister,
and its sincerity
is used for defense and battle.
In this way,
the affairs of the Mín Sè Fū are fulfilled.
The Lì Sè Fū fully possess estimates, regulations, and laws for affairs,
discussing legal punishments,
balances and weights, dry and liquid measures,
and written indictments, not based on private opinion
but using the matter itself as the standard.
In this way,
the affairs of the Lì Sè Fū are fulfilled.
After the Mín Sè Fū complete instruction
and the Lì Sè Fū complete the laws,
then even those who are sincere and loyal
cannot be unfairly favored,
and those who are playful and lazy
cannot cause ruin.
In this way,
the affairs of the ruler of men are fulfilled.
Therefore, he who is a ruler of men
follows their occupations,
makes use of their affairs,
and audits them with measures.
To those who have merit,
he rewards them with the honor of noble ranks
and the abundance of land,
and the people will not be envious.
To those who have faults,
he punishes them with the disgrace of dismissal and exile
and the penalty of death,
and the people will not be resentful.
Taking and giving life does not deviate from the law,
and none of the people will abandon their kin;
this is only because those above have enlightened laws
and those below have constant tasks.
Heaven has constant phenomena,
Earth has constant forms,
and humans have constant rituals;
once established, they do not change,
and these are called the Three Constants.
To combine them into one
is the Way of the ruler of men;
to divide them into duties
is the task of the ministers.
If the ruler loses his Way,
he has no means to hold his state;
if the minister loses his task,
he has no means to hold his position.
Thus, the cultivation of those below by those above will not be reckless,
and the service of those above by those below will not be hollow.
When the cultivation of those below by those above is not reckless,
then those who issue laws and systems
are enlightened;
when the service of those above by those below is not hollow,
then those who follow righteousness and obey orders are careful.
When those above are enlightened and those below are careful,
and those above and below share the same virtue,
they succeed each other in order.
The ruler does not lose his authority,
and those below do not neglect their production,
and they do not treat each other as debtors of gratitude.
Therefore, those above strive for virtue,
and those below maintain their integrity;
rituals take shape above,
and goodness spreads below to the people;
then the common people will look up and feel close to the sovereign,
and below they will devote their full strength to agriculture.
Therefore it is said:
"When the ruler is enlightened, the ministers are trustworthy, the five offices are disciplined, the officers are incorruptible, the farmers are focused, and the merchants and artisans are honest,
then those above and below form one body,
and the external and internal are distinct;
the nature of the people is followed,
and the three social groups are regulated."
He who is a ruler of men
is one who provides the shade of virtue to others;
he who is a minister
is one who looks up to the superior for life.
He who is a superior
measures merit and provides sufficiency;
he who is a minister
receives his appointment and handles it with reverence.
When the distribution of administration is equitable,
and the people have sufficient property,
then the state will be prosperous.
If stipends are granted based on labor,
then the people will not hope for unearned survival.
If punishments and penalties are not biased,
then those below will have no resentment in their hearts.
When names are correct and distinctions are clear,
then the people will not be confused about the *Dào*.
As for the *Dào*,
it is that which the superior uses to lead the people.
Therefore,
the *Dào* and *Dé* originate from the *Jūn*,
commands are transmitted by the *Xiàng*,
tasks are measured by the *Guān*,
and the strength of the common people
moves only according to orders.
Therefore, for one who is a *Jūn*:
nothing is as precious as his words;
for those who are ministers:
nothing is as cherished as their strength.
When words descend and strength ascends,
then the way of minister and sovereign is complete.
Therefore,
the *Zhǔ* plans it,
the *Xiàng* maintains it;
the *Xiàng* plans it,
the *Guān* maintain it;
the *Guān* plan it,
the people labor at it;
then there are tallies, seals, legal codes, and registers to regulate one another.
This is the technique for clarifying the public way and eliminating treacherous falsehoods.
Evaluating talent, measuring ability, and considering *Dé* before promoting them
is the way of the superior;
focusing the mind with single-hearted purpose
and maintaining one’s office without weariness
is the duty of the subordinate.
For one who is a *Jūn*,
if he reaches down into the affairs of the *Guān*,
then the officials will not take responsibility;
for one who is a minister,
if he reaches up to monopolize the position of the superior,
then the *Zhǔ* loses his majesty.
Therefore,
a *Jūn* who possesses the *Dào*
rectifies his *Dé* to oversee the people,
and does not speak of wisdom, ability, cleverness, or intelligence.
Wisdom, ability, cleverness, and intelligence
are the duties of subordinates;
that which employs wisdom, ability, cleverness, and intelligence
is the way of the superior.
The one above
clarifies the *Dào*,
the one below
maintains his office;
the responsibilities of superior and subordinate are different,
yet they unite to form a single body.
Therefore,
knowing what is good
belongs to the *Jūn*.
Being personally good
belongs to those who are servants.
If the *Jūn* is personally good, then he is not impartial.
If the *Jūn* is not impartial,
he will be constantly generous with rewards
but cannot bear to use punishments,
and thus the state will have no law.
If a state is governed without law,
then the people will form cliques and associate with subordinates,
adorning their craftiness to achieve their private ends.
If the legal system is constant,
then the people do not scatter but unite with the superior,
exhausting their sincerity to offer their loyalty.
Thus, without speaking of wisdom or ability,
the court affairs are governed and the state’s troubles are resolved;
this is the responsibility of the *Dà Chén*.
Without speaking of cleverness or intelligence,
good people are promoted
and treacherous falsehoods are punished;
this is because those who see and hear for him are numerous.
Thus, for one who is a *Jūn*,
he sits at the source of all things
and presides over the duties of all living beings.
He selects the worthy and evaluates talent,
and treats them according to the law.
If he promotes and finds the right person,
he sits and receives the benefits, and his blessings
will be more than can be collected.
If the *Guān* are not equal to their duties
and he rushes about to serve them, the resulting failures
will be more than can be saved.
Yet a state is never lacking in scholars equal to the task;
it is only that the superior’s clarity is not sufficient to know them.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler carefully identifies the ministers who are equal to their tasks.
Thus it is said:
When the *Zhǔ*’s way is attained,
worthy talents are successful,
and the common people are well-governed.
Order or chaos lies with the *Zhǔ* alone.
Thus it is said:
The *Zhǔ* himself
is the root of rectified *Dé*;
the governance of *Guān*
is the regulation of his ears and eyes.
When the person is established, the people are transformed;
when *Dé* is rectified, the *Guān* are well-governed.
Governing the *Guān* and transforming the people,
the key lies with the superior.
Therefore, the *Jūn Zǐ* does not seek it from the people.
Thus, for the superior to reach into the affairs of the subordinate
is called encroachment,
and for the subordinate to reach into the affairs of the superior
is called usurpation.
For the superior to encroach
is a perversion;
for the subordinate to usurp
is a rebellion.
When a state has acts of perversion, rebellion, or opposition,
it is because the one who possesses the land and rules the people has lost his principles.
Therefore,
distinguishing interactions and rectifying divisions is called order,
and following order without losing it is called the *Dào*.
When the *Dào* and *Dé* are fixed, the people have a track to follow.
A ruler who possesses the *Dào*
is good at clearly establishing laws
and does not use private interests to block them.
But a ruler without the *Dào*,
having already established laws,
then abandons the laws and acts on private interests.
When the one above
discards the law and acts on private interests,
then those who are ministers use private interests as a pretext for the public good.
If the public way is not violated,
then the private way is also not violated.
By practicing the public way while hiding their private interests within it,
as time passes without being noticed,
how can treacherous hearts not accumulate?
When treacherous hearts accumulate,
the greater cases involve the disaster of encroaching upon and killing the superior,
while the smaller cases involve the chaos of forming cliques and internal strife.
The reason this is so
is that the *Zhǔ*’s *Dé* is not established
and the state has no constant laws.
If the *Zhǔ*’s *Dé* is not established,
then women can manipulate his intentions;
if the state has no constant laws,
then great ministers dare to encroach upon his power.
Great ministers rely on the abilities of the women
to gauge the sovereign's feelings;
favored women rely on the knowledge of men
to secure external power.
Thereupon, they exclude the consort and endanger the heir apparent;
military chaos arises within,
which invites foreign invaders.
These are the signs of a ruler in danger.
Therefore,
a *Jūn* who possesses the *Dào*
has the *Wǔ Guān* above
to shepherd his people,
so the masses do not dare to cross the tracks and act;
he has the *Wǔ Héng* below
to regulate his *Guān*,
so the officials do not dare to abandon the law and act on their own.
The court has fixed measures and balanced instruments
to honor the *Zhǔ*’s position.
Clothing and ceremonial robes and caps,
all have legal regulations,
so the *Jūn* embodies the law and stands established.
The *Jūn* relies on the law to issue commands,
the officials receive the orders and conduct affairs,
and the common people follow the superior to form customs.
When this is clear and long-lasting, it becomes the norm.
Those who violate customs and depart from teachings
will be collectively condemned as treacherous by the masses,
and thus the one who is the superior will be at ease.
The Tiānzǐ issues orders to the world;
the zhūhóu receive orders from the Tiānzǐ;
the dàfū receive orders from the ruler;
sons receive orders from their parents.
The lower obey the upper;
the younger brother obeys the elder brother.
This is the height of compliance.
Weights and stones are standardized for weighing;
pecks and bushels are standardized for measuring volume;
yards and feet are standardized for measuring length;
halberds and weapons follow one standard;
writing uses the same characters;
carriages use the same gauge.
This is the height of correctness.
When the masses are compliant and only one is rebellious,
or when the masses are correct and only one is perverse,
it is like seeking something in the night and obtaining a fire;
treacherous and deceitful people
will have nowhere to hide.
This is how the xiānwáng unified the hearts of the people.
For this reason, when the Tiānzǐ has goodness,
he attributes the virtue to Tiān;
when the zhūhóu have goodness,
they offer congratulations for it to the Tiānzǐ;
when the dàfū have goodness,
they present it to the ruler;
when the people have goodness,
it is rooted in their fathers
and celebrated with the elders.
This is where Dào and law originate;
this is the root of governance.
Therefore, the one who speaks but once a year
is the ruler;
those who inspect periodically are the ministers;
those who audit monthly are the officials;
those who exert the strength of their four limbs
and cultivate the occupation of farming to await orders
are the shùrén.
Therefore, the common people measure their strength among their fathers and brothers,
listen to words regarding the righteousness of ruler and subject,
and the officials evaluate their virtue and ability to wait upon them.
The dàfū manage the affairs within their offices
and do not speak of things outside them;
and the ministers make constant preparations to supply them.
The ministers summarize the essentials;
the official advisors
measure the reality and discuss the merits,
and correct or request clarification on what is doubted.
Then the ruler issues the laws and tallies from the míngfǔ to audit them,
standing above the three steps,
facing south to receive the summaries.
Thus, the one above has spare days,
and the officials are more than equal to their responsibilities;
seasonal orders are not excessive,
and the common people are respectful and well-provided for.
This is only because there are legal systems above
and divided duties below.
The Dào is what brings about the life of man;
it does not reside within man himself.
Sage kings and enlightened rulers are those who are good at knowing and leading it.
Therefore, there is a constant way to govern the people,
and a constant method to generate wealth.
The Dào
is the essential of all things.
One who is a ruler of men
holds onto the essential and awaits them;
then even if those below have treacherous and deceitful hearts,
they will not dare to try them.
The Dào is established as a void;
if the right person is there, it flows;
if the person is gone, it is blocked.
Without this,
there is no way to order the people;
without this,
there is no way to generate wealth.
When the people are governed and wealth is nurtured,
the blessings return to the one above.
Thus, one knows that an enlightened ruler values the Dào and law while treating his state lightly.
Therefore, he who rules a single state
does so because the Dào makes him its ruler;
he who kings the world
does so because the Dào makes him its king.
To king the world on a large scale
or to rule a state on a small scale,
it is the Dào that presides over it.
Thus, what he desires
he can obtain from the people;
what he hates
he can eliminate through the people.
What he desires he can obtain from the people,
so worthy talents are successful.
What he hates he can eliminate through the people,
so treachery and deceit are reduced.
Just as a smith with metal
or a potter with clay,
the shaping lies with the craftsman.
Therefore, if one is about to give,
thick kindness cannot suffice;
if one is about to kill,
severe majesty cannot shake them.
If severe majesty cannot shake them
and thick kindness cannot suffice,
there is a gap between reputation and reality.
When there is good, one does not delay the reward,
so the people do not keep the benefit for themselves;
when there is a fault, one does not let the punishment linger overnight,
so the people do not resent the majesty.
The system of rewards and punishments
does not overstep the people,
so the people return to being close to the one above.
It is like the rain from heaven;
if the moisture descends one foot,
growth rises one foot.
Thus, to appoint officials without personally acting as one,
to employ people without personally serving,
to stand alone and be without audit—
this is the position of the rénzhǔ.
When the xiānwáng were in the world,
the people compared them to the virtue of the shénmíng.
The xiānwáng were good at gathering from the people.
If the people are listened to individually, they are foolish;
if they are listened to collectively, they are sage-like.
Even if one has the virtue of Tāng or Wǔ,
one must still conform to the words of the people in the market.
Thus, the enlightened ruler follows the hearts of the people,
settles their natural dispositions,
and acts upon what is gathered from the hearts of the masses.
Therefore, orders are issued and not hindered;
punishments are established and not used.
The xiānwáng were good at being one body with the people.
To be one body with the people
is to use the state to guard the state
and to use the people to guard the people.
Thus, the people do not find it convenient to do wrong.
Even though there is an enlightened ruler,
beyond a hundred paces,
he listens but does not hear;
