separated by a wall,
he peers but does not see.
Yet the reason he is called an enlightened ruler
is that the ruler is good at employing his ministers,
and the ministers are good at offering their loyalty.
Trust is followed by trust;
goodness is transmitted by goodness.
Thus, within the Sìhǎi,
all can be governed.
Thus, when an enlightened ruler promotes those below,
he fully knows their short and long points,
and knows what they cannot add to,
then employs them in affairs accordingly.
When a worthy person serves his lord,
he fully knows his own short and long points
and where his personal strength does not reach,
then accepts an office by measuring his ability.
The superior uses this to nurture the inferior,
the inferior uses this to serve the superior;
when superior and inferior mutually aim for correctness,
then the common people, men and women, all participate in the governance.
In ancient times, there was no distinction between ruler and minister, superior and inferior;
there was no union of husband and wife, consort and mate;
they lived like beasts in herds
and struggled against each other with force.
Then the wise deceived the foolish,
the strong oppressed the weak,
and the old, the young, the orphaned, and the widowed
did not find their place.
Therefore, the wise borrowed the strength of the masses to prohibit violence and cruelty,
and the violent people were stopped.
To promote benefits and eliminate harms for the people,
and to rectify the virtue of the people,
will cause the people to take the ruler as their teacher.
Therefore, the Way, methods, virtue, and conduct
emerge from worthy men.
When the following of righteousness and principles
takes form in the hearts of the people,
then the people return to the Way.
When names and objects are in their proper places, and right and wrong are distinguished,
then rewards and punishments are carried out.
When upper and lower positions are established,
and the livelihood of the people is organized,
then the capital of the state is established.
Therefore, the reason why a state is a state
is that the people’s substance constitutes the state;
the reason why a ruler is a ruler
is that rewards and punishments constitute the ruler.
To push rewards to the extreme leads to exhaustion;
to push punishments to the extreme leads to cruelty.
When resources are exhausted and commands are cruel,
that is the means by which one loses the people.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler is careful in the teachings regarding daily life,
so that the people can be made to live in order,
win in battle, and hold firm in defense.
If rewards are heavy, the superior cannot provide enough;
if punishments are cruel, the subordinates will not trust.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler cultivates the rituals of eating, drinking, and of mourning the dead and visiting the injured,
and all things will belong to him.
Therefore, encourage them with the *Bā Zhèng*,
distinguish them with clothing,
enrich them with the state’s granaries,
and honor them with the royal prohibitions,
then the people will be close to the ruler
and can be employed.
If the people can be employed,
then the whole world can be reached.
If the world follows its Way,
then it arrives;
if it does not follow its Way,
then it does not arrive.
Now, as for water,
it surges upward in waves,
and after exhausting its motion, it descends again;
its momentum is naturally so.
Therefore, leading them with virtue to make them cherish you,
and awing them with majesty to make them fear you,
will cause the world to return to you.
In a state that possesses the Way,
when orders are issued and commands are given,
husbands and wives all return to being close to the superior;
when laws are spread and decrees are issued,
worthy men and heroic scholars all exert their skills and abilities for the superior.
Within a thousand *lǐ*,
a fine of a bundle of cloth
or a tax of one *mǔ*
can all be known.
Those who handle axes and hatchets do not dare to decline punishing,
and those who handle carriages and caps do not dare to decline rewards,
harmoniously as if they were children of one father,
or the substance of one family,
because righteousness and ritual are clear.
If subordinates do not support their superiors,
and ministers do not support their ruler,
then worthy men will not come.
If worthy men do not come,
then the common people will not be used.
If the common people are not used,
then the world will not be reached.
Therefore it is said:
If virtue is encroached upon, the ruler is in danger;
if judgment is encroached upon, those with merit are in danger;
if orders are encroached upon, officials are in danger;
if punishments are encroached upon, the common people are in danger.
An enlightened ruler
is one who is careful in prohibiting excesses and encroachments.
If there is no discourse of excess or encroachment above,
then there is no heart of opportunistic hoping below.
For one who is a ruler of men,
to turn one's back on the Way and abandon the law,
and to enjoy acting for private interests,
is called disorder.
For one who is a minister of men,
to change precedents and alter constants,
and to use clever words to flatter the superior,
is called soaring.
When disorder arrives, there is cruelty;
when soaring arrives, there is defeat.
If any one of these four arrives,
there is failure, and enemies will plot against it.
Therefore, use distributions and leniency to remedy disorder,
and the common people will be pleased.
Select the worthy and promote the talented,
and honor ritual, filial piety, and fraternal duty,
then treachery and falsehood will stop.
Restrain excess and idleness,
and distinguish between men and women,
then illicit chaos will be blocked.
If honor and meanness have their righteousness,
and ranks and classes are not overstepped,
then those with merit will be encouraged.
If the state has constant standards
and the laws are not hidden,
then the subordinates will have no resentment in their hearts.
These five
are the Way to promote virtue, correct errors,
preserve the state, and stabilize the people.
Now, a ruler of men may have great errors,
and a minister of men may have great crimes.
The state
is what is possessed by the ruler,
and the people
are those over whom he is ruler.
To have a state and rule the people
yet let that which the people hate control them,
this is the first error.
The people have three seasonal pursuits;
if the ruler does not allocate them to his people,
they are not his people.
If the people are not his people,
then they cannot be used for defense or war;
this is the second error of a ruler of men.
As for those who are ministers of men,
receiving from the ruler high rank and heavy salary
and managing great offices.
To turn their back on their office,
neglect their duties,
harmonize with the ruler’s facial expressions,
follow his desires,
and use flattery to gain advantage,
this is the great crime of a minister of men.
If the ruler has errors and does not change,
it is called being upside down;
if a minister deserves punishment and is not executed,
it is called disorder.
If the ruler is an upside-down ruler,
and the minister is a disorderly minister,
the decline of the state
can be awaited while sitting.
Therefore, a ruler who possesses the Way holds the root,
the chancellor holds the essentials,
the high officials hold the laws
to shepherd their various ministers,
and the various ministers exhaust their wisdom and strength
to serve their superior.
If these four observances are maintained, there is order;
if they are changed, there is disorder.
Therefore, it must be clearly established and firmly held.
In the past, the sage kings made the people’s livelihood the root
and carefully understood where misfortune and fortune arise.
Therefore, they were cautious in small matters and subtle details,
avoided the wrong,
and sought distinctions to find the root of things.
Thus, people who were impulsive, treacherous, evil, or deceptive did not dare to try their ways.
This is the Way to rectify the people.
In ancient times, there were two sayings:
“The walls have ears,
and a hidden bandit is at one’s side.”
“Walls have ears”
refers to subtle plans leaking out.
“A hidden bandit is at one’s side”
refers to the way of deep suspicion winning the people.
The leaking of subtle plans
refers to cunning women repeating the requests of the master
and thus supporting wandering evildoers.
Those who use deep suspicion to win the people
are those who were honored before but lowly later who serve as their drivers.
When an enlightened ruler is on the throne,
favorites cannot divine his intentions,
for punishments and penalties are close at hand;
great ministers cannot encroach upon his power,
for those who form cliques are executed;
this is clarity.
For one who acts as a ruler,
if he can distance himself from slander and flattery,
abolish cliques and factions,
and ensure that those of debauched and perverse conduct who eat without merit
have no rank or position at court,
this is the way to stop deception, restrain villainy,
strengthen the state, and preserve oneself.
For one who is a superior,
he controls the various ministers
and the Bǎixìng
by way of the Zhōngyāng zhī rén.
Therefore, the Zhōngyāng zhī rén
are the intermediaries between the ministers and the ruler.
When commands and orders are distributed to the people,
they must pass through the Zhōngyāng zhī rén.
The Zhōngyāng zhī rén,
by treating the relaxed as urgent,
can use urgency to seize authority;
by treating the urgent as relaxed,
the relaxed can be used to bestow favors on the people.
When authority and favors shift to those below,
then the one who is superior is in danger.
Whether the worthy and the unworthy are known to the superior
must depend on the Zhōngyāng zhī rén.
Whether wealth and labor are contributed to the superior
must depend on the Zhōngyāng zhī rén.
They can exchange the worthy for the unworthy and can form factions below.
There are those who can use the people’s wealth and labor to entice their ruler,
and can thus be considered to have performed labor for the superior.
They manipulate both above and below to encircle their private interests,
and if the system of titles cannot be applied against them,
then the one who is superior is in danger.
Those who preempt their ruler in doing good
are those who encroach upon his rewards and snatch away his favors.
Those who preempt their ruler in doing evil
are those who encroach upon his punishments and snatch away his authority.
Those who spread false rumors outside
are those who threaten their ruler.
Those who suppress orders and do not let them out
are those who isolate their ruler.
If these four things occur and the superior does not know,
then the danger to the state can be expected while sitting still.
The divinely sagacious act as Wáng,
the benevolent and wise act as Jūn,
the martial and brave act as Zhǎng;
this is the Tiān zhī Dào
and the nature of humanity.
In the Tiān zhī Dào and human nature, those who are comprehensive are the substance,
those who are limited follow;
this is the cause of the natural order.
Therefore, those who initiate concern for problems
do not participate in the labor;
those who are close to the labor
do not plan the Dào.
Thus, the one who is superior has concerns but does not toil,
while the Bǎixìng toil but do not have these concerns.
When the distinctions between ruler and minister, superior and inferior are clear,
then the Lǐzhì is established.
Therefore, using people to serve the superior,
using strength to serve the enlightened,
and using the physical form to serve the mind,
this is the principle of things.
The Dào of the mind involves advancing and retreating,
while the Dào of the physical form is expansive and winding.
Advancing and retreating are controlled by the ruler;
expansiveness and winding are controlled by labor.
That which governs labor is square;
that which governs control is circular.
The circular revolves;
revolving leads to communication;
communication leads to harmony.
The square holds fast;
holding fast leads to firmness;
firmness leads to trust.
The Jūn creates harmony through benefit;
the minister demonstrates trust through integrity;
then there is no deviance between superior and inferior.
Therefore it is said:
He who rules others controls benevolence;
he who serves others maintains trust.
This refers to the Lǐ between superior and inferior.
The Jūn’s presence in the capital
is like the mind’s presence in the body.
When Dàodé is established above,
then the Bǎixìng are transformed below.
When a cautious mind takes shape within,
then the appearance and demeanor are moved without.
Zhèng
is that by which one clarifies their virtue.
To know how to attain it through oneself
and to know how to attain it through the people
is to follow its principles.
To know how it is lost through the people
and to retreat and cultivate oneself
is to return to the root.
When one demands much of oneself,
virtuous conduct is established.
When one demands little of others,
the people easily provide for him.
Therefore, he who rules others directs his attention upward;
he who serves others directs his attention downward.
Directing attention upward
means recording the seasons of Heaven
and focusing on the people's labor.
Directing attention downward
means developing the resources of the earth
and ensuring sufficient goods for use.
Therefore, being able to adorn great righteousness,
being mindful of the seasons,
above, serving the Shénmíng with Lǐ,
and below, assisting with righteousness—
this is the Dào of the enlightened Jūn.
Being able to rely on the law without favoritism,
above, to correct the ruler's faults,
and below, to relieve the people's suffering—
this is the conduct of a loyal minister.
When an enlightened Jūn is above
and a loyal minister assists him,
then the common people are unified through government and punishment,
and are guided by the benefits of clothing and food;
thus they are honest and easy to employ,
simple and easy to satisfy.
The Jūnzǐ feeds upon the Dào;
the Xiǎorén feeds upon labor;
this is the distinction.
Authority without power
has nowhere to be established;
affairs without action
have nothing from which to arise.
If things are like this,
then the state will be at peace and villainy will diminish.
The Jūnzǐ feeds upon the Dào,
then righteousness is examined and Lǐ is clarified.
When righteousness is examined and Lǐ is clarified,
then the hierarchy of ranks is not overstepped;
even though there may be subordinate Dàfū,
they do not dare to have opportunistic intentions,
and the superior is free from danger.
The common people feed upon labor
and work at the root;
when those who work at the root are many,
the farmers obey commands.
Therefore, when an enlightened Jūn establishes his age,
the people's subjection to the superior
is like the grass and trees' subjection to the seasons.
Therefore, if the people are circuitous, then flow them;
if the people flow and pass through, then make them circuitous.
If breached, they flow;
if blocked, they stop.
Even though there is an enlightened Jūn,
he can breach them
and also block them.
Breaching them
leads the Jūnzǐ to act according to Lǐ;
blocking them
leads the Xiǎorén to be devoted to farming.
When the Jūnzǐ acts according to Lǐ,
the superior is honored and the people are submissive.
When the common people are devoted to farming,
wealth is abundant and provisions are sufficient.
When the superior is honored and the people are submissive,
and wealth is abundant and provisions are sufficient,
when these four are complete in the body,
it is not difficult to become a Wáng in a short time.
The four limbs and the six paths
are the substance of the body.
The Sìzhèng and Wǔguān
are the substance of the state.
If the four limbs do not connect
and the six paths do not reach through,
it is called loss.
If the Sìzhèng are not correct
and the Wǔguān do not act as officials,
it is called disorder.
For this reason, the lord of a state takes a wife from a different clan.
He establishes the nieces and younger sisters,
titled ladies, and palace women,
all of whom are governed by legal regulations;
this is how he manages the internal palace.
He clarifies the distinction between men and women
and makes manifest the rules regarding suspicious behavior;
this is how he prevents illicit conduct.
Consequently, there is no communication between the inner and outer,
slander and evil do not arise,
the talk of women does not concern matters of the government,
and the sons and younger brothers of the various ministers have no private dealings within the palace.
This is how the former kings enlightened virtue and warded off evil,
and how they manifested the public interest and extinguished private interests.
Having clearly established the favored consort as the principal wife,
he does not allow her to displace the rightful heir, which would harm righteousness.
Though ritual may allow for private affection and joy,
their statuses cannot be made equal.
Even if a rank is noble,
ritual must always be implemented.
The legitimate wife is made the most elegant;
she is distinguished by her garments
and heralded by emblems and banners;
this is how her dignity is emphasized.
In this way, brothers will have no rifts or grudges,
and slanderers will not dare to act.
Therefore, in appointing a chancellor,
one displays their achievements and adds to them virtue;
one assesses their labor and clarifies it through law.
One examines and compares their virtues to promote them comprehensively,
honoring their status and manifesting trust in them.
Thus, those below do not have the fear of dying for their remonstrance,
and those standing together at court have no feelings of suppressed resentment.
If things are like this,
then the state will be at peace, and the people will have no evil intentions.
When selecting the worthy and advancing the talented,
one promotes the virtuous to their ranks,
and does not associate with the non-virtuous;
one promotes the capable to their offices,
and does not associate with the incapable.
Let virtue cover the lack of long service,
but do not let it harm the respect for seniority.
In this way,
the ruler will not be troubled,
and the people will not rely on mere luck for their livelihood.
There are four causes for chaos in a state,
and two causes for its downfall.
Internally, having a concubine who rivals the wife—
this is palace chaos.
Among the progeny, having a concubine's son who rivals the legitimate heir—
this is family chaos.
In the court, having a minister who rivals the chancellor—
this is state chaos.
Appointing the incapable to office—
this is general chaos.
If these four are not distinguished,
the ruler loses his structural order.
When the various officials form cliques to pursue their private interests,
he loses the support of his clan.
When the key ministers of the state
make secret pacts and hidden schemes to wait for each other,
he loses his external support.
Losing the clan internally
and losing support externally—
these are the two ways to perish.
Therefore, the status of the wife must be fixed,
the heir must be legitimate,
the chancellor must stand upright to receive orders,
and officials must be loyal, trustworthy, and reverent.
Thus it is said:
there is chaos in the palace,
there is chaos among brothers,
there is chaos among high ministers,
there is chaos among the middle people,
and there is chaos among the common people.
If even one of these five arises,
then the one who is the ruler is in danger.
Chaos in the palace is called "jealous confusion,"
chaos among brothers is called "partisan bias,"
chaos among high ministers is called "self-praising narratives,"
chaos among the middle people is called "fearful murmuring,"
and chaos among the common people is called "depletion of wealth."
Depletion of wealth leads to meanness,
fearful murmuring leads to negligence,
and self-praising narratives, partisan bias, and jealous confusion lead to rebellion.
Therefore, by rectifying names and investigating doubts,
and by executing punishments swiftly on those close at hand,
the internal will be settled.
By governing high ministers according to achievement,
middle people according to their conduct,
and common people according to their tasks,
the state will be prosperous.
By examining the seasons of heaven
and understanding the products of the earth
to coordinate the labor of the people;
by forbidding excessive tasks
and encouraging agricultural work
so that they may attend to their duties without interference,
the common people will be governed.
Above, inspecting them with statistics;
below, organizing them into groups of ten and five for verification;
bringing close those who advance through humility,
to solidify their intentions;
establishing teachers in the districts
to advance their learning.
By appointing them to office based on their ability
and promoting them when they reach the appropriate age,
the scholars will return to proper conduct.
Assessing virtue and measuring achievement,
encouraging what they are capable of,
as if inspecting them through the opinions of the masses,
and entrusting them with the responsibility of the state.
If this is done,
the scholars will return to their true nature.
Guǎnzǐ said:
"Worry about the lack of goodness in your own character;
do not worry that others do not know you.
Cinnabar and azurite are in the mountains,
yet the people know of them and take them;
beautiful pearls are in the deep,
yet the people know of them and take them.
Thus, if I have transgressive actions,
the people's judgment of me will not be in error.
The observation of the people is discerning;
one cannot escape it
to commit ungood acts.
Therefore, if I have goodness,
they immediately praise me;
if I have faults,
they immediately disparage me.
When facing the disparagement or praise of the people,
no one needs to go home and ask their family for confirmation.
Therefore, the former kings stood in awe of the people.
Holding a reputation that follows the people's support,
nothing is not strong;
holding a reputation that loses the people's support,
nothing is not weak.
Even if one is the Son of Heaven or a feudal lord,
if the people all take their reputation and leave them,
then they will abandon their land and flee.
Therefore, the former kings stood in awe of the people.
Of what is in the body, what is most beneficial?
The ears and eyes are most beneficial.
The sages obtained these benefits and relied on them,
thus the people were valued and their reputation was established.
I also rely on them.
The sages relied on what is lovable,
but if I rely on what is loathsome—
if I rely on what is loathsome
to bring about a beautiful reputation,
can that be achieved?
Affection alone cannot make me capable.
Máo Qiáng and Xī Shī
were the beauties of the world;
yet if they wore expressions of resentment on their faces,
they could not be considered lovable.
Suppose I have an ugly face
and furthermore display resentment on it.
When resentment is seen on the face
and wicked words come from the mouth,
while trying to discard the fullness of evil to seek a beautiful reputation,
can that be achieved?
Extreme indeed
is the people's hatred for those who have excessive faults.
Therefore, cut off what is too long,
lengthen what is short,
drain what is full,
and fill what is empty."
Guǎnzǐ said:
"One who is good at blaming themselves
will not be blamed by the people;
one who cannot blame themselves
will be blamed by the people.
Therefore, one who names their own faults is strong;
one who governs their own conduct is wise;
and one who does not attribute their own ungoodness to others
is benevolent."
Therefore, when a wise king has faults,
he reflects on them within himself;
when he has goodness,
he attributes it to the people.
Having faults and reflecting on them himself,
his person becomes vigilant;
having goodness and attributing it to the people,
the people are pleased.
Directing pleasure to the people
and bringing vigilance to himself:
this is how a wise king governs the people.
Now, Jié and Zhòu were not so;
when they had goodness, they reflected it within themselves;
when they had faults, they attributed them to the people.
Attributing them to the people,
the people grew angry;
reflecting it within themselves,
their persons became arrogant.
Directing anger to the people
and bringing arrogance to himself:
this is how he loses himself.
Therefore, a wise king
fears sounds to influence his ears
and fears appearances to influence his eyes.
By these two,
he possesses all under Heaven;
can one not be cautious?
A craftsman has that which influences the axe and hoe,
thus the marking cord can be measured.
Yì had that which influences the bow and arrow,
thus the draw can hit the mark.
Zào Fù had that which influences the reins and whip,
thus swift beasts can be overtaken
and distant roads can be reached.
As for all under Heaven, there is no constant chaos
and no constant order.
When bad people are present, there is chaos;
when good people are present, there is order;
it lies in having achieved goodness, which is the means to influence them."
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"Cultivate humility, respect, love, and courtesy;
eliminate resentment and avoid contention.
If these are used in meeting one another,
then one will not lose people.
Try having much resentment and contending for profit,
being disrespectful to one another,
then one will not possess oneself.
Great indeed is the Way of humility, respect, and love!
In auspicious matters, it can be used for sacrifice;
in inauspicious matters, it can be used for mourning.
Broadly used to regulate all under Heaven, it does not increase;
narrowly used to govern a single person, it does not diminish.
Try going to Zhōngguó,
the Zhūxià, or the lands of the Mányí,
or even to the birds, beasts, and insects;
all depend on this for order or chaos.
If it graces the person, there is glory;
if it leaves the person, there is disgrace.
If one examines its practice in oneself without indolence,
even the people of the Yí and Mò
can be transformed and made to feel love.
If one examines its removal from oneself,
even brothers and parents
can be transformed and made to feel hatred.
Thus the self is what makes others love or hate;
the name is what makes for glory or disgrace.
This way of changing names and things
is like Heaven and Earth;
therefore, the former kings called it the Dào."
When Guǎn Zhòng was ill,
Huán Gōng went to inquire of him, saying:
"Zhòngfù's illness is grave.
If the unavoidable happens and you do not recover from this illness,
what will Zhòngfù instruct me?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Even if Your Lordship had not commanded your servant,
your servant was about to speak of it.
However,
Your Lordship still may not be able to act upon it."
The Duke said:
"If Zhòngfù commands me to go east,
I go east;
if you order me to go west,
I go west.
As for Zhòngfù's commands to me,
how would I dare not follow?"
Guǎn Zhòng straightened his clothes and hat and rose, replying:
"I wish for Your Lordship to distance yourself from Yì Yá, Shù Diāo, Táng Wū, and Gōngzǐ Kāifāng.
Now, Yì Yá served Your Lordship by seasoning food.
Your Lordship said:
'Only steamed infant have I not tasted.'
Thereupon, he steamed his firstborn son and presented him to Your Lordship.
Human nature is such that no one does not love their son.
If he did not love his own son,
what regard will he have for Your Lordship?
Your Lordship loves the inner palace and is jealous.
Shù Diāo castrated himself to manage the inner palace for Your Lordship.
Human nature is such that no one does not love their own body.
If he did not love his own body,
what regard will he have for Your Lordship?
Gōngzǐ Kāifāng served Your Lordship for fifteen years
without returning to see his parents,
yet the distance between Qí and Wèi
is no more than a few days' journey.
I have heard
that what is forced does not last long
and what is hollow is not enduring.
Those whose lives are not good,
their ends will surely not be complete."
Huán Gōng said:
"Good."
Guǎn Zhòng died
and was buried.
The Duke came to hate those four men and dismissed them from office.
He expelled Táng Wū and a harsh illness arose;
he expelled Yì Yá and fine flavors did not arrive;
he expelled Shù Diāo and the palace fell into chaos;
he expelled Gōngzǐ Kāifāng and the court was not governed.
Huán Gōng said:
"Alas!
Can even a sage be mistaken?"
He then restored the four men.
After a year had passed,
the four men caused trouble,
surrounding the Duke in a single room so he could not leave.
There was a woman
who entered through a hole
and reached the Duke's place.
The Duke said:
"I am hungry and want food,
thirsty and want drink,
but I cannot get them;
what is the reason?"
The woman replied:
"Yì Yá,
Shù Diāo,
Táng Wū,
and Gōngzǐ Kāifāng
have divided the State of Qí;
the roads have been blocked for ten days.
Gōngzǐ Kāifāng has taken seven hundred registered units to give to Wèi;
food will no longer be obtainable."
The Duke said:
"Alas!
How far-reaching are the words of a sage!
If the dead have no knowledge, then let it be;
but if they have knowledge,
with what face can I see Zhòngfù in the underworld!"
He then took a piece of raw white silk to cover his head and expired.
Eleven days after he died,
maggots came out from the door,
and only then was it known that Huán Gōng had died.
He was buried with the screen of the Yáng Mén.
The reason why Huán Gōng's body remained for eleven days
until maggots came out of the door without being collected
was because he did not use the worthy until the end.
Huán Gōng,
Guǎn Zhòng,
Bǎo Shūyá,
and Nìng Qī—the four of them were drinking.
When they were merry with wine,
Huán Gōng said to Bǎo Shūyá:
"Why do you not rise to toast to my long life?"
Bǎo Shūyá raised his cup and rose, saying:
"May Your Lordship not forget the time you were in exile in Jǔ;
may Guǎn Zǐ not forget the time he was bound in Lǔ;
may Nìng Qī not forget the time he fed oxen under the cart."
Huán Gōng moved from his mat, bowed twice, and said:
"If I and you two grand officers can avoid forgetting the master's words,
then the state's altars of soil and grain will surely not be in danger."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zǐ, saying:
"I am young, weak, muddled, and foolish,
and do not understand the righteousness between the feudal lords and the four neighbors.
Should not Zhòngfù tell me all about the rulers who possessed the Dào in the past?
I shall take them as a mirror."
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"What Yíwú is capable of and what I am not capable of
are entirely known to you, my lord.
Why does my lord trouble himself to give me orders?"
Huán Gōng asked again:
"Zhòngfǔ,
I am young, weak, confused, and foolish,
and I do not understand the principles of the neighboring feudal lords.
Should Zhòngfǔ not fully inform me about the virtuous rulers of the past?
I wish to take them as a mirror."
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Yíwú heard this from Xú Bó:
The virtuous rulers of the past
respected the mountains and rivers,
the ancestral temples, and the altars of soil and grain,
as well as the high officials of the previous generation.
They gathered them with virtue and made them very wealthy.
They strengthened their military officials
and appropriately employed their strength.
Sages were in front of them,
and the upright and honest were at their side.
They competed to act according to righteousness,
and both superiors and inferiors were refined.
Their conduct was upright and their judgment clear;
they did not slacken throughout the four seasons,
and the people were not troubled.
The five grains flourished.
There was harmony within and without,
the feudal lords submitted,
the state was peaceful,
and weapons of war were not used.
They received gifts of silk
to show their appreciation for virtue;
they clearly received their orders
and used them as laws and models.
This can be called a virtuous ruler of the past."
Huán Gōng said:
"Excellent!"
Huán Gōng said:
"Since Zhòngfǔ has already told me about the virtuous rulers of the past,
should you not also tell me all about the unprincipled rulers of the past?
I wish to take them as a mirror as well."
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Now, as my lord is fine and insightful,
and you already hold a fine office and follow the way,
why would you need to hear about evil?"
Huán Gōng said:
"What kind of talk is this?
If black silk is edged with black silk,
how would I know its beauty?
If white silk is edged with white silk,
how would I know its excellence?
Zhòngfǔ has already told me of the good,
but if you do not tell me of the evil,
how will I know that the good is good?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Yíwú heard this from Xú Bó:
The unprincipled rulers of the past
enlarged their palaces,
raised high their terraces and pavilions,
did not employ good ministers,
and gave refuge to slanderers and thieves.
They had a state but did not govern it,
but relied on others to make plans for them.
Their government orders were not good,
as dark as night.
They were like wild beasts,
with no place to settle.
They did not follow the Way of Heaven,
and did not look at the four quarters as examples.
They had households but did not manage them,
as if they were mad.
They were resented and cursed by the multitude,
and they rarely escaped destruction.
They advanced their actors and jesters,
multiplied their bells and drums,
were swept away by gambling,
and played with artisans and blind musicians.
They executed their good ministers,
were arrogant toward their women,
hunted with nets and arrows,
treated their uncles with cruelty,
galloped about without restraint,
and spent their time in play and laughter.
Their governance and laws were distorted,
and their punishments were severe.
Internally they exploited their people
to carry out attacks and conquests.
Like a leaking cauldron,
how could they not be exhausted?
This can be called an unprincipled ruler of the past."
Huán Gōng said:
"Excellent!"
Huán Gōng said:
"Since Zhòngfǔ has already told me about the virtuous rulers of the past
and the unprincipled rulers of the past,
should Zhòngfǔ not tell me all about the virtuous ministers of the past?
I wish to take them as a mirror."
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Yíwú heard this from Xú Bó:
The virtuous ministers of the past
presented their gifts to become ministers
and did not treat their service among the ruler's attendants as that of a guest.
If the ruler recognized them, they served;
if not, they stopped.
If there were matters of state,
they surely planned for the state,
developing it everywhere.
They followed the virtue of their ancestors,
distinguished between what was natural and what was contrary,
promoted and nurtured worthy people,
and slander and wickedness did not arise.
They served the ruler with righteousness,
and directed their subordinates with ritual propriety.
The noble and the lowly were close to each other,
like brothers.
They were loyal to the state,
and superiors and inferiors attained proper behavior.
When resting they reflected,
when speaking they planned,
and when acting they conducted business.
Residing in the state, they enriched it;
being in the army, they were victorious.
Facing difficulties, they stood by their duties,
and even unto death, they did not regret.
Close to the ruler they were corrective supports,
and far from the ruler they were assistants.
They associated with others through righteousness,
and they lived with others through integrity.
Attending to their office they governed well,
and when presented with wine and food they declined.
They did not slander their ruler,
nor did they hide their words.
If the ruler had faults,
they offered remonstrance without hesitation;
if the ruler had worries,
then the ministers would handle them.
This can be called a virtuous minister of the past."
Huán Gōng said:
"Excellent!"
Huán Gōng said:
"Since Zhòngfǔ has already told me about the virtuous ministers of the past,
should you not also tell me about the unprincipled ministers of the past?
I wish to take them as a mirror too."
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Yíwú heard this from Xú Bó:
The unprincipled ministers of the past
presented their gifts to become ministers
but treated their service among the ruler's attendants as that of a guest.
They used persuasive speech to advance,
and did not seek selflessness.
They moved forward and never retreated,
borrowing favor to sell nobility.
They exalted their bribes and goods,
and degraded their ranks and offices.
Coming forward they claimed to assist,
but going back they said it was impossible,
to cause the downfall of their ruler;
and they all said, 'It was not me.'
The inhumane gathered together
to attack the worthy.
They saw nobility like merchandise,
and saw lowliness as a fault.
They were greedy for bribes,
and competed for wine and food.
They did not associate with good people,
but only served their own interests.
They were arrogant and disrespectful,
not befriending good scholars,
but communicating with slanderers and thieves.
They did not resolve people's disputes,
but only hastened people toward lawsuits.
Deeply immersed in wine,
conduct and righteousness are not followed.
Not cultivating old relationships,
changing and altering the constants of the state,
arbitrarily creating new orders,
deluding and confusing their ruler,
forcibly seizing the administration,
maintaining noble status and favor while being arrogant.
Dismissing and discarding virtuous scholars,
supporting and aiding those who offer bribes,
entering, they ride as equals with the ruler,
exiting, they form cliques,
bribes and gifts are exchanged,
drinking and eating bring them close,
together they bring chaos to their ruler.
If the ruler faces disaster,
each looks after his own self.
These are what were called unprincipled ministers of old."
Huán Gōng said:
"Excellent!"
(Chapter missing).
Short Sayings Nine.
Asking:
"Are the times of old the same as the times of now?"
Answer:
"They are the same."
"Are the people the same
or different?"
Answer:
"They are different;
they can be dealt with through administrative punishment.
In the times of Kù and Yáo,
the beauty of Hùn Wú was below.
Their Dào was not uniquely superior to others."
The mountains were different yet used for firewood,
the marshes were not exhausted and the nourishment was sufficient,
plowing to nourish themselves,
and using the surplus to respond to the needs of the Tiānzǐ,
therefore all was level.
The pasturing of cattle and horses did not overlap,
the customs of the people were unknown to each other,
not going beyond a hundred lǐ to seek sufficiency,
therefore they were high officials but did not manage,
they were tranquil.
In their trials, for one crippled leg or one shoe, one deserved death.
Now, Zhōu Gōng cut off heads until they filled the baskets,
severed heads filled the baskets,
severed feet filled the baskets,
yet the dying people did not submit;
this is not human nature,
it is exhaustion.
The earth is heavy and the people carry it;
when ruined and exhausted, nourishment is insufficient.
Engaging in secondary occupations, the people are stirred up;
this is to have the name below while the reality is above.
As for the Sages,
they examine the roots and wander in joys;
it is a great darkness,
an extensive night.
Asking,
"How does one bring about the transformation of the times? Nothing is better than Chǐ Mí.
Treat the essential as cheap,
and respect the useless,
then the people can be shaped.
Therefore, cheapen grain and rice while respecting pearls and jade;
be fond of rites and music while cheapening practical affairs;
this is the beginning of the root.
Pearls are the Yáng within Yīn,
thus they overcome fire;
jade is the Yīn within Yáng,
thus it overcomes water.
Its transformation is like that of a god.
Therefore, the Tiānzǐ stores pearls and jade,
the feudal lords store gold and stone,
the high officials keep dogs and horses,
the common people store cloth and silk.
If not so,
then the strong could hold them,
and the wise could herd them,
treating the precious as cheap and the cheap as precious.
If not so,
the widowers, widows, orphans, and the elderly would not benefit from it.
At the beginning of equalization,
which is more urgent: administration or instruction?"
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"Administration and instruction are similar but take different directions.
As for instruction,
it is lofty like the distance of autumn clouds,
moving the hearts of people to sorrow;
it is luxuriant like the quiet clouds of summer,
reaching the bodies of people;
it is distant like the stillness of the white moon,
moving the minds of people to resentment;
it is vast like flowing water,
making people contemplate it,
the place where life goes.
At the beginning of instruction,
the person must embody it himself.
Likening it to the first appearance of autumn clouds,
the worthy and the unworthy are transformed by it.
Treat them with respect and wait for them,
love them and employ them,
like offering sacrifices at Fán Shén Shān.
The worthy are few,
the unworthy are many.
If you make use of the worthy,
how could the unworthy not be transformed?
Now, as for administration, there is a slight difference,
it is like the signs of awe-inspiring forms.
If these are removed, can people be made to serve?
Using the poor and the rich,
how should it be done?
Said: The extremely rich cannot be commanded;
the extremely poor do not know shame.
When water is level it does not flow;
without a source it soon dries up.
When clouds are level, the rain is not heavy;
without accumulated clouds,
the rain soon stops.
When administration is level but lacks awe,
it will not be effective.
If there is love without intimacy, then it drifts.
Being intimate with those on the left and right, and employing
the useless, then compare it
to the blind leading the blind, it portends resentment.
When those above are short and those below are long,
using things without measure,
then the root is endangered. Not acknowledging
while sacrificing to Tán, then the secondary ancestors.
Violating oaths and breaking alliances harms one's words.
Respecting the ancestors and deceased fathers
is to honor the beginning.
The trustworthiness of covenants
is how conduct is judged.
Honoring the principles of Heaven and Earth
is how awe is judged.
Scanty virtue is the rotting soil of the masses.
One must rely on awe and punishment to judge the people,
then the administration will be effective.
Can one become a King?
May I ask how to apply this?
One must be clear about the Dào of Heaven and Earth,
then merit and fame can flourish.
Be clear about the benefits of the earth,
and the people can become rich;
understand Chǐ Mí,
and the scholars can be made to care.
The ruler should be intimate by liking good deeds,
strong by establishing decisiveness,
and benevolent by being fond of appointing others.
If the ruler is long-lived and reaches his years,
the people will not suffer from premature death or pestilence,
the six domestic animals will all be reared,
the five grains will all ripen,
then the people's strength can be utilized.
If the rulers of neighboring states are all unworthy,
then one can become a King.
What if they are all worthy?
Said:
Suddenly change the ministers and shift,
suddenly change the affairs and transform,
changes that are sufficient to establish a name.
Compassionately rescuing the exhausted, then fame will encourage others,
planting so that the people become rich;
responding to changes and waiting for resonance,
growing along with all things,
emitting the brilliance of the sun and moon,
moving in response to the wind and rain.
What Heaven covers,
what Earth bears,
of these people, you are the leader.
To not possess yet to be ashamed before Heaven and Earth
is not the business of the Tiānzǐ.
If the people change but you cannot change with them,
it is like attaching leather to a pillar.
If there is a change but you cannot adapt,
you cannot make them submit.
When the people submit, it is through trust.
When the feudal lords submit, it is through transformation.
May I ask how to address the exhaustion of the feudal lords' transformation?
The cause of exhaustion
lies in the private interests of the Great Houses.
As for these Great Houses,
act by following what the people value.
If our lord comes to hunt, provide the lord with the skins of tigers and leopards. For
a lord who employs effort and labor, offer gold, jade, and currency.
For a lord who loves war, offer armor and weapons.
The basis of armor and weapons
must first lie in the fields and houses.
Now, if our lord goes to war, please implement what the people value.
Food and drink
and extravagant music
are what the people desire.
If you satisfy their desires
and fulfill their wishes,
then you can employ them.
If you now make them wear skins and caps of horn, eat wild grass
and drink wild water,
who could employ them?
Those with wounded hearts cannot achieve merit.
Therefore, taste the finest flavors
and then,
exhaust the finest music
and then,
carve eggs before boiling them,
and carve firewood before burning it.
If the cinnabar caves are not blocked,
then the merchants will not stay away.
The wealthy spend extravagantly,
and the poor work for them.
This is how the common people's idleness is prevented; they exert themselves a hundred times to eat,
not just for themselves,
but to store up for transformation.
To employ one's ministers:
give and then take away,
employ and then dismiss,
enrich them solely for their services,
restrain them with fatherly authority and humble them.
Bestow empty titles to make them proud,
take away their labor during the spring and autumn harvests to deplete them,
house them within a mixture of ritual and righteousness,
and periodically promote the strong among them to praise them.
If they are strong, they can be made to serve:
use eloquence for debate,
use wisdom for invitations,
and use integrity to mark others.
Use firmness to override subordinates,
broaden their virtue to slight superiors;
if you cannot employ them, they will drift away.
This is called the crack through which a state perishes.
Therefore, follow the law and maintain constancy,
honor ritual and change customs,
value trust and despise flowery writing,
love the natural order and dislike brokers;
this is called the law of a successful state.
Those who govern a state
reverse the nature of the people,
and only then can they be close to the people.
The people desire ease,
but are taught through labor;
the people desire life,
but are taught through death.
When the teaching of labor is established, the state is wealthy;
when the teaching of death is established, authority is exercised.
The sage
manages *Yīn* and *Yáng*;
therefore, he is smooth on the outside but rugged on the inside.
Thus, those who trust their emotions harm their spirit;
those who beautify their essence harm their refinement.
A beautiful transformation corresponds to its name;
a beautiful change corresponds to its time.
Those who cannot perceive the omen of its beginning will be reached by disaster.
Therefore, follow the benefits of the land,
obey the instructions of Heaven,
humbly count the casualties,
open the state gates,
and know the order of the spirits. Following the benefits of the land
is how one aligns with the auspicious guidelines of Heaven and Earth.
Obeying the instructions of Heaven
means every movement must be clear.
Humbly counting the casualties
means being as one with the ancestors;
in public affairs, the Way must be followed.
Opening the state gates
means amusing them with good words.
Humbly knowing the order of the spirits
means handling the sacrificial animals and the jade tablets
to hold the sacrificial cups.
Small harms to the Great Houses
allow the small to overcome the great.
Be round on the inside,
be timely on the outside,
and yet fear the strong.
Increase the emptiness,
and things will be corrected; observe their inner feelings.
The *Gōng* said:
If the state gates are blocked,
and the common people are clamoring and arrogant,
how should we prepare for it?
Choose what Heaven pardons,
choose what the spirits enrich,
choose what the people support,
and quickly entrust oneself to them;
this is how to bring peace.
To establish strength and address shortcomings
in the state of *Qí*, what should be done?
Give them high reputations to promote them,
give them heavy offices to endanger them,
and then demand performance according to their ability.
If they are too close, distance them,
do not let people plot against them;
if they are too distant, bring them close,
do not let people bend them.
This is how it is done.
If a minister becomes too great,
he will conversely become a harm.
I wish to ease the worry and remove the harm;
to use the small to observe the great,
what should be done?
Do not cut the deep roots,
do not sever the firm stalks,
do not drain the deep springs.
Do not assist the towering heights,
do not extinguish the clear brightness,
do not lose the living glory.
Ten words are not as good as this one.
Even if there is bad luck, it will become good;
therefore, use peace to reach fullness. When there are no affairs,
gather resources to wait for affairs,
and how should this be done?
For those who accumulate, establish surplus food and be extravagant,
beautify carriages and horses and gallop,
have much wine and ale and be lavish.
For a thousand years let no food leave;
this is called the fundamental business.
The district revenue has a master;
if it enters for management and use,
yet things are not managed,
accumulate it in the market.
One entry is accumulated when prices are low,
one entry is accumulated when prices are high;
this is called profit having no constant state.
The common people have no treasure;
they take profit as their priority.
One up and one down,
they stay only where profit is.
Only with profit can there be circulation;
only with circulation can a state be completed.
If profit is stagnant and does not transform,
observe where it comes from
and move it accordingly.
See those who cannot be employed,
and treat them as the common ranks.
Choose those who love fame
and make them leaders of the people;
if they love it without ceasing,
take this as the discipline of the state.
For those whose merit is not yet achieved,
they cannot have a singular name;
for those whose affairs are not yet on the Way,
they cannot speak of names.
Only after merit is achieved can one have a singular name;
only after affairs follow the Way can one speak of names;
only then can one receive and offer the sacrificial toast.
To put one's officers first is to invite offense;
to put one's people last is to sustain oneself.
He who treats the national position lightly will surely see the state fall;
he who distances his noble relatives will find his plans leaked.
Do not employ people from foreign states in office;
this is called losing the guiding principle.
Do not make frequent changes;
this is called ruining what has been accomplished.
When high ministers commit an offense,
do not allow them to leave the borders;
this is called leaking intelligence.
Do not frequently gather at the homes of high ministers to drink wine;
this is called causing the state to greatly diminish.
Even if a Yáo were present in a state that is dissolving,
hidden in the wilderness
and returning to the connected,
for those like this, they must surely follow this path to ruin!
Comparing it to a ceremonial vessel, if the top outweighs the base,
it will tip and flow downward
without being level.
If orders are not implemented below,
then the high and the low will not be able to rely on each other;
this is called a reduction.
Affairs are established but then fail;
why is this?
The army is distant but feared;
why is this?
The people have gathered but then scatter;
why is this?
Peace is interrupted by danger;
why is this?
Those who achieve success but are not trusted are in
peril;
those whose army is strong but lack righteousness will be
destroyed;
those who are not cautious with what is near but seek what is far will find their
army untrustworthy;
if one neglects close ministers to join with those far away,
then affairs will fail once established.
To destroy the principles of a state
and ruin the state's clans
will result in an army that is distant and not feared.
For a state that is small but acts big,
that is benevolent but not profitable,
and yet still has those competing for fame,
how burdensome this is!
Delighting in gathering one's own strength
to incorporate the power of others
while waiting for harm—
even if gathered, they will surely scatter.
If the Dàwáng does not rely on the masses but relies on himself,
the common people will gather on their own;
provide for them first and then benefit them,
then it will be accomplished without harm.
Distancing relatives and favoring outsiders,
aspiring to benevolence while plans are leaked,
despising the few and loving the large—
these are the reasons for danger.
If the masses are unified by a pact,
taking in reality while speaking of yielding,
acting secretly while speaking openly,
benefiting from others' misfortune,
and harming those without trouble—
I wish to possess this alone;
how is this done?
At such a time, the way of distributing wealth
can be practiced.
Now, profits are scattered and the people are discerning;
you must release it, and only then will it work.
The Gōng asked: "What do you mean?"
Lengthening mourning periods to waste their time,
elaborate funerals to circulate their wealth,
one relative going,
one relative coming—
this is how relatives are brought together.
This is called the mass pact.
He asked: "How should this be used?"
Making large burial pits
is to provide work for the poor;
beautifying tomb mounds
is to provide work for the Wénméng;
making large inner and outer coffins
is to promote carpentry;
providing many burial robes and quilts
is to promote women's textile work.
If there is still more,
then there are secondary ornaments,
there are tiered fences,
and there are buried treasures.
By doing this they feed one another,
and then the people benefit each other;
thus the preparations for defense and warfare are complete.
If villages have different customs
and states have different rites,
then the people will not drift away;
if laws are not identical,
then the people will not be distressed;
if the village elders do not see across to one another
and those who drift and scatter are punished,
then the people will not look elsewhere.
Settled in their villages and happy in their homes, the sacrifices,
songs, and titles are all different;
this is how local customs are preserved.
Determining the numbers for the square well-fields
and the multitude of fields for horses,
regulate them;
establish deities for hills and streams and be diligent in sacrifices;
all are differentiated by ability to determine food rations,
showing the importance of the foundation.
Thus for one whose territory is a thousand lǐ wide,
emoluments are heavy and sacrifices are honored.
Their ruler has no surplus land,
and for those who act as one with the land,
they follow and manage it.
For a ruler starting out
who manages as if unified,
it follows the principle of reduction.
For those participating in the reduction, if acting as one
with those who follow
and manage as if unified,
they follow the reduction.
For those participating in the reduction, act as if
following from the beginning without enfeoffment.
For a Wáng,
he elevates affairs;
for a Bàzhě, he generates merit.
To speak of emphasizing the foundation
is called the Shíyú;
dividing land without conflict
is to speak of putting others first and oneself last.
The officials in charge of rites,
the separation of the Zhāomù order;
prioritizing merit and implements,
the management of affairs,
honoring spirits and maintaining traditions;
the responsibilities of warfare,
to value merit and despise death;
the primary task, rewarding merit and reducing personal profit;
to encourage ministers, value righteousness and do not provide small profits.
As for the five offices,
if people strive in their duties,
only then does the ruler hear of them.
Investigate them; at this time,
it is about exalting the worthy.
Thus the ruler and ministers hold their roles.
If ruler and ministers hold their roles,
then high and low are balanced;
from this, we know that exalting the worthy is of no benefit,
and its destruction is suitable.
One who exalts the worthy perishes,
while one who employs the worthy prospers.
Valuing righteousness to forbid violence,
honoring ancestors to show respect to ancestors,
gathering the clan to participate in the court's reductions,
to show that being a ruler is not taken lightly.
Carrying out sacrifices and clearly arranging them,
Gāo Zǐ heard of this
and told the Zhōngqǐn Zhūzǐ.
The Zhōngqǐn Zhūzǐ told Guǎrén:
"Leaving the court without food being served in tripods."
The Zhōngqǐn Zhūzǐ told the women in the palace,
"The Gōng is about to travel,
therefore we do not see the Gōng off."
The Gōng said, "I am not traveling;
where did you hear of this?"
They said:
"We heard it from the Zhōngqǐn Zhūzǐ."
He sent for the Zhōngqǐn Zhūzǐ and asked them,
"Guǎrén is not traveling;
where did you hear of this?"
"We heard it from our predecessors:
If a feudal lord leaves the court and food is not served in tripods,
if there is no external business,
there must be internal worry."
The Gōng said,
“I did not wish to speak with you about this,
but your words have reached this point,
and I cannot but speak with you about it.
I wish to summon the feudal lords;
if the feudal lords do not come, what shall I do?
A mere girl cannot handle the matter of summoning the feudal lords.
Ever since I have ceased being a man who engages in base and murderous deeds,
official duties cannot be fulfilled and clothes cannot be worn;
therefore, even if there were a sage, how could he be put to use?
Can one polish the old ways and the new ways,
stabilize the state, and then transform the times?
When the state is poor but the border regions are rich,
nothing is more beautiful than coarse hemp at court;
when the state is rich but the borders are poor,
nothing is as good as the market.”
The market
is for encouragement.
Encouragement
is that from which the fundamental arises.
When well-managed, secondary affairs will arise.
Without extravagance,
the fundamental business cannot be established.
If selecting the worthy and promoting the capable cannot be achieved,
how can one punish the disobedient?
If a hundred men have no leader,
they cannot be overseen;
if a thousand chariots follow the Way,
they cannot be invaded.
When Zhòu was on high,
how could he punish the disobedient?
If forces are equal, they fight;
if one defends, the other attacks.
A hundred covers without a foundation
or a thousand gatherings without a shrine
are called crude;
they will be taken in one move.
In times of turmoil under Heaven,
when the myriad feudal lords are equal in power
and the myriad people have no one to listen to,
if the superiors cannot perform deeds or change the system,
how can they rule as kings?
By following old precedents and refining laws
to govern according to the Way,
then equals would kill
my lord. Therefore I take
Yí Wú as a substitute.”
The Gōng said:
“What is it like?”
He replied:
“By being unified.
If the overseeing lasts for long,
it can be achieved immediately.
When the spirits and gods are not clear,
there is no reward for the food in the sacks
to make clear the abundance of virtue.
Sinking and floating
is to show that wealth is lightly regarded.
First establish the images and set the dates,
and the people will follow.
Therefore, in offering prayers
with court threads and silk,
one clarifies that wealth is light and reputation is heavy.”
“Together?” The Gōng said, “Oversee?”
“That which is called unified
is to use wisdom to change those who come earlier or later.
If equals are unified, they contend;
if they are doubled, they are pleased;
if tenfold, they follow and submit;
if ten-thousandfold, they are transformed.
When success is achieved but cannot be recognized,
and the people expect what follows—once the form is completed and the name is changed, then one oversees.
I ask about managing the borders, what is it like?”
He replied:
“The borders change daily;
they cannot be viewed through permanent knowledge.
If the people have not yet changed but the affairs change,
this is called self-disorder.
I ask you to consult the borders and participate in their disorder,
assign them tasks,
and follow their plans.
In a territory of a hundred square lǐ,
where signal markers are in sight of each other,
the men flee from disaster and the women prepare food,
and the inner and outer prepare for each other.
In a single day of spring or autumn,
a defeat is called a thousand pieces of gold;
move by weighing your resources.
The scouts cannot be given too much weight;
only through connection with the superior
can the reports from the border be certain.
Can the envoys not have private interests?
No. Having private interests
is how they become internal agents.
Let the capable have a master, wait
and then attend to internal affairs.
A state of ten thousand generations
must have treasures of ten thousand generations.
One must follow the Way of Heaven and Earth;
employ the internal
and do not employ the external;
employ the small
and do not employ the large.
To discard the state treasure
and employ the external
is to leave it to others and be defeated. Weighing the treasure
and employing the small
can be the Way.
If one is capable, one focuses;
focusing brings ease.
If a rafter can overleap,
then the rafter will overleap.
If one is capable of office,
then even without guarding, things do not disperse.
Having many capable ones makes a Hegemon;
otherwise, one will face opposition.
The gentleman
is one who exerts himself to organize people,
not one who organizes things personally.
Thus, let the light be light
and the heavy be heavy.
Before and after,
there is no partiality.
Generally, that which is light
handles the reality.
Using the light makes one employable;
the heavy cannot be raised.
Light and heavy have their proper balance.
Use the heavy for the state;
use the light for death.
Do not give full stipends, lest the state be impoverished
and resources be insufficient.
Do not give full rewards, lest the love of virtue
be used as a routine.
I ask how to first unite with the world without private resentment,
and how to confront the strong without private harm;
how is this done?”
He replied:
“Though the state be strong,
its commands must be loyal and righteous.
Though the state be weak,
its commands must be respectful and sorrowful.
If the strong and the weak do not violate each other,
then people will desire to listen.
Putting others first and oneself last
without doing it to appear benevolent,
bestowing merit on others without claiming it—
then what is entrusted will go far,
and what is contended for will be external.
If it is clear there are no private associations,
then there will be no internal resentment.
Giving to the great leads to victory;
if private associations are numerous, resentment will kill. I, Yí Wú, say:
Giving people wealth
is not as good as not taking away their time;
giving people food
is not as good as not taking away their livelihood.
This is called having no external or internal calamities.
Loyalty and respect
are the nexus between ruler and subject.
Rites and righteousness
are the spirit of the ruler.
Furthermore, the relationship between ruler and subject is one of righteousness;
the love of kin
is one of nature.
To make the nexus between ruler and kin seek the same thing is the relationship of respect.
That which makes a ruler uneasy
is the relationship of scrutiny;
this must be handled with caution.
The worthy cannot be intimidated,
and the capable cannot be detained.
To block matters before they arise
is easy.”
Where water and springs gush forth,
people gather there;
where the soil is beautiful,
people dwell there until death.
As for the vastness of the Jiāng and Hú,
those who seek pearls and shells do not abandon them.
Pursuing the divine and distancing oneself from heat,
those who exchange goblets do not remain,
and brothers leave profit behind
indeed! For those who serve the people of the Zhōngguó,
to observe endangered states and errant rulers and seek to exploit their skills—
is this not close to endangering the lords of the altars of state!
Profit cannot be made a law,
hence the people drift;
the divine cannot be made a law,
hence it is served.
Heaven and Earth cannot be held still,
hence they move; they transform
and thus follow the new.
Therefore, one who attains the way of Heaven
is high yet does not collapse;
one who attains the way of man
is humble yet cannot be overcome.
Therefore, the Shèngrén values this;
the ruler of men values this.
Thus, ultimate uprightness generates ultimate trustworthiness;
ultimate trustworthiness generates ultimate association.
To produce the ultimate, there is a natural way:
do not strive to let outward ornament overcome inner feeling;
do not strive to let the many overcome the few.
If one does not move, the gaze meets a wall;
conduct is practiced throughout the self.
Laws, systems, degrees, and measurements
are the canonical instruments of a King.
Holding to old principles and the Way
is out of fear of change.
Heaven and Earth are like the movement of the divine; transformation and change
are the ultimate manifestations of Heaven and Earth.
To be able to rise with transformation and use it well
means one cannot be stopped by any single path.
The benevolent use it well;
the wise use it well.
If it is not the right person,
they depart with the spirit.
Food and clothing for humans
cannot be departed from for even a single day,
yet relatives can be left from time to time.
Therefore, the Shèngrén establishes himself where the myriad people find it difficult to dwell.
When people die, they are easily forgotten,
but while alive, it is difficult to bring them into harmony.
Thus, the first time is a reward;
the second time becomes a custom;
the third time becomes a matter of course.
When practiced on a small scale,
it is desire;
after a long time,
it becomes Lǐ and Yì.
Thus, do not force subordinates to comply;
the superior must practice it first, and then it will transfer.
Merchants in a state
are not for employing as officials.
They do not choose a village to dwell in,
nor a ruler to serve;
they go out to follow profit
and come in without defending.
Regarding the mountains and forests of the state,
they take from them and profit.
Wherever the marketplaces reach,
they rely on their basis.
Thus, if the superior is extravagant, the subordinates will be wasteful;
but if the ruler, ministers, and those above and below are close to one another,
then the wealth of the ruler and ministers is not hidden away privately.
In this way, by moving one's limbs, one obtains food.
Moving a city or shifting a market
is also a primary matter.
It was asked:
"Can many worthy men be gathered?"
The reply was:
"Fish and turtles that do not eat bait
do not leave their deep pools;
trees that withstand frost and snow
do not listen to Heaven;
scholars who can govern themselves
do not follow a Shèngrén."
How could they be gathered?
Yíwú heard that:
"If they have no desire, even the strong cannot make them submit;
if they are wise, they cannot be herded."
If the ten-day period and the monthly cycle match,
and the Lǜlǚ emerge from one source clearly,
then they can be dwelled with.
Therefore, if you obstruct their way and give them little,
then the scholars will be scattered.
To give without choosing the person
is called being a lover of people;
to take without choosing the person
is called loving profit.
Examine these two things
and use them to guide conduct and dwelling,
then they will gather.
Policy that is not upright
cannot govern a state;
words that are crooked and quiet
cannot be the Way.
Regulating time in policy means
moving along with the seasons.
Taking non-action as the Way
and uniformity as conduct—
this way of withdrawing from the world
cannot be used for advancement and acquisition.
The Yáng advances schemes;
the subtle responds to stimuli;
when killing is repeated, there is uniformity,
and then movement occurs. (May I ask) What does this mean?
The reply was:
"Operating schemes involves the emptiness and fullness of Heaven and Earth,
joining and separating,
and the victory of spring, autumn, winter, and summer.
Thus one knows the causes of strength and weakness,
and then responds to the feudal lords and forms alliances;
thus one knows where the safety or peril of the state resides.
Serve Heaven according to the seasons,
serve the spirits according to Heaven,
serve the ghosts according to the spirits.
Thus the state has no punishments, the ruler lives long,
and the people do not suffer
pestilence. Wisdom operates schemes and puts away the scabbard and blade.
Fullness creates sensation;
emptiness creates disappearance.
The union of fullness and emptiness
is at times reality
and at times movement.
Yīnyáng alternate seasonally;
if the winter is severe, the summer will be hot;
if the Yáng is thick, the Yīn will be cold.
Therefore, the King is cautious regarding the solstices,
thus knowing where emptiness and fullness reside to issue government orders.
When giving life and killing are settled,
and they are joined but not yet dispersed,
one can decide matters.
When they are about to join, one can observe
their following and use them for military force,
and divide their amounts
to form detailed policies.
May I ask, does form change according to the season?
The reply was:
When the divisions of Yīnyáng are fixed,
then sweet and bitter herbs grow.
Following what is appropriate,
then sour and salty are harmonized,
and forms and colors are fixed,
becoming music and sounds.
The advance and retreat of Yīnyáng,
and the times of fullness, emptiness, and disappearance—
their dispersal and union can be seen in the year.
Only the Shèngrén is not
exhausted by the year; he knows fullness and emptiness,
takes from the excess of fullness,
and supplements the insufficient,
so as to facilitate government affairs
and provide for the people's livelihood.
The changing Qì of Earth
responds to its origin.
The changing Qì of water
is responded to with essence
and received with preparedness.
The changing Qì of Heaven
is responded to with correctness.
Furthermore, the essential Qì of Heaven and Earth are five;
they do not necessarily cause obstruction,
but their urgency and reversal
accumulate and become heavy. The advance and retreat of movement and destruction
are precisely these numbers that are difficult to grasp;
these are the seasonal changes of form.
When the Yang of the balanced Qì is obstructed,
how can one remain calm and quiet?
When excessive Qì moves covertly,
and cherished Qì becomes sorrowful in secret,
how can one control such movement?
The answer says:
When obtained during a time of decline,
observe it from its position;
only when there is true beauty will there be brilliance. Cultivating
the mind,
its fluctuations treat one another accordingly,
therefore there are the Qì of fullness and emptiness, of sorrow and joy.
Therefore, in the records of the Dì Bā,
Shénnóng is not included among them,
because he lacked the position
and could not be employed with them.
Question: Where are the cycles of combination and fullness stored?
At twenty years it can be expanded;
at twelve years it is subtly expanded;
at one hundred years it harms the Shén.
When the rites of Zhōu and Zhèng are altered,
then the Lǜ of Zhōu are abandoned,
then the plants and trees of Zhōngguó will migrate to inaccessible wilds.
Thus, when the ruler’s music and attire change,
then ministers have the stipend of a thousand chariots,
women take part in government,
and the value of iron conversely exceeds that of gold.
When music favors low melodies,
and food favors salty and bitter flavors,
if these become extreme, the ruler will decline daily.
Then the sacrifices to the Shén of streams, mounds, mountains, and valleys change,
and the titles of the responding state also change.
Observe this through celestial changes,
and watch it through the wind and Qì.
In ancient sacrifices,
sometimes there were stars,
sometimes there was Xī,
sometimes there was Ǒu,
and sometimes there was Xù.
The mouse corresponds to the substance of expansion,
which is the numerical principle of Yīnyáng;
Huá Ruò Luò is the
name and the title of the sacrifice.
Therefore, when the Tiānzǐ governs the state, he plans and arranges its established things.
The mind’s presence in the body
is the position of the ruler;
the nine orifices’ possession of functions
is the division of the officials.
If the mind abides in its Dào,
the nine orifices will follow the natural Lǐ;
if desires are overabundant,
the eyes will not see colors,
and the ears will not hear sounds.
Therefore it is said:
If the superior departs from his Dào,
the inferiors will fail in their duties.
Do not run in place of a horse,
but let it exert all its strength;
do not fly in place of a bird,
but let it wear out its wings;
do not move before things do,
so as to observe their principles.
To move is to lose one’s position;
to be still is to find oneself.
The Dào is not far away, yet it is difficult to reach its limit;
it dwells together with humans, yet it is difficult to obtain.
Emptying one's desires,
the Shén will enter its dwelling;
if the sweeping is not clean,
the Shén will not remain.
Everyone desires wisdom,
yet no one seeks that by which they become wise.
Wisdom! Wisdom!
Even if cast beyond the seas, it cannot be taken away by itself.
Those who seek it are not as good as those who empty themselves.
The Shèngrén has no seeking,
therefore he is able to be empty.
To be empty and without form is called Dào;
to transform and nourish the myriad things is called Dé;
the affairs among people such as ruler and minister, father and son, are called Yì;
ascending and descending, bowing and yielding,
the hierarchy of the noble and the lowly,
and the forms of intimacy and distance
are called Lǐ;
simplifying things, whether small or great, into a single path,
and using execution, massacre, prohibition, and punishment are called Fǎ.
The Great Dào can be settled in, but cannot be explained.
The words of the Zhēnrén
are neither biased nor skewed; they do not issue from the mouth
and are not seen in the countenance.
Among the people of the Sìhǎi,
who then knows its principle?
Heaven is called empty,
Earth is called still;
thus they do not err.
Cleanse one's palace,
open one's gates,
cast aside selfishness and do not speak,
and the Shénmíng will seem to be present.
Though things be as confused as chaos,
keep them still and they will govern themselves.
Strength cannot establish everything,
and wisdom cannot plan everything.
Things inherently have forms,
and forms inherently have names;
when names are appropriate, one is called a Shèngrén.
Therefore, one must know the wordless words and the Wúwéi affairs,
then one knows the guiding thread of the Dào.
Despite different forms and different holdings,
they do not differ from the principles of the myriad things;
therefore, it can serve as the beginning of the Tiānxià.
That people can be killed
is because they hate death;
that they can be disadvantaged
is because they love profit.
For this reason, the Jūnzǐ is not enticed by what he loves
and not coerced by what he hates;
he is tranquil and follows Wúwéi,
discarding cleverness and past precedents.
His responses
are not preconceived;
his movements
are not calculated.
Error lies in following one’s own will;
fault lies in shifting and changing.
Therefore,
the noble
man who possesses the Dào,
when at rest
appears to have no knowledge,
and when responding to things
appears to be a mere counterpart to them.
This is the Dào of stillness and following.
"The mind’s presence in the body
is the position of the ruler;
the nine orifices’ possession of functions
is the division of the officials."
The ears and eyes
are the officials of seeing and hearing;
if the mind does not interfere with the affairs of seeing and hearing,
then the officials can maintain their divisions.
When the mind has desires,
things pass by but the eyes do not see,
and sounds arrive but the ears do not hear.
Therefore it is said:
"If the superior departs from his Dào,
the inferiors will fail in their duties."
Therefore it is said:
The Xīnshù
is to control the orifices through Wúwéi.
Thus it is called
"the ruler."
"Do not run in place of a horse,"
"do not fly in place of a bird"—
this means not usurping the
abilities of the capable, and not competing with subordinates.
Regarding "Do not move before things do,"
one who wavers is not stable,
and one who is rash is not still;
this means that if one moves first, one cannot observe properly.
"Position"
refers to where one stands.
The ruler of men stands in *Yīn*;
*Yīn* is stillness;
therefore it is said, "If one moves, one loses one's position."
*Yīn* can control *Yáng*;
stillness can control movement;
therefore it is said, "Through stillness, one attains oneself."
The *Dào* exists between Heaven and Earth;
its greatness has no outside;
its smallness has no inside;
therefore it is said, "It is not far, yet difficult to reach the limit."
There is no gap between emptiness and man;
only the *Shèngrén* attains the *Dào* of emptiness;
therefore it is said, "They dwell together, yet it is difficult to attain."
That which the people of the world attend to is the *Jīng*.
If desires are removed, then there is openness;
if there is openness, then there is stillness;
if there is stillness, then there is *Jīng*.
If there is *Jīng*, then one stands independent;
if independent, then there is *Míng*;
if there is *Míng*, then one is *Shén*.
The *Shén* is the most noble;
therefore, if the lodging is not cleared and cleaned,
the noble person will not stay there.
Therefore it is said, "If it is not clean, the spirit will not dwell there."
Everyone wishes to know but none seek it correctly.
That by which they know is how they know that [external thing];
that by which they know is this [the mind].
If one does not cultivate this,
how can one know that?
If one cultivates this,
none can fail to be empty.
Emptiness means having no storage.
Therefore,
if one discards knowledge, what would one seek?
If one has no storage, what would one establish?
Having no seeking and no establishing,
then there is no anxious thought;
if there is no anxious thought, one returns repeatedly to emptiness.
The *Dào* of Heaven
is empty and formless.
Being empty, it is inexhaustible;
being formless, there is nothing it collides with.
Without any collision,
it flows through the myriad things without changing.
*Dé* is the lodging of the *Dào*.
Things attain it to be
born; knowledge attains it to attend to the *Jīng* of the *Dào*.
Therefore *Dé* means "attaining."
"Attaining"
refers to that which is attained to make things as they are.
Non-action is called the *Dào*;
lodging it is called *Dé*.
Therefore, there is no gap between the *Dào* and *Dé*;
thus, those who speak of them do not distinguish them.
The principle of the "gap"
refers to that which serves as the lodging.
*Yì*
means each staying in its proper place.
*Lǐ*
follows human emotions,
complies with the principle of *Yì*,
and provides them with regulation and refinement.
Therefore, *Lǐ* means having principle.
Principle
clarifies distinctions to illustrate the meaning of *Yì*.
Therefore *Lǐ* emerges from principle,
principle emerges from *Yì*,
and *Yì* is based on what is proper.
*Fǎ* is that by which things come forth together;
it is what must be so.
Therefore, execution, slaughter, prohibition, and punishment are used to unify them.
Thus, affairs are supervised by the law;
law emerges from *Quán*;
*Quán* emerges from the *Dào*.
As for the *Dào*,
its movement does not show its form,
its bestowing does not show its *Dé*.
The myriad things all attain by it,
