yet none know its limit.
Therefore it is said,
"It can be settled in, but cannot be described."
*Zhēnrén*
refers to the ultimate.
"Not being fixed"
refers to responding.
Responding
is not something I establish;
therefore one can be without fixed propriety.
"Not being biased" means
following.
Following
is not something I
take for myself; therefore there is no bias.
"It does not come out of the mouth,
nor does it appear in the countenance,"
which means it is formless.
"Of the people within the four seas,
who knows its principle?"
which means it is deeply enclosed.
The *Dào* of Heaven is empty;
the *Dào* of Earth is still.
Being empty, it is inexhaustible;
being still, it does not change.
Not changing, there is no error;
therefore it is said, "It does not boast."
"Cleanse its palace,
open its gates":
The palace
refers to the *Xīn*.
The *Xīn*
is the lodging of wisdom;
thus it is called a "palace."
To cleanse it
is to remove likes and excesses.
The gates
refer to the ears and eyes.
The ears and eyes
are that by which one hears and sees.
"Things inherently have form;
forms inherently have names."
This means that names must not exceed reality,
and reality must not be stretched by names.
Treating forms as forms,
using forms to seek names,
supervising speech and rectifying names—
therefore one is called a *Shèngrén*.
"The wordless word"
refers to responding.
Responding
is done for the sake of others.
Grasping the name
and attending to that
by which it is accomplished—
this is the way of responding.
"The non-action task" refers to following.
Following
means having no addition or subtraction.
Using its form
to follow and create its name—
this is the technique of following.
Names
are that by which the *Shèngrén* records the myriad things.
Ordinary people stand on strength,
strive for goodness,
value ability, and
move by artifice.
The *Shèngrén* is without these.
Being without these,
he is different from things.
Being different, he is empty.
Emptiness is the beginning of the myriad things;
therefore it is said, "He can be the beginning of all under heaven."
When people are pressured by what is disliked,
they lose what they like;
when they are enticed by what they like,
they forget what they dislike.
This is not the *Dào*.
Therefore it is said:
"Do not be enticed by what is liked,
do not be pressured by what is disliked."
When dislike does not lose its principle,
and desire does not exceed its essence,
therefore it is said:
"*Jūnzǐ*." "Being tranquil, pleased, and practicing non-action;
discarding wisdom and artifice"
refers to emptiness and simplicity.
"Its response is not what was pre-arranged,
its movement is not what was pre-selected,"
this speaks of *yīn* (accordance).
*Yīn*
means setting aside oneself and taking external things as the law.
To respond only after being stimulated
is not to have pre-arranged it;
to move by following *lǐ* (principle)
is not to have pre-selected it.
"Error lies in self-reliance;
guilt lies in changeability."
Self-reliance means one is not empty;
being not empty, one clashes with things.
Changeability leads to artificiality;
artificiality leads to chaos.
Therefore, the *Dào* values *yīn*.
*Yīn*
means to follow their abilities
when speaking of what is employed.
"The *Jūnzǐ* dwells as if having no knowledge,"
this refers to the ultimate emptiness.
"His response to things is like an accompaniment,"
which refers to timely suitability,
like a shadow depicting a shape
or an echo responding to a sound.
Therefore, when a thing arrives, one responds;
when it has passed, one lets go of it.
Letting go
means returning to the state of emptiness.
When the form is not upright, *Dé* (Virtue) does not come;
when the center is not refined, the heart is not ordered.
Rectify the form and adorn *Dé*,
and the myriad things will all be attained.
They will come of their own accord in a flock,
and the *shén* (spirit) will not know its limit.
One will clearly know all under Heaven
and reach the four extremes.
Therefore it is said:
Do not let things disturb the sensory organs;
do not let the sensory organs disturb the heart.
This is called inner *Dé*.
Therefore, when the *yì* (intent) and *qì* (vital breath) are settled,
only then can one return to the correct state.
*Qì*
is the fullness of the body;
conduct is the manifestation of what is correct.
If the fullness is not beautiful,
the heart will not attain it;
if conduct is not upright,
the people will not submit.
Therefore,
the *Shèng Rén* (Sage) is like Heaven,
covering all without partiality;
he is like the Earth,
supporting all without partiality.
Partiality
is what brings chaos to all under Heaven.
All things come bearing names;
the *Shèng Rén* follows them and regulates them,
and all under Heaven is ordered.
Realities are not harmed and do not bring chaos to all under Heaven,
and all under Heaven is ordered.
Focus the *yì*,
unify the heart,
make the ears and eyes upright,
and one can know the far from the near.
Can you focus?
Can you be unified?
Can you know good and bad luck without divination?
Can you stop?
Can you cease?
Can you avoid asking others
and obtain it from within yourself?
Therefore it is said:
Think on it.
If thinking does not yield it,
the *guǐshén* (ghosts and spirits) will teach it.
It is not the power of the *guǐshén*,
but the culmination of one’s *jīngqì* (essence and vital breath).
To be able to transform a single thing is called *jīng* (essence);
to be able to transform a single affair is called *zhì* (wisdom).
Selection and choice
are how one prioritizes affairs;
the peak of transformation
is how one responds to things.
Select and choose without chaos;
reach the peak of transformation without exhaustion.
The *Jūnzǐ* who holds to the One
holds to the One and does not lose it;
he can master the myriad things.
He shares the same light as the sun and moon
and shares the same *lǐ* as Heaven and Earth.
The *Shèng Rén* regulates things
and is not controlled by things.
When the heart is at peace,
the state is at peace;
when the heart is ordered,
the state is ordered.
Order comes from the heart;
peace comes from the heart.
Ordering the heart lies within;
ordered words come from the mouth;
ordered affairs are applied to the people.
Thus, when work is performed and the people follow,
then the common people are ordered.
That which restrains them is not punishment;
that which makes them wary is not anger.
When the people are restrained
and the commoners are ordered,
the *Dào* is its root
and its culmination.
When the culmination reaches nothingness,
it is not a place for men to cause chaos.
The regulations of those officials who hold to rules
are not the *Dào*.
The *Dào* of the *Shèng Rén*
seems to exist and yet not to exist;
drawing upon it and using it,
it does not perish even after one's life ends.
It changes with the times but is not transformed;
it responds to things but does not shift;
though used daily, it is not depleted.
Those who can be upright and quiet
will have supple tendons and strong bones.
They can bear the Great Round and embody the Great Square.
Their mirror is the Great Purity, and they see with the Great Clarity.
If uprightness and quietude are not lost,
one daily renews their *Dé*,
clearly knows all under Heaven,
and reaches the four extremes.
When a whole heart is within, it cannot be hidden;
externally it appears in the form and appearance
and can be known from the complexion.
A good *qì* greeting others
is as close as brothers;
an evil *qì* greeting others
is more harmful than weapons.
The wordless word
is heard like thunder and drums.
The form of a whole heart
is brighter than the sun and moon
and more observant than parents.
In the past, the *Míng Wáng* (Enlightened Kings) loved all under Heaven,
so all under Heaven could be attached to them;
the *Bào Wáng* (Tyrant Kings) hated all under Heaven,
so all under Heaven could be estranged from them.
Therefore, rewards are not enough to be considered love,
and punishments are not enough to be considered hatred.
Rewards are the end-products of love;
punishments are the end-products of hatred.
In the life of all people,
they must be upright and balanced.
That which causes them to lose this
must be joy, pleasure, sorrow, and anger.
To moderate anger, nothing is better than music;
to moderate music, nothing is better than *lǐ* (ritual);
to maintain *lǐ*, nothing is better than *jìng* (reverence).
When there is external reverence and inner quietude,
one will surely return to their nature.
Are there no profitable affairs?
I have no heart for profit.
Are there no peaceful places?
I have no heart for seeking peace.
Within the heart, there is another heart.
The *yì* precedes words;
after the *yì*, there is the form;
after the form, there is thought;
after thought, there is knowledge.
The forms of all hearts
surpass the knowledge of the *Xiān Wáng* (Former Kings).
Therefore, gather within to form the source.
The spring will not run dry,
and the inner and outer will be connected.
If the spring does not run dry,
the four limbs will be firm and strong.
If one can make use of it,
it will reach to the four borders.
Therefore, the Shèng Rén explains it in a single word:
above, he observes Tiān;
below, he observes Dì.
Twelve Short Sayings: Establish the constant as the lead,
take tranquility as the ancestor,
take timeliness as the treasure,
take governance as the standard;
if there is harmony, then one can endure.
If it is not my standard,
though it be profitable, I do not do it;
if it is not my proper place,
though it be profitable, I do not act;
if it is not my Dào,
though it be profitable, I do not take it.
Primarily, one follows Tiān;
next, one follows man.
If man does not lead, one does not harmonize;
if Tiān does not initiate, one does not follow.
Therefore, his words
are not discarded,
and his affairs
do not fail.
Trace the origin and calculate the reality;
base it on that from which it arises.
Knowing its images,
then seek its forms; following
its principles,
then know its essence;
seeking its beginnings,
then know its names.
Therefore, among that which contains many things, none is greater than Tiān Dì;
among that which transforms many things, none is more prolific than the sun and moon;
among what the people urgently need,
none is more urgent than water and fire.
However, Tiān does not warp its seasons for a single thing;
the Míng Jūn and Shèng Rén also do not warp their laws for a single person.
Tiān moves as it moves,
and the myriad things receive its benefit;
the Shèng Rén also acts as he acts,
and the Bǎi Xìng receive his benefit.
Therefore, all things are equalized and made abundant.
Thus, in the governance of the Shèng Rén,
he quiets his person to wait for it.
When things arrive, their names govern themselves.
Correct names govern themselves;
if the person is eccentric, names are discarded.
When names are correct and laws are complete,
then the Shèng Rén has nothing to do.
One cannot always stay in one place,
nor can one discard or abandon it;
follow changes to decide matters,
and know the time to take it as the measure.
The great is broad,
the small is constrained;
things have that which is in surplus
and that which is insufficient.
The mobilization of weapons
comes from people;
when those people return,
they return to the self.
Victory in battle
follows from being appropriate;
the arrival of Dé
follows from the self.
Therefore it is said:
To be auspicious toward spirits is to be righteous toward men;
weapons without righteousness are not permissible.
Those who are strong and arrogant diminish their strength;
those who are weak and arrogant swiftly perish;
those who are strong and humble
extend their strength;
those who are weak and humble
avoid culpability.
Therefore, the remnant of arrogance is humility;
the remnant of humility is arrogance.
As for the Dào,
if one person uses it,
it is not heard to be in surplus;
if the whole world practices it,
it is not heard to be insufficient.
This is called the Dào.
Take a little from it
and one gains a little blessing;
take much from it
and one gains much blessing;
practice it fully
and the whole world submits;
if one takes nothing at all from it,
then the people rebel,
and one's person will not escape harm.
The left is that which goes out;
the right is that which comes in.
If that which goes out does not harm others,
that which comes in will harm [only] itself.
Without looking to the sun or moon,
affairs follow accordingly;
without divination by turtle shell or yarrow stalks,
one clearly knows good and bad fortune.
This is called being lenient with punishments,
and achieving fame while merely dwelling in place.
Utter good words,
perform good deeds;
when the deed is accomplished and one looks back, there is no name for it.
The capable have no name;
they attend to affairs as if there were no affairs.
Examine and weigh outgoing and incoming,
and observe what things contain.
Who can govern without governing?
Begin without beginning?
End without ending?
Be weak without being weak?
Therefore it is said: "How beautiful and flourishing!"
Therefore it is said: "In the center where there is no center,"
who can attain the inner essence of that center?
Therefore it is said:
One who achieves success will decline;
one who achieves fame will diminish.
Therefore it is said:
Who can discard fame and success
and return to being the same as the common people?
Who can discard success and fame
and return to a state of non-achievement?
In non-achievement, there is that which values achievement;
in achievement, there is that which values non-achievement.
When the sun reaches its zenith, it declines;
when the moon is full, it wanes.
The peak leads only to decline;
fullness leads only to waning;
greatness leads only to extinction.
Who can lose the self?
Mimic the order of Tiān Dì.
If people speak of good,
do not listen;
if people speak of evil,
do not listen.
Maintain and wait for it;
be empty and do not vacillate between the two;
then it will be pure and clear of itself.
Do not take side-talk as the accomplishment of an affair;
examine and verify it;
do not listen to clever arguments;
let the myriad things return to it,
then beauty and ugliness will appear of themselves.
Tiān perhaps sustains it;
Dì perhaps supports it.
If Tiān did not sustain it,
then Tiān would fall;
if Dì did not support it,
then Dì would sink.
Since Tiān does not fall
and Dì does not sink,
there must be something that sustains and supports them!
How much more so for man?
There is that which governs man,
comparable to the movement of the thunder-drum.
That which cannot shake itself
is perhaps moved by something else.
What is this "something else"? It is "that which is just so."
Looked at, it is not seen;
listened to, it is not heard;
it overflows and fills the world,
yet no obstruction is seen.
It gathers in the complexion,
it is known in the skin and flesh;
seeking its coming and going,
no one knows its time;
thin is its squareness,
vast is its roundness;
so vast, so vast, none can find its gate.
Thus the mouth is for sound,
the ears are for hearing,
the eyes possess sight,
the hands possess pointing,
the feet possess treading,
and affairs and things possess their counterparts.
"What should live, lives;
what should die, dies";
it is said there is West and there is East,
and each dies in its own region.
If one establishes constants and sets up models,
can one maintain integrity?
If one manages constant affairs to open the way,
can one employ people as officials?
Therefore, those who record the evil
speak of the superficial.
Among people of the highest sagehood,
the mouth has no idle habits,
the hands have no idle gestures;
when things arrive, they simply name them.
What is manifested in reputation
and solidified in physical appearance,
these are what can be explained.
What is not manifested in reputation
and not solidified in physical appearance,
these are what cannot be explained.
Upon reaching the ultimate,
it is fine if teaching exists,
and it is fine if teaching perishes.
Therefore it is said:
One who crosses by boat harmonizes with the water;
one who is righteous toward people is auspicious to the spirits.
Affairs have their suitability,
yet they have no suitability, even while appearing to have suitability;
like untying with a horn tool, only after there is no suitability is there suitability;
like untying with a horn tool, only after it is impossible to untie is it untied.
Therefore, of those who are good at handling affairs,
the state knows not their solution.
In doing good,
do not be boastful;
in doing what is not good,
one will fall into punishment.
Whether good or not good,
attain trust and then stop.
Whether to the left or to the right,
it is just the exact center.
It hangs like the sun and moon without end.
Those who are outspoken do not worry about the world;
those who are talkative do not take the myriad things as a plan. Who can
discard talkativeness and become outspoken?
It is difficult to speak of the arts of law;
one must wait for commonality to emerge.
With no words of gain and no words of loss,
one can nearly be exempt from harm.
Therefore it is said:
What is known through knowing?
What is planned through planning?
For one who emerges through careful scrutiny,
the other comes naturally.
To know oneself is called alignment;
to know others is called succor.
If knowledge is suitable, one can
be the sovereign of the world;
strengthening it within and
remaining unified, one can endure long;
if one evaluates and employs it,
one can be the king of the world.
Heaven’s vision is refined;
the four
directions open and it knows the requests; it provides for the soil and grants life.
Can one be like the wind and the waves?
Going only where they wish to go.
Thus, for a son to succeed his father is called righteousness;
for a minister to succeed his ruler is called usurpation.
How can a usurper be sung of?
Wǔ Wáng was such a person.
Therefore it is said:
Who can discard disputation and cleverness
and return to the same path as the common people?
Therefore it is said:
For those whose thoughts are refined, their clarity diminishes;
for those whose virtuous conduct is cultivated, the Kingly Way is narrow;
for those who rest on fame and profit, their life is endangered.
For those whose knowledge encompasses the six directions,
I know that purposeful action in life creates obstacles.
Holding and filling it to the brim
is where the danger lies.
To have fame fill the world
is not as good as stopping.
For fame to advance while the self retreats
is the Way of Heaven.
A state at its peak of fullness
is not a place to serve in office;
a family at its peak of fullness
is not a place to marry off a child;
a person who is arrogant, haughty, and violent
is not one to associate with.
The Dào’s greatness is like Heaven,
its breadth is like the Earth,
its weight is like stone,
its lightness is like a feather.
That which the people rely upon,
those who know it are few.
Therefore it is said:
What Way is so near
yet no one is able to follow it?
To abandon what is near and pursue what is far,
why waste such effort?
Therefore it is said:
If one wishes to love one's body,
first one must know one's nature.
Survey the six directions
to examine the inner self.
By this one knows the signs,
and then one knows the nature of actions.
Having known the nature of actions,
then one knows the cultivation of life.
Left and right, front and back,
circling around and returning to the place.
Holding the model and following the signs,
respectfully welcome what comes.
Now, regarding what comes, it must follow its way;
without shifting or overflowing,
then life will be long.
Harmonize to return to the center,
and form and nature will preserve each other.
Be unified without duality;
this is called knowing the Dào.
If one wishes to follow it,
one must unify its beginning
and solidify what one maintains.
Observe its coming and going;
no one knows its timing.
Seek it in Heaven,
make an appointment with it;
if one does not miss the appointment,
then one can obtain it.
Therefore it is said:
I tell you of the ultimate of Great Brilliance;
the brilliance of Great Brilliance
is not that it loves people, but that people do not give themselves to it.
If they are the same, they follow each other;
if they are opposite, they distance each other.
I observe the distancing of opposites,
and by this I know the sameness of those that follow the same.
The Earth
is the source of the myriad things,
the root and luxuriant growth of all living things;
it is where the beautiful and ugly, the worthy and unworthy, the foolish and the talented are born.
Water
is the blood and Qì of the Earth,
flowing like sinews and veins.
Therefore it is said: Water is a complete substance.
How do we know it is so?
It is said:
Water is soft and weak yet clear,
and likes to wash away people's filth;
this is benevolence.
Viewed it is dark yet white;
this is essence.
Measured it cannot be leveled,
stopping only when full;
this is uprightness.
There is nowhere it does not flow,
stopping only at perfect levelness;
this is righteousness.
People all rush toward the high,
while it alone rushes toward the low;
this is humility.
Humility
is the dwelling of the Dào,
the vessel of kings,
and water takes it as its capital residence.
The level is
the ancestor of the five measures.
Plain white is
the substance of the five colors.
The bland is
the center of the five flavors.
Therefore, water is the level of the myriad things,
the blandness of all living beings, and
the substance of right and wrong, gain and loss.
Thus, there is nothing it does not fill, and nowhere it does not dwell.
It gathers in Heaven and Earth
and is stored in the myriad things;
it is produced in metal and stone,
and gathers in all living beings.
Therefore it is called Shuǐ Shén.
When it gathers in grasses and trees,
their roots obtain their measure,
their flowers obtain their number,
and their fruits obtain their quantity.
When birds and beasts obtain it,
their physical forms become fat and large,
their feathers and fur become lush and abundant,
and their patterns and markings become clear and distinct.
Among the myriad things, there are none that do not fulfill their potential
or return to their constant state;
this is because the internal measure of water is appropriate.
As for why jade is valued,
the nine virtues emerge from it.
That jade is warm, moist, and glossy
is benevolence.
That its markings are organized by principle
is wisdom.
That it is firm and yet not brittle
is righteousness.
That it has sharp edges but does not cut
is conduct.
That it is bright and stainless
is purity.
That it can be broken but not bent
is courage.
That its flaws and perfections are both visible
is essence.
That its lush brilliance and luster
penetrate together without encroaching upon each other
is tolerance.
When struck,
its sound is clear, resonant, and far-reaching,
pure and not muddled;
this is rhetoric.
Thus the sovereign values it,
storing it as a treasure
and carving it into tallies and auspicious tokens,
for the nine virtues emerge from it.
Man
is water.
When the essential energy of male and female combine,
the water flows into form.
At three months it is like a morsel.
What is a morsel?
It is said to be the five flavors.
What are the five flavors?
They are the five viscera.
Sourness governs the spleen,
saltiness governs the lungs,
acridity governs the kidneys,
bitterness governs the liver,
and sweetness governs the heart.
Once the five viscera are complete,
the internal organs are then produced.
The spleen produces the diaphragm,
the lungs produce the bones,
the kidneys produce the brain,
the liver produces the skin,
and the heart produces the flesh.
Once the five internals are complete,
they then manifest as the nine orifices.
The spleen manifests as the nose,
the liver manifests as the eyes,
the kidneys manifest as the ears,
and the lungs manifest as the orifices.
In the fifth month it is completed,
and in the tenth month it is born.
Having been born, the eyes see,
the ears hear, and the heart thinks.
That which the eyes see
is not only the sight of mountains and hills,
but also discerning the vague and indistinct.
That which the ears hear
is not only the sound of thunder and drums,
but also discerning the faint chirping.
That which the heart thinks
is not only knowing the coarse and crude,
but also discerning the minute and subtle.
Thus water gathers in jade
and the nine virtues emerge.
It congeals and hardens to become man,
and the nine orifices and five thoughts emerge.
This is its essence,
which, though coarse, turbid, and hardened,
can exist but cannot vanish.
Those hidden in darkness that can exist and can vanish
are the milfoil, the tortoise, and the dragon.
The tortoise is born in water
and is manifested through fire;
thus it is the precursor of all things
and the arbiter of fortune and misfortune.
The dragon is born in water
and roams covered in the five colors;
therefore it is spiritual.
Wishing to be small, it transforms like a silkworm or caterpillar;
wishing to be large, it encompasses Heaven and Earth;
wishing to ascend, it soars into the clouds and mist;
wishing to descend, it enters the deep springs.
Its transformations have no fixed day,
and its rising and falling have no fixed time;
this is called spiritual. The tortoise and the dragon
are those hidden in darkness that can exist and can vanish.
Those that are seen in some generations
and not seen in others
are the wéi and the Qìng Jì.
Therefore, in a dried-up marsh of several hundred years
where the valley does not move
and the water does not run dry, the Qìng Jì is born.
As for the Qìng Jì,
its form is like a human,
its height is four inches,
it wears yellow clothes,
a yellow cap,
and carries a yellow canopy,
riding a small horse.
It loves to gallop swiftly.
If called by its name,
it can be made to return with a report from a thousand lǐ away within a single day.
This is the essence of the dried-up marsh.
The essence of the dried-up river
is born as the wéi.
As for the wéi, it has one head and two bodies,
its form is like a snake,
and its length is eight feet.
If called by its name,
it can be made to catch fish and turtles.
This is the essence of the dried-up river water.
Thus, the essence of water that is coarse, turbid, and hardened,
which can exist but cannot vanish,
produces man and jade.
Those hidden in darkness that can exist and vanish
are the milfoil, the tortoise, and the dragon.
Those that are seen in some generations
or not seen
are the wéi and the Qìng Jì.
Therefore, all people submit to it,
and Guǎn Zǐ makes it his model;
all people possess it,
and Guǎn Zǐ makes use of it.
Therefore, what is the complete?
It is water.
There is none among the myriad things that does not depend on it for life,
and only those who know its dwelling can be its master.
The complete
is water.
Therefore it is said:
What is water?
It is the root and source of all things,
the ancestral home of all living beings,
and the origin of beauty and ugliness, the worthy and the unworthy, the foolish and the talented.
How do we know it is so?
As for the water of Qí,
it is swift, turbulent, and recirculating;
therefore its people are greedy, coarse, and fond of bravery.
The water of Chǔ
is soft, weak, and clear;
therefore its people are light, resolute, and daring.
The water of Yuè
is turbid, heavy, and thick;
therefore its people are foolish, sickly, and dirty.
The water of Qín is sweet, dense, and sluggish,
stagnant and mixed;
therefore its people are greedy, perverse,
deceptive, and fond of making trouble.
The water of Qí and Jìn
is dry, arid, and churning,
stagnant and mixed;
therefore its people are fawning, flattering, deceptive,
artful, glib, and fond of profit.
The water of Yān
is lowly and weak,
sinking, stagnant, and mixed;
therefore its people are foolish, simple-minded, and fond of uprightness,
light, quick, and ready to die.
The water of Sòng
is light, strong, and clear;
therefore its people are simple, easy-going, and fond of correctness.
This is why when a sage transforms the world,
the solution lies in water.
Thus, if the water is unified, the people's hearts will be corrected;
if the water is clear, the people's hearts will be at ease.
If the people's hearts are corrected, then desires will not be defiled;
if the people's hearts are at ease, then behavior will not be perverse.
This is why when a sage governs the world,
they do not instruct people individually,
nor do they go from house to house speaking;
the pivot lies in water.
Guǎnzǐ said:
Orders have their proper times.
If there is no proper time,
then one must observe the way Heaven follows,
which is vast and boundless,
and obscured by darkness—who can know it?
Only the sage knows the four seasons.
If one does not know the four seasons,
one loses the foundation of the state.
If one does not know the reasons for the five grains,
the state will fall into ruin.
Therefore, Heaven is called Trustworthy and Bright,
Earth is called Trustworthy and Sage,
and the four seasons are called Correct.
If the King is trustworthy, bright, and sage,
then his ministers will be correct.
How do we know the King is trustworthy, bright, and sage?
It is said: By being cautious in employing the capable and being good at listening and trusting. Employing the capable is called "Bright,"
and listening and trusting is called "Sage."
Those who are trustworthy, bright, and sage
all receive rewards from Heaven.
Employing the incapable is called "Darkness."
Those who are dark and forgetful
all receive calamities from Heaven.
Therefore, if those above see completed tasks and value merit,
then the people's affairs will involve labor without scheming.
If those above see merit but treat it as cheap,
then those below will be lazy,
and those above will be arrogant.
Therefore, Yīn and Yáng
are the great principles of Heaven and Earth;
the four seasons
are the great order of Yīn and Yáng;
punishments and virtues
are the counterparts of the four seasons.
When punishments and virtues match the seasons,
then blessings are produced;
when they are contrary, then calamities are produced.
So then, what should be done in Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter?
The East is called Xīng,
its season is called Spring,
its Qì is called Wind,
and Wind produces wood and bones.
Its virtue is joy and abundance,
and it sends forth and brings out according to the proper seasons.
Its affairs: issuing orders to
repair and clean the altars of the spirits,
carefully praying to remove obstructions,
honoring the correct Yáng,
repairing dikes and embankments,
plowing, weeding, and planting trees,
correcting ferries and bridges,
repairing ditches and canals,
tiling roofs and directing the flow of water,
resolving grievances and pardoning crimes,
and opening the ways to the four directions.
Then gentle winds and sweet rains will arrive,
the hundred families will live long,
and the hundred insects will multiply;
this is called the Virtue of the Star.
The Star governs sending forth, and sending forth creates wind.
Therefore, if in Spring one executes the administration of Winter, things will wither;
if one executes the administration of Autumn, there will be frost;
if one executes the administration of Summer, there will be parching heat.
Therefore, in the three months of Spring, on the days of Jiǎ and Yǐ, five administrative acts are issued.
The first act: Examine the young and the orphaned,
and pardon those who have committed crimes.
The second act: Distribute ranks and orders,
and grant stipends and positions.
The third act: When the ice thaws, repair the ditches and canals,
and return the displaced people.
The fourth act: Level the dangerous and difficult places,
repair the boundaries and borders,
and correct the field paths.
The fifth act: Do not kill fawns or the young of animals,
and do not break flowers or sever buds.
If these five acts are timely,
the Spring rains will come.
The South is called Sun,
its season is called Summer,
its Qì is called Yáng,
and Yáng produces people and Qì.
Its virtue is bestowing, granting, cultivating, and rejoicing.
Its affairs: issuing orders for
rewards and gifts, distributing ranks,
receiving stipends, and following the local customs.
Carefully perform the sacrifices to the spirits,
measure merit and reward the worthy,
to assist the Yáng Qì.
Then the great heat will arrive,
the seasonal rains will fall,
and the five grains and hundred fruits will ripen;
this is called the Virtue of the Sun. , , , . . , , : , , , , , , , .
The Sun governs rewards,
and rewards create heat. , .
If in Summer one executes the administration of Spring, there will be wind;
if one executes the administration of Autumn, there will be floods;
if one executes the administration of Winter, things will fall.
Therefore, in the three months of Summer, on the days of Bǐng and Dīng, five administrative acts are issued.
The first act: Seek those who have merit and have exerted labor and promote them.
The second act: Open long-stored grain,
open old storehouses,
and open old storage pits
to grant loans.
The third act: Issue orders to ban fans and remove hats, do not wear ceremonial caps,
and remove urgent leaks in field huts.
The fourth act: Seek those who have virtue and have bestowed charity upon the people and reward them.
The fifth act: Issue orders to ban the setting of nets for birds and beasts,
and do not kill flying birds.
If these five acts are timely,
the Summer rains will come.
The Center is called Earth.
The Virtue of Earth truly assists the four seasons in their entry and exit,
regulating the wind and rain, and Earth increases its strength.
Earth produces skin and flesh.
Its virtue is harmony, peace, and equal use,
being central, correct, and selfless,
truly assisting the four seasons:
in Spring, it brings abundance and nurturing;
in Summer, it nurtures growth;
in Autumn, it gathers the harvest;
in Winter, it closes and stores.
When the great cold reaches its extreme,
the state will flourish,
and the four directions will submit;
this is called the Virtue of the Year.
The Year governs harmony,
and harmony creates rain.
The West is called Chén,
its season is called Autumn,
its Qì is called Yīn,
and Yīn produces metal and armor.
Its virtue is sorrow and mourning,
stillness and correctness, severity and obedience,
dwelling without daring to be licentious or wasteful.
Its affairs: issuing orders to
not let the people be licentious or violent,
follow the traveling troops to gather the harvest,
and measure the people's resources to accumulate and store.
Felling those various trunks,
gathering those various materials,
the hundred things are then gathered,
so that the people will not be idle.
What is hated must be scrutinized,
what is desired must be obtained,
if righteousness and trustworthiness prevail, then one is victorious;
this is called the Virtue of Chén.
Chén governs gathering,
and gathering is Yīn.
If in autumn one carries out spring policies, there will be blooming;
if summer policies, there will be flooding;
if winter policies, there will be depletion.
For this reason, in the three months of autumn, the five policies are issued on Gēng and Xīn days.
The first policy says: prohibit gambling and games of chance,
restrain trivial arguments,
and avoid disputes and jealousy.
The second policy says: do not display the blades of the five weapons.
The third policy says: be cautious with traveling farmers,
and urge the collection of the harvest.
The fourth policy says: repair gaps and block cracks.
The fifth policy says: repair walls and fences,
and secure the neighborhood gates.
If the five tasks follow the season,
the five grains will all be gathered.
The north is called the Moon,
its season is Winter,
its Qi is Cold,
and Cold produces water and blood.
Its virtue is pure and expansive,
warm and forgiving, thorough and secret.
Its affairs: issue commands to
maintain prohibitions and relocate the people,
order stillness and cessation,
so that the earth does not leak.
Decide on punishments and apply penalties,
showing no amnesty to those with guilt,
in order to correspond with the Yīn Qi.
The great cold will then arrive,
armor and weapons will be strong,
the five grains will ripen,
the state will prosper,
and the four directions will be prepared;
this is called the Virtue of the Moon.
The Moon governs punishment,
and punishment is Cold.
If in winter one carries out spring policies, there will be leakage;
if summer policies, there will be thunder;
if autumn policies, there will be drought.
For this reason, in the three months of winter, the five policies are issued on Rén and Guǐ days.
The first policy says: deliberate on the orphaned and solitary,
and care for the elders.
The second policy says: be good at following Yīn,
maintain the sacrifices to the spirits,
distribute ranks and emoluments,
and bestow the prepared positions.
The third policy says: verify the accounts,
and do not release the treasures of the mountains and rivers.
The fourth policy says: apprehend the wicked and those in flight;
those who capture thieves and rebels shall be rewarded.
The fifth policy says: prohibit migration, stop drifting people, and restrain the separation of households.
If the five policies follow the season,
winter affairs will not exceed their limits,
what is sought will surely be obtained,
and what is hated will surely be subdued.
Thus, if there is wilting in spring or blooming in autumn,
thunder in winter or frost and snow in summer,
these are all bandits of Qi.
When Punishment and Virtue switch their periods and lose their order,
the bandit Qi arrives swiftly;
when bandit Qi arrives swiftly,
the state suffers many disasters and calamities.
For this reason, the Sage King is diligent with the seasons and entrusts his policies to them;
he establishes teachings and entrusts his military might to them;
he establishes sacrifices and entrusts his virtue to them.
These three are the means by which the Sage King harmonizes with the movements of Heaven and Earth.
The Sun governs Yáng,
the Moon governs Yīn,
and the Year governs Harmony.
Yáng is Virtue,
Yīn is Punishment,
and Harmony is Affairs.
For this reason, when the sun is eclipsed,
the state that has lost Virtue hates it;
when the moon is eclipsed,
the state that has lost Punishment hates it;
when a comet appears,
the state that has lost Harmony hates it;
when the wind contends with the sun for brightness,
the state that has lost Rectitude hates it.
Therefore, the Sage King cultivates Virtue when the sun is eclipsed,
cultivates Punishment when the moon is eclipsed,
cultivates Harmony when a comet appears,
and cultivates Rectitude when the wind contends with the sun for brightness.
These four are the means by which the Sage King avoids the punishment of Heaven and Earth.
If one can truly practice this,
the five grains will proliferate,
the six domestic animals will multiply,
and the armor and weapons will be strong.
If governance accumulates, there is prosperity;
if cruelty and tyranny accumulate, there is ruin.
The Dào produces Heaven and Earth,
and Virtue produces worthy men.
The Dào produces Virtue,
Virtue produces Rectitude,
and Rectitude produces Affairs.
Thus, as the Sage King governs all under heaven:
at the limit, things return;
at the end, things begin again.
Virtue begins in Spring
and grows in Summer;
Punishment begins in Autumn
and flows in Winter.
If Punishment and Virtue do not lose their place,
the four seasons will be as one.
If Punishment and Virtue leave their proper direction,
the seasons will run in reverse.
Affairs will not be completed,
and there will surely be great calamity.
The moon has three policies;
the King's affairs must be ordered
so that they may surely be long-lasting.
Those who do not hit the mark die;
those who lose the principle perish.
The state has four seasons;
firmly hold to the King's affairs.
The four guards have their places;
the three policies hold the support.
The first is the Root,
the second is the Vessel,
the third is the Filling,
the fourth is the Ruler,
the fifth is the Teacher,
the sixth is the Guard,
the seventh is the Establishment,
the eighth is the Preceder,
and the ninth is the Ender.
Once there are nine,
one then provides the five offices within the six departments,
and the five notes within the six pitch-pipes.
In the sixth month, the sun reaches its solstice;
for this reason, humans have the six lines,
and the six lines are how they connect with Heaven and Earth.
The Way of Heaven is regulated by nine,
the Principles of Earth are regulated by eight,
and the Way of Man is regulated by six.
Taking Heaven as father
and Earth as mother,
so as to open up the myriad things
and consolidate the single unity.
Connecting with the nine regulations,
the six departments, and the three fillings,
one becomes an enlightened Tiānzǐ.
Cultivate and level the water and soil
to await the celestial famines;
examine the five internal organs
to see those who are not loyal;
beneath the management of sacrifices,
observe the positions on earth;
distribute wealth to illuminate the spiritual dwellings,
and harmonize with the essential Qi.
Once harmonized, there is constancy;
having constancy, there are guiding principles.
Carefully harmonize the sounds,
and tune the twelve bells
to regulate human emotions.
Once human emotions are grasped,
the myriad things reach their limit;
then there is Virtue.
Therefore, connecting with the Yáng Qi
is the means to serve Heaven,
weaving the sun and moon
to use them for the people;
connecting with the Yīn Qi
is the means to serve Earth,
By determining the longitudes and latitudes of the stars and the calendar,
one observes their movements.
When these ways are understood, actions may then be taken;
thus, the divine stalks need not be spiritual,
nor the divine tortoise be used for divination;
Huángdì’s benevolence was all-encompassing,
reaching the ultimate state of governance.
Formerly, Huángdì obtained Chīyóu and became enlightened in the Way of Heaven;
he obtained Dàcháng and became observant of the advantages of the Earth;
he obtained Cānglóng and became discerning regarding the East;
he obtained Zhùróng and became discerning regarding the South;
he obtained Dàfēng and became discerning regarding the West;
he obtained Hòutǔ and became discerning regarding the North.
Huángdì obtained these six ministers and the realm was governed;
this was the pinnacle of spiritual brilliance.
Chīyóu was enlightened in the Way of Heaven,
thus he was appointed as the Regulator of Seasons;
Dàcháng was observant of the advantages of the Earth,
thus he was appointed as the Granary Keeper.
Cānglóng was discerning regarding the East,
thus he was appointed as the Gōngshī;
Zhùróng was discerning regarding the South,
thus he was appointed as the Sītú;
Dàfēng was discerning regarding the West,
thus he was appointed as the Sīmǎ;
Hòutǔ was discerning regarding the North,
thus he was appointed as the Lǐ.
Therefore, Spring corresponds to the Gōngshī,
Summer to the Sītú,
Autumn to the Sīmǎ,
and Winter to the Lǐ.
Formerly, Huángdì, based on the modulation of tones,
created the Five Tones
to regulate the Five Bells.
He named the Five Bells:
the first is called the Azure Bell,
of the Great Sound;
the second is called the Red Bell,
of the Heavy Heart;
the third is called the Yellow Bell,
of the Sprinkled Radiance;
the fourth is called the Bright Bell,
of Dimming Brilliance;
the fifth is called the Black Bell,
of Hidden Constancy.
Once the Five Tones were tuned,
he then established the Five Phases
to rectify the heavenly seasons,
and the Five Offices to rectify human positions.
When humans and Heaven are in harmony,
then the beauty of Heaven and Earth is produced.
When the solstice arrives,
observing the Jiǎzǐ day, the Wood phase governs.
The Son of Heaven issues commands,
ordering the Shìshī on the left and right to manage internal affairs.
He organizes and distinguishes the ranks of nobility,
evaluating the worthy and unworthy among the officials and clerks;
he distributes treasures and grants rewards within the four borders.
He releases old grain based on the size of the fields.
Going out from the capital, the Forest Wardens
follow the mountains and forests,
prohibiting the people from cutting wood,
which is the way to cherish the grass and trees.
In this way, the ice thaws and the frost melts,
and the grasses and trees sprout in their patches.
He protects hibernating insects and eggs of waterfowl;
during the spring opening, he does not violate the seasons;
the sprouts have sufficient roots;
the fledglings are not diseased,
and the young deer and elk do not perish prematurely.
Do not press for speed;
do not harm the infants in swaddling clothes.
Thus the seasons will not wither.
This concludes in seventy-two days.
Observing the Bǐngzǐ day,
the Fire phase governs.
The Son of Heaven issues commands,
ordering the Xíngrén to manage internal affairs.
He orders the digging of ditches and irrigation channels, and the dredging of old paths.
He releases stored goods, and the lords bestow rewards and grants.
The noble men practice riding and racing to release the Earth's qi.
He brings out furs and silks,
ordering the Xíngrén to practice the rites of spring and autumn throughout the realm;
the feudal lords communicate,
and all who meet under heaven achieve harmony.
In this way, the heavens have no violent winds;
the grasses and trees flourish;
the stagnant air dissipates;
the people are not sick, and the flowers and blossoms are abundant.
This concludes in seventy-two days.
Observing the Wùzǐ day,
the Earth phase governs.
The Son of Heaven issues commands,
ordering the Sītú on the left and right to manage internal affairs.
He does not execute those who are not upright;
he treats agricultural matters with reverence.
He widely spreads benevolent words,
lightens capital punishment,
and pardons criminals.
Going out from the capital, the Sītú
orders that the people's labor be directed to follow the seasons to nourish the five grains.
The noble men live in quietude,
while the farmers apply their labor to the utmost.
In this way, Heaven becomes mild and yielding;
the grasses and trees are nourished and grow;
the five grains flourish, ripen, and grow large;
the six domestic animals and sacrificial victims are prepared;
the people have sufficient wealth;
the state is rich;
superiors and subordinates are close;
and the feudal lords are in harmony.
This concludes in seventy-two days.
Observing the Gēngzǐ day,
the Metal phase governs.
The Son of Heaven issues commands,
ordering the Zhùzōng to select prohibited animals and birds
and the first of the five grains to ripen,
to offer them in the ancestral temple and the five sacrifices;
the ghosts and spirits enjoy their aroma,
and the noble men eat their flavors.
In this way, the cool breeze arrives,
and white dew falls.
The Son of Heaven issues commands,
ordering the Sīmǎ on the left and right
to assemble armor and sharpen weapons,
organizing groups of ten and five to conduct drills within the four borders,
solemnly informing the people of military matters;
this is to prepare for the killing and harvesting of Heaven and Earth.
In this way, the days are scorched by the sun,
and at night the dew falls;
the earth becomes firm;
the five grains ripen together;
the grasses and trees yield abundant fruit;
the harvest of the year is bountiful,
and the growth is great.
This concludes in seventy-two days.
Observing the Rénzǐ day,
the Water phase governs.
The Son of Heaven issues commands,
ordering the Shǐrén on the left and right to manage internal affairs. If their energy
is sufficient, they act and then stop;
if their energy is insufficient,
then violent unrest and bandits will arise.
Many times they harvest bamboo for arrows,
cut down sandalwood and mulberry trees,
and order the people to go out hunting.
They kill animals and birds without sparing the large or small;
this is to honor the closing and storing of Heaven and Earth.
In this way, the feathered and egg-laying ones are not broken;
the haired and womb-bearing ones do not miscarry;
pregnant women do not waste away or lose their children;
and the roots of grasses and trees are beautiful.
This concludes in seventy-two days.
Observing the Jiǎzǐ day,
the Wood phase governs.
If the Son of Heaven does not distribute grain
or grant rewards,
but instead carries out massive felling and wounding,
the ruler will be in danger.
Otherwise,
the Crown Prince will be in danger,
the consort will die;
or else
the eldest son will die.
This concludes in seventy-two days.
Observing the Bǐngzǐ day,
the Fire phase governs.
If the Son of Heaven reverently implements urgent policies,
there will be droughts and pestilence,
the sprouts will die, and the people will suffer.
This concludes in seventy-two days.
When observing *Wùzǐ*,
the Element Earth governs.
If the *Tiānzǐ* repairs palaces and halls
or builds terraces and pavilions,
the ruler will be in danger;
if he builds outer city walls,
the ministers will die.
This concludes after seventy-two days.
When observing *Gēngzǐ*,
the Element Metal governs.
If the *Tiānzǐ* attacks mountains and strikes stones,
there will be military action and defeat, soldiers will die,
and the administration will be lost.
This concludes after seventy-two days.
When observing *Rénzǐ*,
the Element Water governs.
If the *Tiānzǐ* breaches dams and moves great waters,
the Queen and the royal consorts will pass away;
if not,
then those with feathers and eggs will be crushed,
those with hair and wombs will be miscarried,
pregnant women will waste away and be abandoned,
and the roots of grass and trees will not be healthy.
This also concludes after seventy-two days.
To go to war and fear water,
this is called the destruction of the gallbladder. In small matters, others will not follow;
in great matters, it is not auspicious.
To go to war and fear danger,
this is called being lost within.
By dividing the army's ranks,
the men will become confused and dazed;
this is surely the path to the general's downfall.
To overvalue stillness is akin to death;
to overvalue action is akin to ghosts;
to overvalue trust is akin to a spur;
to overvalue submission is akin to avoidance.
As for stillness and action,
sometimes one is the host,
and sometimes one is the guest;
what is valued is attaining the proper measure.
Knowing the preparation of stillness, one dwells
and benefits oneself;
knowing how to follow action,
every movement will result in achievement.
Therefore it is said: he who practices non-action is a Sovereign;
this is what is meant.
When contrary seasons sprout,
and Heaven and Earth have not yet taken form,
if one carries out government beforehand,
the matters will not succeed,
and one will erroneously receive punishment.
Heaven follows man;
the Sage follows Heaven. If the time of Heaven does not act,
do not be the guest;
if human affairs do not arise,
do not be the initiator.
Harmonize with the multitude
to follow the compliance of Heaven and Earth.
If man precedes them,
Heaven and Earth will punish him;
if the Sage completes them,
then he reaches the same limit as Heaven.
Upright and still, not contending;
acting and moving without error;
pure essence not lingering—
he reaches the same limit as Earth.
If the Heavenly Limit is not yet attained,
then remain hidden in virtue;
once the Heavenly Limit is attained,
then apply one's strength.
Having completed the work,
follow and maintain its course,
and others cannot replace you.
The way to successful achievement
lies in regarding expansion and contraction as treasures.
Do not lose the Heavenly Limit,
but stop when the numbers are exhausted.
If the matter is not yet completed,
do not change its form
and do not lose its beginning.
Quiet the people and observe the time;
wait for the command and then arise.
Therefore it is said:
follow the compliance of *Yīnyáng*
and guide the constancy of Heaven and Earth.
Expanding and contracting,
thereby acting appropriately;
dying and living,
following the forms of Heaven and Earth.
Heaven and Earth form it;
the Sage completes it.
He who takes a little gains a little benefit;
he who takes much gains much benefit;
he who practices it fully possesses all under Heaven.
Therefore, the worthy is sincere and faithful to show benevolence;
he is compassionate and kind to show love;
with an upright government and appearance,
he does not dare to precede others.
Being centered and still without lingering, abundant in virtue without seeking,
it manifests in a feminine manner.
Where he dwells, he is soft,
peaceful, still, and happy; when he acts,
it is with virtue and without contention,
to await the erupting actions of all under Heaven.
Therefore, the worthy is peaceful, slow, upright, and still;
his soft moderation is first settled.
He acts from what he dares not do,
and stands upon what he cannot do,
holding to the moderation of weakness and firmly dwelling in it.
Therefore, he does not violate the Heavenly seasons
and does not disrupt the people's work.
Grasping the time, he nourishes the people;
he puts virtue first and punishment last.
He is compliant with Heaven
and subtly measures men.
As for one who is good at being comprehensive,
the brilliant cannot see him;
as for one who is good at being brilliant,
the comprehensive cannot obscure him.
If Great Brilliance overcomes Great Comprehensiveness,
then the people will have no Great Comprehensiveness;
if Great Comprehensiveness overcomes Great Brilliance,
then the people will have no Great Brilliance.
The predecessor of Great Comprehensiveness
can exert faith;
the ancestor of Great Brilliance
can take the place of Heaven. Search below
and do not find it;
seek it under the *Zhāoyáo* star.
Beasts grow weary of running, yet there are hidden nets to catch them. Now tilting, now turning—
otherwise, they cannot be caught.
Great Civility is layered thrice,
valuing righteousness and virtue;
Great Militancy is layered thrice,
setting aside weapons and force.
Establish and judge the *Wǔxíng*,
each corresponding to its name.
The guilty do not feel resentment,
and the good are not alarmed;
this is called Punishment.
Correcting them, submitting them, overcoming them, and adorning them;
one must be strict with the orders,
and the people will model themselves after them; this is called Government.
Unfailing like the four seasons,
unchanging like the stars and constellations,
like the night and like the day,
like *yīn* and like *yáng*,
like the brightness of the sun and moon;
this is called Law.
Loving them, giving them life,
nourishing them, and completing them;
the people benefit without effort,
and all under Heaven feel close to him;
this is called Virtue.
Without virtue and without resentment,
without likes and without dislikes,
the myriad things honor the One,
and *Yīnyáng* share the same measure;
this is called the *Dào*.
Use punishment to eliminate evils,
use government to command them,
use law to restrain them,
use virtue to nourish them,
and use the *Dào* to enlighten them. When using punishment to eliminate evils,
do not lose the people's lives;
order them so as to cut off their desires,
and do not let the people take shortcuts;
restrain them so as to cut off their intentions,
and do not let the people seek luck.
To nurture them in order to transform their evil,
one must begin with one's own self.
One must be enlightened to observe their lives
and follow their principles.
When punishments are applied to the ultimate degree, the people
use their hearts to be respectful.
When governance is applied to the ultimate degree, the people
submit with trust and listen.
When virtue is applied to the ultimate degree, the people
are harmonious and tranquil.
When the Way is applied to the ultimate degree, the people
entrust themselves and do not struggle.
Assigning a criminal the appropriate name is called punishment.
Issuing orders at the proper time is called rectification.
Adhering to precedents without change is called law.
Loving the people without selfishness is called virtue.
Assembling where the people gather is called the Way. In establishing constants and conducting administration,
can one make people submit with trust?
Centered in harmony and cautious in respect,
can one be said to renew daily?
With an upright balance and unified tranquility,
can one maintain caution?
By abolishing the private and establishing the public,
can one promote the worthy?
In approaching governance and presiding over the people,
can one put one's own person last?
Being able to make people submit with trust
is called the rectification of the discipline.
Being able to renew daily
is called acting according to principle.
Maintaining caution and rectifying names,
falsehood and deception will stop of their own accord.
Promoting people without selfishness,
the ministers' virtues will all follow the Way.
Being able to put one's own person last,
one can assist the Tiānzǐ above.
As for why the common people maintain defense and fight unto death without feeling indebted to their superiors,
there are methods by which this is reached. It is said:
The primary reason is
the location of their relatives and ancestral graves,
and their fields and residences being rich and sufficient to dwell in.
If not that,
then the districts, counties, townships, and villages, along with their clans, are sufficient to cherish and enjoy.
If not that,
then the superior's teachings and
customs, and their benevolence toward the people, are profound,
such that the people could go nowhere else to find the same.
If not that,
then the benefits of the mountains, forests, marshes, and valleys are sufficient for their livelihood.
If not that,
then the terrain is treacherous and obstructed,
easy to defend and difficult to attack.
If not that,
then the punishments are severe and fearsome.
If not that,
then the rewards are clear and sufficient to encourage them.
If not that,
then there is deep resentment toward the enemy.
If not that,
then there is great merit owed to the superior.
These are the reasons why the people maintain defense and fight unto death without feeling indebted to their superiors.
Now, relying on untrustworthy people
while seeking to use wisdom; employing
people who do not maintain their positions
while wishing for stability;
leading soldiers who will not fight
while hoping for victory;
these are the three darknesses of military affairs.
A Sage Sovereign relies on the law and not on wisdom;
he relies on methods and not on persuasion;
he relies on the public and not on the private;
he relies on the Great Way and not on trivial matters;
only then is his person at ease and the world is well-governed.
A failing ruler is not like this;
he abandons the law and relies on wisdom;
therefore, the people abandon their work and love reputation.
He abandons methods and relies on persuasion;
therefore, the people abandon substance and love talk.
He abandons the public and loves the private;
therefore, the people depart from the law and act recklessly.
He abandons the Great Way and relies on trivial matters;
therefore, the superior is exhausted and troubled,
the common people are deluded and confused,
and the state is not well-governed.
A Sage Sovereign is not like this;
he maintains the essentials of the Way,
abides in ease and joy,
gallops in the hunt,
enjoys bells, drums, pipes, and zithers,
and the pleasures of the palace,
without prohibition or restraint.
He does not contemplate or deliberate,
he does not worry or plot;
he benefits his person and body,
gives comfort to his physical form,
nurtures his longevity,
and with robes folded and hands clasped, the world is well-governed.
Therefore, if a ruler of men can use this Way, he does not burden his mind,
does not fatigue his intent,
and does not exert his strength,
yet the lands are naturally opened,
the granaries are naturally filled,
the stores and accumulations naturally increase,
the armor and weapons naturally become strong,
the ministers are without deception or falsehood,
the various officials are without treachery or wickedness,
and people of unusual skills or techniques
do not dare to use lofty words or boastful conduct
to exceed their true circumstances
or to manipulate their ruler.
Formerly, when Yáo governed the world,
it was like clay on a potter's wheel,
following only what the potter made of it;
it was like metal in a furnace,
following freely what the smith cast.
His people came when led,
went when pushed,
succeeded when employed,
and stopped when forbidden.
Therefore, Yáo's governance
was simply about being good at clarifying the orders of laws and prohibitions.
When Huángdì governed the world,
his people came without being led,
went without being pushed,
succeeded without being employed,
and stopped without being forbidden.
Therefore, Huángdì's governance
consisted of establishing the law and not changing it,
making the people feel secure within his laws.
What are called benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music all emerge from the law.
This is how the former sages unified the people.
The Zhōushū says:
"If the laws of the state are not unified,
it is inauspicious for those who possess the state;
if the people do not follow the law, it is inauspicious; if the state repeatedly establishes laws to preside over the people, it is inauspicious;
if the various ministers do not use ritual and righteousness for teaching, it is inauspicious;
if the various officials who attend to affairs depart from the law in their governance, it is inauspicious."
Therefore it is said:
The law
cannot be constant in its specificities,
yet it is that from which survival and destruction, order and chaos, emerge;
it is the Great Standard by which the Sage Sovereign governs the world.
Ruler and minister, superior and inferior, noble and base, all originate from it;
therefore it is called
"the Law." In the laws of antiquity,
the world had no people who sought favors or appointments through personal influence,
no scholars of broad knowledge and eloquent persuasion,
no grand attire,
and no strange conduct;
all were encompassed within the law to serve their ruler.
Therefore, there are two things that an enlightened king maintains as constants:
first is to clarify the law and firmly uphold it;
second is to forbid the people from private interests and collect them for service;
these two
are what a ruler maintains as constants.
For the law
is that by which the superior unifies the people and employs the inferiors;
private interests
are that by which the inferiors encroach upon the law and bring chaos to the ruler.
Therefore, the Sage Sovereign establishes standards and institutes laws and firmly upholds them;
in this way, talented men and practiced scholars,
and those of broad knowledge, cannot cause disorder;
the numerous and powerful, the rich and noble, or the privately brave cannot encroach;
those who are trusted, close, or beloved cannot cause estrangement;
rare and strange objects cannot cause delusion;
and of the myriad things and hundred affairs, those not within the law cannot cause movement.
Thus, the law is the Ultimate Way of the world
and the precious instrument of the Sage Sovereign.
Today, the world is not so;
all have good laws but are unable to maintain them.
For this reason, capable talents and practiced *shì*,
leisured acquaintances and widely learned *shì*,
can use their wisdom to disrupt the law and confuse the superior.
The strong, the wealthy, the noble, and the privately brave
can use their power to violate the law and commit encroachment and oppression.
Neighboring *zhūhóu* can use their influence to place sons and establish ministers.
*Dàchén* can use their private means to attach the common people,
cutting from public wealth to reward private *shì*.
In all such cases, seeking the implementation of law
and the order of the state
is impossible.
A *shèngjūn* is not so.
*Qīngxiàng* are not permitted to cut for their private interests.
*Qúnchén* are not permitted to favor those they are close to or love.
The *shèngjūn* also clarifies his laws and firmly adheres to them.
*Qúnchén* cultivate themselves and converge like spokes to serve their *jūn*.
The *mín* are harmonious and obedient, listening to orders and following the law to attend to their affairs. Thus it is said:
There is the creation of law,
there is the maintenance of law,
and there is modeling oneself on the law.
The one who creates the law is the *jūn*;
the one who maintains the law is the *chén*;
those who model themselves on the law are the *mín*.
When *jūn* and *chén*, superior and inferior, noble and base, all follow the law,
this is called *dàzhì*.
Thus a *jūn* has three *shù*:
To love people without private rewards,
to hate people without private punishments,
and to establish standards and set laws so that judgment and decision are by measure—
such is a *shàngzhǔ*.
To love people and reward them privately,
to hate people and punish them privately,
to turn against the *dàchén*,
to distance those close to him,
and to decide solely by his own heart—
such is a *zhōngzhǔ*.
When *chén* have those they love and reward them privately,
or have those they hate and punish them privately,
violating the public law
and damaging their upright hearts,
while the *jūn* listens solely to his *dàchén*—
such is a *wēizhǔ*.
Therefore, one who is a *jūn*
does not overly value loving people
and does not overly value hating people.
Overvaluing love is called losing *dé*;
overvaluing hatred is called losing *wēi*.
When both *wēi* and *dé* are lost,
then the *jūn* is in peril.
Therefore, there are six things a *míngwáng* wields:
giving life, taking life,
making rich, making poor,
making noble, making base.
These six handles
are what the *jūn* wields.
There are four positions where the *jūn* resides:
first is *wén*, second is *wǔ*, third is *wēi*, and fourth is *dé*.
These four positions
are where the *jūn* resides.
To lend to others what one wields
is called the seizure of the handles;
to lend to others where one resides
is called the loss of position.
When the handles are seized and the position lost,
yet one seeks for orders to be carried out,
it is impossible.
If the law is not impartial
and orders are not complete,
this is also the way to the seizure of handles and loss of position.
Therefore, acting to pervert the law
or acting to destroy orders
are things a *shèngjūn* forbids himself from doing.
Thus, the noble cannot use *wēi* against him,
the wealthy cannot use rewards to influence him,
the base cannot use subservience to move him,
those close cannot use intimacy to sway him,
and the beautiful cannot entice him to excess.
Standing firm and immovable,
the strange and deviant are then afraid.
When the strange are reformed and the deviant transformed,
orders go forth and the *mín* shift.
Therefore, the *shèngjūn* establishes measures
and sets standards and laws
as firm as Heaven and Earth,
as stable as the arrayed stars,
as bright as the sun and moon,
as reliable as the four seasons.
Thus, orders go forth and the *mín* follow them.
But a *shījūn* is not so.
He establishes a law and then abolishes it;
he issues an order and then reverses it;
he perverts the law to follow private interests;
he destroys orders so they are not complete.
Thus, the noble can use *wēi* against him,
the wealthy can use rewards,
the base can use subservience,
those close can use intimacy,
and the beautiful can entice him to excess.
Because these five
are not forbidden within himself,
the *qúnchén* and common people
each harbor their private interests
and seek favor from their *jūn*.
When they seek favor and obtain it,
then the *jūn* is daily encroached upon.
When they seek favor and do not obtain it,
then resentment daily arises.
To be daily encroached upon and for resentment to arise
is what a *shījūn* follows.
Generally, for a *jūn* who cannot use his laws
and cannot satisfy his intent,
but acts while looking to his *chén*
and listens to noble *chén* while abandoning the law—
this is what is meant by "the noble exerting *wēi*."
When wealthy people use gold and jade to serve the *jūn* and make requests,
and the *jūn* abandons the law to listen to them,
this is what is meant by "the wealthy using rewards."
When base people use submissive, humble, and respectful looks and sorrowful countenances to appeal to their *jūn*,
and the *jūn* consequently abandons the law to listen to them,
it is what is meant by "the base serving him."
When those close to him use their proximity and affection to seek something from their *jūn*,
and the *jūn* consequently abandons the law to listen to them,
this is what is meant by "those close using intimacy."
When beautiful people use clever words and pleasing countenances to request something of their *jūn*,
and the *jūn* consequently abandons the law to listen to them,
this is what is meant by "the beautiful enticing him."
An ordered age is not so.
It does not distinguish between kin or stranger, distant or near, noble or base, beautiful or ugly,
but decides by measure and law.
Those who are executed do not feel resentment;
those who are rewarded do not attribute it to the *jūn*'s personal *dé*.
Laws and regulations are implemented
with the impartiality of Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, in officialdom there is no private discourse,
among *shì* there is no private debate,
and among the *mín* there is no private talk.
All empty their hearts to listen to their superior.
The superior uses public justice to discourse
and laws and regulations to decide;
thus, he employs the world without it being a burden.
Now, a *luànjūn* is not so.
He has private visions,
and thus there are things he does not see;
he has private hearings,
and thus there are things he does not hear;
he has private thoughts,
and thus there are things he does not know.
Privacy
is the way to obstruction, delusion, and loss of position.
When the superior abandons public law to listen to private talk,
then the *qúnchén* and common people all set up private ways and establish their own methods
to teach within the state.
They form cliques and factions
to establish their private interests,
and use petitions and recommendations
to disrupt the public law.
Each person uses their own mind
to seek favor from the superior.
The superior has no measures to forbid this,
so private talk increases daily
while public law is daily damaged.
The lack of order in the state
arises from this.
*Jūn* and *chén*
occupy the positions of Heaven and Earth;
the *mín*
are the image of the many things.
Each stands in his assigned duty to await the *jūn*'s orders.
How can the *qúnchén* and common people each use their own minds to establish private interests?
Therefore, if one follows the ruler's commands and acts upon them,
even if there is loss or failure, there is no punishment;
if one acts without the ruler's command,
even if there is success or profit,
the crime is punishable by death.
Thus, the way inferiors serve superiors
is like an echo responding to a sound;
the way ministers serve the ruler
is like a shadow following the form.
Therefore, when the superior commands and the inferior responds,
when the ruler acts and the ministers follow,
this is the way of good governance.
Now, if without the ruler's command
one acts and achieves success or profit,
and is rewarded because of it,
this is to teach people to act recklessly.
If one follows the ruler's command and acts upon it,
but suffers loss or failure and is punished for it,
this causes the people to weigh profit and harm and distance themselves from the law.
If the various ministers and the common people each weigh profit and harm
and take actions according to their private interests,
then the legal system will be destroyed and commands will not be carried out.
What is called "governing the state"
means the ruler's way is clear.
An enlightened ruler
possesses techniques and methods such that he cannot be deceived,
is careful regarding laws and prohibitions such that they cannot be violated,
and is discerning regarding the division of duties such that they cannot be thrown into disorder.
Therefore, the various ministers dare not act on their private interests;
noble ministers may not obscure those of low status;
those close to the ruler may not block those who are distant;
the orphaned, the widowed, the elderly, and the weak do not lose their assigned duties;
within the borders, distinctions are clear and there is no overstepping.
This is what is called governing the state.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"What is called governing the state
means the ruler's way is clear."
What is called a "disordered state"
is one where the ministers' techniques prevail.
An enlightened ruler
is the means by which the superior unifies the people and employs inferiors.
Private techniques
are the means by which inferiors encroach upon the superior and disorder the ruler.
Therefore, when laws are discarded and private interests are pursued,
the ruler of men becomes isolated and stands alone,
while the ministers form factions and cliques.
In such a case,
the ruler is weak and the ministers are strong;
this is what is called a disordered state.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"What is called a disordered state
is one where the ministers' techniques prevail."
Now, that the ruler is honored and the ministers are humble
is not due to personal affection
but because the ruler holds the power to prevail.
When an enlightened ruler occupies the high position
and possesses the power to ensure order,
then the various ministers dare not do wrong.
Therefore, that the various ministers dare not deceive the ruler
is not because they love the ruler,
but because they fear the ruler's awe-inspiring power.
That the common people strive to be of use
is not because they love the ruler,
but because they fear the ruler's laws and commands.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler wields the methods of certain victory
to govern the people who must be employed;
he occupies the position of certain honor
to control the ministers who must be submissive.
Thus, commands are carried out and prohibitions are effective,
the ruler is honored and the ministers are humble.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"That the ruler is honored and the ministers are humble
is not a matter of personal affection
but because of the power to prevail."
That the various officials are orderly
is not due to benevolence
but because punishments are certain.
In the governance of an enlightened ruler,
he suspends ranks and stipends to encourage his people;
since the people derive profit from the superior,
the ruler has the means to employ them.
He establishes punishments to overawe his inferiors;
since inferiors have fear of the superior,
the ruler has the means to shepherd them.
Therefore, without ranks and stipends, the ruler has no way to encourage the people;
without punishments, the ruler has no way to overawe the masses.
Therefore, that a minister acts with reason and obeys commands
is not because he loves the ruler,
but rather to pursue profit and avoid harm.
That the various officials uphold the law without wickedness
is not because they love the ruler,
but because they desire to receive ranks and stipends and avoid punishments.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"That the various officials fulfill their duties
is not due to benevolence
but because punishments are certain."
Therefore, if the ruler and minister share the same way, there will be disorder.
The ruler of men
exclusively holds the power of life and death,
occupies a position of awe-inspiring power,
and wields the handle of commands being carried out and prohibitions being effective
to govern his various ministers;
this is the way of the ruler.
The minister
occupies a humble position,
obeys the ruler's commands,
keeps to his original responsibilities,
and manages his divided duties;
this is the way of the minister.
Therefore, if the ruler acts according to the way of the minister, there will be disorder;
if the minister acts according to the way of the ruler, there will be peril.
Thus, when there is no distinction between high and low
and the ruler and minister share the same way,
it is the root of disorder.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"If the ruler and minister share the same way, there will be disorder."
To delegate authority exclusively is to lose it.
The reason ministers are fearful and serve the ruler with caution
is that they desire life and hate death.
If people are made not to desire life
and not to hate death,
then it is impossible to control them.
Now, for the power of life and death to reside exclusively with the high ministers
without the ruler being in peril
is something that has never occurred.
Therefore, when order and disorder are not decided by law but are determined by high ministers,
and the power of life and death is not controlled by the ruler but resides with the inferiors,
this is a parasitic ruler.
Therefore, if the ruler of men exclusively gives his awe-inspiring power to others,
then there will surely be the disaster of being coerced or murdered.
If he exclusively gives his legal systems to others,
then there will surely be the calamity of disorder and ruin.
To act in such a manner
is the way of a doomed ruler.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"To delegate authority exclusively is to lose it."
Now, a state has four types of ruin:
when commands essentially do not go forth,
it is called extinction.
In general, if one is a ruler but cannot have his commands carried out,
discards the law and indulges the various ministers,
his awe and dignity are already discarded,
and his power and authority are already seized,
his commands cannot go forth,
the various ministers will not be of use to him,
and the common people will not be employed by him.
If the masses within the borders are not controlled,
then the state is not his state,
and the people are not his people.
To act in such a manner
is the way of an extinguished ruler.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"When commands do not go forth, it is called extinction."
When commands go forth but are blocked along the way,
it is called obstruction.
According to the way of an enlightened ruler,
those of humble status do not wait for those of high status to have an audience,
high ministers do not rely on those close to the ruler to be promoted,
the various officials are connected in an orderly fashion,
and the various ministers are clearly visible.
For those who are punished,
the ruler sees their crime.
For those who are rewarded,
the ruler knows their merit.
What is seen and known is not contradictory,
rewards and punishments do not err,
and there are methods to prevent being obscured;
thus, there is no trouble of blockage or obstruction.
A ruler in chaos is not like this:
laws and decrees cannot reach the people;
he is distant, isolated, and blocked off,
and he cannot hear what is going on.
Such a state
is the way of blockage and obstruction.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"When orders are issued but detained,
it is called blockage."
When the sentiments of those below seek but fail to reach those above,
it is called obstruction.
The means by which ministers take advantage to commit wickedness
is by usurping the ruler's authority.
When there are ministers who usurp the ruler's authority,
then the ruler's orders cannot be carried out
and the sentiments of those below do not reach those above.
The power of such ministers
can block the space between the lord and his ministers and prevent the expression of good and evil sentiments;
news of disaster and fortune does not penetrate through,
and the ruler is deluded with no way to realize it.
Such a state
is the way of an obstructed ruler.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"When the sentiments of those below do not reach those above,
it is called obstruction."
When the sentiments of those below move upward but the path is stopped,
it is called encroachment.
An enlightened ruler
listens to all but decides alone,
multiplying his doors and gates.
According to the way of the various ministers,
