those below are able to enlighten those above,
and the lowly are able to speak to the noble;
therefore, wicked people do not dare to deceive.
A ruler in chaos is not like this:
he listens without methods or techniques,
and decides matters without cross-examination or comparison.
Consequently, incompetent scholars reach those above,
corrupt and crooked ministers monopolize the state,
the ruler's vision is obscured and his hearing is obstructed,
and loyal ministers who wish to advise and remonstrate cannot enter.
Such a state
is the way of an encroached ruler.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"When the sentiments of those below move upward but the path is stopped,
it is called encroachment."
Thus, that which gives rise to destruction, encroachment, obstruction, and blockage
stems from the failure to establish law.
When a ruler governs a state,
none are without laws and decrees.
When rewards and punishments are fully prepared,
his laws and decrees are clear;
and when the application of rewards and punishments is appropriate,
then the ruler is honored and prominent, and wickedness does not arise.
When his laws and decrees are contrary to principle
and the application of rewards and punishments is inappropriate,
then the various ministers establish private interests and block and obstruct him,
forming cliques to threaten or kill him.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"That which gives rise to destruction, obstruction, encroachment, and blockage
stems from the failure to establish law."
For this reason, when the *Xiānwáng* governed the state,
they did not let their intentions stray outside the law.
The legal system
is the means by which the ruler controls the world and forbids wickedness and depravity,
and the means by which he leads the people within the seas and serves the ancestral temple.
Private intentions
are what give rise to chaos, foster wickedness, and harm public justice;
they are what cause blockage, obscurity, loss of correctness, and peril leading to ruin.
Therefore, when the legal system is implemented, the state is well-governed;
when private intentions are implemented, the state is in chaos.
Although there may be someone the enlightened ruler loves in his heart,
he does not reward them if they have no merit;
although there may be someone he hates in his heart,
he does not punish them if they have no guilt.
He examines gains and losses according to the legal statutes
and pays no attention to anything that is not within the legal system.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"When the *Xiānwáng* governed the state,
they did not let their intentions stray outside the law."
They did not grant favors within the law.
When an enlightened ruler governs a state,
he examines what is appropriate
and carries out correct principles;
thus, those who deserve reward
cannot be refused by the ministers,
and those who deserve punishment
do not dare to avoid it.
Now, rewarding merit and punishing crime
is the means to bring benefit to the world and remove harm.
If weeds and rushes are not removed,
they will harm the grain;
if thieves and bandits are not executed,
they will injure good citizens.
To abandon public law and practice private favors
is to benefit the wicked and depraved and foster violence and chaos.
To practice private favors and reward those without merit
is to make the people seek luck through laziness and have expectations of those above.
To practice private favors and pardon those with guilt
is to make the people belittle those above and easily commit wrongdoings.
To abandon public law
and use private favors
is something an enlightened ruler does not do.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"They did not grant favors within the law."
To have every action be in accordance with the law
is the means to forbid errors and exclude private interests.
Among all rulers, none fail to desire that their people be useful;
that which makes people useful
is the necessary establishment of law and the carrying out of orders.
Therefore, in governing a state and directing the masses, nothing is as effective as law;
in forbidding excess and stopping violence, nothing is as effective as punishment.
Thus, it is not that the poor do not desire to seize the wealth of the rich,
yet they do not dare to do so
because the law does not allow it.
It is not that the strong are unable to oppress the weak,
yet they do not dare to do so
because they fear execution by the law.
Therefore, when the affairs of the various officials
are examined according to the law,
then wickedness does not arise.
When violent and negligent people
are punished according to the law,
then disaster does not arise.
When the various ministers advance together,
if they are controlled through techniques of calculation,
then private interests have no place to be established.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"To have every action be in accordance with the law
is the means to forbid errors and exclude private interests."
Authority is not placed in two locations;
governance does not come from two gates.
The means by which a ruler controls his subordinates
is authority and power.
Thus, if authority and power are with those below,
then the ruler is controlled by the ministers.
If authority and power are with the one above,
then the ministers are controlled by the ruler.
Those who obscure the ruler
do not necessarily block his gates
or guard his doors;
yet if orders are not carried out,
prohibitions are not stopped,
and what is desired is not attained,
it is because he has lost his authority and power.
Therefore, if authority and power remain solely with the ruler,
then the various ministers will feel awe and respect.
If laws and governance come solely from the ruler,
then the world will submit to his power.
If authority and power are shared with the ministers,
then orders will not be carried out.
If laws and governance emerge from the ministers,
then the people will not listen.
Therefore, when an enlightened ruler governs the world,
authority and power remain solely with the ruler
and are not shared with the ministers;
laws and governance are solely controlled by the ruler
and do not emerge from the ministers.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"Authority is not placed in two locations;
governance does not come from two gates."
Governing the state through law
is merely a matter of taking action.
An enlightened ruler
unifies weights and measures,
establishes standards and models,
and firmly upholds them;
therefore, when orders are issued, the people obey.
The law
is the standard for the world
and the model for all matters.
Officials
are those to whom the people entrust their lives;
thus, in the governance of an enlightened ruler,
those who comply with the law are rewarded,
and those who violate the law are punished;
because punishment for crimes is based on the law,
the people go to their deaths without resentment.
When merit is measured by the law,
the people receive rewards without feeling personal gratitude,
and this is the achievement of taking actions according to the law;
thus the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"To govern a state with law,
then it is simply a matter of taking correct actions."
Therefore, where there are systems of legal measures,
one cannot use cleverness for deception or fraud;
where there are scales and balances,
one cannot be deceived regarding weight;
scales and balances
are how the figures of weight are established;
yet the reason people do not try to manipulate them
is not that they hate profit in their hearts,
but because the weight cannot increase or decrease the numbers for them,
and the balance cannot lighten or sharpen the weight for them;
people know that manipulating scales and balances is useless,
so they do not do it;
therefore, when an enlightened ruler is in the superior position,
officials cannot twist the law,
and clerks cannot act for private gain;
people know that currying favor with clerks is useless,
so wealth and goods do not flow to them.
Scales and balances are level and upright in dealing with objects;
therefore, treacherous and deceitful people cannot carry out their private schemes;
thus the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"Where there are scales and balances,
one cannot be deceived about weight."
Where there are measurements of *xún* and *zhàng*,
one cannot be mistaken about length;
the *chǐ*, *cùn*, *xún*, and *zhàng*
are how the reality of length is obtained;
therefore, using the *chǐ* and *cùn* to measure length,
one can do so ten thousand times without a single error;
therefore, the measures of *chǐ* and *cùn*,
though someone may be wealthy, noble, numerous, or strong,
do not become longer for them;
though someone may be poor, lowly, humble, or disgraced,
they do not become shorter for them;
being fair and without bias,
treacherous and deceitful people cannot create errors;
thus the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"Where there are measurements of *xún* and *zhàng*,
one cannot be mistaken about length."
Now, if a ruler sets aside the law and promotes the capable based on reputation,
then ministers will distance themselves from the superior and form factions below;
if officials are appointed based on cliques,
then the people will focus on social connections and not seek to be useful.
The reason a state falls into chaos
is that the reality of matters is discarded in favor of blame and praise;
therefore, when an enlightened ruler listens,
he holds those who speak accountable to facts,
and tests those who praise others by the performance of the officials they recommended;
those whose words lack substance are punished,
and officials who disrupt their offices are punished.
Consequently, empty words dare not be presented;
the unworthy dare not accept office.
A chaotic ruler is not so;
he listens to words without supervising their reality,
thus the ministers use empty praise to advance their cliques;
he appoints officials without holding them accountable for their achievements,
thus stupid and corrupt officials are in the court.
In this way,
the ministers promote one another with fine reputations,
grant one another credit for achievements,
strive to increase their social ties,
and are not of use to the ruler;
thus the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"If a ruler sets aside the law and promotes the capable based on reputation,
then ministers will distance themselves from the superior and form factions below;
if officials are appointed based on cliques,
then the people will focus on social connections and not seek to be useful."
Therefore, the reason offices lose their order
is that the ruler uses praise as reward
and defamation as punishment.
A chaotic ruler does not examine the merits and labor of his ministers;
he rewards those who are widely praised
and does not investigate their crimes,
but punishes those who are widely defamed.
In such a case,
wicked ministers get rewards without merit,
and loyal ministers receive punishment without crime.
Thus, if there is much merit but no reward,
ministers will not strive to exert their efforts;
if conduct is upright but there is punishment,
then the worthy and sagacious have no way to exhaust their abilities;
if rank and salary are obtained through bribery,
then corrupt and shameful people will be in office;
if those relying on influence are unworthy yet hold high positions,
then the people will turn their backs on public law and flock to those with power.
In this way,
honest and cautious people lose their positions,
and incorruptible officials lose their governance;
thus the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"The reason offices lose their order
is that the ruler uses praise as reward and defamation as punishment."
Consequently, those who love rewards and hate punishments will abandon the public way and practice private arts.
When fair officials govern their offices,
they carry out the law without selfishness,
so treacherous ministers cannot obtain profit;
this is what treacherous ministers strive to harm.
If the ruler does not verify crimes
and punishes based on baseless words,
then treacherous ministers cannot help but serve the noble and powerful to seek promotion and praise,
in order to avoid punishment and receive salary and rewards.
Thus the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"Those who love rewards and hate punishments,
abandon the public way and practice private arts."
Forming factions to hide one another
means forgetting the ruler and dying for social ties to advance their reputations.
The way treacherous ministers ruin their ruler
is gradual and subtle,
causing the ruler to be deluded without knowing it;
above, they watch the ruler's moods for one another,
below, they buy reputation among the people,
they praise their own clique so the ruler honors them,
and they defame those outside their clique so the ruler discards them;
whatever benefits or harms them,
the ruler listens to and acts upon.
In this way,
all the ministers forget the ruler and flock to private associations.
Thus the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"Forming factions to hide evil for one another
is why they forget the ruler and use private associations to advance their reputations."
Therefore, those with many connections receive much praise;
with cliques both inside and outside,
even if there is great treachery,
there are many ways to blind the ruler.
If the ruler lacks methods and techniques,
the ministers will find him easy to deceive;
if the state has no clear laws,
the people will lightly commit wrongdoings;
therefore, when treacherous and evil people handle state affairs,
the ministers look up to them for benefit or harm.
In this way,
many treacherous people will act as their eyes and ears.
Even if there is great righteousness, the ruler has no way to know it; thus the *Míng Fǎ* says: "When connections are numerous and praise is plenty,
with cliques both inside and outside, even if there is great treachery, there are many ways to blind the ruler."
Consequently, loyal ministers die for crimes they did not commit,
while wicked ministers rise based on merit they do not have.
In general, those who are called loyal ministers
strive to clarify law and technique,
assist the ruler day and night,
and understand the principles of measures and numbers to govern the world.
Treacherous and evil ministers
know that if law and technique are clear, there will surely be order;
when there is order, treacherous ministers are constrained and those skilled in law and technique become prominent.
Therefore, that which the treacherous and evil
strive to do is to ensure the law is not
clear and the ruler does not awaken,
so that they can obtain what they desire.
Thus, if upright ministers are employed,
then treacherous and evil ministers will be constrained and harmed;
it is a situation where the upright and the treacherous cannot both advance together.
When treacherous and evil people are at the ruler's side,
they cannot but be hated. If the ruler only hates them
but does not eliminate them, they will surely wait
for the ruler to be at leisure and endanger him day and night. If the ruler
does not investigate and uses their words,
then loyal ministers will be without crime
yet suffer and die, while treacherous ministers will be without merit yet become wealthy and noble.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
“Loyal ministers die for no crime,
and evil ministers rise without merit.”
When those who die have committed no crime
and those who rise have no merit,
then those who serve as ministers will value private interests and disregard the public good.
Wealth, nobility, honor, and prominence,
and possessing the world for a long time—
there is no ruler who does not desire these.
That commands are executed and prohibitions are observed,
and that there is no rival within the four seas—
there is no ruler who does not desire these.
Being obscured, deceived, encroached upon, and bullied—
there is no ruler who does not hate these.
To lose the world
and have the ancestral temple destroyed—
there is no ruler who does not hate these.
Loyal ministers desire to clarify the methods of law to achieve what the ruler desires and eliminate what the ruler hates.
But when treacherous ministers monopolize the ruler,
they use private means to endanger them,
so loyal ministers have no way to present their techniques of public justice.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
“When those who die have committed no crime,
and those who rise have no merit,
then those who serve as ministers will value private interests and disregard the public good.”
They go ten times to the gates of private individuals
but not once to the court.
When a chaotic ruler grants titles and stipends,
he does not use laws and regulations to verify merit;
when he carries out punishments,
he does not use laws and regulations to verify offenses,
but instead listens to what powerful ministers say.
Thus, if a minister wishes someone to be rewarded,
the ruler rewards them for his sake;
if a minister wishes someone to be punished,
the ruler punishes them for his sake.
Abolishing the public law
and listening exclusively to powerful ministers.
In this way,
all ministers strive for their own factions,
honoring powerful ministers while forgetting their ruler,
rushing to the gates of powerful ministers instead of the court.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
“They go ten times to the gates of private individuals,
but not once to the court.”
They plan for their families a hundred times
but do not plan for the state once.
In the governance of an enlightened ruler,
he is clear about the division of duties
and supervises the completion of tasks;
those capable of their responsibilities hold office,
and those not capable are dismissed;
thus all ministers exhaust their ability and effort to govern their affairs.
A chaotic ruler is not so;
therefore, although the ministers hold official positions
and receive generous stipends,
none strive to govern the state,
but rather aim to control the power of the state to monopolize its benefits,
preying upon the people to enrich their own families.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
“They plan for their families a hundred times,
but do not plan for their state once.”
Although their subordinates are numerous,
it is not to honor the ruler;
although the various officials are complete in number,
it is not to take responsibility for the state.
This is called a state being without men.
When an enlightened ruler is in the superior position,
the people within the borders exhaust their strength to serve their ruler,
and the various officials divide their duties to achieve order
and stabilize the state.
A chaotic ruler is not so.
Even if there are men of courage and strength,
the high ministers keep them for their private use
and not to serve their ruler;
even if there are men of sagacity and wisdom,
the high ministers keep them for their private use
and not to govern the state.
Therefore, although subordinates are numerous,
they cannot advance;
although the various officials are complete in number,
they cannot be controlled.
In such a case,
there is the name of a ruler but not the reality.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
“Although subordinates are numerous,
it is not to honor the ruler.
Although the various officials are complete in number,
it is not to take responsibility for the state;
this is called a state being without men.”
A state being “without men”
does not mean the court officials are few,
but that families and households strive to benefit one another
and do not strive to honor the ruler.
An enlightened ruler
makes subordinates exhaust their strength and observe the legal boundaries;
thus the ministers strive to honor the ruler and do not dare look after their private families.
The distinction between minister and ruler is clear,
and the positions of superior and inferior are scrutinized;
thus the high ministers each stay in their positions and do not dare to aggrandize one another.
A chaotic ruler is not so;
legal systems are abandoned and not implemented;
thus ministers are able to strive to benefit their own families.
There is no distinction between ruler and minister,
and no difference between superior and inferior;
thus the ministers are able to strive to aggrandize one another.
In such a case,
it is not that court officials are few,
but that the multitude is not put to use.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
“A state being without men
does not mean court officials
are few;
but that families and households strive to benefit one another,
and do not strive to honor the ruler;
and high ministers strive to aggrandize one another
and do not take responsibility for the state.”
High ministers strive to aggrandize one another and do not take responsibility for the state;
minor officials hold onto their stipends to cultivate social connections
and do not take their official duties as their business;
thus the offices lose their function.
When a ruler establishes offices and appoints officials,
it is not merely to honor their persons
or provide them with generous support.
It is to make them uphold the ruler’s laws,
execute the ruler’s commands,
to govern the common people,
and to punish thieves and rebels.
For this reason, if the office assigned is large,
the rank is noble and the stipend is generous;
if the office assigned is small,
the rank is humble and the stipend is meager.
Ranks and stipends
are the means by which a ruler makes officials manage their duties.
In the governance of a chaotic ruler,
they hold noble positions,
receive generous stipends,
and nurture those they associate with,
yet do not take their office as their duty.
In such a case,
the offices lose their function.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
“Minor officials hold onto their stipends to cultivate associations,
and do not take their official duties as their business;
thus the offices fail in their duties.”
For this reason, when the *Xiānwáng* governed the state,
they made the law select men
and did not promote them personally.
In the enlightened ruler’s selection of worthy men,
those who claim to be courageous are tested in the army;
those who claim to be wise are tested in the office.
Those tested in the army and found to have merit are promoted;
those tested in the office and found to have managed affairs well are employed.
Thus, matters of military merit determine courage or cowardice;
the management of official duties determines stupidity or wisdom.
Therefore, the appearance of courage, cowardice, stupidity, and wisdom
is as distinct as the division between white and black.
A chaotic ruler is not so;
he listens to words without testing them,
thus those who speak recklessly are employed.
He appoints men without assigning them to specific offices,
thus the unworthy do not face hardship;
Therefore, an enlightened ruler (*míngzhǔ*) uses the law to examine words and seek their reality,
assigns offices based on the person and audits their achievements,
and relies solely on the law without personally elevating individuals;
therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
“In the governance of the state by the former kings (*xiānwáng*),
they let the law select people
and did not personally elevate them;”
they let the law measure achievements
and did not personally estimate them.
As for what is called achievement,
it is that which brings peace to the sovereign and benefits the ten thousand people;
breaking armies and killing generals,
winning victories and capturing territories,
ensuring the sovereign has no worry of peril or ruin,
and the common people have no fear of death or captivity—
these are why soldiers are considered to have achievement.
Upholding the sovereign’s laws,
governing within the borders,
ensuring the strong do not oppress the weak,
and the many do not abuse the few,
so that the ten thousand people joyfully exert their strength to support and serve their sovereign—
these are why officials are considered to have achievement.
Correcting the sovereign’s faults,
remedying the sovereign’s lapses,
clarifying principle and righteousness to guide their sovereign,
so that the sovereign has no depraved conduct
or the affliction of being obscured or deceived—
these are why ministers are considered to have achievement;
therefore, in the governance of an enlightened ruler,
he clearly distinguishes duties and audits achievements and efforts;
those with achievement are rewarded,
and those who violate the law are executed;
wherever punishment or reward is applied,
each attains what is appropriate,
and the sovereign does not personally involve himself;
therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
“Let the law measure achievement
and do not personally estimate it.”
Therefore, ability may be hidden but cannot be obscured,
and failure may occur but cannot be glossed over;
in the governance of an enlightened ruler,
he scrutinizes right and wrong,
investigates the facts of matters,
and examines them with standards and measures;
if they accord with the law, he acts;
if they do not accord with the law, he stops;
if the achievement fulfills their words, they are rewarded;
if it does not fulfill their words, they are punished;
thus, regarding those who speak of wisdom and ability,
there must be visible achievement before they are elevated;
regarding those spoken of as wicked or failing,
there must be visible faults before they are dismissed;
in this way,
scholars may rise to the top and none can envy them,
and the unworthy are stranded and dismissed and none can elevate them;
therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
“Ability cannot be obscured,
and failure cannot be glossed over.”
Those who are praised cannot advance,
and those who are slandered cannot be demoted.
The Way (*Dào*) of an enlightened ruler
is to establish what the people desire
to seek their achievement;
therefore, he creates rank and salary to encourage them.
He establishes what the people detest
to prohibit their depravity;
therefore, he creates punishments to overawe them.
Thus, he examines their achievement and carries out rewards,
and examines their crimes and carries out punishments;
in this way,
among the various ministers, those who recommend the meritless dare not step forward,
and those who disparage the innocent cannot cause them to be demoted;
therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
“Those who are praised cannot advance,
and those who are slandered cannot be demoted.”
Thus, the distinction between sovereign and minister is clear;
when the distinction is clear, governance is easy;
controlling the various ministers,
and holding the exclusive power over life and death,
is the duty of the sovereign.
To receive orders and look up to control
is the duty of the minister.
To have authority and power, being honored and manifest,
is the duty of the sovereign.
To be humble and lowly, showing awe and respect,
is the duty of the minister.
To have orders carried out and prohibitions stop actions
is the duty of the sovereign.
To uphold the law and listen and obey
is the duty of the minister.
Thus, in the relationship between sovereign and minister,
their positions are high and low.
They are like heaven and earth;
their distinction is as different as day is from night,
like white and black.
Therefore, when the distinction between sovereign and minister is clear,
the sovereign is honored and the minister is humble;
in this way,
those below follow those above
like an echo responding to a sound;
the minister follows the sovereign’s model
like a shadow following a form;
therefore, when those above command, those below respond;
when the sovereign acts, the minister follows;
by command, things are done;
by prohibition, things are stopped;
by seeking, things are obtained;
this is what is meant by easy governance;
therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
“Between sovereign and minister,
if the distinction is clear, governance is easy.”
Although the sovereign does not personally perform tasks below,
keeping the law and letting it perform them is acceptable.
An enlightened ruler grasps the techniques (*shù*) and employs ministers,
makes the various ministers exert their wisdom and ability
and present their best skills;
thus, the wise exert their schemes and the capable
present their achievements.
He supervises them based on their previous words;
the results of subsequent matters are produced;
if they match, he rewards them; if they do not match,
he punishes them. Establishing offices,
employing officials, and governing the people,
he examines the law to test and audit the completion of work; upholding the law,
and through the person of the law, he is without toil, yet duties are divided;
therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
“Although the sovereign does not personally perform tasks below,
keeping the law and letting it perform them is acceptable.”
In ancient times, those who wished to rectify the world and harmonize All-under-Heaven (*tiānxià*) must first observe the government of the state,
estimate affairs,
investigate the customs of the people,
root out the source of order and chaos,
know where gains and losses lie,
and only then do they act. Therefore, the law can be established and governance can be carried out.
If the ten thousand people are not in harmony,
the state is not at peace,
and the failure is not with those above,
then the fault is with those below.
Now, if a sovereign acts contrary to principle and does not cultivate the Way (*Dào*),
executes people without reason,
imposes heavy taxes,
exhausts the people’s wealth,
is urgent in his commands,
and fatigues the people’s strength,
when wealth is exhausted,
then they cannot help but steal and seize;
when strength is fatigued,
then they cannot help but become lazy and deceitful.
Once the people are stealing, seizing, lazy, and deceitful,
and then the law is used to follow and punish them,
then punishments will be heavy and chaos will arise all the more.
When the people are toiling, suffering, and in want,
they will slight prohibitions and treat crimes lightly;
in this case,
the failure lies with those above.
When the failure lies with those above
and those above do not change,
then the ten thousand people have nowhere to entrust their lives.
Now, if a ruler makes punishments and administration light,
is lenient with the common people,
makes taxes thin,
and relaxes his commands,
yet the people are dissolute and restless, acting selfishly
and not following the regulations,
polishing their cleverness and employing deceit,
and relying on their strength to contend,
then the fault lies with those below.
Errors lie with subordinates
when the ruler of men is not incorruptible and is inconsistent;
then violent people cannot be overcome,
and evil disorder will not cease.
If violent people cannot be overcome
and evil disorder does not cease,
then the power of the one who rules men is damaged
and his prestige daily declines.
Therefore, for one who is a ruler of men,
nothing is more precious than control.
What is called control
is when laws are established and orders are carried out.
When laws are established and orders are carried out,
the various ministers uphold the law and maintain their offices,
and the hundred officials have constant standards.
"When laws are not complex and hidden,"
the myriad people are sincere and honest,
returning to fundamentals and being frugal with their labor.
Thus, rewards must be sufficient to employ them,
and prestige must be sufficient to overcome them,
and only then will subordinates follow.
Therefore, those whom the ancients called Míng Jūn
were not just one ruler.
Their setting of rewards had thin and thick,
their establishing of prohibitions had light and heavy;
their tracks and actions were not necessarily the same,
and it was not that they were intentionally contrary,
but that they all changed with the times
and moved according to customs.
If the people are restless and their behavior is deviant,
then rewards cannot but be thick
and prohibitions cannot but be heavy.
Thus, when the Shèng Rén established thick rewards,
it was not out of extravagance;
when they established heavy prohibitions,
it was not out of cruelty.
If rewards are thin,
then the people see no benefit;
if prohibitions are light,
then evil people do not fear.
To set up what people find of no benefit
and desire to employ them,
then the people will not exert their strength;
to establish what people do not fear
and desire to prohibit,
then evil people will not cease.
For this reason, when laws are set forth and orders issued,
the people do not follow.
Thus, if rewards are insufficient to encourage,
then the soldiers and people will not be of use;
if punishments are insufficient to be feared,
then violent people will lightly violate prohibitions.
The people are those who submit to the prestige of execution
and only then follow,
see profit
and only then are of use,
are governed
and only then become upright,
and obtain security
and only then are tranquil.
If thieves and bandits are not overcome,
evil disorder does not cease,
the strong rob the weak,
and the many oppress the few—
this is the worry of the world
and the suffering of the myriad people.
If worry and suffering are not removed,
then the people will not be at peace in their dwellings;
if the people are not at peace in their dwellings,
then the people's hope in the superiors is severed.
No benefit is greater than order,
and no harm is greater than chaos.
The reason the Wǔ Dì and Sān Wáng achieved success, established their names, and became illustrious to later generations
was that they brought benefit and removed harm for the world.
Their actions and deeds were not necessarily the same,
but their objectives were one.
If the people are greedy and restless while punishments are light,
and crimes and errors are not exposed,
then this encourages debauchery and facilitates evil and deviance.
To have a heart that loves the people
while in reality coinciding with harming the people—
these two things must be examined.
If thieves and bandits are not overcome,
then good people are in danger;
if legal prohibitions are not established,
then treachery and evil will multiply.
Therefore, in affairs, nothing is more urgent than addressing current needs,
and in governance, nothing is more precious than obtaining Qí.
If control over the people is too urgent, then the people are pressured;
if the people are pressured, then they are distressed;
if they are distressed, then the people lose what they cherish;
if it is too lax, they become unrestrained;
if they are unrestrained, they become licentious;
if they are licentious, they act selfishly;
if they act selfishly, they distance themselves from the public;
if they distance themselves from the public, they are difficult to use.
Thus, the reason governance is not established
is because Qí is not obtained. If Qí is not obtained,
then governance is difficult to carry out.
Therefore, the Qí of governing the people
must be examined.
The Shèng Rén
are clear about the way of order and chaos
and are practiced in the beginning and end of human affairs.
In their governing of the people,
they aim to benefit the people and the superiors.
Therefore, in establishing the Qí, they do not admire antiquity
nor linger in the present;
they change with the times
and transform with customs.
In the way of ruling people,
nothing is more precious than control.
Through control, the ruler's way is established;
when the ruler's way is established,
then subordinates follow;
when subordinates follow,
then instruction can be established and transformation can be completed.
If the people do not submit in heart and follow in body,
then they cannot be taught with the refined culture of Lǐ and Yì.
One who rules people must examine this.
Generally, in the way of governing a state,
one must first enrich the people.
When the people are rich, they are easy to govern;
when the people are poor, they are difficult to govern.
How do we know this is so?
When the people are rich, they are content in their villages and value their homes.
When they are content in their villages and value their homes,
they respect superiors and fear committing crimes.
When they respect superiors and fear committing crimes,
they are easy to govern.
When the people are poor, they find danger in their villages and think lightly of their homes.
When they find danger in their villages and think lightly of their homes,
they dare to insult superiors and violate prohibitions.
When they insult superiors and violate prohibitions,
they are difficult to govern.
Therefore, a well-governed state is always rich,
while a chaotic state is surely poor.
For this reason, those who are good at governing a state
must first enrich the people
and then govern them.
In the past, the rulers of seventy-nine generations
had different legal systems
and different commands and orders,
yet they all reigned as kings over the world. Why was this?
It must be because their states were rich and their grain was abundant.
Now, a rich state and abundant grain
originate from agriculture;
therefore, the former kings valued it.
In the urgent tasks of a state,
one must first prohibit secondary crafts and intricate skills.
When secondary crafts and intricate skills are prohibited,
then the people have no means to live as idle wanderers.
When the people have no means to live as idle wanderers,
they must engage in agriculture.
When the people serve in agriculture,
then the fields are cultivated.
When the fields are cultivated,
then grain is abundant.
When grain is abundant,
then the state is rich.
When the state is rich, the military is strong.
When the military is strong, battles are won.
When battles are won, territory is expanded.
For this reason, the former kings knew that a large population, strong military,
expanded territory, and rich state surely originate from grain.
Therefore, they prohibited secondary crafts,
stopped strange skills,
and benefited agricultural affairs.
Now, those who engage in secondary occupations and craft ingenious trifles
work for one day and eat for five.
Farmers work throughout the year,
yet it is not enough to feed themselves.
Thus, the people abandon the fundamental and pursue secondary occupations.
When they abandon the fundamental and pursue secondary occupations,
the fields lie waste and the state becomes poor.
Generally, for farmers, the monthly income is insufficient, while the yearly harvest provides a surplus.
But when the superiors' taxes are violent, urgent, and untimely,
the people must take out double-interest loans to pay the superiors' levies.
Plowing and weeding have their seasons,
and rainfall is not always sufficient;
then the people take out double-interest loans to hire labor.
Buying grain in autumn at a price of five
and selling grain in spring at the price of a bundle,
this is yet another doubling of loans.
Therefore, because of the superiors' levies, there are four ways the people are taken from doubly:
taxes on passes and markets,
levies for storehouses and treasuries,
the ten-percent tax on grain,
and the service of laborers and grooms;
in these four seasons, they must also resort to double-interest loans.
When one commoner supports four masters,
then even if those who flee and migrate are punished
and the superiors cannot stop them,
it is because grain is scarce and the people have no stores.
East of Sōngshān,
and between the Hé and the Rǔ,
things grow early and wither late;
it is where the five grains flourish and ripen.
Four types of seeds lead to five harvests.
In a medium year, one *mǔ* yields two *shí*,
so one man produces two hundred *shí* of grain.
Now, the granaries are empty and the people have no stores,
and farmers sell their children,
because the superiors have no method to equalize it.
Therefore, the former kings made the farmers,
*shì*, merchants, and artisans—the four classes of people—exchange their abilities and alternate their work,
so that the profits of the whole year
had no way to exceed one another.
Thus, when the people's work is unified, they obtain equality.
When the people's work is unified,
the fields are reclaimed,
and deceitful cleverness does not arise.
When fields are reclaimed,
grain is abundant,
and when grain is abundant,
the state is wealthy.
When deceitful cleverness does not arise,
the people are well-governed. Being wealthy
and well-governed—this is the Way of the King.
A state that does not produce grain perishes;
one where grain is produced but people die is a hegemon;
one where grain is produced and no one dies is a King.
Grain
is what the people flock to;
grain
is what wealth flocks to;
grain
is what land flocks to.
If grain is abundant, all things in the world will arrive.
Therefore, Shùn moved once and formed a village,
moved twice and formed a city,
moved thrice and formed a state.
Shùn did not use severe punishments
or heavy prohibitions,
yet the people flocked to him,
because those who left would surely suffer harm,
and those who followed him would surely gain profit.
The former kings
were good at removing harm and promoting profit for the people,
so the people of the world flocked to them.
What is called "promoting profit"
is to benefit agricultural affairs.
What is called "removing harm"
is to prohibit what harms agricultural affairs.
If agricultural affairs prevail, then the grain collected is abundant;
if the grain collected is abundant, then the state is wealthy;
if the state is wealthy, then they find peace in their villages and value their homes;
if they find peace in their villages and value their homes,
then even if customs are changed and habits altered,
or the masses are driven to move,
even to the point of death,
the people will not feel resentment.
This is the achievement of prioritizing grain.
If the superiors do not benefit agriculture,
then grain will be scarce;
if grain is scarce, the people will be poor;
if the people are poor, they will treat their homes lightly;
if they treat their homes lightly, they will easily leave;
if they easily leave, then the superiors' orders cannot be carried out with certainty;
if the superiors' orders cannot be carried out with certainty,
then prohibitions cannot be stopped with certainty;
if prohibitions cannot be stopped with certainty,
then battles will not necessarily be won
and defenses will not necessarily be firm.
When orders are not necessarily followed,
prohibitions are not necessarily stopped,
battles are not necessarily won,
and defenses will not necessarily be firm,
he is called a "parasitic ruler."
This results from the harm of not benefiting agriculture
and having little grain.
Grain
is the fundamental business of a King,
the great task of a ruler,
the path to possessing the people,
and the Dào to governing the state.
Generally, the essence of all things,
when aligned, becomes life.
Below, it gives life to the five grains;
above, it becomes the ranked stars.
Flowing between heaven and earth,
it is called ghosts and spirits;
stored within the breast,
it is called a Sage.
Therefore, this Qì,
is as bright as if ascending to heaven,
as dark as if entering an abyss,
as vast as if in the sea,
and as sudden as if within oneself.
Therefore, this Qì
cannot be stopped by force,
but can be settled by virtue;
it cannot be summoned by voice,
but can be welcomed by tone.
Respectfully guard it and do not lose it;
this is called perfected virtue.
When virtue is perfected, wisdom emerges,
and the ten thousand things are all attained.
Generally, the form of the mind
naturally fills and overflows,
naturally generates and completes.
The reason for losing it
must be because of sorrow, joy, happiness, anger, desire, or profit.
If one can remove sorrow, joy, happiness, anger, desire, and profit,
the mind then returns to its proper state.
The nature of that mind
benefits from tranquility and peace;
do not trouble it or confuse it,
and harmony will naturally be achieved.
Vividly as if at one's side,
suddenly as if about to be lost,
distantly as if reaching the limit of the infinite.
The investigation of this is not far;
daily one uses its virtue.
The Dào is what fills the form,
but people cannot hold it firm.
It goes and does not return;
it comes and does not stay.
Secretly, none hear its sound,
suddenly, it is in the mind;
obscurely, one does not see its form,
yet copiously, it is born together with me.
One does not see its form,
nor hear its sound,
yet it orders its completion; this is called the Dào.
Generally, the Dào has no specific place;
in a good heart, it peacefully abides.
When the heart is quiet and the Qì is regulated,
the Dào can then stay.
That Dào is not far;
the people obtain it to produce;
that Dào does not depart;
the people follow it to know.
Therefore,
suddenly, it seems as if it can be sought;
distantly, it seems as if it is exhausted and has no place.
The nature of that Dào
dislikes clamor and noise;
cultivate the heart and quiet the noise,
and the Dào can then be obtained.
As for the Dào,
it is what the mouth cannot speak,
what the eyes cannot see,
and what the ears cannot hear.
It is that by which one cultivates the heart and rectifies the form.
When humans lose it, they die;
when they attain it, they live.
When endeavors lose it, they fail;
when they attain it, they succeed.
Generally, the Dào
has no root and no stem,
no leaf and no flower.
The myriad things are born by it,
the myriad things are completed by it,
and one names it Dào.
Heaven governs through uprightness,
Earth governs through levelness,
and Man governs through peace and stillness.
Spring, autumn, winter, and summer
are the seasons of Heaven.
Mountains, hills, rivers, and valleys
are the resources of Earth.
Joy, anger, taking, and giving
are the schemes of Man.
Therefore, the Shèngrén changes with the times but does not transform,
and follows things without shifting.
Being able to be upright and still,
only then can one be stable.
With a stable heart within,
the ears and eyes are keen and clear,
the four limbs are firm and strong,
and they can become an abode for the Jīng.
As for the Jīng,
it is the essence of Qì.
When Qì flows, the Dào then arises.
With life, there is thought.
With thought, there is knowledge.
With knowledge, one then stops.
Regarding the form of the heart:
excessive knowledge leads to the loss of life.
To be able to transform things through the One is called spiritual.
To be able to change matters through the One is called wise.
Transformation does not change the Qì,
and change does not change the wisdom.
Only the Jūnzǐ who holds to the One is able to do this!
Holding to the One without losing it,
one can lord over the myriad things.
The Jūnzǐ employs things
and is not employed by things,
because he has attained the principle of the One.
Ordering the heart lies within,
ordering speech comes from the mouth,
ordering affairs is applied to others,
and thus the world is ordered.
"With one word attained, the world submits;
with one word settled, the world listens"
—this is what is meant.
If the form is not upright,
Dé will not come.
If the interior is not still,
the heart will not be ordered.
Rectify the form and gather Dé;
then heavenly benevolence and earthly righteousness
will copiously arrive of themselves.
The ultimate of Shénmíng
shines forth to know the myriad things.
If the center is guarded without error,
one does not let things disorder the senses,
and one does not let the senses disorder the heart;
this is called "attainment within."
There is a spirit that naturally resides in the body,
now going, now coming,
and none are able to fathom it.
To lose it is certainly chaos;
to gain it is certainly order.
Respectfully clean its abode,
and the Jīng will naturally come.
Think upon the Jīng and reflect on it,
calmly contemplate and order it.
With a solemn appearance and reverent awe,
the Jīng will reach stability.
Attain it and do not let it go,
and the ears and eyes will not be licentious.
The heart will have no other designs;
when an upright heart is within,
the myriad things obtain their measure.
The Dào fills the world
and is everywhere among the people,
yet the people cannot know it.
Through the explanation of a single word,
one examines Heaven above,
reaches the limits of Earth below,
and encompasses the Jiǔzhōu.
What is meant by explaining it?
It lies in the ordering of the heart.
When my heart is ordered,
the senses are then ordered.
When my heart is at peace,
the senses are then at peace.
That which orders them is the heart;
that which pacifies them is the heart.
The heart uses the heart to store the heart;
within the heart there is yet another heart.
That heart within the heart
is the intention that precedes speech.
After the intention, there is the form;
after the form, there is speech.
After speech, there is command;
after command, there is order.
Without order, there is certainly chaos;
chaos leads to death.
When Jīng is preserved, life arises of itself;
outwardly there is peace and flourishing,
and internally it is stored as a source and spring.
Vast and peaceful,
it serves as an abyss for the Qì.
When the abyss does not dry up,
the four limbs are then firm.
When the spring does not run dry,
the nine orifices are then clear.
Then one can exhaust Heaven and Earth
and cover the Sìhǎi.
Within there is no confused intention,
and without there are no evil calamities.
The heart is whole within,
and the form is whole without.
Not encountering heavenly calamities
and not meeting with human harm,
such a person is called a Shèngrén.
If a person can be upright and still,
the skin is relaxed and ample,
the ears and eyes are keen and clear,
and the tendons are flexible and the bones are strong.
Then one can bear the Dàhuán
and tread upon the Dàfāng,
reflecting the Dàqīng
and seeing by the Dàmíng.
Respectful and cautious without error,
daily renewing one's Dé,
knowing all under Heaven
and reaching to the four extremities.
Respectfully manifesting one's fullness—
this is called "inner attainment."
Yet if one does not return to this,
this is the error of life.
Generally, the Dào
must be pervasive and fine,
must be broad and relaxed,
and must be firm and stable.
Hold to the good and do not let it go;
discard licentiousness and let shallow luster fade.
Once its ultimate is known,
return to the Dào and Dé.
With a whole heart within,
it cannot be hidden or concealed;
it is known through the appearance
and seen in the complexion.
When a good Qì meets people,
it is more intimate than brothers.
When an evil Qì meets people,
it is more harmful than weapons of war.
The sound of the unspoken
is faster than thunder and drums.
The form of the heart's Qì
is brighter than the sun and moon
and more observant than parents.
Rewards are not enough to encourage the good,
and punishments are not enough to penalize the transgressive.
When Qì and intention are attained, the world submits;
when heart and intention are settled, the world listens.
Concentrating the Qì as if divine,
the myriad things are all preserved.
Can you concentrate it?
Can you be one?
Can you know good and bad fortune without divination?
Can you stop?
Can you cease?
Can you refrain from seeking it in others and obtain it within yourself?
Think about it, think about it,
and think about it yet again.
If you think about it and do not understand,
the ghosts and spirits will reveal it.
This is not through the power of ghosts and spirits,
but is the utmost reach of refined vital energy (*jīngqì*).
Once the four limbs are correctly aligned
and the blood and vital energy (*xuèqì*) are tranquil,
unify your intent and concentrate your mind,
so that ears and eyes are not led astray;
though far away, it seems near.
Careful searching produces knowledge;
negligence produces worry;
arrogance produces resentment;
melancholy produces illness;
and when illness is dire, death follows.
If you think about it without letting go,
you will be distressed within and emaciated without.
If you do not plan for it early,
your life will abandon its lodging.
For eating, nothing is better than not being overfull;
for thinking, nothing is better than not exhausting it.
When moderation and fitness are balanced,
it will arrive of its own accord.
In the life of every person,
Heaven provides the essence (*jīng*),
Earth provides the form (*xíng*),
and combining these makes a person.
When they are in harmony, there is life;
when not in harmony, there is no life.
Examine the way of harmony;
its essence is not seen,
and its manifestations are not unsightly.
With equanimity and rectitude filling the chest,
and the regulation of order residing in the heart,
one achieves longevity.
When anger loses its measure,
one must plan for it.
Moderate the five desires,
and discard the two evils.
Do not be joyful and do not be angry,
so that equanimity and rectitude fill the chest.
In the life of every person,
one must rely on equanimity and rectitude.
The reason one loses it
is surely because of joy, anger, worry, and anxiety.
Therefore, to stop anger, nothing is better than the *Shī*;
to remove worry, nothing is better than *yuè*;
to moderate *yuè*, nothing is better than *lǐ*;
to maintain *lǐ*, nothing is better than *jìng* (reverence);
to maintain *jìng* (reverence), nothing is better than *jìng* (stillness).
Stillness within and reverence without,
one can return to one's nature,
and that nature will become greatly settled.
Regarding the way of all eating:
Overfilling
causes injury and the form is not good.
Excessive restriction
causes bones to wither and blood to stagnate.
Between fullness and restriction,
this is called the completion of harmony;
it is where the essence (*jīng*) lodges
and where knowledge is produced.
When hunger and satiety lose their measure,
one must plan for it.
When full, move quickly;
when hungry, broaden your thoughts;
when old, lengthen your reflections.
If full but not moving quickly,
vital energy (*qì*) will not flow to the four extremities.
If hungry but not broadening thoughts,
hunger will not be alleviated even if full.
If old but not lengthening reflections,
exhaustion will quickly lead to depletion.
Expand the mind and let it be open;
relax the vital energy and let it be broad.
If the form is tranquil and unmoving,
one can maintain the One and discard the myriad distractions.
Seeing profit, do not be enticed;
seeing harm, do not be afraid.
Be relaxed and benevolent,
finding joy within oneself alone.
This is called "cloud-like vital energy" (*yúnqì*);
its movement of intent is like Heaven.
In the life of every person,
it must be by means of joy.
Worry causes the loss of order;
anger causes the loss of the starting point.
Worry, grief, joy, and anger—
when these exist, the *Dào* has no place to reside.
Use stillness to quiet love and desire;
use rectitude to encounter disorder.
Neither pull nor push,
and fortune will return of its own accord.
That *Dào* comes of itself;
one can rely on it to plan.
If still, you obtain it;
if agitated, you lose it.
The spiritual vital energy (*língqì*) is in the heart;
it comes and goes.
So small there is nothing inside it,
so large there is nothing outside it.
The reason it is lost
is that agitation causes harm.
If the heart can maintain stillness,
the *Dào* will settle itself.
For the person who has attained the *Dào*,
the pores are clear and the hair radiates,
and there is no decay within the chest.
Following the way of moderating desires,
the myriad things cannot cause harm.
Having assembled the feudal lords at *Kuíqiū*,
[Lord Huán] wished to perform the *Fēng* and *Shàn* sacrifices.
*Guǎn Zhòng* said:
"In antiquity, there were seventy-two houses that performed the *Fēng* sacrifice at *Tàishān* and the *Shàn* sacrifice at *Liángfù*,
but of those, I, *Yíwú*, remember only twelve.
In the past, *Wúhuáishì*
performed the *Fēng* sacrifice at *Tàishān*,
and the *Shàn* sacrifice at *Yúnyún*;
*Fùxī* performed the *Fēng* sacrifice at *Tàishān*,
and the *Shàn* sacrifice at *Yúnyún*;
*Shénnóng* performed the *Fēng* sacrifice at *Tàishān*,
and the *Shàn* sacrifice at *Yúnyún*;
*Yándì* performed the *Fēng* sacrifice at *Tàishān*,
and the *Shàn* sacrifice at *Yúnyún*;
*Huángdì* performed the *Fēng* sacrifice at *Tàishān*,
and the *Shàn* sacrifice at *Tíngtíng*;
*Zhuānxū* performed the *Fēng* sacrifice at *Tàishān*,
and the *Shàn* sacrifice at *Yúnyún*;
*Dì Kù* performed the *Fēng* sacrifice at *Tàishān*,
and the *Shàn* sacrifice at *Yúnyún*;
*Yáo* performed the *Fēng* sacrifice at *Tàishān*,
and the *Shàn* sacrifice at *Yúnyún*;
*Shùn* performed the *Fēng* sacrifice at *Tàishān*,
and the *Shàn* sacrifice at *Yúnyún*;
*Yǔ* performed the *Fēng* sacrifice at *Tàishān*,
and the *Shàn* sacrifice at *Kuìjī*;
*Tāng* performed the *Fēng* sacrifice at *Tàishān*,
and the *Shàn* sacrifice at *Yúnyún*;
*Zhōu Chéng Wáng* performed the *Fēng* sacrifice at *Tàishān*,
and the *Shàn* sacrifice at *Shèshǒu*.
All of them received the Mandate of Heaven before they could perform the *Fēng* and *Shàn* sacrifices."
Lord *Huán* said:
"I campaigned in the north against the *Shānróng*,
passing through *Gūzhú*;
I campaigned in the west against *Dàxià*,
crossing the *Liúshā*,
binding the horses and suspending the chariots
to ascend *Bēi’ěr* Mountain;
I campaigned in the south as far as *Zhàolíng*,
and climbed *Xióng’ěr* Mountain
to look out over the *Jiāng* and *Hàn* rivers.
There were three assemblies of war chariots
and six assemblies of passenger chariots;
nine times I united the feudal lords,
bringing order to the world once and for all,
and none of the feudal lords disobeyed me.
In the past, when the Three Dynasties received the Mandate,
how was it any different from this?"
At this, *Guǎn Zhòng* saw that Lord *Huán* could not be dissuaded by words,
so he set before him specific requirements, saying:
"For the *Fēng* and *Shàn* sacrifices of old,
the millet from *Hàoshàng*
and the grain from *Běilǐ*
were used for the sacrificial offerings;
between the *Jiāng* and *Huái* rivers,
there was a type of couch grass with three ridges,
which was used for the sacrificial mats.
The Eastern Sea yielded the *Bǐmù* fish,
and the Western Sea yielded the *Bǐyì* bird,
and thereafter fifteen kinds of things that were not summoned arrived of their own accord."
"Now that the fènghuáng and qílín do not come,
auspicious grains do not grow,
and yet fleabane, mugwort, goosefoot, and weeds flourish,
and owls frequently arrive,
yet you wish to perform the fēngshàn?
Would that not be perhaps unacceptable?"
Thereupon Huán Gōng desisted.
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zǐ:
"To govern without disorder,
and to be enlightened without being obscured—
how is this done?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"By clearly defining divisions and assigning duties,
then there will be order without disorder,
and enlightenment without being obscured."
The Duke said:
"I ask, how can one enrich the state?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"By exerting effort upon the land and acting according to the seasons,
then the state will certainly be rich."
The Duke again asked:
"I wish to practice broad benevolence and great righteousness
to benefit the world;
what must be done for this to be possible?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"By punishing the violent and forbidding wrongdoing,
preserving those that are perishing and continuing lines that are severed,
and pardoning the innocent,
then benevolence will be broad and righteousness will be great."
The Duke said:
"I have heard
that to punish the violent and forbid wrongdoing, and to pardon the innocent,
one must have the tools for victory in battle
and the methods for attacking and capturing,
only then can one punish the violent and forbid wrongdoing, and pardon the innocent.
I ask about the tools for victory in battle?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"By selecting the heroes of the world,
gathering the finest materials of the world,
and attracting the skilled craftsmen of the world,
then one will have the tools for victory in battle."
The Duke said:
"What about the methods for attacking and capturing?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"By destroying their defenses,
scattering their stores,
and seizing their food,
then there will be no fortified cities."
The Duke said:
"If so, then how does one recruit scholars?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"If you treat them with courtesy
and are generous without deceiving them,
then the scholars of the world will arrive."
The Duke said:
"How does one gather the finest materials of the world?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"By turning five into six
and nine into ten;
they will be beyond counting."
The Duke said:
"How does one attract craftsmen?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"By paying three times the wages,
they will not consider a thousand lǐ too far."
Huán Gōng said:
"I already know the tools for victory in battle
and the methods for attacking and capturing.
I ask about marching the army and raiding cities,
knowing what to do first and what to do later in maneuvers,
and not losing the advantages of the terrain—
how is this done?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Use currency and examine maps."
The Duke said:
"How does one ensure victory in open-field battles?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"By using unconventional tactics."
The Duke said:
"I wish to know the whole world—how is this done?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"If the small things are not known to me,
then the world is not worth knowing."
The Duke said:
"In defense, battle, and foresight, there are worries.
If the people are not necessarily willing to die,
then one cannot face the difficulties of defense and battle with them;
if they are not necessarily trustworthy,
then one cannot rely on them for external knowledge.
To rely on people who are unwilling to die
and seek success in defense and battle,
or to rely on people who are untrustworthy
and seek external knowledge,
these are the three darknesses of the military.
How can I make the people necessarily willing to die and necessarily trustworthy?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Make clear the three fundamentals."
The Duke said:
"What are called the three fundamentals?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"As for the three fundamentals:
the first is called stability,
the second is called esteem,
and the third is called the pledge."
The Duke said:
"What does that mean?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"The ancestral state and the location of one's parents' graves
constitute stability;
fields, residences, noble titles, and stipends
constitute esteem;
wives and children
constitute the pledge.
When these three are prepared,
and then you increase your majesty
and sharpen their intent,
then the people will certainly be willing to die and will not deceive me."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zǐ about governing the people.
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Generally, for one who shepherds the people,
they must know their ailments
and care for them with virtue;
do not frighten them with punishment,
and do not restrain them with force.
Being careful with these four things
is sufficient to govern the people."
Huán Gōng said:
"I see the goodness in this,
but what if the population is small?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Being few in number is not a worry for one who possesses a state.
In the past, the Tiānzǐ stood in the center
with a territory of a thousand lǐ,
and these four principles were inclusive within it;
why would he be concerned with being few?
If one shepherds the people without knowing their ailments,
then the people will be ill;
if one does not care for them with virtue,
then the people will have much resentment;
if one frightens them with punishment,
then the people will be very deceitful;
if one restrains them with force,
then those who leave will not return,
and those who come will resist stubbornly.
Therefore, when a sage king shepherds the people,
he does not focus on their numbers."
Huán Gōng said:
"Excellent.
Do not stop;
how then should these be put into practice?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Substantial trustworthiness, ultimate benevolence, sternness
combined with propriety—
being careful with these four things
is how to put them into practice."
Huán Gōng said:
"I request to hear the explanation."
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"As for trustworthiness,
the people will trust it;
as for benevolence,
the people will cherish it;
as for sternness,
the people will fear it;
as for propriety,
the people will admire it.
A saying goes:
'When blessings and commands do not change,'
that is trustworthiness."
"That which is not what one desires,
do not impose it on others;
this is humaneness (rén).
Being firm within and
upright without; this is severity (yán).
To be of substance and trust, yet yielding;
this is ritual propriety (lǐ)."
Huán Gōng said:
"Excellent!
In governing the people, what should come first?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"There are times to put governance first,
and there are times to put virtue first."
"When fierce winds and torrential rains
do not harm people,
and droughts are not a distress to the people,
the rivers are well-channeled,
the year's grain ripens,
grain and loans are cheap,
birds and beasts gather with people
to eat the people's food,
and the people suffer no epidemics."
"At such a time,
the people are wealthy and arrogant.
Those who govern the people should collect heavily in good years
to fill the granaries,
and prohibit access to marshes and lakes.
This is called preceding them with tasks,
following them with punishments,
and revering them with ritual and music
to restrain their excesses.
This is called putting governance first."
"When fierce winds and torrential rains harm the people,
and droughts are a distress to the people,
the year's grain does not ripen,
the year is famished,
grain and loans are expensive,
and the people suffer from epidemics."
"At such a time,
the people are poor and exhausted.
Those who govern the people should open the granaries, mountain forests, and marshes to share their wealth.
Put tasks last,
and put compassion first,
to relieve their exhaustion.
This is called putting virtue first."
"When collecting from them,
do not seize the people's wealth;
when bestowing upon them,
do not fail those who have virtue.
To make those above wealthy and those below sufficient,
this is the ultimate task of the Sagely Kings."
Huán Gōng said:
"Good."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"I desired to be a hegemon,
and through the efforts of you gentlemen,
I have already attained hegemony.
Now I desire to be a King;
is that possible?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"You should summon Yì Yá and ask him."
Bǎo Shū arrived,
and the Duke asked him as well.
Bǎo Shū replied:
"You should summon Bīn Xū Wú and ask him."
Bīn Xū Wú hurried forward,
and the Duke asked him as well.
Bīn Xū Wú replied:
"Among the kings of antiquity,
the ruler was abundant,
and his ministers were diminished.
Now, your ministers are abundant."
The Duke withdrew and stood far off in deep contemplation.
The three gentlemen then slowly advanced.
The Duke said:
"In the past, Dà Wáng was worthy,
Wáng Jì was worthy,
Wén Wáng was worthy,
and Wǔ Wáng was worthy;
Wǔ Wáng attacked Yīn and conquered it,
dying seven years later.
Zhōu Gōng then assisted Chéng Wáng in governing the world,
and was only just able to maintain control within the Four Seas."
"Now my sons are not like me,
and I am not like you gentlemen.
Looking at it this way,
then it is certain I will not be a King."
Huán Gōng said:
"I wish to overcome the people,
how should I do it?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"These are not the words of a ruler of men.
Overcoming the people is easy.
But the way of overcoming the people
is not the Great Way of the world."
"If you wish to overcome the people,
then have the officials manage the litigation,
and command those who have committed crimes to pay compensation,
frequently inspecting and strictly punishing;
if it is like this, the people are overcome."
"However, the way of overcoming the people
is not the Great Way of the world.
If you make the people fear you
without feeling close to you,
disaster will soon reach your person."
"Even if you can hold on for a short time,
then no one will be able to stop
your assassination.
How dangerous!
Your state is precarious!"
Huán Gōng was observing the stables,
and asked the stable official:
"What task in the stable is the most difficult?"
The official did not reply.
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I, Yí Wú, was once a stable hand;
putting up the stall partitions is most difficult.
If you first put up the crooked timber,
the crooked timber then seeks more crooked timber;
once the crooked timber is in place,
straight timber has nowhere to be used."
"If you first put up the straight timber,
the straight timber then seeks more straight timber;
once the straight timber is in place,
crooked timber also has nowhere to be used."
Huán Gōng said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"I wish to attack those of the large states who are not submissive;
how should I do it?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"First love those within your four borders,
and then you can loathe the bad ones outside your borders."
"First stabilize the houses of the high officials and dignitaries,
and then you can endanger the neighboring enemy states.
Therefore, the former kings certainly had what they established,
and then they had what they abolished;
they certainly had what they benefited,
and then they had what they harmed."
Huán Gōng ascended the throne,
and ordered a blood-sacrifice at the altar of the soil to fulfill a prayer.
The priest Fù Yǐ Bì presented the sacrificial meat,
and the prayer said:
"May it remove the ruler's harsh ailments and his tendency toward much emptiness and little substance."
Huán Gōng was displeased,
and glared at Fù Yǐ Bì.
Fù Yǐ Bì offered the wine and made a sacrifice, saying:
"And also grant the ruler more of those like his worthies."
Huán Gōng was angry,
and intended to execute him, but had not yet done so.
He reported this to Guǎn Zhòng.
Guǎn Zhòng then knew that Huán Gōng was capable of attaining hegemony.
Huán Gōng was riding a horse,
and a tiger, seeing him, crouched down.
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"Just now I was riding my horse,
and a tiger saw me and did not dare to move;
what is the reason for this?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I suspect
you were riding a Bó horse, wandering about,
and galloped facing the sun?"
The Duke said:
"Indeed."
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"This horse resembles a Bó.
The Bó eats tigers and leopards,
so the tiger was suspicious of it."
Chǔ attacked Jǔ;
the ruler of Jǔ sent someone to seek help from Qí
Huán Gōng. He was about to save them,
when Guǎn Zhòng said:
"You must not save them."
The Duke said:
"What is the reason for this?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I spoke with his envoy;
three times I insulted his lord,
but his expression did not change.
I ordered the officials not to fulfill the proper rites;
three times I used force, but the envoy
contested it to the death.
The ruler of Jǔ is a petty man.
Your Highness should not rescue him."
Huán Gōng indeed did not rescue him, and Jǔ fell.
Huán Gōng celebrated the spring festival,
and in the third month, he went to observe the countryside.
Huán Gōng said:
"What thing can be compared to the virtue of a gentleman?"
Xí Péng replied:
"Consider grain:
it resides within a shell,
having a coiled city in the middle
and armed weapons on the outside.
It does not dare to rely on its own strength,
calling itself 'sù' (grain).
This can indeed be compared to the virtue of a gentleman!"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Seedlings, when they first begin small,
how gentle and child-like they are!
When they reach maturity,
how dignified and like a scholar they are!
When they reach completion,
how easy and diligent they are,
how like a gentleman they are!
If the world obtains them, there is peace;
if not, there is danger;
therefore they are named 'hé' (standing grain).
This indeed can be compared to the virtue of a gentleman."
Huán Gōng said:
"Good."
Huán Gōng went north to attack Gūzhú;
when he was ten lǐ from the stream of Bēi'ěr,
he suddenly stopped.
He stared blankly,
reached for his bow to shoot,
but drew it and did not dare release it.
He said to his attendants:
"Do you see the person ahead?"
The attendants replied:
"We do not see him."
The Duke said:
"Will the matter not succeed?
I am greatly perplexed.
Just now I saw a person
a foot tall but with human features complete:
wearing a cap, with his right sleeve tucked up,
running swiftly in front of the horse.
Will the matter not succeed?
I am greatly perplexed.
Could there be a person like this?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I have heard that the god of climbing mountains is named Yú Ér,
who is a foot tall but with human features complete.
When a hegemonic or kingly ruler rises,
the god of climbing mountains appears.
Moreover, running swiftly in front of the horse
is showing the way.
Tucking up the sleeve
indicates there is water ahead.
Tucking up the right sleeve
indicates that one should wade across from the right side."
When they reached the stream of Bēi'ěr,
there was someone assisting with the water
who said:
"If you wade from the left side,
its depth reaches the cap;
if you wade from the right side,
its depth reaches only the knees.
If you wade from the right,
you will surely succeed."
Huán Gōng stood and bowed to Guǎn Zhòng in front of his horse, saying:
"Zhòngfù’s sagacity is such as this;
I have been in error for a long time."
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I, Yíwú, have heard
that a sage knows before things take shape.
Now that they have already taken shape and I know them,
I am not a sage,
but rather good at following teachings."
Huán Gōng sent Guǎn Zhòng to seek Nìng Qī;
Nìng Qī responded to him by saying:
"How vast and boundless!"
Guǎn Zhòng did not understand
and pondered it until the midday meal.
A servant girl said:
"What are you pondering, My Lord?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It is not something a servant girl would know."
The servant girl said:
"My Lord, do not look down on the young,
nor despise the lowly.
In the past, during the war between Wú and Gān,
those who had not lost their milk teeth could not enter the army gates.
Guózǐ knocked out his own teeth
and thus entered,
doing much for the state of Gān.
Bǎilǐ Xī
was a cattle feeder in the state of Qín.
Mù Gōng raised him up and made him Chancellor,
and he subsequently became hegemon over the feudal lords.
Looking at it from this perspective,
how can the lowly be despised,
and how can the young be looked down upon?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Indeed. The Duke sent me to seek Nìng Qī;
Nìng Qī responded to me saying, 'How vast and boundless!'
and I did not recognize its meaning."
The servant girl said:
"The Odes have a verse:
'Vast is the water,
thriving are the fish;
I have no home or family,
so how can you summon me to stay?'
Master Nìng likely desires a home."
Huán Gōng and Guǎn Zhòng closed the doors to plan an attack on Jǔ;
it had not yet been launched,
but it was already heard of throughout the state;
what was the reason?
Guǎn Zhòng said:
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"There must be a sage in the state."
Huán Gōng said:
"True.
Among those on duty,
there was one holding a mat and food who looked up at us;
could it be that person?"
Thereupon he ordered him to return to duty
and not to be replaced.
After a short while,
Dōngguō Yóu arrived.
Huán Gōng ordered the usher to invite him up,
stood with him on the same level,
and questioned him,
saying:
"Was it you who spoke of attacking Jǔ?"
Dōngguō Yóu said:
"Yes,
it was I."
Huán Gōng said:
"I did not speak of attacking Jǔ,
yet you spoke of attacking Jǔ;
what was the reason?"
Dōngguō Yóu replied:
"I have heard that
gentlemen are good at planning,
while petty men are good at inferring;
I inferred it."
Huán Gōng said:
"How did you infer it?"
Dōngguō Yóu said:
"A joyful and happy expression
is the color of bells and drums;
a deep and quiet expression is the color of mourning garments;
a fierce and full expression
with fingers and toes twitching
is the color of soldiers and armor.
The other day, I saw you two lords on the terrace;
your mouths opened but did not close,
which means you were saying 'Jǔ'; you raised your hands and pointed, and the direction was toward Jǔ.
Furthermore, I observed that among the lords of small states who are not submissive,
only Jǔ remains.
Therefore
I said you were attacking Jǔ."
Huán Gōng said:
"Excellent!
To use the subtle to hit the obvious—
is this not what is meant?
Please take a seat;
I shall share this matter with you."
A guest wanted to be presented to Qí Huán Gōng,
and requested to be appointed as a high official,
with a salary of one thousand zhōng.
The Duke informed
Guǎn Zhòng of this. Guǎn Zhòng said:
"My Lord, give it to him."
When the guest heard this, he said:
"I will not serve as an official."
The Duke said:
"For what reason?"
He replied:
"I have heard that those who select people based on others' words
will also dismiss people based on others' words.
I will not serve."
Someone used Píng Xū to request a discussion on the ways of seven rulers,
finding six faults and one correctness;
he used this as a mirror for himself
to know gains and losses. Using it to measure seven ministers,
he found six faults and one correctness.
Oh, how beautiful!
The matter is accomplished.
The Shēn Zhǔ: Employs power and maintains techniques as his constant rule,
and listens comprehensively to those near and far to extend his clarity.
When all essentials are scrutinized,
then laws and orders are firm;
when rewards and punishments are certain,
then subordinates submit to the standards.
When harmony is obtained without exhaustive preparation,
then the people return to simplicity.
Therefore, the ruler is at ease and secure,
officials are solemn and austere,
the people are simple and affectionate,
offices have no corrupt clerks,
the court has no treacherous ministers,
subordinates do not encroach or compete,
and the generation has no punished people.
The Huì Zhǔ: Uses abundant rewards and generous gifts to exhaust the treasury,
and pardons the treacherous and overlooks faults, thereby damaging the law.
When the treasury is exhausted, the ruler's power declines;
when the law is damaged, the door to treachery opens.
Thus it is said: "Extreme excess leads to reverse defeat."
The Qīn Zhǔ: His likes and dislikes run contrary to the law, thereby harming himself;
he delights in deciding what is difficult to know, thereby blocking clarity.
He follows sycophants and loves small scrutinies;
affairs have no constancy, and laws and orders are dragged along.
If he does not stop,
then the state loses its power.
The Máng Zhǔ: His eyes extend toward the five colors,
his ears are constant to the five sounds;
he does not calculate for the four neighbors,
and does not listen to the voice of overseers.
Then subordinates act willfully
and the state's power greatly tilts.
If he does not stop,
then what he hates will reach his own person.
The Láo Zhǔ: He does not clarify the division of duties;
superiors and inferiors interfere with each other;
and minister and ruler follow the same standards.
Punishments are shaken by laxity,
and laxity is shaken by harshness.
Leaving leads to chaos,
and approaching leads to danger;
what then will future generations obtain?
The Zhèn Zhǔ: His joy and anger have no measure;
his severe executions have no pardon;
subordinates are terrified and shaken,
not knowing what to do;
then people turn back to their old ways.
If he does not stop,
then laws and techniques diminish daily
and the state loses its firmness.
The Wáng Zhǔ: He uses human sentiments to settle doubts;
therefore, subordinates have no trust.
He completely governs all affairs himself,
so affairs are many;
when many, he is confused;
when confused, the urgent and the non-urgent are both established.
If he does not stop,
then he sees what is not good;
his remaining strength is lost, and he is punished.
Therefore, the order or chaos of a person lies in his heart;
the survival or ruin of a state lies in its ruler.
The gains and losses of the world
emerge from the way of one person.
If the ruler loves the foundation,
then the people love to clear the wild lands;
if the ruler loves goods,
then people trade in the markets;
if the ruler loves palaces,
then craftsmen are skillful;
if the ruler loves patterns and colors,
then female laborers are extravagant.
The Chǔ Wáng loved small waists,
and the beauties reduced their food;
the Wú Wáng loved swords,
and the state's knights treated death lightly.
Death and not eating
are what all under heaven commonly dislike,
yet why do they do them?
They follow what the ruler desires.
How much more so is the transformation of pleasure, music, and sound?
If men do not farm
and women do not weave,
and craftsmen exert effort on the useless,
