yet one desires the produce of the land
and the granaries to be full and solid,
it cannot be obtained.
If the land is not productive,
then the people are insufficient;
if the people are insufficient,
then contrary spirit arises;
when contrary spirit arises,
then orders are not carried out.
Then, if strong enemies launch an attack,
even a good ruler cannot survive.
How can we show this to be so?
Say:
In the past, Zhòu was like this.
He executed the worthy and loyal,
drew near to slanderous and thieving officials,
and valued women;
he loved killing but was not brave;
he loved wealth and forgot the poor.
He hunted without end;
he played music without satiety;
the Yáo Tái and Yù Pǔ were not enough for him to dwell in;
a thousand chariots and teams of four were not enough for him to ride;
talented female musicians were three thousand;
the sounds of bells, stones, strings, and flutes never ceased.
The common people were exhausted;
the gentlemen would not die for him;
in the end there were no people;
the people had hearts of rebellion.
He encountered Zhōu Wǔ Wáng
and thus became the prey of the Zhōu clan.
This is one who was deluded by objects and lost the true nature,
who rejoiced in excessive pleasure and forgot future calamities.
Therefore, if expenditures are set without measure,
the state will fall.
If disputes are raised at the wrong time,
one will surely receive calamity.
Granaries do not become empty for no reason;
commerce and officialdom do not fail for no reason;
laws and orders do not become chaotic for no reason;
a state does not perish for no reason.
In time there are spring and autumn;
in the year there are relief and disaster;
in government there are urgency and leisure.
Because government has urgency and leisure,
goods have lightness and weight;
because the year has relief and disaster,
the people have surplus and insufficiency;
because time has spring and autumn,
grain has high and low prices.
And if the superior does not regulate excesses,
then traveling merchants can increase their capital tenfold or a hundredfold.
That the common people do not farm,
and that poverty and wealth are not compared,
all arise from this.
That city walls are not defended,
and soldiers are not utilized,
all begin from this path.
Those who perish states and ruin families
are not without territory;
it is that what they attend to is not their proper work.
In disastrous years of thunder and drought,
it is not that there is no rain or dew;
it is that dryness and moisture are not at their proper times.
In a chaotic age of vexatious government,
it is not that there are no laws or orders;
it is that those executed or rewarded are not the right people.
Violent rulers and confused lords
are not without hearts and minds;
it is that what they choose and discard are not the right methods.
Therefore, a bright ruler has six tasks and four prohibitions.
What are the six tasks?
The first is called moderation in expenditure;
the second is called worthy assistants;
the third is called laws and measures;
the fourth is called certain punishment;
the fifth is called the seasons of Heaven;
the sixth is called the suitability of the Earth.
What are the four prohibitions?
In spring, there should be no killing or military campaigns,
no cutting into great mounds,
no baring of the great floodplains,
no felling of great trees,
no hacking at great mountains,
no setting of great fires,
no execution of great ministers,
and no collection of grain taxes.
In summer, there should be no damming of waters,
no diverting of famous rivers,
no blocking of great valleys,
no commencing of earthworks,
and no shooting of birds and beasts.
In autumn, do not pardon errors, release the guilty, or delay punishments.
In winter, there should be no granting of ranks or rewarding with emoluments,
which would harm and damage the five internal organs.
Thus, if the spring policies are not prohibited,
then the hundred growths will not emerge.
If the summer policies are not prohibited,
then the five grains will not mature.
If the autumn policies are not prohibited,
then the wicked and depraved will not be overcome.
If the winter policies are not prohibited,
then the *qì* of the Earth will not be stored.
If all four are violated,
then *Yīn* and *Yáng* will be in disharmony,
wind and rain will not come at the proper times,
great floods will submerge provinces and wash away towns,
great winds will blow down houses and break trees,
and violent fires will burn the land and scorch the grass.
There will be thunder in winter,
and lightning in winter;
plants and trees will wither in summer and bloom in autumn;
hibernating insects will not hide;
those that should die will live,
and those that should hibernate will cry out.
Hemp will be filled with pests and frogs;
the mountains will be full of insects and vermin.
The six domestic animals will not multiply,
and the people will suffer many premature deaths.
The state will be poor and the laws in chaos;
rebellious *qì* will arise from below.
Therefore it is said:
When terraces and pavilions face each other,
these are the verandas of a doomed state.
When galloping chariots fill the country,
these are the horses of pursuing invaders.
When swords are decorated with feathers and pearls,
these are the axes that cut down life.
When patterns and embroidery are woven together,
these are the kilns that burn away merit.
The bright king knows this is so;
therefore, he keeps them distant and does not draw them near.
If he can discard the latter and take up the former,
then the Way of the ruler of men is complete.
Now, the law
is that by which merit is raised and the violent are intimidated.
Statutes
are that by which duties are fixed and disputes are stopped.
Orders
are that by which the people are made to know their affairs.
Laws, statutes, government, and orders
are the compass, square, and marking line for officials and people.
If the square is not correct,
one cannot seek a square shape;
if the marking line is not reliable,
one cannot seek a straight line.
Laws and orders
are established jointly by the ruler and ministers.
Power and authority
are held solely by the ruler of men.
Therefore, if the ruler of men loses his hold, there is danger;
if the ministers and officials lose his hold, there is chaos.
When crimes are decided by officials, there is order;
when authority is wielded by the ruler, there is majesty;
when the people trust the law, there is closeness.
For this reason, the bright king examines the law and is cautious with authority;
there is a distinction between those below and those above.
All selfishness that arises
must originate with the ruler.
If the superior loves the fundamentals,
then upright gentlemen will be in front.
If the superior loves profit,
then slanderous and flattering men will be at his side.
If the superior often delights in giving rewards
without following merit,
then gentlemen will not be of use.
If he frequently issues heavy laws
but does not overcome the crimes,
then wickedness will not be stopped.
The bright king knows this is so;
therefore, he manifests inevitable governance
and establishes certain punishments.
Thus, the people know what they must pursue
and know what they must avoid.
Push them and they go;
call them and they come;
it is like dropping a weight from a height,
or like channeling water onto the ground.
Thus, the laws are not burdensome and the officials are not weary;
the people do not violate the prohibitions;
and therefore, the hundred surnames have no resentment toward the superior.
The Law Minister: When the law
decides names and determines judgments,
there is no slander or praise.
Thus, if the ruler follows the law, his position is secure;
if the ministers follow the law, bribery stops
and the people are without wickedness.
Oh, how beautiful it is!
Names are determined and words are beneficial.
The Adorned Minister: He overcomes his kin and the noble to make a name for himself,
and feigns indifference to rank and emolument to appear lofty.
Loving fame, he lacks reality;
being lofty, he is ungovernable.
The *Gù Jì* says:
"Without reality, there is no power;
if the reins are lost, how can the horse be controlled?"
The Encroaching Minister: He attends to small details to subvert the laws and orders,
and loves making friends to carry out private requests.
Thus, when private ways are followed, the laws and measures are encroached upon;
when punishments and laws are numerous, wickedness is not prohibited.
If the King is strict with executions, he will first capture the people's hearts.
The Flattering Minister: When they are numerous, they build bells and drums,
and present many adorned women to confuse the superior.
Thus, if the superior is confused, the four neighbors are not considered,
and those in charge of music just collect their salaries.
Therefore, the flattering ministers are noble while the law ministers are lowly;
this is called "subtle isolation."
The Foolish Minister: He takes severe crimes and heavy punishments as his conduct,
and takes heavy taxes
and many toll roads as his service to the superior.
He causes himself to be hated while the ruler receives the blame.
The *Gù Jì* refers to this as:
"Foolish loyalty is a slandering thief";
this is what is meant.
The Treacherous Minister: He speaks poignantly of human emotions to startle the ruler,
and exposes the cliques of the guilty to eliminate
his enemies.
By eliminating enemies, crimes fall upon the innocent;
when crimes fall upon the innocent,
then the ruler dwells with his enemies.
Thus, he speaks well of the hateful to gain trust,
and the ruler loses those close to him.
The Chaotic Minister: Secretly he declines merit and emolument,
but openly he requests heavy rewards for those below.
In private he acts as if he is not the source,
yet in action he acts as a virtuous pillar.
He uses wrongs to buy fame,
and uses rights to harm the superior,
yet the multitude does not know.
This is called "subtle attack."
Prohibitions are stored within the chest,
while calamity is avoided ten thousand *lǐ* away.
One who can use this to control that
is only one who can use self-knowledge to know others.
That the winter sun is not excessive
is not because it loves ice;
that the summer sun does not scorch
is not because it loves fire.
It is because they do not suit the person's comfort or the body's convenience.
Now, an enlightened Míng Wáng does not value the beauty of palaces and chambers,
not because he likes small things;
he does not listen to bells and drums,
not because he hates music.
It is because they cause harm to the fundamental occupation and hinder instruction.
Therefore, he is first cautious regarding himself and then others;
officials are also cautious regarding internal matters and then external ones;
the people also devote themselves to the fundamental and abandon the trivial.
Settle the people in what they enjoy,
employ them in what they find profitable,
reward them for what they do well,
punish them for what they dislike,
earn their trust by letting them keep their surplus wealth,
and gain their service by the absence of executions.
Among those below, if no one is executed,
it is because those who must be executed certainly are;
if there are those executed,
it is because those who must be executed are not certain.
By using punishments to reach a state of no punishments,
the laws are easy and the people are preserved;
by using no punishments to reach a state of having punishments,
the punishments are troublesome and villainy is plentiful.
To do the easy first is to have difficulty later;
to do the difficult first is to have ease later;
all things are thus.
An enlightened Míng Wáng knows this is so;
therefore, he must punish without pardoning
and must reward without shifting,
not because he delights in giving or enjoys killing,
but to bring benefit and remove harm for the people.
Thus the elderly are cared for and the weak are raised,
and the myriad people are kept alive and whole;
nothing is more enlightened than this.
Now, when the law is upheld as the law, there is order.
Law is
the standard for the world,
used to resolve doubts and clarify right and wrong,
and that upon which the lives of the Bǎixìng are suspended.
Therefore, the enlightened Míng Wáng is cautious with it;
he does not change his laws for the sake of relatives or the noble;
officials do not dare to use the dignity of high office to endanger its mandates;
the people do not use pearls, jade, or heavy treasures to violate its prohibitions.
Thus, the ruler views the law as more solemn than his relatives; the officials carry out orders
with more respect than for their teachers;
the people receive instruction
with more weight than for divine treasures. Thus, the law is established and not violated,
and punishments are set but not carried out.
If rewards for merit are not equal,
though the position is high,
those who serve will be few;
if pardons for crimes are not uniform,
though virtue is thick,
those who do not praise will be many;
if affairs are undertaken at the wrong time,
though strength is exhausted,
success will not be achieved;
if punishments are not appropriate,
though executions are many,
violence will not be stopped.
When justice is applied,
though the crime is heavy,
those below will have no resentment;
when private interest is applied,
though the reward is great,
the Shì will not be joyful.
If the implementation of law is not according to the Dào,
the masses of people cannot be obedient;
if actions and omissions are inappropriate,
the masses of people cannot achieve success.
He who does not attack the unprepared
should be named a fool.
Therefore, when the Shèng Rén regulates affairs,
he can moderate palaces and chambers
and make carriages and horses appropriate to fill the storehouses;
then the state will certainly be wealthy
and the position certainly honored.
He can make clothing appropriate
and discard toys and curios to support the fundamental;
then resources will certainly be sufficient
and the person certainly secure.
He can remove useless tasks
and unhelpful expenses,
circulate currency and practice rituals;
then his party will certainly be many
and his relations certainly close.
As for the common crowd, they are often occupied with things,
embittering their strength
and laboring their minds;
therefore they are impoverished and lack sufficiency;
the great lose their states,
and the small endanger their persons.
Generally, human nature is such:
to be happy when obtaining what one desires,
and to be sorrowful when encountering what one hates;
this is shared by both the noble and the lowly.
What is near cannot but be desired;
what is far cannot but be forgotten;
human nature is all like this.
But likes and dislikes differ,
and each person follows what they desire,
yet safety and danger differ for them;
then the forms of the worthy and the unworthy are revealed.
Things have quantity,
but feelings cannot be equalized;
affairs have success or failure,
but intentions cannot be the same;
actions have advancement or retreat,
but strength cannot do both.
Therefore, one establishes oneself in the center,
and nourishment has its moderation:
Palaces and chambers are sufficient to avoid dryness and dampness;
food and drink are sufficient to harmonize blood and Qì;
clothing is sufficient to suit cold and warmth;
rituals and ceremonies are sufficient to distinguish the noble and the lowly;
leisure and amusement are sufficient to generate joy;
inner and outer coffins are sufficient to decay the bones;
shrouds and burial clothes are sufficient to decay the flesh;
tombs are sufficient for markers and records.
Do not perform unhelpful labor,
do not do useless tasks;
thus the intent is settled and does not disturb the Qì and emotions.
When Qì and emotions are not disturbed,
then ears and eyes are keen
and food and clothing are sufficient.
When ears and eyes are keen
and food and clothing are sufficient, then encroachment and contention do not arise,
and resentment and anger do not exist.
Superiors and subordinates are close to each other,
and weapons of war are not used.
Therefore, to regulate the body and act with righteousness,
to be frugal, moderate, respectful, and reverent;
even if there is no blessing,
misfortune will also not come.
To be arrogant, proud, extravagant, and excessive,
to deviate from standards and cut off reason;
even if there is no misfortune,
blessing will also not arrive.
For this reason, the Jūnzǐ looks up at those who have cut off reason
to caution himself;
he looks down at those who fall short
to keep himself in check.
Therefore it is said:
"Reputation does not arise without cause,
and trouble does not occur in isolation;
blessing does not choose a house,
misfortune does not seek a person."
This is what is meant.
If one can use what is heard to observe and examine,
then affairs will certainly be clear.
Generally, the conditions of order and chaos
all begin with the ruler. Therefore, the good ruler restrains them with harm
and leads them with profit.
For one who can handle profit and harm,
wealth will be plenty and errors will be few.
Generally, human nature is such that
when seeing profit, none can but pursue it,
and when seeing harm, none can but avoid it.
As for merchants engaged in trade,
they double their pace and travel day and night,
continuing through the night,
and do not consider a thousand lǐ to be far,
because profit is before them.
Fishermen go into the sea;
the sea is ten thousand fathoms deep;
they go against the current there,
riding danger for a hundred lǐ,
staying out all night,
because profit is in the water.
Therefore, where profit is located,
though it be a mountain of a thousand fathoms,
there is nowhere they will not climb;
beneath the deep abyss,
there is nowhere they will not enter.
Therefore, one who is good at governing grasps where benefit lies,
and the people spontaneously find beauty and peace;
without being pushed, they go forward;
without being pulled, they come;
without being troubled or disturbed,
the people spontaneously become wealthy.
Like a bird brooding over its eggs,
there is no visible form or sound,
yet one only sees the accomplishment.
Now, the foundation of governing a state
is to obtain the seasons of Heaven to serve as the warp
and to obtain the hearts of the people to serve as the woof;
laws and decrees are the main ropes of the net,
officials are the mesh,
the *shí* and *wǔ* serve as the ranks,
and rewards and executions serve as the civil and military powers.
Repairing agricultural tools
corresponds to preparing weaponry;
farming and cultivation correspond to attacking and battling.
Pushing and pulling the *diào* and *nòu*
correspond to wielding swords and halberds;
wearing rain capes corresponds to wearing armor and tunics;
and sedge hats correspond to shields and barricades.
Therefore, when the tools for plowing are complete, the weapons for war are prepared;
when agricultural tasks are practiced, the skills for battle are refined.
During the three months of spring,
smoking out the rooms and heating the stoves,
drilling the fire-sticks to change the fire,
and dredging the wells to change the water,
are the means by which to eliminate lingering toxins.
Performing the spring sacrifices,
fulfilling long-standing prayers,
using fish as sacrificial animals,
and using malt for wine,
and inviting one another to gather,
are the means by which to unite relatives.
Do not kill livestock,
do not destroy eggs,
do not cut down trees,
do not prematurely end flowering plants,
and do not strike down young stalks;
these are the means to allow the growth of all living things.
Granting gifts to the widowed and orphaned,
relieving the solitary and childless,
lending to those without seeds,
and exempting the landless from taxes,
are the means by which to encourage the weak among the people.
Dispatching the *Wǔzhèng*,
pardoning minor offenses,
releasing imprisoned people,
and resolving feuds,
are the means to establish the achievements of the season
and bestow the grain of life.
In summer, rewarding the *Wǔdé*,
bestowing full titles and stipends, promoting officials, honoring filial piety and fraternal duty, and restoring the talented and strong,
are the means by which to encourage merit.
In autumn, carrying out the *Wǔxíng*,
and executing those for major crimes,
are the means by which to prohibit licentiousness and evil,
and stop thieves and bandits.
In winter, gathering the *Wǔzàng*,
and collecting the myriad things,
are the means by which to keep the people working within.
When the tasks of the four seasons are complete,
the people’s achievements will be increased a hundredfold.
Therefore, spring is benevolent, summer is loyal,
autumn is urgent, and winter is closed.
Following the timing of Heaven,
conforming to the suitability of the Earth,
and harmonizing with the concord of the people;
therefore the wind and rain are timely,
the five grains are substantial,
the grasses and trees are beautiful and abundant,
the six kinds of livestock multiply,
the state is wealthy and the military is strong,
the people are capable and orders are carried out.
Internally, there is no government of harassment or disturbance;
externally, there is no worry of powerful enemies.
Now, only when movement and stillness follow the natural order is there harmony;
only after one does not miss the proper time is there wealth;
only after one does not lose the laws is there order.
Therefore, a state is not wealthy without cause,
and a people are not well-governed without cause.
That which flourishes without being well-governed,
or perishes without being in chaos,
from ancient times until today,
has never existed.
Therefore, in a state where many possess private courage,
its military is weak;
where officials possess much private cleverness,
its laws are in disorder;
where the people pursue many private interests,
its state is poor.
Therefore, for virtue, nothing is better than being broad and deep,
to make the people willing to die for it;
for rewards and punishments, nothing is better than being certain and inevitable,
to make the people trust in them.
Now, he who is good at shepherding the people
does not rely on city walls,
but supports them with the *shí*
and supervises them with the *wǔ*.
Within the *wǔ*, there is no one who is not their own person;
among the people, there is no one who is not in their own neighborhood;
within the neighborhood, there is no one who is not in their own household.
Therefore, those who flee have no place to hide,
and those who migrate have no place to be accepted;
without being sought, they are restrained;
without being summoned, they come.
Thus the people have no intention of wandering,
and officials have no worry of preparing for pursuit.
Therefore, the ruler’s policies can reach the people,
and the people’s hearts can be tied to the ruler.
Now, the way laws control the people
is like a potter with clay
or a smith with metal.
Therefore, by carefully examining where benefit and harm lie,
the people’s choices to leave or stay
are like fire toward the dry or the damp,
or water toward the high or the low.
Now, that which sustains the people
is clothing and food;
that which produces food
is water and soil.
There is an essential method for enriching the people,
and a standard for feeding them;
the standard is that thirty *mǔ* are sufficient for a person to complete the year.
Taking both good and bad years into account,
if one *mǔ* yields one *shí*,
then a person has thirty *shí*;
fruit and vegetables used as simple food are equivalent to ten *shí*;
husks and bran used for the six kinds of livestock are equivalent to ten *shí*;
then a person has fifty *shí*.
Cloth, silk, hemp, and thread,
along with incidental income and extraordinary profits,
are not yet included in this.
Therefore, the state has surplus stores,
and the people have surplus food.
Now, calculating and equalizing
are the means to manage abundance and scarcity;
weights and balances
are the means to observe heaviness and lightness;
household registers and land records
are the means to know the extent of poverty and wealth.
Therefore, one who is good at governing must first know his lands,
and then he will know his people;
only after the land is well-managed can the people be sufficient.
In general, of those who possess the world,
those who campaign by means of sentiments are Emperors;
those who campaign by means of affairs are Kings;
those who campaign by means of governance are Hegemons.
And there are five ways to plot for success.
One: observe those whom the ruler loves
in order to divide his authority;
if one person has two hearts,
his internal state will surely decline.
If ministers are not used,
his state can be endangered.
Two: observe those whom he secretly hates,
give them generous bribes,
and the information obtained can be deep.
With the body inside but the heart outside,
his state can be understood.
Three: listen to his licentious music
to indulge his mind.
Send him *yú* pipes, *sè* zithers, and beautiful women
to block him from within;
send him flattering ministers and patterned horses
to obscure him from without.
When the outside and inside are blocked and obscured,
his failure can be accomplished.
Fourth, one must become deeply close to them,
as if they were one's own siblings.
Secretly introduce persuasive speakers
to cause them to plot their own schemes;
introduce brave warriors
to embolden their spirit.
Introduce people into other countries
to make them break their treaties,
cut off their envoys,
and thwart their intentions;
this will inevitably lead them to fight each other.
When two countries oppose each other,
one must take advantage of their exhaustion.
Fifth, examine their plans deeply,
be cautious of their loyal ministers,
create estrangement among those they employ,
cause internal distrust,
and make them have intentions of desertion.
When intentions of desertion cannot be reconciled,
they will inevitably destroy themselves from within.
Once the loyal ministers are dead,
then the government can be seized.
These five are
the ways of strategic success.
Within forty days of entering a state,
implement the Jiǔ Huì zhī Jiào (Teachings of the Nine Benevolences).
The first is Lǎo Lǎo (Honoring the Elderly),
the second is Cí Yòu (Caring for the Young),
the third is Xù Gū (Pitying the Orphaned),
the fourth is Yǎng Jí (Nurturing the Sick),
the fifth is Hé Dú (Uniting the Solitary),
the sixth is Wèn Bìng (Inquiring after the Ill),
the seventh is Tōng Qióng (Relieving the Destitute),
the eighth is Zhèn Kùn (Succoring the Distressed),
the ninth is Jiē Jué (Continuing the Extinguished).
What is meant by Lǎo Lǎo is
that all states and capitals have a Zhǎng Lǎo (Overseer of the Elderly).
For those aged seventy and above,
one son is exempt from labor service,
and every three months they are provided with meat;
for those eighty and above,
two sons are exempt from labor service,
and they are provided with meat every month;
for those ninety and above,
the entire household is exempt from labor service,
and they are provided with wine and meat every day.
Upon death,
the superior provides the inner and outer coffins.
Encourage the sons and younger brothers: provide fine meals,
ask what they desire,
and seek what they crave.
This is what is meant by Lǎo Lǎo.
What is meant by Cí Yòu is
that all states and capitals have a Zhǎng Yòu (Overseer of the Young).
When officers and commoners have children,
and the children are young and weak such that they cannot be supported and become a burden,
those with three young children
are exempt from the wife's labor tax,
those with four young children have the entire family exempt from labor service,
and those with five young children are further provided with a wet nurse,
and they receive food for two people,
stopping only after the children are capable of service.
This is what is meant by Cí Yòu.
What is meant by Xù Gū is
that all states and capitals have a Zhǎng Gū (Overseer of Orphans).
When officers or commoners die
and their children are orphaned and young,
without parents to raise them
and unable to support themselves,
they are entrusted to their local community,
acquaintances, and old friends.
Those who raise one orphan
have one son exempt from labor service,
those who raise two orphans
have two sons exempt from labor service,
those who raise three orphans
have the entire household exempt from labor service.
The Zhǎng Gū frequently visits them,
inevitably knowing their food and drink, hunger and cold,
and whether their bodies are thin or healthy, and pities them.
This is what is meant by Xù Gū.
What is meant by Yǎng Jí is
that all states and capitals have a Zhǎng Yǎng Jí (Overseer of Nurturing the Sick).
For the deaf, the blind, the mute, the dumb, the lame, those with paralyzed limbs, and those with hands and feet contracted,
who cannot support themselves,
the superior takes them in and nurtures them
in the Jí
Guān (Bureau of the Sick), providing them with clothing and food.
This stops only after they have passed away.
This is what is meant by Yǎng Jí.
What is meant by Hé Dú is
that all states and capitals have a Zhǎng Méi (Overseer of Matchmaking).
A man without a wife is called guān,
and a woman without a husband is called guǎ.
Take these guān and guǎ and unite them in harmony,
give them fields and houses to establish a household,
and only after three years do they perform labor service.
This is what is meant by Hé Dú.
What is meant by Wèn Bìng is
that all states and capitals have a Zhǎng Bìng (Overseer of Illness).
When officers or commoners are ill,
the Zhǎng Bìng follows orders to inquire after them.
For those ninety and above,
they are visited once a day;
for those eighty and above,
once every two days;
for those seventy and above,
once every three days;
for the general populace, once every five days.
If the illness is severe, it is reported to
the superior, who visits in person.
The Zhǎng Bìng travels throughout the state,
making the inquiry of the ill their duty.
This is what is meant by Wèn Bìng.
What is meant by Tōng Qióng is
that all states and capitals have Tōng Qióng (Relieving the Destitute) officials.
If there are destitute couples without a place to live,
or destitute guests who have run out of food,
those living in their local community
who report it will be rewarded,
and those who do not report it will be punished.
This is what is meant by Tōng Qióng.
What is meant by Zhèn Kùn is
that in years of crop failure, when the common
people suffer from disease
and many die;
relax punishments,
pardon the guilty,
and distribute grain from the granaries to feed them.
This is what is meant by Zhèn Kùn.
What is meant by Jiē Jué is
that when officers or commoners die in service to the superior
or in battle,
make their acquaintances and old friends
receive resources from the superior
to perform sacrifices for them.
This is what is meant by Jiē Jué.
Be calm, leisurely, and quiet;
let gentle measures be determined first,
keeping the mind empty and the intent peaceful to wait for the necessary moment.
The above is the Zhǔ Wèi (Ruler's Position).
The eyes value clarity,
the ears value sharpness of hearing,
and the mind values wisdom.
Seeing with the eyes of all under heaven,
then there is nothing unseen;
listening with the ears of all under heaven,
then there is nothing unheard;
contemplating with the mind of all under heaven,
then there is nothing unknown.
When information comes in from all sides like spokes to a hub,
then clarity is not obstructed.
The above is the Zhǔ Míng (Ruler's Clarity).
The technique of listening is as follows:
do not reject upon a glance,
and do not grant upon a glance.
If you grant it, you lose control;
if you reject it, you are blocked and obstructed.
Like a high mountain, when you look up at it,
it cannot be exhausted;
like a deep abyss, when you measure it,
it cannot be fathomed.
The virtue of the divine and the bright,
correctness and stillness are its ultimate state.
The above is the Zhǔ Tīng (Ruler's Listening).
Those who use rewards value sincerity;
those who use punishments value certainty.
When rewards and punishments are trustworthy and certain to what is seen by ears and eyes,
then in what is not seen, none will not be secretly transformed.
Sincerity permeates heaven and earth,
and connects with the divine and the bright;
how much more so with the treacherous and the false?
The above is the Zhǔ Shǎng (Ruler's Rewards).
The first is called that of Heaven,
the second is called that of Earth,
the third is called that of Man.
Within the four directions, above and below, left and right, and front and back,
where is the position of *Yínghuò*?
The above is "The Lord's Inquiries."
When the heart does not act on behalf of the nine orifices,
the nine orifices will be well-ordered;
when the ruler does not act on behalf of the five officials,
the five officials will be well-ordered.
For those who do good,
the ruler grants them rewards;
for those who do wrong,
the ruler grants them punishments.
The ruler follows the way by which they come
and accordingly grants to them;
thus he does not toil.
The sage follows along with things,
and therefore he can manage them.
By following them and adhering to principle,
he can endure for a long time.
The above is "The Lord's Following."
A ruler of men cannot but be comprehensive;
if a ruler of men is not comprehensive,
then the various ministers below will be in disorder.
How silent, having no beginning!
If the external and internal do not communicate,
how can he know where resentment lies?
If the gates are closed and not opened,
good and bad will have no source.
The above is "The Lord's Comprehensiveness."
The first is called "long eyes,"
the second is called "flying ears,"
the third is called "planting brilliance."
Clearly knowing what is beyond a thousand *lǐ*,
or within what is hidden and subtle,
is called "detecting villainy."
When villainy is detected, then changes will be made.
The above is "The Lord's Comparison."
Follow the name to supervise the reality;
examine the reality to determine the name.
Name and reality produce each other
and return to become each other's essence.
When name and reality correspond, there is order;
when they do not correspond, there is disorder.
Name is born from reality;
reality is born from virtue;
virtue is born from principle;
principle is born from wisdom;
wisdom is born from appropriateness.
The above is "Supervising Names."
Duke *Huán* of *Qí* asked *Guǎn Zǐ*, saying:
"I think of possessing something and not losing it,
or obtaining it and not having it vanish;
is there a Way for this?"
He replied:
"Do not initiate and do not innovate;
when the time arrives, follow it.
Do not let private likes and dislikes harm public justice.
Observe what the people hate and take it as a warning for yourself.
When *Huángdì* established the discussions of the *Míng Tái*,
he looked up to the worthy;
when *Yáo* had the inquiries of the *Qú Shì*,
he listened down to the people;
*Shùn* had the banner for reporting good deeds
so that the ruler would not be obscured;
*Yǔ* set up the drum in the court
to prepare for inquiries;
*Tāng* had the courtyard of the public streets
to observe people's criticisms;
*Wǔ Wáng* had the restoration of the *Líng Tái*,
so that the worthy would come forward.
These are the means by which the ancient sage-emperors and brilliant kings possessed without losing
and obtained without forgetting."
Duke *Huán* said:
"I wish to emulate them and do this;
what should its name be?"
He replied:
"Its name is 'Discussions of the *Zè Shì*.'
It is said: Let the laws be simple and easy to carry out,
let the punishments be scrutinized so they are not violated,
let the affairs be concise and easy to follow,
and let the demands be few and easy to satisfy.
If there are people who criticize the faults of those above,
call them upright officers
and bring them into the discussions of the *Zè Shì*.
Let the officials and those in charge all perform their duties according to their tasks and not forget their actions.
This is the business of the *Zè Shì*;
I request that *Dōngguō Yá* be appointed to it.
This is a man who can contend with the ruler over upright matters."
Duke *Huán* said:
"Good."
Formerly, Duke *Huán* asked *Guǎn Zhòng*, saying:
"I beg to ask about surveying the terrain to establish a state;
how should it be done to be acceptable?"
*Guǎn Zhòng* replied:
"From what I, *Yíwú*, have heard,
those who can become hegemons or kings
are truly the sages of the world.
Therefore, when a sage settles a state,
it must be on land that does not tilt,
and he selects terrain that is fertile and rich,
facing the mountains, with
arterial rivers or marshes on the left and right,
and constructing drainage channels within
that flow into large rivers according to their course.
The land then, through its natural resources and what it produces,
will profitably nourish its people and raise the six kinds of livestock.
The people of the Son of Heaven
will all return to his virtue and benefit from his righteousness.
Then he separately regulates and demarcates it:
a *zhōu* is called a *shù*,
and what does not fill a *shù* is called a *lǐ*.
Thus, a hundred households make a *lǐ*,
ten *lǐ* make a *shù*,
ten *shù* make a *zhōu*,
ten *zhōu* make a *dū*,
and ten *dū* make a hegemonic state.
Those not equal to a hegemonic state are called states.
They serve the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven has ten thousand feudal lords,
among whom are dukes, marquises, counts, viscounts, and barons.
The Son of Heaven resides in the center;
this is called following the resources of Heaven
and returning to the benefits of the Earth.
Within, he builds a city wall;
outside the city wall, he builds an outer wall;
outside the outer wall, he builds earthen embankments:
where the ground is high, he digs moats;
where it is low, he builds dikes.
He names it the 'Golden City.'
He plants brambles and thorns;
those that grow dense and thick together
are the means to make it solid.
Repair and increase them year by year without ceasing;
repair and increase them seasonally without ceasing;
the blessings will reach one's grandsons and sons.
This is called the inexhaustible benefit for ten thousand generations of human life,
and the treasure to be guarded by a ruler of men.
Ministers submit to it to exhaust their loyalty to the ruler;
the ruler embodies it to oversee the world;
thus he can be a leader for the people of the world.
This is the responsibility of the prime minister
and the duty of the minister.
Therefore, one who is good at governing a state
must first eliminate its five harms;
the people will then be free from suffering and harm all their lives and will be filial and compassionate."
Duke *Huán* said:
"I wish to hear the explanation of the five harms."
*Guǎn Zhòng* replied:
"Floods
are one harm;
drought
is one harm;
wind, fog, hail, and frost
are one harm;
pestilence
is one harm;
insects
are one harm.
These are called the five harms.
Among the categories of the five harms,
floods are the greatest.
Once the five harms are eliminated,
the people can then be governed."
Duke *Huán* said:
"I wish to hear about the harm of floods."
*Guǎn Zhòng* replied:
"Waters have large and small sizes,
and also distances of far and near.
Water that comes out of the mountains and flows into the sea
is called cardinal water;
water that branches off from other waters
and enters large waters or the sea
is called branch water."
In the ravines of the mountains,
those that sometimes have water
and sometimes do not
are called valley waters;
water that emerges from the ground and flows
into large waters or the sea
is called river water;
those that emerge from the ground but do not flow
are called abyssal ice.
Regarding these five waters,
one may proceed according to their benefits,
or one may restrain them,
but if done for a long time
there will constantly be dangers."
Huán Gōng said:
"Can water be restrained and made to go east, west, south, north, or to high places?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"It can.
Now, the nature of water
is to run from high to low;
then it is swift,
reaching even to the floating stones;
but if it goes from low to high,
it stays and does not flow.
Therefore, if you raise its upper reaches and guide it like a tilted pitcher,
with a slope of one and three-tenths chǐ
for every forty-nine units of a lǐ,
the water can be made to run.
Then make its path winding to lengthen it
and move it by using its momentum.
The nature of water
is that when it reaches a curve
it must stay and recede;
when full, the back pushes the front;
where the land is low it flows levelly;
where the land is high it is controlled;
where it is blocked by a curve it pounds and destroys.
If blocked by a curve and agitated it leaps;
if it leaps it leans;
if it leans it circles;
if it circles it centers;
if it centers it submerges;
if it submerges it blocks;
if it blocks it shifts;
if it shifts it is controlled;
if it is controlled the water flows recklessly;
if water flows recklessly it harms people;
if it harms people they are impoverished;
if they are impoverished they treat laws lightly;
if they treat laws lightly they are difficult to govern;
if they are difficult to govern they are not filial;
if they are not filial they will not be loyal subjects.
Therefore, the category of the five harms
and types of injury and killing
share the same source for misfortune and fortune.
One who knows how to prepare for these five
is a ruler on par with Heaven and Earth."
Huán Gōng said:
"May I ask about the way to prepare for the five harms?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"To eliminate the five harms,
start with water.
Please establish water officials
and appoint those practiced in water matters as officers:
one Dàfū and one Assistant Dàfū each,
with a sufficient number of unit commanders, school heads, and official assistants.
Then take one person each from the left and right sides of the water
to serve as the capital artisan and water engineer.
Order them to patrol the watercourses,
city walls,
river dikes,
ditches and ponds,
government offices,
temples and residences, and within the districts; where repairs are needed,
provide a sufficient number of laborers and materials.
The decree should say:
Always at the end of the year in autumn,
review the common people,
examine the households
according to their land,
determine the number of people in groups of tens and fives,
and distinguish between male and female, old and young.
Those who cannot be employed
shall be exempted;
those with chronic illnesses who cannot work
shall be treated;
those who can perform reduced labor
shall be given half-tasks.
Simultaneously determine the number of armored soldiers
who should be conscripted
and report to the capital.
The capital shall oversee those below
and see where there is surplus or deficiency,
then report to the water officials.
The water officials shall also use the number of armored soldiers due for conscription,
and together with the Sānlǎo,
the village officials,
and the heads of the five-family groups
patrol the villages,
following the heads of families on their inspection.
Review the tools prepared for water management
during the idle time of winter.
Baskets, shovels, boards, and rammers: six for every ten men;
soil carts: one for every ten;
rain mats: two for every ten.
Two sets of eating utensils
for each person
should be stored securely in the village,
and also provided as funeral equipment.
Afterwards, always order the water officials
and the capital artisan, together with the Sānlǎo,
the village officials,
and the heads of the five-family groups
to inspect them.
They should always start on the first day of the month to review the equipment,
taking those that are complete and strong,
repairing those that are worn or old,
and discarding those that are inferior.
Always during the idle time of winter,
order the armored soldiers in turns to gather firewood,
and pile it by the water's edge.
The Zhōu Dàfū shall lead them,
ensuring they do not miss the proper time.
The piling of firewood
is for when matters have concluded;
the earthwork
is for before matters have begun.
When Heaven and Earth are in harmony,
and the days are growing longer,
viewed in this way,
the benefits are a hundredfold.
Therefore, always prepare equipment when there is no business
so that it can be used when there is business;
thus water can always be controlled
and prevented from causing ruin.
This is what is called having constant preparation and prior readiness."
Huán Gōng asked:
"At what time should the work be done?"
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"In the third month of spring,
Heaven and Earth are dry,
and it is the time when waters are collected and aligned.
Mountains and rivers are dried and low,
the celestial qi descends,
the terrestrial qi rises,
and all things communicate and exchange.
Therefore, old matters have concluded
and new matters have not yet begun;
the sprouts of plants and trees are growing and edible.
Cold and heat are balanced,
and day and night are of equal length;
after they are equal,
the nights become shorter day by day,
and the days become longer day by day.
It is advantageous to perform earthworks at this time,
as the earth will then become increasingly firm.
Order the armored soldiers to build dikes beside the large waters,
making them wide at the bottom
and narrow at the top,
following the course of the water.
For land where grass does not grow,
bags must be made for it.
Large ones are made into dikes,
and small ones are made into embankments.
If they flank the water on all sides,
the grain crops will not be harmed.
Each year, raise and increase them,
plant them with thorns and brambles
to consolidate the ground,
and intersperse them with cypress and poplar
to prepare against breached waters.
The people will obtain abundance therefrom;
this is called 'flowing fat.'
Order the lower poor to guard them,
making boundaries here and there;
then there can be no ruin.
During the three months of summer,
the vital energy of Heaven and Earth is robust.
The great heat arrives,
and the ten thousand things bloom and flourish.
It is beneficial to quickly weed
and kill the overgrown grass.
One should not wish to disturb the administrative orders;
the life-force is called "not long-lasting."
It is not beneficial to undertake earthworks;
leave the farmers to their tasks.
Profits would be depleted by five-tenths,
and earthworks would not be completed.
During the three months of autumn,
the mountains, rivers, and hundred springs gush forth.
Rains descend,
mountain waters emerge,
sea routes are obstructed,
rain and dew follow one another,
and the vapors of Heaven and Earth converge.
It is beneficial to work quickly
to harvest and gather without delay.
What is grasped in one day
provides food for a hundred days.
Among the people, whether male or female,
all go out to the fields.
It is not beneficial to undertake earthworks.
Moisture and dampness arise daily,
and the soil is weak and difficult to form.
Profits are depleted by six-tenths,
and the work of the earth-laborers will not stand.
During the three months of winter,
Heaven and Earth close and store away.
The heat and rain stop,
the great cold arises,
and the ten thousand things are ripened and solid.
It is beneficial to fill and block empty gaps,
repair the border walls,
plaster the inner and outer city roads,
standardize measures of length,
rectify weights and balances,
empty the jails,
and fill the granaries.
The Ruler cultivates music
and gazes toward the Shén Míng.
The affairs of the entire year are concluded.
Promote those with merit,
reward the worthy,
punish the guilty,
and evaluate the officials of the various departments to rank them.
It is not beneficial to undertake earthworks.
Profits are depleted by seven-tenths,
and the soil is hard and will not stand.
The days grow shorter,
and the nights grow longer.
It is beneficial for building inner rooms,
but not for building outer halls.
When the four seasons are thus obtained,
the four harms are all subdued."
Huán Gōng said:
"I am confused.
I do not know how the four harms are subdued.
How is it so?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"If earthworks are undertaken in winter,
exposing what the earth has stored,
then in summer there will be many violent storms,
and in autumn the soaking rains will not stop.
If in spring one does not collect dry bones and rotten remains
and cut down dead trees to remove them,
then the summer drought will arrive.
In summer, there are heavy dews and mists from the plains
that smother the various grasses.
If people gather and eat them,
it will harm them.
Diseases among the people will be numerous and will not cease;
the people will then be afraid and in danger.
The Ruler should order the officials of the five departments, along with the Sān Lǎo,
the Lǐ Yǒusī,
and the Wǔzhǎng
to go through the villages to harmonize them.
Order the households to light fires for warmth.
Their fields and the wells within their courtyards should all be covered.
Do not let the poisonous mist descend
upon the eating utensils, as drinking from them will harm people.
There are descending insects that harm the grain crops.
Whenever the disasters of Heaven descend,
the Jūnzǐ carefully avoids them;
therefore, they do not die in eight or nine cases out of ten.
Great cold, great heat,
great winds, and great rains—
when they arrive out of season,
these are called the Four Punishments.
Some encounter them and die;
some encounter them and live.
The Jūnzǐ avoids them;
these also harm people.
Thus, the officials are those who teach and harmonize;
the Sān Lǎo,
Lǐ Yǒusī,
and Wǔzhǎng
are those who act as leaders.
When these five are prepared,
the people have no unfulfilled desires;
they only desire to complete their work.
Therefore, always use the winter days to harmonize with the Sān Lǎo,
Lǐ Yǒusī,
and Wǔzhǎng.
Use winter for rewards and punishments,
making each correspond to their reward or submit to their punishment.
If these five are not harmed,
then the Ruler's laws will be upheld.
This is shown to the people and is easy to see;
therefore, the people do not conspire together."
Huán Gōng said:
"In the twelve months of a year,
regarding earthworks,
if there is a time when they must be done,
yet it is the wrong season and they fail,
how should one prepare for it?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Always order the officials of the water department
to inspect the dikes and embankments in winter.
Those that can be repaired
should be marked and reported to the capital.
The capital should undertake the work in spring when there are few tasks.
After the work is done,
regular inspections should be made.
If a dike is damaged, it should be repaired.
When there is great rain,
each should guard their post, and those parts that can be fixed should be fixed immediately,
using the labor of convicts and servants.
During great rains, if the dikes need covering, cover them.
If the waters crash against them, if they can be reinforced, reinforce them.
To go through the whole year without failure is the goal.
This is called constant preparedness;
where would disaster come from?
The reason for this is that
turbid water carrying silt blocks itself as it flows;
this refers to the Jiāng and the Hé.
Heighten the dikes every year
so they are not submerged.
In spring and winter, take soil from the inside;
in autumn and summer, take soil from the outside.
When the turbid water enters,
it cannot cause failure."
Huán Gōng said:
"Good.
Zhòngfù's words to me are complete.
However, what else should I do?
Quickly teach my close attendants for me."
When Guǎn Zhòng rectified the world,
his measures reached seven Chǐ deep.
He dredged the fields and rested the laborers,
and none of the five kinds of grain were unsuitable.
He established the foundations and left behind fruits.
For that soil, the suitable trees were Yuán, Lún, Dù, and Sōng;
the suitable grasses were Chǔ and Jí.
Seeing this soil,
it was named Wǔshī.
At five times seven, thirty-five Chǐ deep,
one reaches the springs.
The sound of a shout corresponds to the Jué note.
Its water is dark green,
and its people are strong.
Chìlú is coarse, strong, and fertile;
none of the five kinds of grain are unsuitable.
Its hemp is white,
its cloth is yellow,
its suitable grasses are Báimáo and Guàn,
and its suitable tree is the Chìtáng.
When one sees this soil,
it is named *Sìshī*.
Four times seven is twenty-eight *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring.
Its call matches the *shāng* pitch.
Its water is white and sweet,
and its people are long-lived.
As for *Huángtáng* soil, it is suitable for nothing,
except for broomcorn and glutinous millet.
It is suitable for hanging marshes.
When constructing walls and fences,
the ground is moist and frequently collapses,
making it difficult to establish cities or build walls.
Its grasses are suitable for *qiáo* and *máo*,
and its trees are suitable for *chūn*, *rǎo*, and *sāng*.
When one sees this soil,
it is named *Sānshī*.
Three times seven is twenty-one *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring.
Its call matches the *gōng* pitch.
Its spring is yellow and grainy,
and the water shifts its flow.
*Chìzhí* soil is suitable for large beans and wheat.
As for reed marshes, its grasses are suitable for *fù*,
and its trees are suitable for *qǐ*.
When one sees this soil,
it is named *Zàishī*.
Two times seven is fourteen *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring.
Its call matches the *yǔ* pitch.
Its spring is salty,
and the water shifts its flow.
*Hēizhí* soil is suitable for rice and wheat.
Its grasses are suitable for *píng* and *tiáo*,
and its trees are suitable for *báitáng*.
When one sees this soil,
it is named *Yīshī*.
Seven *chǐ* and one reaches the spring.
Its call matches the *zhǐ* pitch.
Its water is black and bitter.
Generally, hearing the *zhǐ* pitch is like carrying a pig on the back
and being startled upon waking.
Generally, hearing the *yǔ* pitch is like a neighing horse in the wild.
Generally, hearing the *gōng* pitch is like an ox lowing in a pit.
Generally, hearing the *shāng* pitch is like a sheep separated from its flock.
Generally, hearing the *jué* pitch is like a pheasant climbing a tree to cry out;
the sound is rapid and clear.
Whenever one is to set the five pitches,
for the first of all,
one first takes one as the master and triples it,
then squares it to match eighty-one;
using this to generate the head of the *Huángzhōng* and the base element to form the *gōng* pitch.
Divide this by three and add one part back to it,
making one hundred and eight,
which forms the *zhǐ* pitch.
Then divide by three and remove its portion,
and it is exactly enough
to generate the *shāng* pitch.
Divide this by three and add one part back to it,
and using this one forms the *yǔ* pitch.
Divide this by three and remove its portion,
and it is exactly enough
to form the *jué* pitch.
For *Fényán* terrain, it is six layers,
six times seven is forty-two *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring.
By the side of the *Xiá*, it is seven layers,
seven times seven is forty-nine *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring.
At *Èxiá*, it is eight layers,
seven times eight is fifty-six *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring.
At *Dùlíng*, it is nine layers,
seven times nine is sixty-three *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring.
At *Yánlíng*, it is ten layers,
seventy *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring.
At *Huánlíng*, it is eleven layers,
seventy-seven *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring.
On *Mànshān*, it is twelve layers,
eighty-four *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring.
On *Fùshān*, it is thirteen layers,
ninety-one *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring.
At the white soil of *Fùshān*, it is fourteen layers,
ninety-eight *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring.
At *Zhōnglíng*, it is fifteen layers,
one hundred and five *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring.
On *Qīngshān*, it is sixteen layers,
one hundred and twelve *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring;
this is the dwelling place of the *Qīnglóng*,
where there is thick clay,
and water cannot be obtained.
At the red soil of *Áoshān*, it is seventeen layers,
one hundred and nineteen *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring;
beneath it is *qīngshāng*,
and water cannot be obtained.
At the white soil of *Shāshān*, it is eighteen layers,
one hundred and twenty-six *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring;
beneath it is contiguous stone,
and water cannot be obtained.
On *Dǒushān*, it is nineteen layers,
one hundred and thirty-three *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring;
beneath it is ash-soil,
and water cannot be obtained.
On the earth-hills of *Gāolíng*, it is twenty layers,
one hundred and forty *chǐ*,
and at that depth one reaches the spring.
On the top of a mountain, it is named *Xiànquán*;
its ground does not dry up,
its grasses are like *máo* and *zǒu*,
its trees are *mán*;
if one digs two *chǐ*,
one then reaches the spring.
On the top of a mountain, it is named *Fùlǚ*;
its grasses are *yúcháng* and *yóu*,
its trees are *liǔ*;
if one digs three *chǐ*,
one reaches the spring.
On the top of a mountain, it is named *Quányīng*;
its grasses are *qí* and *báichāng*,
its trees are *yáng*;
if one digs five *chǐ*,
one reaches the spring.
On the side of a mountain,
its grasses are *jīng* and *qiáng*,
its trees are *gé*;
if one digs two times seven, which is fourteen *chǐ*,
one reaches the spring.
On the side of a mountain,
its grasses are *fú* and *lóu*,
its trees are *ōuyú*;
if one digs three times seven, which is twenty-one *chǐ*,
one reaches the spring.
Generally, the way of grasses and soils
is that each produces its own grain.
Whether high or low,
each has its own grasses and soils.
*Yè* is lower than *qì*,
*qì* is lower than *guǎn*,
*guǎn* is lower than *pú*,
*pú* is lower than *wěi*,
*wěi* is lower than *guàn*,
*guàn* is lower than *lóu*,
*lóu* is lower than *píng*,
*píng* is lower than *xiāo*,
*xiāo* is lower than *bì*,
*bì* is lower than *huán*,
*huán* is lower than *máo*.
Generally, those grassy things
have twelve levels of gradation,
each having its proper place.
The soils of the *Jiǔzhōu*
constitute ninety types.
Every soil has its constant nature,
and things have their order.
The best among all soils
are the *Wǔsù*.
Of the *Wǔsù* types,
some are red, some azure, some white, some black, or some yellow.
The *Wǔsù* have five distinct colors.
The characteristics of *Wǔ Sù*
are that it is moist but not tough,
firm but not brittle.
It does not clog carriage wheels
nor does it stain the hands or feet.
As for its crops, the large heavy and small heavy varieties,
with white stems and white flowers,
are all suitable.
Regarding the soil of *Wǔ Sù*,
whether it is on hills or mountains,
on embankments or plains,
on the shady or sunny side, it is entirely suitable for
*Tóng* and *Zuò*; none fail to flourish and grow tall.
Its *Yú* and *Liǔ*,
its *Yǎn* and *Sāng*,
its *Zhè* and *Lì*,
its *Huái* and *Yáng*,
all these trees flourish and proliferate,
their branches being straight and long.
Its marshes abound in fish,
and its pastures are suitable for cattle and sheep.
Its lands and fences
are all suitable for *Zhú*, *Jiàn*, *Zǎo*, *Guī*, *Yóu*, and *Tán*.
Five fragrances grow there:
*Bìlì* and *Báizhǐ*,
*Míwú*, *Jiāo*, and *Lián*.
Where the five fragrances are gathered,
diseases are few and aging is slow,
the men and women are all handsome,
and the people are skillful.
Its springs are yellow and white,
and its people are peaceful and virtuous.
The soil of *Wǔ Sù*
is dry but not hard,
soaked but not muddy;
regardless of elevation, it remains moist.
This is called *Sù Tǔ*.
Next after *Sù Tǔ* is *Wǔ Wò*.
The substances of *Wǔ Wò*
are either red, blue-green, yellow, white, or black. Among the five substances of *Wǔ Wò*,
the five substances of *Wǔ Wò* each have different principles.
The characteristics of *Wǔ Wò*
are a draining and loose soil;
insects can easily live there.
Though loose and draining, it is not barren;
underneath it is moist.
As for its crops, the large sprout and small sprout varieties,
with red stems and black flowers,
grow long like arrows.
The soil of *Wǔ Wò*,
whether on mounds or mountains,
on hills or ridges,
or on the sunny side of valleys or hills,
to its left and right,
is suitable for those various trees:
*Tóng*, *Zuò*, *Fú*, *Chūn*, and the *Báizǐ*.
Its *Méi* and *Xìng*,
its *Táo* and *Lǐ*,
their flowers bloom and their stems rise.
Its *Jí* and *Táng*,
its *Huái* and *Yáng*,
its *Yú* and *Sāng*,
its *Qǐ* and *Fāng*,
these trees are numerous and large,
their branches being straight and long.
In the shade grow *Zhálí*,
and in the sun are planted the *Wǔmá*;
whether high or low,
it does not matter where they are.
The large hemp is like arrows or reeds,
being large, long, and beautiful;
the small hemp is like rushes or small sticks.
They each have their desired place.
The large ones are incomparable,
and the small ones are well-ordered;
when measured and stored,
they are like many strands of refined silk.
Five fragrances grow in the fields:
*Lián*, *Yú*, and *Míwú*,
*Gǎoběn* and *Báizhǐ*.
Its marshes abound in fish,
and its pastures are suitable for cattle and sheep.
Its springs are white and blue-green,
and its people are strong and vigorous;
they rarely have scabies or sores,
and they never suffer from wasting diseases or hangovers.
The soil of *Wǔ Wò*
is dry but not salty,
soaked but not muddy;
regardless of elevation, it remains moist.
This is called *Wò Tǔ*.
Next after *Wò Tǔ* is *Wǔ Wèi*.
The substances of *Wǔ Wèi*
are a mixture of five colors,
each having different patterns.
The characteristics of *Wǔ Wèi*
are that it is not cloddy or ashy;
it is blue-green, loose, and mossy.
As for its crops, the large *Wěiwú* and
small *Wěiwú* varieties,
with red stems and white flowers.
The soil of *Wǔ Wèi*,
whether on ridges or hills,
on embankments or plains,
on mounds or mountains,
is all suitable for *Zhú*, *Jiàn*,
*Zǎo*, *Guī*, *Yóu*, and *Tán*.
In the shallow areas of its mountains,
there are *Lóng* and *Jiè*.
Various trees flourish there,
their branches being long and numerous:
its *Sāng* and *Sōng*,
its *Qǐ* and *Róng*.
Various kinds of trees are accommodated,
such as *Yú*, *Táo*, *Liǔ*, and *Dòng*.
Various medicinal herbs grow there,
such as *Jiāng* and *Jiégěng*,
*Xiǎoxīn* and *Dàméng*.
On the mountain peaks,
there are many *Jú*, *Fú*, and *Yú*;
at the foot of the mountains,
there are *Jiàn* and *Yuàn*;
on the mountain sides,
there are *Huángmáng*,
and *Báichāng*,
*Shānlí* and *Wěimáng*.
Various medicinal herbs gather there
to ward off calamities for the people.
In its forests and clearings,
there are *Huái* and *Dòng*,
*Zuò* and *Gǔ*;
all sorts of trees grow there,
and birds and beasts find their place.
There are elks and stags,
and also many deer.
Its springs are blue-green and black,
and its people are nimble and upright,
efficient in affairs and eating little.
Regardless of elevation, it remains moist.
This is called *Wèi Tǔ*.
Next after *Wèi Tǔ* is *Wǔ Yǐn*.
The characteristics of *Wǔ Yǐn*
are black soil and black moss,
blue-green, loose and rich,
fine like ash.
As for its crops, the *Lěigé*,
with red stems and yellow flowers that strike the eye;
its leaves are like those of the *Yuàn*.
For the cultivation of fruit and trees,
it is two-tenths less productive than the first three soils.
This is called *Yǐn Tǔ*.
Next after *Yǐn Tǔ* is *Wǔ Rǎng*.
The characteristics of *Wǔ Rǎng*
are fine like a marsh or heaped earth.
As for its crops, the large *Shuǐcháng* and
small *Shuǐcháng* varieties,
with red stems and yellow flowers,
and they are lush. They endure flood and drought;
none are unsuitable.
For the cultivation of fruit and trees,
it is two-tenths less productive than the previous soil.
This is called *Rǎng Tǔ*.
Next after *Rǎng Tǔ* is *Wǔ Fú*.
The characteristics of *Wǔ Fú*
are hard like rice grains.
It retains moisture
and does not separate or crack.
As for its crops, the *Rěnyǐn*.
The *Rěn* leaves are like reed leaves,
and it grows fox-fur-like tassels.
It has yellow or black stems with black flowers;
its grains are large,
and all are suitable.
In the cultivation of fruit and timber trees,
it does not equal the top soil of the three grades by two-tenths.
Of the thirty products of superior soil,
twelve items are planted. Middle soil is called *Wǔshù*.
The appearance of *Wǔshù*
is granary-like as if in a pit,
and it is situated in moist and humid places.
Its seeds are
Large *Jì* and Small *Jì*,
with red stalks and yellow flourishing ears.
It withstands floods and droughts,
and its fine grain is like hemp.
In the cultivation of fruit and timber trees,
it is not as good as the top soil of the three grades by three-tenths.
Next after *Shù* soil is called *Wǔlú*.
The appearance of *Wǔlú*
is strong, hard, and firm.
Its seeds are Large *Hándān* and
Small *Hándān*,
with stalks and leaves like the *Fú* and *Chūn* trees,
and its grain is large.
In the cultivation of fruit and timber trees,
it is not as good as the top soil of the three grades by three-tenths.
Next after *Lú* soil is called *Wǔlàn*.
The appearance of *Wǔlàn*
is fragrant like chaff and fertile.
Its seeds are Large *Lì* and Small *Lì*,
with green stalks and yellow flourishing ears.
In the cultivation of fruit and timber trees,
it is not as good as the top soil of the three grades by three-tenths.
Next after *Làn* soil is called *Wǔpiāo*.
The appearance of *Wǔpiāo*
is flowery like fragrance and moist.
Its seeds are Large *Jù* and Small *Jù*,
with black stalks and green flourishing ears.
In the cultivation of fruit and timber trees,
it is not as good as the top soil of the three grades by four-tenths.
Next after *Piāo* soil is called *Wǔshā*.
The appearance of *Wǔshā*
is grainy like dust and grit.
Its seeds are Large *Bèi* and Small *Bèi*,
with white stalks and green flourishing ears on vines.
In the cultivation of fruit and timber trees,
it is not as good as the top soil of the three grades by four-tenths.
Next after *Shā* soil is called *Wǔgé*.
The appearance of *Wǔgé*
is piled up like snails;
it cannot withstand floods or droughts.
Its seeds are Large *Lùshū* and Small
*Lùshū*, with black stalks and black flourishing ears.
In the cultivation of fruit and timber trees,
it is not as good as the top soil of the three grades by four-tenths.
Of the thirty items of middle soil,
twelve are planted.
Lower soil is called *Wǔyóu*.
The appearance of *Wǔyóu* is like dung.
Its seeds are Large *Huá* and Small *Huá*,
with white stalks and black flourishing ears.
In the cultivation of fruit and timber trees,
it is not as good as the top soil of the three grades by five-tenths.
Next after *Yóu* soil is called *Wǔzhuàng*.
The appearance of *Wǔzhuàng* is like a rat's liver.
Its seeds are Green *Liáng*,
with black stalks and black flourishing ears.
In the cultivation of fruit and timber trees,
it is not as good as the top soil of the three grades by five-tenths.
Next after *Zhuàng* soil is called *Wǔzhí*.
The appearance of *Wǔzhí*
is very glossy and porous,
and it is cracked and lean.
Its seeds are *Yànshàn*
with black fruit, and red calyxes with yellow fruit.
In the cultivation of fruit and timber trees,
it is not as good as the top soil of the three grades by six-tenths.
Next after *Wǔzhí* is called *Wǔhú*.
The appearance of *Wǔhú* is hollow and loose,
and it cannot withstand floods or droughts.
Its seeds are Large *Shū* and Small *Shū*,
with many white fruits.
In the cultivation of fruit and timber trees,
it is not as good as the top soil of the three grades by six-tenths.
Next after *Hú* soil is called *Wǔxì*.
The appearance of *Wǔxì*
is firm but not skeletal.
Its seeds are upland rice: *Hēi'é* and *Mǎfū*.
In the cultivation of fruit and timber trees,
it is not as good as the top soil of the three grades by seven-tenths.
Next after *Xì* soil is called *Wǔjié*.
The appearance of *Wǔjié*
is very salty and bitter;
its products are of the lowest grade.
Its seeds are white rice, long and narrow.
In the cultivation of fruit and timber trees,
it is not as good as the top soil of the three grades by seven-tenths.
Of the thirty items of lower soil,
twelve are planted.
In total, there are ninety soil items,
and thirty-six are planted.
When the *Xiānshēng* imparts instruction,
the *Dìzǐ* take it as their rule.
Being gentle, respectful, and self-effacing,
what they receive is thorough.
Seeing good, they follow it;
hearing of righteousness, they submit to it.
Gentle, kind, filial, and fraternal,
they are not arrogant and do not rely on their strength.
Their will is not empty or crooked;
their conduct must be upright.
In their travels and dwelling, they have constancy;
they must associate with those of virtue.
Their countenance is orderly;
their inner heart must be disciplined.
Rising early and retiring late,
their clothes and belts must be tidy.
Gaining in the morning and practicing in the evening,
they are cautious and reverent.
Focusing on this without neglect,
this is called the rule of learning.
As for the duties of the young,
they retire late and rise early.
Having swept and washed their hands and mouths,
they perform their duties with reverence.
Holding up their robes and providing water for washing,
the *Xiānshēng* then rises.
They pour water for washing and remove the basin,
broadly sweep and straighten the mat,
and the *Xiānshēng* then sits.
Coming and going with respect,
as if seeing an honored guest.
Sitting upright facing the Master,
their countenance shows no shame.
The protocol for receiving lessons
must begin with the eldest;
once a cycle is completed, it remains so,
otherwise not.
When beginning to recite, one must stand;
for the next one, it is finished.
In all words and actions,
think of the Mean as the guide.
Those of old who were about to flourish
necessarily began from this.
Those arriving later take their mats;
if the seating is cramped, they stand.
If there are guests,
the *Dìzǐ* quickly rise.
Facing the guest without declining,
they respond and then proceed,
hastening forward to receive orders.
Even if what is sought is not there,
they must return and report.
Returning to their seats, they resume their lessons.
If there are doubts,
they clasp their hands and ask.
When the Master goes out, everyone rises.
When it comes time for the meal,
as the *Xiānshēng* is about to eat,
the *Dìzǐ* prepare and serve the food.
Gathering their hems, washing, and rinsing,
they kneel and serve the food.
Placing the sauce and arranging the food,
they display the meal without disorder.
Whenever placing that food:
whether birds, beasts, fish, or turtles,
the vegetable soup must come first.
The soup and sliced meat are separated in the middle;
the meat is in front of the sauce;
the arrangement should be square.
Rice comes at the end,
with wine on the left and syrup on the right.
Announcing that all is ready, they withdraw
and stand with hands clasped.
After the teacher has eaten three helpings of rice and two ladles of soup,
the student holds the empty *dòu* vessel in the left hand,
and the ladle in the right hand.
Refill by circulating;
only observing for insufficiency.
If there is equal insufficiency, follow seniority;
the circulation has a starting point;
hold the handle at a distance of one foot and do not kneel;
this is called the rules of refilling.
When the Xiān Shēng has finished eating,
the Dì Zǐ then clear away.
Hasten forward to present the mouth-rinse;
sweep the area in front and collect the sacrificial offerings.
When the Xiān Shēng gives the command,
the Dì Zǐ then eat.
Assemble according to seniority;
when seated, occupy the full space of the mat.
For rice, one must hold the bowl with both hands;
for soup, do not use the hands.
One may rest the hands on the knees,
but do not lean on the elbows.
Having eaten until satiated,
wipe the mouth and cover it with the hand.
Shake the lapels and sweep the mat;
those who have finished eating rise,
and lift their robes to descend.
Turn around to face the mat;
each clears away their own food,
as if serving guests.
Having cleared and put the vessels together,
they return to their standing positions.
The general way of sweeping:
fill a basin with water,
roll up the sleeves to the elbows;
in the hall, sprinkle the water broadly;
in the inner room, wet the hands to sprinkle.
Hold the dustpan against the chest,
with the broom inside it.
Enter the door and stand;
the demeanor must not be remiss.
Hold the broom and set down the dustpan,
leaning it against the side of the door.
The general rule for sweeping
is that it must begin from the southwest corner.
Bend and bow deeply like a chime-stone;
when sweeping, do not let dust scatter.
Sweep forward while moving backward,
gathering the dust inside the door.
Kneel and use the board to push it,
bringing the refuse toward oneself,
and put the broom into the dustpan.
If the Xiān Shēng rises,
then stand up and excuse oneself.
Kneel to pick up the tools and stand;
then go out to discard them.
Having finished sweeping, return to stand;
this is to harmonize and examine.
For the evening meal, repeat the same rituals.
At dusk, when the fire is to be lit,
hold the candle and sit in a corner.
The method for arranging the fuel bundles:
place them horizontally at the seating area.
Align them at the proper distance,
then receive the fire;
the posture should be bent like a square.
Leave space between the stalks for more stalks.
Those already burning should be placed below,
holding the lamp-bowl to maintain the flame.
Hold the candle with the right hand,
and adjust the alignment with the left hand.
If there are fallen fragments, replace the candle;
when shifting positions, do not turn your back to the honored one.
Then take the candle-snuffers,
and then go out to leave.
When the Xiān Shēng is about to rest,
the Dì Zǐ all rise.
Respectfully present the pillow and mat,
and ask where his feet should be placed;
when arranging the bedding, request instructions;
if there is a regular custom, then do not ask.
Once the Xiān Shēng is resting,
each joins his fellow students.
They polish one another through discussion,
each improving his own demeanor.
When the cycle is complete, it begins again;
this is called the discipline of the Dì Zǐ.

Mountains
are the highest of things.
Benevolence
is the highest conduct of a ruler.
Compassion
is the highest conduct of parents.
Loyalty
is the highest conduct of a minister.
Filial piety
is the highest conduct of sons and daughters-in-law.
Therefore, if a mountain is high and does not collapse, sacrificial sheep will arrive.
If a ruler is benevolent and does not slacken, the people will support and sustain him.
If parents are compassionate and do not slacken, sons and daughters-in-law will be obedient.
If ministers are loyal and do not slacken, rank and emolument will arrive.
If sons and daughters-in-law are filial and do not slacken, a good reputation will follow them.
Therefore, if one’s integrity is high and one does not slacken,
then what one desires will be attained.
If one slackens, one will not attain it.
Thus it is said:
“If a mountain is high and does not collapse, sacrificial sheep will arrive.”
Abysses
are where many things are born;
if they can be deep and not run dry,
then sunken jade will arrive.
A ruler
is he whom the people look up to for life;
if he can be magnanimous, pure, and generous, and not harsh or harmful,
then the people will attach themselves to him.
Parents
are those from whom sons and daughters-in-law receive instruction;
if they can be compassionate, kind, and instructive without losing track of reason,
then sons and daughters-in-law will be filial.
Ministers
are those whom a ruler employs;
if they can exert their full effort in serving their superior,
then they will be in accord with the ruler.
Sons and daughters-in-law
are those by whom parents find peace;
if they can be filial, fraternal, and obedient to their parents,
then they will be in accord with their parents.
Therefore, if an abyss runs dry and has no water, sunken jade will not arrive;
if a ruler is harsh and lacks generosity, the myriad people will not attach themselves to him;
if parents are violent and lack kindness, sons and daughters-in-law will not be close to them;
if ministers are indolent and not loyal, they will suffer debasement, disgrace, hardship, and poverty;
if sons and daughters-in-law do not bring peace to their parents, misfortune and sorrow will arrive.
Therefore, if an abyss does not run dry,
then what is desired will arrive;
if it runs dry, it will not arrive.
Thus it is said:
“If an abyss is deep and does not run dry, sunken jade will reach its peak.”
Heaven covers the myriad things,
regulates cold and heat,
moves the sun and moon,
and arrays the stars and constellations;
this is the constancy of Heaven.
It governs them with principle,
ending and then beginning again.
A ruler shepherds the myriad people,
governs all under Heaven,
and oversees the hundred officials;
this is the constancy of a ruler.
He governs them with law,
ending and then beginning again.
Harmonizing descendants
and gathering relatives
is the constancy of parents.
They govern them with righteousness,
ending and then beginning again.
Being sincere, respectful, loyal, and trustworthy
is the constancy of ministers.
They use these to serve their ruler,
ending and then beginning again.
Loving parents, being good at providing for them,
thinking of respect, and following instructions
are the constancy of sons and daughters-in-law.
They use these to serve their parents,
ending and then beginning again.
Therefore, if Heaven does not lose its constancy,
then cold and heat obtain their proper seasons,
and the sun, moon, stars, and constellations obtain their proper order.
If a ruler does not lose his constancy,
then the various ministers obtain their righteousness,
and the hundred officials maintain their duties.
If parents do not lose their constancy,
then descendants are harmonious and obedient,
and relatives are joyful with one another.
If ministers do not lose their constancy,
then there are no errors in affairs,
and official posts and governance are orderly.
If sons and daughters-in-law do not lose their constancy,
then the old and young are in order and the close and distant are harmonious.
Therefore, those who use the constants achieve order;
those who lose the constants fall into chaos.
Heaven has never changed;
that is how it achieves order.
Thus it is said:
“Heaven does not change its constancy.”
Earth giving birth to and nourishing the myriad things
is the rule of Earth.
Securing and governing the common people
is the rule of the ruler.
Teaching and protecting family matters
is the rule of parents.
Correcting through admonition and dying for one’s principles
is the rule of ministers.
Exerting full effort to provide for parents
is the rule of sons and daughters-in-law.
Earth does not change its rule,
thus the myriad things are born there.
A ruler does not change his rule,
thus the common people are at peace there.
Parents do not change their rule,
thus family matters are managed there.
Ministers do not change their rule,
thus the ruler has no errors.
Sons and daughters-in-law do not change their rule,
thus provision for parents is complete and prepared.
Therefore, those who use
“rules”
are secure;
those who do not use
“rules”
are in danger.
Earth has never changed;
that is how it remains secure.
Thus it is said:
“Earth does not change its rule.”
In spring,
the yáng qì begins to rise,
thus the myriad things are born.
In summer,
the yáng qì has fully risen,
thus the myriad things grow.
In autumn,
the yīn qì begins to descend,
thus the myriad things are harvested.
In winter,
the yīn qì has fully descended,
thus the myriad things are stored.
Thus spring and summer are for birth and growth,
while autumn and winter are for harvesting and storing;
this is the rhythm of the four seasons.
Rewards and punishments
