are the rhythm of the ruler.
The four seasons have never failed to give life or to kill;
the ruler has never failed to reward or to punish.
Thus it is said:
“Spring, autumn, winter, and summer do not alter their rhythm.”
Heaven covers the myriad things and regulates them;
Earth carries the myriad things and nourishes them;
the four seasons
give birth to and grow the myriad things, and then harvest and store them.
From ancient times until now,
they have not changed their Dào.
Thus it is said:
“The past and the present are one.”
The jiāolóng
is the spirit among water creatures.
When it rides on the water, its spirit is established;
when it loses the water, its spirit is discarded.
The ruler of men
is the one who possesses majesty in the world.
When he wins the people, his majesty is established;
when he loses the people, his majesty is discarded.
The jiāolóng waits to obtain water before its spirit can be established;
the ruler of men waits to obtain the people before his majesty can be perfected.
Thus it is said:
“When the jiāolóng obtains water, its spirit can be established.”
Tigers and leopards
are the fierce ones among beasts.
When they dwell within deep forests and vast marshes, people fear their majesty and uphold it.
The ruler of men
is the one who possesses power in the world.
When he dwells in seclusion, people fear his power.
Therefore, if tigers and leopards leave their seclusion and come near to men,
then men will capture them and hold their majesty in contempt.
If the ruler of men leaves his gates and draws too close to the people,
then the people will belittle him and be arrogant toward his power.
Thus it is said:
“Tigers and leopards rely on seclusion, so their majesty can be upheld.”
Wind is that which blows things about.
That which the wind blows
does not avoid the noble or the base, the beautiful or the ugly.
Rain is that which moistens things.
That which the rain falls upon
does not avoid the small or the great, the strong or the weak.
Wind and rain are perfectly impartial and without selfishness;
where they go has no constant direction;
though people encounter blowing and soaking, no one resents them.
Thus it is said:
“Wind and rain have no fixed direction, and so resentment and anger do not reach them.”
The reason why a ruler’s commands are carried out and his prohibitions are observed
is that he must command what the people like and prohibit what the people dislike.
Among the sentiments of the people, there is none who does not desire life and dislike death,
and none who does not desire benefit and dislike harm.
Therefore, if the superior issues commands regarding life
and benefiting people,
then the commands will be carried out;
if he issues prohibitions regarding killing
and harming people,
then it is prohibited.
The reason why orders are implemented
is that the people must find joy in the governance;
then the orders are carried out.
Thus it is said:
“What is valued is having the means to carry out orders.”
The reason why a ruler of men can make those below exert their full strength and be close to those above
is that he must bring benefits and eliminate harms for the world.
Thus, when his moral favor reaches the world
and his kindness is generously bestowed upon all things,
fathers and sons are able to live in peace,
and all living creatures are able to be nurtured;
thus the myriad people joyfully exert their full strength and take pleasure in being of use to their superior.
At home, they focus on the fundamental work and labor diligently to fill the granaries;
abroad, they exhaust their integrity and die for the enemy to secure the state;
though they endure toil, hardship, lowliness, and disgrace, they do not dare to complain.
This is how the humble forget their lowliness.
Thus it is said:
“The humble have the means to forget their lowliness.”
When rising and resting are timely,
food and drink are moderate,
and cold and heat are properly adjusted,
then the body benefits and life is extended.
When rising and resting are untimely,
food and drink are immoderate,
and cold and heat are not properly adjusted,
then the physical form is burdened and life is diminished.
If people are lazy and extravagant, they will be poor;
if they are industrious and frugal, they will be wealthy.
Now, nothing comes about without cause;
there must be a reason for it.
Thus it is said:
“Longevity, early death, poverty, and wealth do not arrive without reason.”
When laws are established and the people find joy in them,
and orders are issued and the people cherish them;
when the laws and orders correspond to the hearts of the people
like the matching halves of a tally,
then the ruler is honored and prominent.
Thus it is said:
“Those who cherish the orders are the source of the ruler’s honor.”
When a ruler issues words
that follow principle
and accord with the people’s feelings,
then the people accept his words.
When the people accept his words, his reputation becomes manifest.
Thus it is said:
“The acceptance of words is the operation of one’s reputation.”
In the governance of the world by an enlightened ruler,
he keeps his people quiet without disturbing them
and gives them leisure without tiring them.
If they are not disturbed, the people will follow the path of their own accord;
if they are not tired out, the people will prove themselves of their own accord.
Thus it is said:
“When those above are without action, the people prove themselves.”
The ruler of men establishes his standards and measures,
arrays the duties of offices,
and clarifies the laws and regulations
to preside over his people,
without putting words before them;
then the people follow what is correct.
The so-called *bàoshǔ*
is a ritual vessel.
Thus it is said:
“The *bàoshǔ* does not speak, yet the ancestral hall is already in order.”
The stately *hónghú*
is a creature of beautiful appearance.
Because its appearance is beautiful,
the people sing of it.
Virtue and righteousness
are the beauty of conduct.
Because virtue and righteousness are beautiful,
the people take joy in them.
What the people sing of and take joy in
are beautiful appearance, virtue, and righteousness,
and the enlightened ruler possesses these like the *hónghú*.
Thus it is said:
“The *hónghú* are stately,
and only the people sing of them.”
Stateliness (*jǐjǐ*)
means sincerity, gravity, and decisiveness in affairs;
many officers (*duōshì*)
means many worthy men.
*Zhōu Wénwáng* was sincere, grave, and decisive,
and so the state was well-governed.
His various ministers understood principles to assist the ruler,
and so the ruler was enlightened.
When the ruler is enlightened and the state is well-governed,
the entire territory receives his benefits and grace;
the people of *Yīn* raised their heads and looked toward *Wénwáng*,
wishing to be *Wénwáng*’s subjects.
Thus it is said:
“With many stately officers,
the people of *Yīn* were transformed by him.”
When *Zhòu* was the ruler,
he exhausted the people’s strength,
seized the people’s wealth,
and endangered the people’s lives.
Orders of injustice and tyranny
were imposed upon the hundred surnames;
cruel and poisonous messengers
were sent throughout the world.
Thus the high officials were not loyal,
and the common people felt hatred and resentment;
that the world rebelled against him and wished to be subjects of *Wénwáng*
was something *Zhòu* brought upon himself.
Thus it is said:
“This was the failure of *Zhòu*.”
Having no standards, laws, or protocols,
and drifting without a fixed place,
is called the “questions of drifting *fēipéng*.”
As for the questions of drifting *fēipéng*,
an enlightened ruler does not listen to them.
Words without standards
are not permitted by an enlightened ruler.
Thus it is said:
“The questions of drifting *fēipéng*
are not among those to be received.”
When the Way is followed, then ruler and minister are close,
father and son are at peace,
and all living things flourish.
Therefore, the task of an enlightened ruler
lies in practicing the Way
and not looking back at small things.
Swallows and sparrows (*yànjué*)
are small things.
Thus it is said:
“When swallows and sparrows gather,
one who practices the Way does not look back.”
The actions of an enlightened ruler attain principle and righteousness,
his orders accord with the people’s hearts,
his executions match the crimes,
and his rewards match the achievements.
Therefore, although he does not use animal sacrifices or jade tablets to pray to the spirits and gods,
the spirits and gods assist him,
heaven and earth support him,
and his undertakings are blessed.
The actions of a chaotic ruler lose righteousness and principle,
his orders go against the people’s hearts,
his executions do not match the crimes,
and his rewards do not match the achievements.
Therefore, although he uses animal sacrifices and jade tablets to pray to the spirits and gods,
the spirits and gods do not assist him,
heaven and earth do not support him,
and his undertakings lead to calamity.
Thus it is said:
“Animal sacrifices and jade tablets are not enough to please the spirits.”
That by which a ruler achieves success
is wealth and strength.
Therefore, when a state is wealthy and its army is strong,
the feudal lords submit to its influence,
and neighboring enemies fear its majesty;
even if he does not use precious gifts to serve the feudal lords,
the feudal lords do not dare to invade.
That by which a ruler commits a fault
is poverty and weakness.
Therefore, when a state is poor and its army is weak,
it will not be victorious in battle
and its defenses will not be firm;
even if he offers famous ritual vessels and heavy treasures to serve neighboring enemies,
he cannot escape the calamity of destruction.
Thus it is said:
“When the ruler’s achievements have a foundation,
what use are precious gifts?”
*Yì* was an ancient master of archery.
He adjusted his bow and arrows and held them firmly.
In handling the bow,
he examined its height
and had a method for hitting the target with certainty;
thus he could shoot many times and hit the mark many times.
An enlightened ruler
is like *Yì*.
He balances his laws,
examines their abolition or establishment, and adheres to them firmly;
he has a method for ensuring certain governance;
thus he can undertake many things and have them all be appropriate.
The Way
is the means by which *Yì* hit the mark with certainty
and the means by which a ruler governs with certainty.
Archery
consists of the bowstring releasing the arrow.
Thus it is said:
“The Way of *Yì* is not merely archery.”
*Zàofù*
was a master of driving horses.
He looked after his horses well,
moderated their food and drink,
estimated the horses’ strength,
and examined their gait;
thus he could travel long distances without the horses becoming exhausted.
An enlightened ruler
is like *Zàofù*.
He governs his people well,
estimates their strength,
and examines their skills;
thus he achieves success without the people becoming distressed or harmed.
Thus, technique
is the means by which *Zàofù* traveled long distances
and the means by which a ruler establishes achievements and fame.
Driving
consists of handling the reins.
Therefore it is said:
"Zào Fù's art is not merely driving."
When Xī Zhòng made carriages,
the squares, circles, curves, and straights all conformed to the compass, square, hook, and line.
Thus the mechanical parts rotated in harmony with each other,
their use was sturdy and efficient,
and the completed implements were strong and durable.
An enlightened ruler
is like Xī Zhòng.
His words and actions
all conform to methods and techniques;
therefore, all principles correspond,
and those above and below are close to each other.
"Skill"
is that by which Xī Zhòng made implements,
and that by which a ruler conducts governance.
As for "hewing and carving,"
these are the axes and knives.
Therefore it is said:
"Xī Zhòng's skill is not merely hewing and carving."
As for the people, if you benefit them, they come;
if you harm them, they leave.
The people's following of benefit
is like water running downward;
toward the four directions, they have no preference.
Therefore, one who wishes to attract the people
must first initiate their benefit;
then, although not summoned, the people will arrive on their own.
If you establish what they loathe,
even if you summon them, the people will not come.
Therefore it is said:
"To summon those far away, cause there to be no active seeking."
If one oversees the people like a father and mother,
then the people will be close to and love them.
If the Way is pure and generous,
and one treats them with substance,
even without saying "I am close to the people,"
the people will indeed be close.
If one oversees the people like enemies,
then the people will be distant from them.
If the Way is not generous,
and one treats them without substance,
while deception and hypocrisy arise together,
even if one says "I am close to the people,"
the people will not be close.
Therefore it is said:
"To make those nearby close, words require no effort."
An enlightened ruler's making those far away come and those nearby close
depends on the action within the heart.
That which is called "walking at night"
is the action of the heart.
If one can act with virtue from the heart,
then no one in the world can contend with them.
Therefore it is said:
"Is it only the one who walks at night who possesses it?"
To be a ruler yet be a predator,
to be a parent yet be cruel,
to be a minister yet be disloyal,
to be a child or daughter-in-law yet be unfilial—
these four are the great failures of humans.
When great failures reside in one's person,
even if one has small virtues,
one cannot be considered worthy.
That which is called a "level plain"
is a low-lying marsh.
Even if it has small mounds,
it cannot be considered high.
Therefore it is said:
"Regarding the hillocks of a level plain,
what do they have of height?"
To be a ruler and be kind,
to be a parent and be compassionate,
to be a minister and be loyal,
to be a child or daughter-in-law and be filial—
these four are the high conducts of humans.
When high conduct resides in one's person,
even if one has small faults,
one is not considered unworthy.
That which is called a "great mountain"
is the high part of mountains.
Even if it has small hollows,
one does not consider it deep.
Therefore it is said:
"Regarding the hollows of a great mountain,
what do they have of depth?"
Defaming and slandering a worthy person is called *zǐ*,
promoting and praising an unworthy person is called *wèi*.
If people of slander and falsehood are employed,
then the ruler's brilliance is obscured,
and words of defamation and false praise arise.
If they are entrusted with great matters,
then the matters will not succeed and disaster will arrive.
Therefore it is said:
"People of slander and falsehood,
do not entrust them with great things."
When an enlightened ruler considers matters,
those who plan for the sake of the world
are called *mú jù*.
When greatness is planned, then all within the seas receive its bounty;
when bounty is spread across the world,
later generations enjoy its achievements for a long time, and the benefits increase more and more.
Therefore it is said:
"One who plans greatness can be joined in far-reaching undertakings."
The Sage selects what can be said and only then speaks;
he selects what can be done and only then acts.
To steal a gain and then have harm follow,
or to steal a joy and then have worry follow—
the Sage does not do these.
Therefore, the Sage, in selecting his words, must consider their consequences;
in selecting his actions, he must consider their potential for sorrow.
Therefore it is said:
"One who considers sorrow can be joined in attaining the Way."
As for the petty man,
he perverts the Way to gain acceptance,
accommodates the ruler's whims to steal favor,
and follows profit to steal gain.
In such cases,
although his gain is swift,
the arrival of disaster is also rapid.
Therefore, the Sage dismisses and does not use him.
Therefore it is said:
"One whose plans are swift but whose sorrow is near,
let him go and do not summon him."
To promote one thing and make it a long-term benefit for the world
is called "promoting the enduring."
When the enduring is promoted, then those who receive its benefit are many,
and the visibility of virtue and righteousness reaches far.
Therefore it is said:
"One who promotes the enduring can be seen from afar."
Heaven's capacity is vast;
therefore, it can cover the myriad things.
Earth's capacity is vast;
therefore, it can support the myriad things.
A ruler's capacity is vast;
therefore, he accommodates many things, and the multitude can align with him.
Therefore it is said:
"One whose capacity is vast is one with whom the multitude aligns."
To be noble, wealthy, honored, and prominent—
the people turn toward and delight in this;
there is no ruler who does not desire it.
Therefore, one who wishes for the people to cherish and delight in him
must practice virtue and the Way without becoming weary;
then the people will cherish and delight in him.
Therefore it is said:
"If you wish people to cherish you,
firmly practice and do not become weary."
In the Sage's seeking of matters,
he first evaluates their logic and righteousness
and calculates their feasibility.
Thus, if it is righteous, he seeks it;
if it is not righteous, he stops;
if it is feasible, he seeks it;
if it is not feasible, he stops.
Thus, the matters he obtains
are always treasures for his person.
In the petty man's seeking of matters,
he does not evaluate their logic or righteousness
and does not calculate their feasibility.
He seeks even what is unrighteous;
he seeks even what is unfeasible.
Thus, the matters he obtains
have never been reliable.
Therefore it is said:
"A matter that must be obtained
is not worth relying upon."
When the Sage makes a promise,
he first evaluates its logic and righteousness
and calculates its feasibility;
if it is righteous, he promises;
if it is not righteous, he desists;
if it is feasible, he promises;
if it is not feasible, he desists.
Therefore, his promises have never lacked trustworthiness.
The petty man promises even what is unrighteous,
promises even what is unfeasible,
and makes promises whenever he speaks.
Therefore, his promises are not necessarily trustworthy.
Therefore it is said:
"A word that must promise
is not worth believing."
If one is careful with one family,
then one is established in one family;
if one is careful with one village,
then one is established in one village;
if one is careful with one state,
then one is established in one state;
if one is careful with the world,
then one is established in the world.
Thus, if that which one is careful about is small,
then that which one establishes is also small;
if that which one is careful about is large,
then that which one establishes is also large.
Therefore it is said:
"One whose care is small does not establish greatly."
The sea does not reject water,
therefore it can achieve its greatness;
the mountain does not reject earth and stone,
therefore it can achieve its height;
an enlightened ruler does not tire of people,
therefore he can achieve his multitude;
A scholar does not tire of learning,
therefore he can achieve his status as a Shèngrén.
One who is picky with food
is one who dislikes many things.
Admonition
is the means to secure the ruler;
food
is the means to nourish the body.
If a ruler dislikes admonition, he will not be secure;
if a person is picky with food, he will not be well-nourished.
Therefore it is said:
“One who is picky with food does not nourish the body.”
When speaking, those who talk of morality, virtue, loyalty, trustworthiness, filial piety, and fraternal duty,
these are words that should not be discarded.
Tiān is fair and without partiality,
therefore there is nothing, whether beautiful or ugly, that it does not cover;
Dì is fair and without partiality,
therefore there is nothing, whether small or large, that it does not sustain.
Words that should not be discarded
are fair and without partiality,
therefore there is no one, whether worthy or unworthy, that they do not employ.
Thus, words that should not be discarded
are aligned with the impartiality of Tiān and Dì.
Therefore it is said:
“He who possesses words that should not be discarded
must be aligned with Tiān and Dì.”
When a Míngzhǔ manages things,
he employs them according to their strengths
and does not employ them for their weaknesses,
so that no task is unsuccessful and no merit is unestablished.
A Luànzhǔ does not know that things each have their own strengths and weaknesses,
yet he demands perfection.
Now, deliberating on affairs and determining the nature of things,
and distinguishing the principles of rites and righteousness,
are the strengths of humans and the weaknesses of monkeys;
scaling heights and traversing dangers
are the strengths of monkeys and the weaknesses of humans.
If one demands from humans the strengths of monkeys,
then his orders will be abandoned and his expectations will not be met.
Therefore it is said:
“Descending a cliff of three rèn
is a great difficulty for humans,
but monkeys drink there.”
When a Míngzhǔ initiates an undertaking,
he relies on the deliberations of Shèngrén,
employs the strength of the masses,
and does not participate personally.
Thus, the undertaking succeeds and blessings arise.
A Luànzhǔ considers himself wise,
and does not depend on the deliberations of Shèngrén;
he boasts and exerts himself for his own merit,
and does not depend on the strength of the masses;
he acts solely by himself,
and does not listen to upright admonitions.
Thus, the undertaking fails and disaster arises.
Therefore it is said:
“Boasting of oneself and being fond of acting alone
is the disaster of undertaking an affair.”
Horses
are what one rides to travel through the wilderness.
Therefore, even if they are not traveling through the wilderness,
in the feeding and care of the horses,
one is never remiss or lazy.
The people
are the means for defense and warfare.
Therefore, even if they are not defending or fighting,
in the governing and nurturing of the people,
one is never remiss or lazy.
Therefore it is said:
“Even if not traveling through its wilderness,
do not neglect its horses.”
Tiān produces the four seasons,
Dì produces the myriad resources,
to nourish the myriad things without taking anything from them.
A Míngzhǔ is the match of Tiān and Dì.
He teaches the people according to the seasons,
encourages them in plowing and weaving,
to enrich the people’s livelihood,
but he does not boast of his merit,
nor does he take the profit for himself.
Therefore it is said:
“He who can give without taking
is the match of Tiān and Dì.”
Remissness, laziness, neglect, and arrogance—
to serve a ruler with these is to be disloyal;
to serve parents with these is to be unfilial;
to initiate an undertaking with these is to be unsuccessful.
Therefore it is said:
“The lazy and weary do not attain their goals.”
Using compasses and squares to make circles and squares leads to success;
using feet and inches to measure short and long leads to accuracy;
using laws and methods to govern the people leads to peace.
Thus, if affairs do not deviate from reason,
their success seems divine.
Therefore it is said:
“That which does not deviate seems like the divine.”
Serving a ruler without exerting full effort results in punishment;
serving parents without exerting full effort results in lack of intimacy;
receiving instruction and pursuing studies without diligence results in failure to achieve.
Therefore, if one does not exert effort to advance in the morning,
no merit will be seen by the evening.
Therefore it is said:
“If one forgets his tasks in the morning,
he loses his merit by evening.”
If the inner sentiments are sincere and honest, then one’s reputation will be beautiful;
if one’s cultivation and conduct are cautious and respectful, then honor and prominence will follow.
If the inner self lacks genuine sentiment, then one’s reputation will be bad;
if one’s cultivation and conduct are negligent and careless, then disgrace and insult will arise.
Therefore it is said:
“When corrupt energy invades the interior,
the righteous complexion then fades.”
If one acts as a ruler but does not clarify the righteousness between ruler and minister to rectify his ministers,
then the ministers will not know the principles of being a minister to serve their ruler.
Therefore it is said:
“If the ruler does not act as a ruler, the minister will not act as a minister.”
If one acts as a father but does not clarify the righteousness between father and son to teach and regulate his son,
then the son will not know the way of being a son to serve his father.
Therefore it is said:
“If the father does not act as a father, the son will not act as a son.”
When ruler and minister are close,
superiors and subordinates are in harmony,
and the myriad people are unified,
then when the ruler gives an order, the people carry it out;
when the superior has a prohibition, the people do not violate it.
If ruler and minister are not close,
superiors and subordinates are not in harmony,
and the myriad people are not unified,
then orders will not be carried out,
and prohibitions will not stop people.
Therefore it is said:
“If superiors and subordinates are not in harmony,
then orders will not be carried out.”
If words are trustworthy,
movements are dignified,
and robes and caps are correct,
then the subordinate ministers will be respectful.
If words are negligent,
movements are flawed,
and robes and caps are sloppy,
then the subordinate ministers will treat him with contempt.
Therefore it is said:
“If robes and caps are not correct, then guests will not be respectful.”
Ritual demeanor
is the standard for the myriad things.
Laws and regulations
are the models for the myriad people;
rites and righteousness
are the models for the noble and the lowly.
Thus, if actions have proper demeanor, orders will be carried out;
if they lack proper demeanor, orders will not be carried out.
Therefore it is said:
“If advancing and retreating lack proper demeanor, then government orders will not be carried out.”
As for the ruler of men,
if he is warm, kind, magnanimous, and generous, the people will love him;
if he is orderly, strict, and dignified, the people will stand in awe of him.
Thus, if the people love him, they will be close to him;
if they stand in awe of him, they can be employed.
Now, having the people close and available for use
is the urgent concern of the ruler.
Therefore it is said:
“To be both cherished and held in awe means the way of the ruler is complete.”
If the ruler of men can pacify his people,
then they will serve their ruler as they serve their parents.
Thus, if the ruler has worries, they worry for him;
if he has difficulties, they will die for him.
If the ruler views the people as dirt,
then the people will not be useful to him.
If the ruler has worries, they will not worry;
if he has difficulties, they will not die for him.
Therefore it is said:
“If no one finds joy in him, then no one will grieve for him;
if no one gives life to them, then no one will die for him.”
The reason the people defend and fight to the death without faltering
is that the favors the superior bestows upon the people are generous.
Thus, if the superior’s favors are generous,
the people’s repayment to the superior will also be generous;
if the superior’s favors are meager,
the people’s repayment to the superior will also be meager.
Thus, to bestow meager favors but demand generous repayment
is something a ruler cannot obtain from a minister,
nor a father from a son.
Therefore it is said:
“If what goes out does not reach,
what comes back will not be maximal.”
The Dào
supports the myriad things,
allowing them to be born and grow,
and each to complete its natural life.
Therefore, it may be used to govern a village,
or to govern a state,
or to govern the world.
Therefore it is said:
“What the Dào speaks of is one,
but those who use it are different.”
Hearing the Dào and using it to govern a village,
one brings closeness to its fathers and sons,
harmony to its brothers,
and rectitude to its customs,
making the people find joy in their superiors
and be at peace in their land.
The one who acts as the backbone of a village is
a person of that village.
Therefore it is said:
"One who has heard the Way and likes to serve the village is
a person of the village."
The people's following of those who possess the Way is
like the hungry prioritizing food,
like the cold prioritizing clothing,
and like the hot prioritizing shade.
Therefore, when there is the Way, the people return to it;
when there is no Way, the people leave it.
Therefore it is said:
"Where the Way departs, no one comes;
where the Way arrives, no one departs."
The Way is
that by which one transforms one's person and proceeds toward correct principles.
Therefore, when the Way is in the person, their words are naturally compliant,
their actions are naturally correct,
their service to the ruler is naturally loyal,
their service to their father is naturally filial,
and their dealings with others are naturally principled.
Therefore it is said:
"Where the Way is established,
the person is transformed."
The Way of Heaven
is full but does not overflow,
and flourishes but does not decline.
An enlightened ruler models himself after the Way of Heaven;
thus he is noble but not arrogant,
wealthy but not extravagant,
and acts with principle without laziness.
Thus he can long preserve wealth and nobility,
and long possess the world without losing it.
Therefore it is said:
"He who maintains fullness is aligned with Heaven."
An enlightened ruler rescues the world from disaster
and secures the world from danger.
To rescue from disaster and secure from danger,
one must rely on the utility of the myriad people
before one can achieve it.
Therefore it is said:
"Security and danger are aligned with the people."
Large territory and a wealthy state,
numerous people and a strong military—
this is a flourishing and full state.
Although already flourishing and full,
if there is no generous virtue to stabilize it
and no regulations or methods to govern it,
then the state will not be his state,
and the people will not be his people.
Therefore it is said:
"Losing the measure of Heaven,
though full, it must dry up."
If ministers are not close to their ruler,
and the common people do not trust their officials,
then high and low are separated and not in harmony;
thus, although they may consider themselves secure,
they will surely be endangered.
Therefore it is said:
"When high and low are not in harmony,
though secure, they will surely be endangered."
If a ruler possesses the Way of Heaven
to govern his people,
then the people will be of one heart in serving their superior;
thus he can be noble and wealthy and long rule the world as king.
If he loses the Way of Heaven,
then the people will rebel and not follow;
thus the ruler will be endangered and cannot long rule the world as king.
Therefore it is said:
"To desire to rule the world but lose the Way of Heaven
makes it impossible to rule the world."
If a ruler focuses on learning methods and techniques
and focuses on practicing correct principles,
then transformation and change will advance daily
until great merit is achieved,
yet the ignorant do not know it.
A chaotic ruler is licentious and crooked,
daily acting without the Way
until he reaches destruction,
yet he does not know it himself.
Therefore it is said:
"No one knows how it is done,
yet the achievement is completed;
no one knows where it is kept,
for it is hidden without form."
Anciently, the Sān Wáng and Wǔ Bà were all rulers who benefited the world;
thus their persons were noble and illustrious, and their descendants received their blessings.
Jié, Zhòu,
Yōu, and Lì were all rulers who harmed the world;
thus their persons were distressed and injured, and their descendants suffered their calamities.
Therefore it is said:
"Those who doubt the present should examine the past;
those who do not know the future should look at what has gone before."
Shénnóng taught farming and the production of grain
to bring benefit to the people.
Yǔ personally cleared channels,
cutting through heights and clearing depths,
to bring benefit to the people.
Tāng and Wǔ went on expeditions against those without the Way
and executed the violent and chaotic
to bring benefit to the people.
Thus, although the actions of enlightened kings may differ,
their benefiting the people is the same.
Therefore it is said:
"The tasks of ten thousand things
arise differently but return to the same point;
past and present are one."
If a ridgepole grows crooked and cannot bear its weight, the house collapses,
yet people do not harbor resentment
because the principle makes it so.
A weak child
is loved by a compassionate mother.
If he unprincipledly
drops a tile, the compassionate mother whips him.
Thus, if something moves according to its principle,
even a collapsing house causes no resentment;
if it does not move according to its principle,
then dropping a tile must lead to whipping.
Therefore it is said:
"A raw ridgepole collapses the house,
yet resentment and anger do not reach it;
a weak child drops a tile,
and the compassionate mother wields the switch."
Practicing the Way of Heaven
and manifesting public principle
makes those far away become naturally close;
discarding the Way of Heaven
and practicing private actions
causes mother and son to resent each other.
Therefore it is said:
"The ultimate of the Way of Heaven
makes the distant naturally close;
the arising of human affairs
makes close kin create resentment."
Anciently,
King Wǔ's territory did not exceed a hundred lǐ,
and his soldiers did not exceed ten thousand,
yet he could win battles and capture territory,
established himself as the Son of Heaven,
and generations called him a Shèng Wáng
because he knew the techniques for doing so.
Jié and Zhòu were noble as the Son of Heaven,
wealthy within the four seas,
their territory was very large,
and their soldiers very numerous,
yet they died and their states perished,
becoming the laughingstock of the world
because they did not know the techniques for doing so.
Thus, if one can do it,
the small can become large
and the humble can become noble.
If one cannot do it,
then even as the Son of Heaven,
people will still seize it from him.
Therefore it is said:
"The skillful have a surplus, while the clumsy have a deficiency."
An enlightened ruler does not go against Heaven above
and does not exhaust the earth below;
thus Heaven gives him the seasons
and Earth produces wealth for him.
A chaotic ruler goes against the Way of Heaven above
and cuts off the principles of the earth below;
thus Heaven does not give him the seasons
and Earth does not produce wealth.
Therefore it is said:
"Achievements that follow Heaven
receive Heaven's help;
achievements that go against Heaven
receive Heaven's opposition."
Anciently,
King Wǔ
was helped by Heaven.
Thus, though his land was small and his people few,
he still became the Son of Heaven.
Jié and Zhòu
were opposed by Heaven.
Thus, though their land was large and their people numerous,
they still suffered distress, humiliation, and death.
Therefore it is said:
"What Heaven helps,
though small, must become large;
what Heaven opposes,
though large, must be diminished."
To associate with others
with much deceit and lack of sincerity,
seeking only immediate gain,
is called a crow-gathering association.
A crow-gathering association,
though joyful at first,
will surely result in mutual blame later.
Therefore it is said:
"A crow-gathering association,
though seemingly good, is not close."
When a Shèng Rén enters into an agreement with others,
he observes their service to their ruler above
and their service to their parents within;
there must be discernible principles
before he enters the agreement.
If an agreement is made without following principle,
they will surely betray each other later.
Therefore it is said:
"A knot that is not doubled,
though firm, will surely loosen.
In the application of the Dào,
value its weight."
An enlightened lord consults with Shèng Rén,
so his plans are successful;
he undertakes affairs with them,
so his affairs are accomplished.
A disorderly lord consults with those who are unworthy,
so his plans fail;
he undertakes affairs with them,
so his affairs are ruined.
Now, the failure of plans and the ruin of affairs
is the fault of associating with the unsuitable.
Therefore it is said:
"Do not associate with the unsuitable."
An enlightened lord measures what human strength is capable of doing,
and only then employs them.
Thus, when he gives orders regarding what people are capable of doing,
then the orders are carried out;
when he employs them for what people are capable of doing,
then affairs are accomplished.
A disorderly lord does not measure human strength,
giving orders for what people are incapable of doing,
so his orders are discarded;
employing them for what people are incapable of doing,
so his affairs are ruined.
Now, when orders are issued but discarded,
and affairs are undertaken but ruined,
this is the fault of forcing the incapable.
Therefore it is said:
"Do not force the incapable."
For a person who is deranged and confused,
if one tells them of the righteousness between lord and minister,
the principles of father and son,
and the distinctions between the noble and the base,
they will not believe the words of the Shèng Rén,
but will instead cause them harm and injury.
Therefore, the Shèng Rén does not inform them.
Therefore it is said:
"Do not inform the ignorant."
Undertaking affairs with the unworthy
results in the ruin of affairs;
employing people for what they are incapable of doing
results in the discarding of orders;
informing a person who is deranged and confused
results in harm to oneself.
Therefore it is said:
"Associating with the unsuitable,
forcing the incapable,
and informing the ignorant,
is called laboring without merit."
If one constantly uses words to boastfully clarify one's association with others,
one's love for others,
or one's virtue toward others,
if one uses this to be a friend, they will not be close;
if one uses this to form a connection, it will not be bound;
if one uses this to have virtue toward others, they will not be repaid.
Therefore it is said:
"A friendship based on shown association
is nearly devoid of closeness;
a connection based on shown love
is nearly devoid of bonding;
a virtue based on shown bestowal
is nearly devoid of repayment.
That to which the four quarters return
is the conduct of the heart."
An enlightened lord does not use his own wisdom,
but relies on the wisdom of the Shèng Rén;
he does not use his own strength,
but relies on the strength of the masses.
Therefore, by using the wisdom of the Shèng Rén for deliberation,
there is nothing he does not know;
by using the strength of the masses to initiate affairs,
there is nothing he does not accomplish.
Being able to set himself aside and rely on the wisdom and strength of the world to rise up,
then his person is at ease and blessings are many.
A disorderly lord solely uses his own wisdom
and does not rely on the wisdom of the Shèng Rén;
he solely uses his own strength
and does not rely on the strength of the masses;
thus his person is toiled and misfortunes are many.
Therefore it is said:
"A state that relies on one alone
is toilsome and full of misfortune."
An enlightened lord internally carries out his laws and measures,
and externally carries out principles and righteousness.
Therefore, neighboring states are close to him,
and allied states trust him.
When there is trouble, neighboring states worry for him;
when there is difficulty, neighboring states rescue him.
A disorderly lord internally loses his own people
and externally is not trusted by neighboring states.
Therefore, when there is trouble, none worry for him;
when there is difficulty, none rescue him.
Losing both the external and the internal,
he is solitary and without allies;
thus the state is weak and the lord is disgraced.
Therefore it is said:
"The ruler of a solitary state
is base and lacks prestige."
In an enlightened lord's governing of the world,
he must employ Shèng Rén,
and only then is the world governed;
when a woman seeks a husband's family,
she must use a matchmaker,
and only then are family matters accomplished.
Therefore, if one governs the world without using Shèng Rén,
then the world is perverse and chaotic, and the people are not close;
if one seeks a husband's family without using a matchmaker,
then it is shameful and people do not trust her.
Therefore it is said:
"A woman who acts as her own matchmaker
is ugly and not trusted."
An enlightened lord is one
whom people have not yet seen but toward whom they have a close heart,
for he possesses the Dào that makes the people close to him.
Thus his position is secure and the people go to him.
Therefore it is said:
"When one is close to him before having seen him,
one can go to him."
Yáo and Shùn
were enlightened lords of antiquity;
the world promoted them without tiring,
praised them without becoming weary,
and after a long time and far distance did not forget them,
because they possessed the Dào that made the people not forget.
Thus their positions were secure and the people came to them.
Therefore it is said:
"When one does not forget after a long time,
one can come to him."
The sun and moon
are what brightly observe the myriad things;
if the sky has much cloud and vapor,
and those that obscure and cover are many,
then the sun and moon are not bright.
A lord of men
is like the sun and moon;
if the various ministers are full of villainy and establish private interests
to block and obscure the lord,
then the lord cannot brightly observe his subordinates,
and the sentiments of the subordinates cannot communicate upward.
Thus villainy and evil increase daily, while the lord of men is increasingly obscured.
Therefore it is said:
"When the sun and moon are not bright,
it is that the sky is not clear."
Mountains are the highest of things.
If the ground is treacherous, filthy, and not level,
then the mountain cannot be seen.
A lord of men
is like a mountain;
if those to his left and right form factions and cliques to block their lord,
then the lord cannot be seen.
Therefore it is said:
"When a mountain is high but not seen,
it is because the ground is not level."
When a lord of men speaks words that do not oppose the people's hearts
and do not contradict principles and righteousness,
such that what he says is sufficient to bring peace to the world,
people only fear that he will not speak again.
If one speaks words that alienate the closeness of father and son,
distance the Dào of lord and minister,
and harm the masses of the world,
these are words that cannot be repeated;
therefore, an enlightened lord does not speak them.
Therefore it is said:
"If a word cannot be repeated,
the lord does not speak it."
When a lord of men's own conduct is upright,
making people have ritual propriety,
and treating people with trustworthiness,
such that his actions originate from himself and serve as a model for the world,
people only fear that he will not act again.
If his own conduct is not upright,
making people violent and cruel,
and treating people without trust,
such that his actions originate from himself and become a laughingstock for the world,
these are actions that cannot be repeated;
therefore, an enlightened lord does not perform them.
Therefore it is said:
"If an action cannot be repeated,
the lord does not perform it."
Words that cannot be repeated
are words that are not trustworthy;
actions that cannot be repeated
are actions that are harmful and violent.
Therefore, if words are not trustworthy, the people will not be attached;
if actions are harmful and violent, the world will be resentful.
When the people are not attached
and the world is resentful,
this is where destruction and downfall arise;
therefore, an enlightened lord forbids them.
Therefore it is said:
"In all cases, words that cannot be repeated
and actions that cannot be repeated
are the great prohibitions for those who possess a state."
If the ruler of men listens to the talk of putting away weapons,
then the various ministers and guests will not dare to speak of military matters.
Consequently, internally he will not know the order or chaos of the state,
and externally he will not know the strength or weakness of the *Zhūhóu*.
In this state, the city walls will fall into ruin
and none will repair or mend them;
the armor will wear out and the weapons will decay,
and none will restore or fix them.
In this state, the preparations for defense and guarding will be destroyed.
Those in distant lands will plot,
the soldiers at the borders will make preparations,
and the common people will have no heart to resist the enemy.
Therefore it is said:
“If the theory of putting away weapons prevails,
then the strategic passes and obstacles will not be guarded.”
If the ruler of men listens to the theory of *Jiān'ài*,
then he will view the people of the world as his own people
and view other states as his own state.
In this state, he will have no heart for annexation or seizure,
and there will be no incidents of destroying armies or defeating generals.
Consequently, those skilled in archery, charioteering, and bravery will not receive generous stipends,
and officials who destroy armies and kill generals will not be honored with noble ranks.
In this state, those skilled in archery, charioteering, and bravery will go abroad.
I may be able to refrain from attacking others,
but I cannot make others refrain from attacking me.
If they demand land and I give it to them,
it is not what I desire;
if I do not give it and go to war with them,
I will certainly not win.
They use trained soldiers,
while I use a driven mob;
they use excellent generals,
while I use the incompetent.
The defeat will certainly result in the destruction of the army and the killing of the general.
Therefore it is said:
“If the theory of *Jiān'ài* prevails,
then the soldiers will not fight.”
If the ruler of men loves nothing but the preservation of life,
then the various ministers will all preserve their lives,
and furthermore nurture their lives.
What is meant by nurturing life?
It is said: rich flavors,
and music and beauty;
then it is considered nurturing life.
Consequently, they will follow their desires and act licentiously,
with no distinction between male and female,
returning to the level of birds and beasts.
Consequently, *Lǐ*, *Yì*, *Lián*, and *Chǐ* will not be established,
and the ruler of men will have no way to maintain himself.
Therefore it is said:
“If the theory of preserving life prevails,
then *Lián* and *Chǐ* will not be established.”
If the ruler of men listens to private discourse and self-valuation,
then the people will withdraw into quietude and seclusion,
living in caves and going to the mountains,
disparaging the worldly authorities,
slighting noble ranks and stipends and despising the officials.
Consequently, orders will not be carried out and prohibitions will not be stopped.
Therefore it is said:
“If the theory of private discourse and self-valuation prevails,
then the orders of the superior will not be carried out.”
If the ruler of men loves nothing but gold, jade, and wealth,
he will certainly desire to obtain what he likes;
consequently, there must be something given in exchange for them.
What is used to exchange for them?
High offices and honorable positions;
if not those, then noble ranks and heavy stipends.
In this state, the unworthy will be in high positions.
Consequently, the worthy will not serve under them,
the wise will not provide counsel,
the trustworthy will not enter into agreements,
and the brave will not die for the cause.
In this state, it is as if driving the state toward abandonment.
Therefore it is said:
“If the theory of gold, jade, and wealth prevails,
then noble ranks and regalia will flow to the unworthy.”
If the ruler of men listens to cliques and cabals,
then the various ministers will form factions,
concealing the good and publicizing the bad.
Consequently, the true and false conditions of the state will not be seen by the superior.
In this state, those in factions will be in the front,
and those without factions will be in the back.
When those in factions are in the front
and the worthy and unworthy are not distinguished,
then the chaos of contention and seizure will arise,
and the ruler will be in a position of peril.
Therefore it is said:
“If the theory of cliques and cabals prevails,
then the worthy
and unworthy will not be distinguished.”
If the ruler of men listens to the pursuit of spectacles, music, and amusements,
then he will be ruined.
Generally, spectacles and music consist of
palaces,
terrace ponds,
pearls and jade,
and vocal and instrumental music.
These are all ways that waste wealth, exhaust labor, and harm the state.
And those who serve the ruler with these things
are all *Jiānrén*.
If the ruler of men listens to them,
how can he not be ruined?
Consequently, the treasuries and granaries will be empty,
the reserves will be exhausted,
and with *Jiānrén* in high positions,
they will obstruct the worthy and prevent them from advancing.
Consequently, when the state happens to face disaster,
then entertainers and dwarfs will rise up to discuss the affairs of state.
This is driving the state toward abandonment.
Therefore it is said:
“If the theory of spectacles, music, and amusements prevails,
then *Jiānrén* will be in high positions.”
If the ruler of men listens to soliciting favors and recommendation based on reputation,
then the various ministers will all solicit favors for one another.
Consequently, favors will be obtained from the superior,
and factions will be formed in the villages.
In this state, wealth and goods will circulate throughout the state,
and the legal system will be destroyed in the government offices.
The various ministers will focus on cleverness to seek employment;
consequently, there will be honor without noble rank
and wealth without a stipend.
Therefore it is said:
“If the theory of soliciting favors and recommendation based on reputation prevails,
then the *Shéngmò* will not be straight.”
If the ruler of men listens to flattery and the glossing over of faults,
then he will be ruined.
How is it known to be so?
A flattering minister
always ensures that his lord does not regret his errors and does not change his mistakes;
therefore, the lord is deluded and does not realize it himself.
In this state, the counseling ministers will die, and the flattering ministers will be honored.
Therefore it is said:
“If the theory of flattery, slander, and glossing over faults prevails,
then the artful and deceitful will be employed.”
Law is that which
models itself on the positions of Heaven and Earth,
imitates the movement of the four seasons,
and is used to govern Tiānxià.
The movement of the four seasons
has cold and has heat;
the Shèngrén models himself on this,
therefore there are civil and military aspects.
The positions of Heaven and Earth
have front and back,
have left and right;
the Shèngrén models himself on this
in order to establish the guidelines and principles.
Spring brings life on the left,
Autumn brings death on the right;
Summer brings growth in the front,
Winter brings storage in the back.
Matters of birth and growth
are civil;
matters of collection and storage
are military.
For this reason, civil matters are on the left,
military matters are on the right;
the Shèngrén models himself on this
in order to execute laws and orders
and to govern the principles of affairs.
In all matters of law,
one's maintenance must not be incorrect.
If maintenance is incorrect, then hearing and governing will not be impartial.
If hearing and governing are not impartial, then governance will not be fully principled,
and affairs will not be fully responded to.
If governance is not fully principled,
then those who are distant or low-born will have nowhere to voice their grievances;
if affairs are not fully responded to,
then merit and benefits will not be fully promoted.
If merit and benefits are not fully promoted, the state will be poor;
if those who are distant or low-born have nowhere to voice their grievances, then the subordinates will be resentful.
Therefore it is said:
"Whenever about to establish an undertaking,
straighten that Tiānzhí."
Tiānzhí
is the heart.
When Tiānzhí is straight,
then one is not partial to close relatives,
and does not mistreat those who are distant.
Not being partial to close relatives
and not mistreating those who are distant,
then no benefit is left behind,
and no governance is hidden.
When no benefit is left behind
and no governance is hidden,
then all affairs are promoted,
and nothing is neglected.
If one wishes to see Tiānxīn,
observe the clarity of wind and rain.
Therefore it is said:
"When wind and rain do not deviate,
far and near, high and low,
each obtains its succession."
The myriad things honor Heaven and value wind and rain.
The reason they honor Heaven
is because none does not receive its mandate from it;
the reason they value wind and rain
is because none does not wait for the wind to move and wait for the rain to be moistened.
If the myriad things were to cast aside Heaven and instead receive mandates elsewhere,
cast aside the wind and instead look elsewhere for movement,
cast aside the rain and instead look elsewhere for moisture,
then there would be no reason to honor Heaven and value wind and rain.
Now, that which a ruler of men is honored and secured by
is because his authority is established and his orders are executed.
The reason he can establish authority and execute orders
is because the handle of authority and benefit resides entirely with the ruler.
If the handle of authority and benefit did not reside exclusively with the ruler,
but were divided,
then the ruler would daily become lighter and authority and benefit would daily decline;
this is the way of encroachment and violence.
Therefore it is said:
"When the Sānjīng are prepared,
then the ruler possesses the state."
Taking advantage of Summer while it is growing,
examine carefully the management of punishments and rewards.
One must clarify the guidelines and principles,
set forth righteousness and establish laws,
and decide matters by principle.
Empty the breath and calm the heart,
then cast away anger and joy.
If one turns against the law and abandons orders to act on anger and joy,
then disaster and chaos will arise,
and the position of the superior will be endangered.
Therefore it is said:
"Do not reward because of joy,
do not kill because of anger.
If one rewards because of joy
and kills because of anger,
then resentment will arise
and orders will be abandoned.
When orders are issued suddenly but not executed,
then the people's hearts will turn outward;
when those who have turned outward have followers,
then disaster begins to sprout.
That which the masses are indignant about,
the few cannot plot against."
When Winter has closed and stored,
all matters come to an end;
past affairs are fully recorded,
and future affairs have not yet arisen.
In the midst of Winter when there are no affairs,
carefully observe the end and the beginning,
and examine the principles of affairs.
There are matters that are easy at first and difficult later;
there are those that are insufficient to be seen at the start but unattainable at the end.
This is why constant benefits are not promoted,
and why affairs become distressed.
Of matters that are easy at first,
people act on them lightly;
if people act on them lightly,
then they will surely find them difficult and hard to complete.
Of those that are insufficient to be seen at the start,
people abandon them lightly;
if people abandon them lightly,
then they will surely lose unattainable merit.
To frequently have difficult and hard-to-complete matters
and to constantly lose unattainable merit
is the way of decline and exhaustion.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler examines the principles of affairs
and carefully observes the end and the beginning;
before acting, he must know what will be accomplished;
once accomplished, he must know how it will be used;
when used, he must know its benefits and harms.
To act without knowing what will be accomplished,
to accomplish without knowing how it will be used,
to use without knowing its benefits and harms,
is called reckless action.
With reckless action,
one's affairs are not accomplished
and one's merit is not established.
Therefore it is said:
"In promoting what is good, one must observe its end;
in discarding what is bad, one must calculate its exhaustion."
In general, a ruler of men
wishes for the people to have ritual and righteousness.
If the people lack ritual and righteousness,
then superior and inferior will be in chaos, and the noble and base will struggle.
Therefore it is said:
"Reward and encourage sincerity and respect to make them manifest,
enrich with stipends those with merit to encourage them,
and grant noble rank to those with a reputation to dignify them."
In general, a ruler of men
wishes for the masses to be close to the superior and turn toward his intent,
and wishes for them to be equal to their tasks in their endeavors.
But as for the masses,
if they are not loved, they will not be close;
if they are not taught to be obedient, they will not turn toward his intent.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler loves all to make them close,
clarifies teachings of obedience to guide them,
makes their circumstances convenient,
makes their preparations beneficial,
cherishes their strength,
and does not snatch away their time so as to benefit them.
In this way, the masses will be close to the superior and turn toward his intent,
and they will be equal to their tasks in their endeavors.
Therefore it is said:
"Inclusive love without exception
is called the ruler's heart.
One must first provide obedient teaching,
and the myriad people will turn toward the wind.
Benefit them day and night,
and the masses will be equal to their tasks."
The roots of governance are two:
the first is called people,
the second is called affairs.
People must be desired to be employed,
affairs must be desired to be skillful.
People have defiance and obedience,
affairs have weighing and measurement.
If people's hearts are defiant, they cannot be employed;
if weighing and measurement are lost, then affairs will not be skillful.
If affairs are not skillful, there will be injury;
if people are not employed, there will be resentment.
Therefore it is said:
"Select people by using oneself as a standard;
complete affairs by using substance."
Completing affairs by using substance
is to use weighing and measurement;
selecting people by using oneself as a standard
is to act by measuring with empathy.
To measure with empathy
is to measure it against oneself;
what one is not comfortable with oneself,
do not impose on others.
Therefore it is said:
"Be careful in the use of wealth,
be cautious in giving rewards,
and examine weighing and measurement.
Therefore, in using wealth one cannot be stingy,
in using strength one cannot be harsh.
If the use of wealth is stingy, then there will be waste;
if the use of strength is harsh, then there will be exhaustion."
How do we know this is so?
If the use of strength is harsh, then affairs will not be skillful,
If a task is not skillfully done and is repeatedly redone,
it is therefore said to be toilsome.
If expenditures are stingy, they will not meet with people's hearts;
if they do not meet with people's hearts, then resentment will arise.
To spend wealth and yet generate resentment
is therefore said to be wasteful.
When resentment arises and does not subside,
and the masses toil without obtaining rest,
then there will surely be a mind toward collapse and destruction.
Therefore it is said:
"When the people have not enough,
orders will be held in contempt;
when the people suffer calamity,
orders will not be carried out.
When rewards for service are not obtained,
misfortune will then begin to flourish;
when misfortune flourishes and there is no realization,
the people will then look to their own schemes."
Generally, in a state without laws, the masses do not know what to do;
without standards, affairs have no pattern.
If there are laws but they are not upright,
or there are standards but they are not straight,
then governance will be crooked.
When governance is crooked, the state will be in chaos.
Therefore it is said:
"When laws are upright and standards are straight,
crimes and killings are not pardoned,
and executions are carried out with certainty,
then the people will be in awe and fear.
When martial majesty is clearly manifested,
orders need not be issued a second time."
Generally, as for the people,
there are none who do not hate punishment and fear guilt.
Therefore, the ruler of men uses stern teaching to show them,
and clear penalties and punishments to make them respectful.
Therefore it is said:
"Use weariness and exhaustion to discipline them,
use punishments for crimes and errors to chasten them,
and use executions for violating prohibitions to awe them."
For governing a state, there are three instruments;
for ruining a state, there are six attacks.
If an enlightened ruler can overcome the six attacks and establish the three instruments,
then the state will be well-governed.
If an unworthy ruler cannot overcome the six attacks and establish the three instruments,
then the state will not be well-governed.
What are the three instruments?
It is said: orders,
axes and halberds,
and salaries and rewards.
What are the six attacks?
It is said: relatives,
nobility,
goods,
beauty,
cunning sycophancy,
and playthings.
What is the use of the three instruments?
It is said: without orders, there is no way to employ subordinates;
without axes and halberds, there is no way to strike awe into the masses;
without salaries and rewards, there is no way to encourage the people.
How do the six attacks cause failure?
It is said: when one may survive despite not listening,
when one may be pardoned despite violating prohibitions,
and when one may become rich despite having no merit.
In a state where one may survive despite not listening,
then orders are insufficient to employ subordinates;
where one may be pardoned despite violating prohibitions,
then axes and halberds are insufficient to strike awe into the masses;
where one may become rich despite having no merit,
then salaries and rewards are insufficient to encourage the people.
When orders are insufficient to employ subordinates,
axes and halberds are insufficient to strike awe into the masses,
and salaries and rewards are insufficient to encourage the people,
then the ruler of men has no way to maintain his position.
That being so, what does an enlightened ruler do?
An enlightened ruler does not change orders for the sake of those six things,
does not waver in the use of axes and halberds for those six things,
and does not increase or decrease salaries and rewards for those six things.
Therefore it is said:
"When the foundation is firm and unmoving,
the strange and deviant will then be afraid.
When the strange are reformed and the deviant transformed,
orders will go forth and the people will be moved."
Generally, as for the ruler of men,
he covers and supports the myriad people and possesses them all;
he shines upon the myriad tribes and employs them in service.
Therefore, he takes Heaven,
the Sun and Moon,
and the Four Seasons as his masters
and models
to govern the world.
Heaven covers and has no outside;
its virtue is nowhere absent.
Earth supports and has no abandonment;
it is peaceful, firm, and unmoving.
Therefore, there is nothing that does not grow and propagate.
The sage models himself after them to cover and support the myriad people;
thus, none fail to obtain their proper station and name.
When they obtain their proper station and name,
then none are not put to use.
Therefore it is said:
"He matches his virtue with Heaven,
and he is without partiality like Earth."
The brilliance of the Sun and Moon is without selfishness;
therefore, there is none who does not receive their light.
The sage models himself after them
to illuminate the myriad people;
thus, he is able to examine and observe,
so that no good is left out
and no wickedness is hidden.
When no good is left out
and no wickedness is hidden,
then punishments and rewards are certain and reliable.
When punishments and rewards are certain and reliable,
then the good are encouraged and the wicked are stopped.
Therefore it is said:
"He aligns himself with the Sun and Moon."
The movement of the Four Seasons
is certain and clearly manifested.
The sage models himself after them
to employ the myriad people;
thus, he does not lose the merit of the seasons.
Therefore it is said:
"He ranks himself with the Four Seasons."
Generally, as for the masses,
if you love them, they will be close to you;
if you benefit them, they will come to you.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler establishes benefits to attract them
and manifests love to bring them close.
If there is benefit alone without love,
then the masses will come but will not be close;
if there is love alone without benefit,
then the masses will be close but will not come.
When love and the granting of benefits are carried out together,
then ruler and minister are pleased with each other,
friends are pleased with each other,
brothers are pleased with each other,
and father and son are pleased with each other.
Wherever love and the granting of benefits are established,
even the strongest fortresses cannot hold out.
Therefore it is said:
"Pleasing the masses lies in love and the granting of benefits."
Generally, the reason a ruler possesses the masses
is the virtue of love and the granting of benefits.
If love is displaced
and benefit is monopolized,
then he cannot possess them all.
Therefore it is said:
"Possessing the masses lies in abolishing selfishness."
Even if the virtue of love and the granting of benefits is practiced and there is no selfishness,
if internal conduct is not cultivated,
then one cannot cause the rulers of distant lands to come to court.
Therefore, he rectifies the righteousness between ruler and minister, superior and inferior;
he refines the righteousness between father and son, brothers, and husband and wife;
he refines the distinction between men and women,
and distinguishes the degrees of distance and closeness.
He causes the ruler to be virtuous and the minister to be loyal,
the father to be kind and the son to be filial,
the elder brother to be loving and the younger brother to be respectful,
so that ritual and righteousness are clearly manifested.
If things are like this, then those who are near will be close to him,
and those who are far will turn to him.
Therefore it is said:
"Summoning those afar lies in cultivating what is near."
Shutting out calamity lies in removing resentment;
it is not that one removes resentment only when it exists,
but that in the place where one handles affairs, there is constantly no resentment.
Generally, that from which misfortune and chaos arise
is born of resentment and grievance;
that from which resentment and grievance arise
is born of being contrary to reason.
For this reason, the enlightened ruler's handling of the masses is always based on principle;
his employing of them is always according to the proper Way;
rewards for service are always appropriate;
his words always hit the mark;
and punishments are always reasonable.
If things are like this, then the masses will have no heart of suppressed resentment
and no intention of regret or hatred.
If things are like this, then misfortune and chaos will not arise,
and the superior position will not be endangered.
Therefore it is said:
"Shutting out calamity lies in removing resentment."
Generally, that by which a ruler of men is honored and secure
is his worthy assistants.
If the assistants are worthy, then the ruler is honored,
the state is secure,
and the people are well-governed.
If there are no such assistants, then the ruler is debased,
the state is endangered,
and the people are in chaos.
Therefore it is said:
"Enduring preservation lies in employing the worthy."
Generally, among people,
there are none who do not desire benefit and hate harm.
For this reason, if one shares benefit with the world,
the world will uphold him;
if one monopolizes the benefit of the world,
the world will plot against him.
What the world plots against,
though it be established, it will surely fall.
That which the world upholds,
though high, is not in danger.
Therefore it is said:
“The security of a high position lies in sharing benefits.”
As for what is meant by being able to benefit others with what does not benefit oneself,
Shùn was such a person.
Shùn farmed at Lì Shān,
made pottery at Hé Bīn,
and fished at Léi Zé,
yet he did not take the profits for himself
in order to teach the common people,
and all the common people benefited from it.
This is what is meant by being able to benefit others with what does not benefit oneself.
As for what is meant by being able to give to others what one does not possess,
Wǔ Wáng was such a person.
Wǔ Wáng attacked Zhòu;
of the soldiers who went,
every man was granted a village register.
On the day they entered Yīn,
he opened the granaries of Jù Qiáo
and distributed the wealth of Lù Tái,
and the people of Yīn were greatly pleased.
This is what is meant by being able to give to others what one does not possess.
Huán Gōng said to Guǎn Zǐ:
“Now you teach me to model myself after Heaven and unite with its virtue;
uniting with virtue brings longevity.
If one unites with virtue and covers all things universally, then the myriad things receive their destiny.
Modeling oneself after Earth and being without partiality;
being without partiality brings stability and firmness.
If one is without partiality and supports all things universally, then all living beings will flourish.
Being equal to the Sun and Moon,
one is without selfishness and protects the light.
If one is without selfishness and shines upon all things universally, then the beautiful and the ugly are not hidden.
In that case, for a gentleman’s self-cultivation,
is it simply a matter of having no likes and no dislikes?”
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
“Not so.
Learning is the means by which one transforms oneself
and the means by which one nurtures oneself.
Therefore, the gentleman dislikes speaking of the faults of others;
he dislikes those who are disloyal yet harbor resentment and envy;
he dislikes those who do not deliberate impartially yet seek a reputation that fits their title;
he dislikes those who have not held lower positions yet occupy higher ones;
he dislikes those who are not kind to those without yet are unrestrained within.
These five things are what the gentleman fears doing,
but they are the reasons why the petty man perishes.
How much more so for a ruler of men?”
An enlightened ruler
possesses administrative techniques and cannot be deceived;
he is discerning regarding laws and prohibitions and cannot be violated;
and he is observant of the division of duties and cannot be thrown into disorder.
Therefore, the various ministers do not dare to act on their private interests,
noble ministers may not obscure those of low rank,
those close to the ruler may not block those far away,
the orphaned, widowed, elderly, and weak do not lose their proper places,
and within the borders, distinctions are clear and there is no mutual overstepping.
This is called governing the state.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"That which is called governing the state
is the clarity of the ruler’s Way."
Clarity of law
is how the superior unifies the people and employs the subordinates;
private schemes
are how subordinates encroach upon the superior and disorder the ruler.
Therefore, when laws are discarded and private interests prevail,
the ruler of men is isolated and stands alone,
while the ministers form factions and parties.
In this case, the ruler is weak and the ministers are strong;
this is called a disordered state.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"That which is called a disordered state
is the triumph of the ministers’ schemes."
When an enlightened ruler is in the superior position,
possessing the power that ensures order,
then the various ministers do not dare to do wrong.
Thus, that the ministers do not dare to deceive the ruler
is not because they love the ruler,
but because they fear the ruler’s awe-inspiring power;
that the common people strive to be employed
is not because they love the ruler,
but because they fear the ruler’s laws and orders.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler wields the technique of certain victory
to govern the people who must be employed;
he occupies a position of certain honor
to control the ministers who must submit.
Therefore, commands are carried out and prohibitions are effective;
the ruler is honored and the ministers are humble.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"Honoring the lord and humbling the ministers
is not a matter of calculating kinship,
but of prevailing through power."
In the governance of an enlightened ruler,
he holds out titles and stipends to encourage his people;
since the people gain benefits from the superior,
the ruler has the means to employ them;
he establishes punishments to overawe his subordinates;
since subordinates have fear toward the superior,
the ruler has the means to manage them.
Therefore, without titles and stipends, the ruler has no means to encourage the people;
without punishments, the ruler has no means to overawe the masses.
Therefore, that ministers act with reason and follow orders
is not because they love the ruler,
but rather to pursue benefit and avoid harm;
that the hundred officials uphold the law without villainy
is not because they love the ruler,
but because they desire to receive titles and stipends and avoid punishment.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"That the hundred officials attend to their duties
is not due to kindness,
but because punishments are certain."
The ruler of men
monopolizes life and death,
occupies a position of awe-inspiring power,
and wields the handle of commands being carried out and prohibitions being effective to drive his ministers;
this is the Way of the ruler.
The ministers
occupy humble positions,
follow the ruler’s orders,
keep to their primary responsibilities,
and manage their allotted duties;
this is the Way of the minister.
Therefore, if the ruler acts according to the Way of the minister, there is disorder;
if the minister acts according to the Way of the ruler, there is danger.
Therefore, when there are no distinctions between superior and inferior
and lord and minister share the same Way,
it is the root of disorder.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"If the lord and minister share the same Way, there is disorder."
The reason ministers are fearful and serve the ruler with care
is that they desire life and hate death.
If people are made not to desire life
and not to hate death,
then they cannot be controlled.
If the handle of life and death
lies exclusively with the high ministers,
yet the ruler is not in danger,
such a thing has never occurred.
Therefore, if order or disorder is not decided by law but by powerful ministers,
and if the power to execute is not controlled by the ruler but lies with the subordinates,
this is a parasitic ruler.
Thus, if the ruler of men exclusively grants his awe-inspiring power to others,
then there will certainly be the peril of being coerced or murdered;
if he exclusively grants his legal systems to others,
then there will certainly be the disaster of disorder and ruin.
One who acts like this
follows the way of a doomed king.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"Exclusive delegation leads to loss."
Whenever a ruler cannot carry out his orders,
discards the law and indulges the ministers,
his awe-inspiring dignity is already discarded,
his power and influence are already seized,
orders cannot go forth,
the ministers will not work for him,
the people will not be employed by him,
and the masses within the borders are not controlled,
then the state is not his state
and the people are not his people.
One who is like this
follows the way of an extinguished ruler.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"When orders basically do not go forth, it is called extinction."
The Way of the enlightened ruler:
the humble and lowly do not wait for the honorable and noble to be seen,
high ministers do not rely on attendants to advance,
the hundred officials are in communication,
and the various ministers are clearly visible.
When there is punishment, the ruler sees the crime;
when there is reward, the ruler knows the merit.
Observation and knowledge are not contradictory,
and rewards and punishments do not miss their mark.
Possessing the technique of non-obscuration,
there is thus no peril of being blocked or obstructed.
A disordered ruler is not like this;
laws and orders cannot reach the people,
and those who are distant are blocked off and cannot be heard.
One who is like this
follows the way of an obstructed ruler.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"When orders are issued but detained, it is called obstruction."
The reason ministers take advantage to commit villainy
is that they manipulate the ruler.
If there are ministers who manipulate the ruler,
then the ruler’s orders cannot be carried out
and the conditions of the subordinates are not communicated upward.
The power of the ministers
is able to separate the lord and the ministers,
making the true state of good and evil not heard or known
and matters of disaster and fortune not clearly communicated,
so the ruler is deluded and has no way to realize it.
One who is like this
follows the way of a blocked ruler.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"When the conditions of subordinates are not communicated upward, it is called blocking."
An enlightened ruler
listens to all but decides alone,
and multiplies his channels of information.
In the Way of the ministers,
subordinates can clarify matters to the superior
and the lowly can speak about the noble.
Therefore, villainous people do not dare to deceive.
A disordered ruler is not like this;
he listens without administrative techniques
and decides matters without systematic cross-checking.
Therefore, incompetent scholars communicate with the superior,
corrupt ministers monopolize the state,
the ruler’s vision is obscured and his hearing is blocked,
and loyal ministers who wish to advise and remonstrate cannot enter.
One who is like this
follows the way of an encroached ruler.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"When subordinates' conditions go up but the Way is stopped,
it is called encroachment."
When a ruler of men governs a state,
there are always laws, orders, rewards, and punishments.
Therefore, if his laws and orders are clear and the rewards and punishments established are appropriate,
then the ruler is honored and prominent, and villainy does not arise;
if his laws and orders are contrary and the rewards and punishments established are inappropriate,
then the ministers will establish private interests and obstruct him,
form factions and coerce or murder him.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"Extinction,
blockage, encroachment,
and obstruction arise
from the failure to establish laws."
Laws and standards
are how the ruler controls the realm and prohibits villainy and evil,
how he manages all within the seas and serves the ancestral temple.
Private intentions
are what generate disorder, nourish villainy, and harm public justice,
what cause obstruction, obscuration, loss of correctness, and peril of ruin.
Therefore, if laws and standards are practiced, the state is ordered;
if private intentions are practiced, the state is in disorder.
