Even if someone is loved by the heart of the enlightened ruler, if they have no merit, they are not rewarded;
even if someone is hated by his heart, if they have no crime, they are not punished.
He refers to the legal patterns and examines success and failure;
he does not pay attention to anything that is not according to the laws and standards.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"In the *Xiān Wáng*’s governance of the state,
they did not let their intentions wander outside the law."
In an enlightened ruler’s governance of the state,
he examines what is appropriate
and carries out the correct principles.
Therefore, those who deserve reward,
the ministers may not decline;
those who deserve punishment,
the ministers do not dare to evade.
Now, rewarding merit and punishing crime
are the means by which benefit is brought to the world and harm is removed.
If weeds are not removed,
they will harm the grain crops;
if thieves and robbers are not executed,
they will injure the good people.
To set aside public law and practice private favors
is to benefit the wicked and evil and to encourage violence and disorder.
Practicing private favors and rewarding those without merit
causes the people to be indolent and to look for lucky favors from those above;
practicing private favors and pardoning the guilty
causes the people to slight those above and easily commit wrongs.
To set aside public law and use private whims
is something an enlightened ruler does not do.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"Do not grant favors within the scope of the law."
Of all rulers, none do not desire their people to be of use.
To make the people useful,
laws must be established and orders must be carried out.
Therefore, for governing the state and employing the masses, nothing is like law;
for forbidding debauchery and stopping violence, nothing is like punishment.
It is not that the poor do not desire to seize the wealth of the rich;
however, the reason they do not dare
is that the law does not allow it.
It is not that the strong are unable to abuse the weak;
however, the reason they do not dare
is that they fear the punishment of the law.
Therefore, regarding the affairs of the various officials,
if one examines them according to the law,
then wickedness will not arise;
regarding violent and arrogant people,
if one punishes them with physical penalties,
then calamity will not occur;
when the ministers come forward together,
if one manages them with techniques,
then private interests will have no place to be established.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"When no action is outside the law,
it is the means to forbid errors and exclude private interests."
That by which the ruler controls his subordinates
is majesty and power.
Therefore, if majesty and power are below,
then the ruler is controlled by the ministers;
if majesty and power are above,
then the ministers are controlled by the ruler.
Those who blind the ruler
do not block his gates or guard his doors;
however, when orders are not carried out,
prohibitions are not stopped,
and what is desired is not obtained,
it is because he has lost his majesty and power.
Therefore, if majesty and power reside solely with the ruler,
then the various ministers will be in awe and respectful;
if laws and governance originate solely from the ruler,
then the world will be submissive and obedient.
Therefore, if majesty and power are shared with the ministers, then orders will not be carried out;
if laws and governance originate from the ministers, then the people will not obey.
Therefore, in the enlightened ruler's governance of the world,
majesty and power reside solely with the ruler and are not shared with the ministers;
laws and governance are decided solely by the ruler and do not emerge from the ministers.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"Majesty is not placed in two places;
governance does not come from two gates."
The enlightened ruler
unifies weights and measures,
establishes models and standards,
and firmly maintains them.
Therefore, when orders are issued, the people follow.
Law
is the standard for the world
and the model for all things.
Officials
are those to whom the people's lives are entrusted.
Therefore, in the governance of an enlightened ruler,
those who deserve it according to the law are executed.
Therefore, when punishment for crime is according to the law,
then the people go to their deaths without resentment;
when merit is measured according to the law,
then the people receive rewards without feeling indebted.
This is the achievement of taking actions according to the law.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"Governing the state with the law
is simply a matter of taking actions."
The enlightened ruler
has the system of legal standards;
therefore, the various ministers all emerge from a governance of uprightness and do not dare to commit wickedness.
The common people know that the ruler manages affairs according to the law;
therefore, when they are employed by officials,
if there is a law, the people follow them,
and if there is no law, they stop.
The people use the law to resist officials;
subordinates use the law to deal with superiors.
Therefore, deceitful and hypocritical people cannot cheat their ruler;
envious people cannot use their malicious hearts;
slandering and flattering people cannot apply their cleverness.
Even a thousand *lǐ* away,
they do not dare to arbitrarily commit wrongs.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"One who has the system of legal standards
cannot be deceived by cleverness or hypocrisy."
The steelyard and the balance
are that by which the values of light and heavy are established.
However, the reason people do not try to manipulate them
is not because their hearts dislike profit,
but because the balance cannot change the amount for them
and the scale cannot alter the weight for them.
People know that trying to manipulate the balance and scale is useless;
therefore, they do not do it.
Therefore, when an enlightened ruler is in the superior position,
then officials cannot bend the law,
and magistrates cannot act for private interests;
the people know that serving the officials is useless;
therefore, wealth and goods do not flow to the officials.
The balance and scale are level and upright as they await objects;
therefore, wicked and deceitful people cannot carry out their private interests.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"Having the measure of the balance and scale is like being impossible to deceive with light or heavy."
The inch, foot, fathom, and ten-foot measure
are the means to obtain the reality of short and long.
Therefore, using the inch and foot to measure short and long,
then in ten thousand attempts, there will not be a single failure.
For this reason, the standard of the inch and foot,
even for the wealthy, noble, numerous, and strong,
does not increase the length;
even for the poor, lowly, humble, and disgraced,
does not decrease the length.
It is fair and without bias.
Therefore, wicked and deceitful people cannot mislead it.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"Having the numbers of the fathom and ten-foot measure
means one cannot be mistaken about long and short."
The reason a state falls into chaos
is because it abandons the reality of circumstances and relies on praise or blame.
Therefore, when an enlightened ruler listens,
he holds those who speak accountable to their reality;
he tests those who praise others by their official duties.
Those who speak without reality
are executed; officials who throw their offices into chaos
are executed. For this reason, empty words do not dare to be presented,
and unworthy people do not dare to accept office.
A ruler who brings chaos is not like this;
he listens to words but does not supervise their reality.
Therefore, the various ministers use empty praise to promote their factions;
he appoints to office but does not hold them accountable for their results.
Therefore, foolish and corrupt officials fill the court.
If it is like this, then the various ministers push each other forward with fine reputations
and lend each other credit for achievements;
they strive to increase their social circles and are not used by the ruler.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"When the ruler abandons the law to promote the capable based on reputation,
then the ministers will distance themselves from the superior and form cliques below;
when officials are promoted based on factions,
then the people will strive for social circles and not seek to be of use."
A ruler who brings chaos does not examine the merit and labor of the ministers;
those praised by the masses,
he rewards;
he does not investigate their crimes and errors,
and those defamed by the masses,
he punishes.
In such a case,
then wicked ministers gain rewards without merit,
and the loyal and upright suffer punishment without crime.
Therefore, if merit is great but there is no reward,
then the ministers will not strive to exhaust their strength;
if conduct is upright but there is punishment,
then the worthy and sagely will have no way to exhaust their abilities.
If wealth and goods are used to obtain rank and salary,
then corrupt and disgraceful people will be in office;
if people who rely on connections are unworthy yet hold noble positions,
then the people will turn their backs on the public law and rush toward those with influence.
In such a case,
then the sincere and honest people lose their positions,
and the incorruptible officials lose their administration.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"When officials lose their administration,
it is because the ruler uses praise as a reward
and defamation as a punishment."
When a fair official manages an office,
he carries out the law without selfishness;
then wicked ministers cannot gain their benefits there.
This is what wicked ministers strive to damage.
If the ruler does not verify their crimes and errors
but punishes them based on words without reality,
then ministers cannot help but serve the noble and powerful to seek praise
in order to avoid punishment and receive rewards and salaries.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"Those who love rewards and hate punishments
will abandon the public way and practice private techniques."
The way wicked ministers ruin their ruler
is by gradual accumulation and subtle steps,
causing the ruler to be deluded and confused without realizing it.
Above, they watch the ruler for each other;
below, they buy praise from the people.
They praise those of their faction and cause the ruler to respect them;
they defame those who do not praise them and cause the ruler to discard them.
What they find beneficial or harmful,
the ruler listens to and carries out.
In such a case,
then the various ministers all forget the ruler and rush toward private social circles.
Therefore, the *Míngfǎ* says:
"They form cliques to act wickedly together;
for this reason, they forget their ruler and die for their associates
in order to advance their reputation."
If the ruler lacks techniques and methods,
then the ministers can easily deceive him;
if the state lacks clear laws,
then the common people will lightly commit wrongs.
Therefore, if treacherous and wicked people manage state affairs,
then the ministers will look to them for benefit and harm;
in this way,
there will be many wicked people acting as their eyes and ears.
Although there is unrighteousness,
the ruler has no way of knowing it.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"With many associates and much praise,
forming cliques internally and externally,
even if there is great treachery,
the ways to obscure the ruler's vision are many."
All those called loyal ministers
strive to clarify laws and methods,
assisting the ruler day and night to be clear about the principles of measures and standards,
in order to govern the world.
Treacherous and wicked ministers know that if laws and methods are clear, there must be order;
if there is order, the wicked ministers will be in difficulty and the scholars of laws and methods will be prominent.
Therefore, what the wicked strive for
is to keep the laws from being clear
and the ruler from realizing the truth,
so that they themselves can get what they desire.
Therefore, if upright ministers are employed, treacherous and wicked ministers will be troubled and harmed;
this is a situation where the upright and the treacherous cannot both advance.
Those treacherous and wicked ones at the ruler's side
cannot help but hate the upright;
precisely because they hate them,
they must wait for a quiet moment with the ruler to endanger them day and night.
If the ruler does not examine this and uses their words,
then loyal ministers will be troubled and die though they are without guilt,
while treacherous ministers will become wealthy and noble though they are without merit.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"Loyal ministers die for what is not a crime,
while wicked ministers rise for what is not merit."
Wealth, nobility, honor, and prominence,
and holding the world for a long time,
there is no ruler who does not desire these.
That orders are executed and prohibitions are stopped,
and to be without rivals within the seas,
there is no ruler who does not desire these.
Being obscured, deceived, encroached upon, or maltreated,
there is no ruler who does not loathe these.
Losing the world,
and having the ancestral temple destroyed,
there is no ruler who does not loathe these.
Although loyal ministers desire to clarify laws and methods to achieve what the ruler desires and remove what the ruler loathes,
those treacherous ministers who dominate the ruler
will use private means to endanger them;
thus, loyal ministers have no way to advance their impartial and just techniques.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"When those who die are not guilty
and those who rise have no merit,
then those who are ministers will value private interests and belittle the public interest."
When a chaotic ruler confers ranks and stipends,
he does not use laws and decrees to examine merit;
when he carries out punishments and penalties,
he does not use laws and decrees to examine crimes and faults.
Instead, he listens to what his powerful ministers say.
Thus, if a minister wants someone rewarded,
the ruler rewards them for him;
if a minister wants someone punished,
the ruler punishes them for him.
Having discarded the public law,
he exclusively listens to powerful ministers.
Because of this,
all the ministers strive for their cliques;
they value powerful ministers and forget their ruler,
rushing to the gates of powerful ministers instead of attending the court.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"They go ten times to the gates of private individuals,
but not once to the court."
In the governance of an enlightened ruler,
he is clear about the division of duties
and supervises the completion of tasks.
Those capable of their responsibilities hold office;
those incapable of their responsibilities are dismissed.
Thus, all the ministers exhaust their ability and use all their strength to manage their affairs.
A chaotic ruler is not so.
Thus, although the ministers hold official positions
and receive generous stipends,
none of them strive to govern the state;
they only look to control the weight of the state and monopolize its benefits,
preying on the people to enrich their own families.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"They think a hundred times of their families,
but not once of the state."
When an enlightened ruler is in the superior position,
the masses within the borders exhaust their strength to serve their ruler,
and the various officials divide their duties and achieve order to stabilize the state.
A chaotic ruler is not so.
Even if there are men of courage and strength,
the high ministers keep them for their private use
and not to serve the ruler;
even if there are men of sagacity and wisdom,
the high ministers keep them for their private use
and not to govern the state.
Thus, although subordinates are numerous,
they cannot advance;
although the various officials are provided for,
they cannot be controlled.
In such a case,
he has the title of a ruler but lacks the reality.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"Although subordinates are numerous,
they are not used to honor the sovereign;
although various officials are provided for,
they are not used for the responsibility of the state.
This is what is called a state without men."
An enlightened ruler
causes subordinates to exhaust their strength and observe the laws and decrees;
thus, the ministers strive to honor the ruler and do not dare look after their own families.
The division between minister and ruler is clear,
and the positions of superior and inferior are fixed;
thus, the high ministers each stay in their positions and do not dare to aggrandize one another.
A chaotic ruler is not so;
laws and systems are discarded and not implemented;
thus, the ministers are able to strive to benefit their families.
There is no division between sovereign and minister,
and no distinction between superior and inferior;
thus, the ministers are able to strive to aggrandize one another.
In such a case,
it is not that there are few ministers at court,
but that the multitude is not being used.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"That a state is without men
does not mean the court ministers have declined.
It is that families strive to benefit one another
rather than striving to honor the sovereign,
and the high ministers strive to aggrandize one another
rather than taking responsibility for the state."
When a ruler establishes offices and appoints officials,
it is not merely to honor them and provide them with generous support;
it is to make them uphold the ruler's laws
and carry out the ruler's orders
to govern the common people and punish thieves and bandits.
Therefore, if the office assigned is large,
the rank is honorable and the stipend is generous;
if the office assigned is small,
the rank is humble and the stipend is meager.
Ranks and stipends
are the means by which the ruler makes officials manage their duties.
In the rule of a chaotic ruler,
officials occupy honorable positions
and receive stipends
to support those they are associated with,
rather than making their office their primary concern.
In such a case,
then the office loses its function.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"Lesser ministers hold onto their stipends to support their associates
and do not make the office their business;
thus, the office loses its function."
When an enlightened ruler selects worthy men,
he tests those said to be brave in the army
and tests those said to be wise in office.
Those who are tested in the army and have merit are promoted;
those who are tested in office and manage affairs well are employed.
Thus, through the affairs of military merit, bravery or cowardice is determined;
through the governance of official duties, stupidity or wisdom is determined.
Thus, the appearance of bravery, cowardice, stupidity, and wisdom
is like the distinction between white and black.
A chaotic ruler is not so;
he listens to words without testing them;
thus, those who speak recklessly are employed.
He appoints people without
assessing them;
thus, the unworthy are not troubled.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler uses the law to examine their words and seek the reality,
appoints them to office and assesses their merit,
relying exclusively on the law and not promoting them based on his own whims.
Therefore, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"When the former kings governed the state,
they made the law select men and did not promote based on their own whims."
All of what is called merit
is that which brings peace to the ruler
and benefit to the myriad people.
Now, to crush armies and kill generals,
to be victorious in battle and capture territory,
keeping the ruler free from the worry of peril and ruin
and the common people free from the disaster of death and capture,
this is what constitutes merit for soldiers.
To uphold the ruler's laws,
to govern within the borders,
to ensure the strong do not mistreat the weak
and the many do not oppress the few,
so the myriad people joyfully exhaust their strength to serve and support their ruler,
this is what constitutes merit for officials.
To correct the ruler's errors,
to remedy the ruler's mistakes,
and to clarify principles and righteousness to lead their ruler,
so the ruler is without wicked and perverse conduct
or the trouble of being obscured and deceived,
this is what constitutes merit for ministers.
Thus, in the governance of an enlightened ruler,
Clearly divide responsibilities and evaluate merit and labor.
Those with merit are rewarded,
and those who bring disorder to governance are punished.
When punishment and reward are applied,
each should be appropriate,
and the ruler does not act out of personal bias.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"Let the law measure merit,
and do not estimate it oneself."
In the governance of an enlightened ruler,
he examines right and wrong,
investigates the facts of matters,
and examines them using standards and measurements.
If it conforms to the law, he acts;
if it does not conform to the law, he stops.
If the achievement fulfills what was spoken, he rewards;
if it does not fulfill what was spoken, he punishes.
Therefore, regarding those who speak of wisdom and ability,
he must see their achievements before promoting them;
regarding those who speak of evil and failure,
he must see their errors before dismissing them.
In this way, worthy men will advance to the top and none can be jealous of them,
and the unworthy will be distressed and dismissed, and none can promote them.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"Ability cannot be concealed, and failure cannot be glossed over."
The way of the enlightened ruler
is to establish what the people desire to seek their merit,
thus he uses rank and salary to encourage them;
he establishes what the people hate to forbid their wickedness,
thus he uses punishments and penalties to make them fearful.
Therefore, he examines their merit to carry out rewards,
and examines their crimes to carry out punishments.
In this way, when the crowd of ministers praises those without merit,
they will not dare to advance them;
when they slander those without guilt,
they will not be able to demote them.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"Those who are praised cannot be advanced,
and those who are slandered cannot be demoted."
Controlling the ministers
and monopolizing life and death
is the duty of the ruler;
obeying orders and looking up to constraints
is the duty of the ministers.
Majestic power and honored manifestation
are the duty of the ruler;
lowliness, respect, and awe
are the duty of the ministers.
Orders being followed and prohibitions being observed
is the duty of the ruler;
upholding the law and being obedient
is the duty of the ministers.
Therefore, the relationship between ruler and minister,
their positions of high and low,
are like heaven and earth;
the difference in their divisions
is like white and black.
Therefore, when the distinction between ruler and minister is clear,
the ruler is honored and the minister is humble.
In this way,
the subjects following the superior
is like an echo responding to a sound;
the ministers modeling themselves after the ruler
is like a shadow following a form.
Therefore, when the superior orders, the subordinates respond;
when the ruler acts, the ministers follow.
What is ordered will be carried out;
what is forbidden will stop;
what is sought will be obtained.
This is called
"easy governance."
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"When the distinction between ruler and minister is clear,
then governance is easy."
The enlightened ruler wields techniques to employ ministers,
making the crowd of ministers demonstrate their wisdom and ability
and present their greatest skills.
Thus the wise demonstrate their plans,
the capable present their achievements,
and former words are used to supervise subsequent matters.
If the demonstration matches the words, he rewards them;
if it does not match, he punishes them.
He establishes offices and appoints officials to govern the people,
and examines the law to test and assess successful achievements.
By upholding the law and letting the law be the law,
his person has no toil, yet responsibilities are divided.
Thus, the *Míng Fǎ* says:
"Though the ruler does not personally act below,
he can uphold the law to act for him."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zǐ, saying:
"May I ask about the *Chéng Mǎ*?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Whether a state has no reserves
depends on the orders."
Huán Gōng said:
"What does it mean that 'whether a state has no reserves depends on the orders'?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"The capacity of one farmer
is to cultivate one hundred *mǔ*,
and the spring labors are within twenty-five days."
Huán Gōng said:
"What does 'spring labors are within twenty-five days' mean?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Sixty days after the winter solstice, the surface frost thaws;
seventy-five days after, the deep frost thaws.
When the deep frost thaws, the millet is planted.
If it is not planted by the hundredth day, it will not grow.
Thus, spring labors are only within twenty-five days.
Now, if you, my lord, build the *Fú* Terrace,
the crowds from the *Wǔ Qú* will all work on it.
If you exceed the spring season without stopping,
and the people lose those twenty-five days,
then the land within the *Wǔ Qú* will be obstructed and abandoned.
If you raise a labor service for one person,
one hundred *mǔ* will not be cultivated;
if you raise service for ten people,
one thousand *mǔ* will not be cultivated;
if you raise service for a hundred people,
ten thousand *mǔ* will not be cultivated;
if you raise service for a thousand people,
one hundred thousand *mǔ* will not be cultivated.
Once the twenty-five days of spring are lost,
and yet there is still summer work being initiated,
then spring loses its land,
and summer loses its sprouts.
If in autumn you raise labor service without stopping,
this is called the repeated loss of grain and land.
When grain is lost due to missing the seasons,
yet your taxes and levies continue without end,
and if the people eat fifteen units of grain,
but you have already levied nine,
and there are further demands for currency,
this is why bandits and violence arise,
and why punishments and penalties are numerous.
To follow this with violence
is called 'internal war'."
Huán Gōng said:
"Excellent!"
Guǎn Zǐ said: "The calculations of the *Chéng Mǎ* method are not yet exhausted.
A true king does not take away the people's time,
therefore the five grains flourish.
When the five grains flourish,
then officials value their salaries lightly,
and the people care little for rewards.
Those who are good at governing a state
make the farmers plow in the cold and weed in the heat,
so their strength returns to the superior,
and the women work diligently on fine details
so the weaving returns to the storehouses;
this is not to incur the resentment of the people
or to harm their intentions,
but is the principle of the 'high and low' calculation,
which is an unavoidable logic."
Huán Gōng said:
"What should be done?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"The state of *Yú* obtained the calculations of the *Chéng Mǎ*."
Huán Gōng said:
"What is meant by the calculations of the *Chéng Mǎ*?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"To the farmer with one hundred *mǔ*, give him this calculation:
'Let twenty-five days be the time for your spring work.
I will provide you with currency.'
In the *Tài Qiū*, when your grain is harvested in abundance,
the price of the state's grain will drop significantly.
Then say to the farmers:
'The currency you hold
should be exchanged for grain and stored in the granaries of the districts and villages.'
When a portion of the state's grain is held by the superior,
the value of the state's grain will increase tenfold.
Then tell the officials of the distant and near counties, villages, and towns that they must all provide equipment and tools,
and say:
'The state has no currency,
use grain as a standard for currency.'
The price standard of the state's grain
will be set at nine-tenths.
By returning the grain in exchange for the equipment,
all state equipment will be provided,
without levying taxes from the people.
This was the *Chéng Mǎ* calculation of the *Yǒu Yú*."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zǐ, saying:
"The Chéngmǎ strategy of the Yǒu Yú clan has already been implemented.
I wish to establish the Chéngmǎ strategy;
how should I go about it?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Warring states cultivate the labor of their walls and moats;
therefore, their states often lose the utility of their land.
A royal state acts according to the seasons."
Huán Gōng said:
"What is meant by acting according to the seasons?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Issue the decree of equalization,
maintain the strategy for land utility and labor;
thus, opening and closing are both controlled from above,
without seeking from the people."
"A hegemonic state maintains divisions,
where the ruler and those below circulate within the space of these divisions, and resources are sufficient.
A royal state maintains the beginning;
if state resources are insufficient by one part,
then add one part;
if state resources are insufficient by two parts,
then add two parts;
if state resources are insufficient by three parts,
then add three parts;
if state resources are insufficient by four parts,
then add four parts;
if state resources are insufficient by five parts,
then add five parts;
if state resources are insufficient by six parts,
then add six parts;
if state resources are insufficient by seven parts,
then add seven parts;
if state resources are insufficient by eight parts,
then add eight parts;
if state resources are insufficient by nine parts,
then add nine parts;
if state resources are insufficient by ten parts,
then add ten parts.
The ruler controls the high and low prices,
storing three-tenths every year;
in ten years, there will surely be a surplus of three years.
If a year is disastrous with drought or floods,
and the people lose their livelihood,
then repair palace rooms, terraces, and pavilions,
employing those who have no dogs in front and no pigs behind as laborers.
Thus, repairing palace rooms, terraces, and pavilions
is not to beautify them for pleasure,
but to balance the state's strategy.
Now, as for rulers who lose the Chéngmǎ strategy,
through spring, autumn, winter, and summer,
they do not know the beginning or end of the seasons;
they start construction and raise the masses,
building palace rooms, terraces, and pavilions.
The people lose their primary business;
the ruler does not realize the loss in the spring strategy,
and also the loss in the summer and autumn strategies.
The number of people who have no food and sell their children is many.
Fierce and resolute people become excessive and violent,
while the poor and sick
beg and request. If the ruler applies laws and punishments,
then the people suffer punishments and executions and do not follow the sovereign.
This is how the methods of the Chéngmǎ strategy are lost.
The equalization of Chéngmǎ
is equalized with all under Heaven.
When those goods are cheap, they leak away;
when they are heavy, they are targeted.
This leads to states in conflict leaking to one another,
and the masters of 'light and heavy' snatching from one another.
As for a royal state,
it holds the flow and stops it."
Huán Gōng said:
"What is meant by holding the flow?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"There are cases where one person plows and five people eat,
one person plows and four people eat,
one person plows and three people eat,
or one person plows and two people eat.
This depends on equalizing labor and working the land.
Field strategies are balanced with one another;
this is the seasonal maintenance of the state's strategy.
If the ruler does not maintain it through strategy,
then the people will maintain it from below;
this is the state strategy flowing away."
Huán Gōng said: "Are the methods of Chéngmǎ
exhausted here?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Cloth, weaving, and goods
all have their prices established.
The prices of goods
rise and fall with the currency.
Grain alone can be uniquely expensive or uniquely cheap."
Huán Gōng said:
"What is meant by 'uniquely expensive or uniquely cheap'?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"When grain is heavy, the ten thousand things are light;
when grain is light, the ten thousand things are heavy."
The Duke said:
"What is the method for the Chéngmǎ strategy regarding the lowly?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"In the commanderies and counties, for the best soil,
maintain a certain amount.
For medium soil,
maintain a certain amount.
For poor soil,
maintain a certain amount.
Thus, by assessing the soil and fixing the registries,
the people will not move away;
by relieving the poor and supplementing the insufficient,
those below will take joy in those above.
Therefore, use the abundance of the best soil
to supplement the void of the poor soil.
Clarify the four seasons,
maintain the regulation of opening and closing;
the people's not moving away
is like placing a square object on the ground.
This is called the method of the Chéngmǎ strategy."
The chapter is lost.
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zǐ, saying:
"May I hear about the ultimate methods of state affairs?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"What do you mean by ultimate methods?"
Huán Gōng said:
"Qín Shē taught me, saying:
'If curtains and covers are not repaired,
and clothes are not numerous,
then women's work will not flourish.
If the rituals of the sacrificial vessels do not use livestock—
with feudal lords using the tàiláo,
and high officials using the shàoláo—
if it is not like this,
then the six domestic animals will not be bred.
If one does not heighten the terraces and pavilions,
or beautify the palace rooms,
then the various materials will not be distributed.'
What do you think of these words?"
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"This is not the method."
Huán Gōng said:
"Why is it not the method?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"This is the method for stabilizing the soil.
Under the system of the Son of Heaven, the territory is a thousand lǐ square;
a Qí Duke's territory is a hundred lǐ square;
a Count by the sea is seventy lǐ;
a Baron is fifty lǐ.
They should work together like the chest and the arms.
Therefore, by equalizing the slow and fast, the surplus and the insufficient,
although they are below,
they do not cause worry for the ruler.
Those whose territory is narrow yet wish to rise and compete with large states:
their farmers plow in the cold and weed in the heat,
their strength returning to those above;
their women are diligent in spinning and weaving,
their merit returning to the treasury.
It is not that they resent the hearts of the people
or wound the intentions of the people;
but without accumulated stores
one cannot employ people;
without accumulated wealth,
there is no way to encourage those below.
The methods of Tài Shē
cannot be used in a narrow and confined state."
Huán Gōng said:
"Excellent."
Huán Gōng again asked Guǎn Zǐ, saying:
"Yì Tián said to me:
'One who is skilled uses what is not his own
and employs those who are not his own people.
Why not rely on the power of the feudal lords to control all under Heaven?'"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"The words of Yì Tián are incorrect.
Those who are good at governing a state:
when the soil is opened and lands are cleared,
then the people stay and reside;
when the granaries are full,
then they know ritual and etiquette.
Furthermore, to have no reserves is to invite encirclement;
to have a prosperous city is to invite assault.
If the internal affairs are not settled, one cannot maintain authority over the world.
The words of Yì Tián are incorrect."
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"If one stores one part every year,
in ten years there will be ten parts.
If one stores two parts every year,
in five years there will be ten parts.
If grain is ten and five are kept,
and fine silks fill the storehouses,
then five remain with the superior.
Therefore, observe the year and store;
determine the timing by the district and accumulate by the year,
so the state has ten years of reserves.
Wealth overcomes poverty,
courage overcomes cowardice,
wisdom overcomes foolishness,
subtlety overcomes lack of subtlety,
righteousness overcomes lack of righteousness,
trained soldiers overcome a driven crowd.
All ten types of victory will be possessed.
Thus, an offensive is like wind and rain,
movement is like thunder and lightning;
going out and coming in alone,
no one can forbid it,
without waiting for the power of others.
Therefore, the words of Yì Tián are incorrect."
Huán Gōng said:
"Good."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zǐ:
"I wish to levy a tax on archery towers;
how about it?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"This destroys what has been completed."
"I wish to levy a tax
on trees and forests?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"This fells what is living."
"I wish to levy a tax
on the six domestic animals?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"This slaughters life."
"I wish to levy a tax
on the people;
how about it?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"This causes the concealment of true conditions."
Huán Gōng said:
"In that case, how shall I govern the state?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Only taking official control of the mountains and seas will do."
Huán Gōng said:
"What is meant by 'taking official control of the mountains and seas'?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"In a state that would rule the world,
one must carefully regulate the salt policies."
Huán Gōng said:
"What is meant by 'regulating the salt policies'?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"A family of ten mouths
has ten people eating salt;
a family of a hundred mouths
has a hundred people eating salt.
In a month, an adult male eats five and a third shēng of salt,
an adult female eats three and a third shēng of salt,
and a child eats two and a third shēng of salt.
This is the general calculation.
A hundred shēng make a fǔ.
If the price of salt is ordered to increase by a fraction of a qiáng per shēng,
it is fifty per fǔ.
If increased by one qiáng per shēng,
it is a hundred per fǔ.
If increased by two qiáng per shēng,
it is two hundred per fǔ.
A zhōng is two thousand,
ten zhōng are twenty thousand,
a hundred zhōng are two hundred thousand,
a thousand zhōng are two million.
In a state of ten thousand chariots,
the number of mouths to feed is ten million.
Calculating it roughly, the commerce
per day is two million,
ten days is twenty million,
and one month is sixty million.
To levy a tax on a state of ten thousand chariots
of one million people.
A monthly poll tax of thirty coins per person
would be thirty million.
Now, instead of levying it from the people and their children,
I have sixty million—the equivalent of the taxes of two states.
If the ruler were to issue an order saying:
'I shall levy a tax on all the people and their children,'
then they would certainly clamor and shout.
Now, by providing salt through these policies,
a hundredfold returns to the superior,
and the people have no way to avoid this;
such is the method of calculation."
"Now, the method for the Iron Office is:
one woman must have one needle and one knife
for her work to be established.
A plowman must have one plow handle, one plowshare, and one hoe
for his work to be established.
Those who drive light and heavy carriages must have one axe, one saw, one awl, and one chisel
for their work to be established.
To complete one's work without these,
there is no such thing under heaven.
If the price of a needle is increased by one,
then thirty needles equal the tax of one person.
If the price of a knife is increased by six,
five times six is thirty,
so five knives equal the tax of one person.
If the price of plow iron is increased by ten,
then three plow irons equal the tax of one person.
All other price weights follow this standard.
In this way, when the people lift their arms to work,
none will not be paying the levy."
Huán Gōng said:
"In that case, can a state without mountains and seas not rule as a king?"
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"Rely on other people's mountains and seas and make use of them.
Suppose a state that possesses a sea
sells salt to our state
at fifteen per fǔ; I receive it
and the officials sell it for a hundred.
I did not participate in its original labor,
but received the products of others;
this uses
price weights to drive one another. This is the method of calculation for the people."
If a state has ten years of reserves,
yet the people have insufficient food,
they all look to the ruler's bounty based on their skills;
if the ruler has the wealth of the mountains and seas,
yet the people have insufficient resources for use,
they all interact with the ruler through their enterprises.
Therefore, when the ruler holds their food
and guards their resources,
relying on the surplus to control the deficiency,
then the people will all be dependent on the superior.
The five grains and rice
are the masters of the people's lives;
gold, knives, and coins
are the people's means of exchange.
Therefore, those who are skilled hold the means of exchange
to manage the masters of life;
thus the people's strength can be fully obtained.
People trust what is close and will die for profit;
this is true everywhere within the seas.
People rejoice when given to
and are angry when taken from;
such is the nature of human feelings.
The former kings knew this was so,
so they showed the form of giving
and did not show the principle of taking.
Thus, the people's love can be harmonized with the superior.
Household levies
are things that are sought by force;
land taxes
are things that are requested after calculation.
A ruler who rules as a King or Hegemon
removes that which is sought by force
and abolishes that which is requested after calculation;
therefore, the whole world is happy to follow him.
If profit comes from a single source,
the state will have no rival;
if it comes from two sources,
its military strength will be halved;
if it comes from three sources,
it cannot raise an army;
if it comes from four sources,
the state will surely perish.
The former kings knew this to be so;
therefore, they blocked the people’s excess profits
and narrowed their paths to gain.
Thus, giving lies with the ruler,
taking away lies with the ruler,
impoverishing lies with the ruler,
and enriching lies with the ruler.
Hence, the people look up to their superior as they do the sun and moon,
and love the ruler as they do their parents.
In general, for one who would govern a state,
if he does not understand "light and heavy,"
he cannot create a cage to keep the people;
if he cannot regulate and harmonize the people’s profit,
he cannot speak of establishing a system for great order.
Therefore, a state of ten thousand chariots
has merchants with ten thousand pieces of gold,
and a state of a thousand chariots
has merchants with a thousand pieces of gold.
Why is this so?
When the state loses much of its profit,
then officials will not fulfill their loyalty,
and soldiers will not give their lives.
Years have bad or good harvests,
so grain has periods of high and low prices;
orders have slow or urgent phases,
so goods have periods of being "light" or "heavy."
Yet if the ruler cannot manage this,
he allows hoarding merchants to roam the markets
and take advantage of the people’s insufficiency,
making a hundredfold profit on their capital.
If land is divided equally,
the strong can hold onto it;
if wealth is divided equally,
the clever can collect it.
The clever achieve ten times the success of others,
while the foolish suffer losses and cannot recover their capital.
Yet if the ruler cannot harmonize this,
then there will be a hundredfold difference in the people’s livelihoods.
Now, if the people are wealthy, they cannot be employed through rewards;
if they are poor, they cannot be awed by punishments.
The failure of laws and decrees to be implemented
and the lack of order among the ten thousand people
are due to the inequality of wealth and poverty.
Furthermore, when the ruler measures out the seeds and calculates the usage,
plows the fields and clears the weeds,
the superior obtains the statistics;
regarding what the people eat,
each person has a certain number of *bù* and *mǔ*;
if one calculates the harvest and measures the reserves, they should be sufficient.
Yet why are there people who are starving and have nothing to eat?
It is because grain is being hoarded.
The ruler casts coins and establishes currency
for the common people to circulate.
Each person possesses a certain amount in hundreds or thousands.
Yet why are the people’s affairs not attended to
and their resources insufficient?
It is because profits are being consolidated and hoarded.
Therefore, if the ruler cannot disperse accumulations,
equalize excesses and shortages,
break up consolidated wealth and profits,
and harmonize the people’s affairs,
then even if the ruler strengthens agriculture and encourages plowing,
and personally casts currency without end,
he is merely making the people into each other’s servants.
How can this be considered governance?
When a year happens to be good,
then the market grain sales yield no profit,
and dogs and pigs eat the food meant for humans.
When a year happens to be bad,
then one *fǔ* of grain in the market costs ten strings of cash,
and there are starving people on the roads.
So is it that the strength of the soil is inherently insufficient
or that food is inherently inadequate?
In the past year when grain sales were cheap,
dogs and pigs ate the food meant for humans;
therefore, in the following year, the people have an insufficiency.
When goods happen to be cheap,
then half the labor yields no profit;
the people’s work does not recover its costs.
When goods happen to be expensive,
then they cost ten times more and cannot be obtained;
the people lose their means of use.
So is it that wealth and goods are inherently scarce
or that the harvest and reserves are inherently insufficient?
It is because the timing of the people’s profit is lost and the value of goods is unequal.
Therefore, an able ruler distributes reserves where the people have a shortage
and manages affairs where the people have a surplus.
When the people have a surplus, they value goods lightly;
therefore the ruler collects them while they are light.
When the people have a shortage, they value goods heavily;
therefore the ruler disperses them when they are heavy.
Collecting and accumulating when light,
and dispersing and circulating when heavy,
the ruler will surely gain a tenfold profit,
and the fluctuations of wealth can be equalized.
In general, the great advantage of "light and heavy"
is to strike the light with the heavy
and to dispel the expensive with the cheap.
The fullness and emptiness of all things
follow the seasons; if the standard balance is maintained, there is no change;
but if the equilibrium is broken, then the "heavy" appears.
The ruler knows this is so;
therefore he maintains it through the standard balance.
He ensures that a city of ten thousand households must have a reserve of ten thousand *zhōng*,
and ten million strings of cash;
he ensures that a city of a thousand households must have a reserve of a thousand *zhōng*,
and one million strings of cash.
In spring, these are used to support plowing;
in summer, to support weeding.
Plowshares and tools,
food and provisions,
are all supplied by the ruler.
Thus, great merchants and hoarding families cannot forcibly seize from my people.
And why is this?
Because the ruler carefully nurtures the foundation.
By taxing in the spring to collect silk and fabrics,
and lending in the summer to collect the autumn harvest,
the people’s work is never interrupted,
and the state never loses its profit.
In general, the five grains
are the masters of all things.
When grain is expensive, all other things must be cheap;
when grain is cheap, all other things must be expensive.
The two act as rivals
and cannot both be level.
Therefore, the ruler manages the order of grain and goods as they overcome one another,
and handles affairs within the space of their inequality.
Thus, the ten thousand people need not be taxed directly,
yet the state’s profit returns to the ruler.
Now, to tax based on houses and rooms
is called "destroying what has been completed";
to tax based on the six domestic animals
is called "stopping life";
to tax based on the *mǔ* of fields
is called "forbidding plowing";
to tax based on individual persons
is called "estranging their feelings";
to tax based on households
is called "encouraging evasion."
These five methods should not all be used;
therefore, a true King may implement them partially but never to their full extent.
Therefore, the *Tiānzǐ* taxes through currency,
and the feudal lords tax through food.
In a year of average harvest, a *dàn* of grain is sold for ten coins.
An adult male eats four *dàn*,
which amounts to a monthly tax of forty;
an adult female eats three *dàn*,
which amounts to a monthly tax of thirty;
a child eats two *dàn*,
which amounts to a monthly tax of twenty.
In a bad year when grain is expensive,
grain is bought at twenty coins per *dàn*.
Then an adult male has a tax of eighty,
an adult female has a tax of sixty,
and a child has a tax of forty.
In this way, the ruler does not need to issue orders to collect harvests or tax by household;
since that ruler carefully guards the foundation and reserves,
men, women, the various people, and children all unwittingly submit to the tax.
If one person is provided with grain from the granary,
ten people will have a surplus;
if ten people are provided with grain from the granary,
a hundred people will have a surplus;
if a hundred people are provided with grain from the granary,
a thousand people will have a surplus.
Generally, when goods are many, they are cheap;
when they are few, they are expensive.
When they are dispersed, they are "light";
when they are gathered, they are "heavy."
The ruler of men understands that this is so.
Therefore, he observes the state's surpluses and deficiencies to manage its wealth and goods.
When grain is cheap, he uses currency to provide for food;
when cloth and silk are cheap, he uses currency to provide for clothing.
He observes the lightness and heaviness of goods and manages them by means of standardizations.
Thus, prices can be adjusted,
and the ruler obtains his profit.
If a state of ten thousand chariots is in front,
and a state of a thousand chariots is behind,
it is called a Dǐ state.
If a state of a thousand chariots is in front,
and a state of ten thousand chariots is behind,
it is called a Jù state.
If the territory is a perfect square
and is surrounded by enemies on all four sides,
it is called a Qú state.
To occupy a Qú state with a hundred chariots
is to be called a ruler who depends on others for food.
If a state of a thousand chariots occupies a Qú position,
more than half of its territory will be whittled away.
If a state of ten thousand chariots occupies a Qú position,
less than a third of its territory will be whittled away.
What is meant by a ruler with a hundred chariots occupying a Qú position and being dependent on others for food?
With a hundred chariots in a Qú position, one is endangered, terrified, and hemmed in between states of a thousand and ten thousand chariots.
When the rulers of the great states do not get along
and raise troops to attack one another,
they will certainly use the small state as a buffer or a shield.
Any benefits from success will not be directed toward it.
Great ministers die abroad,
and territory is partitioned to reward their merit;
when battle lines are formed and prisoners are captured,
rewards are distributed as emoluments.
Thus, the land is exhausted by rewards for merit,
and tax revenues are depleted by providing for orphans.
This is merely having the empty name of a ruler;
there is no actual land to possess.
Though titled as having a defense of a hundred chariots,
in reality, there is not a foot of soil available for use.
Therefore, such a person is called a ruler dependent on others for food.
However, when the great states are in harmony
and the small states have exhausted their resources,
how does it come to this?
It is said:
In a state of a hundred chariots,
the officials issue tallies and registrations,
follow the morning and evening rhythms of the four seasons,
and manage them with the standard of lightness and heaviness;
only then can a hundred chariots be maintained.
In a state of a thousand chariots, one must secure
where natural resources flourish,
where tools and implements are produced,
and where goods and materials arise.
Observe whether the harvest of the year is full or empty
and adjust the lightness and heaviness of salaries;
only then can a thousand chariots be sufficient.
In a state of ten thousand chariots,
one must monitor the fullness or emptiness of the harvest,
take advantage of the people’s times of leisure or urgency,
rectify commands and orders,
and manage them by the grand standardization;
only then can ten thousand chariots be provided for.
Jade arises in Yúshì,
gold arises in Rǔ and Hàn,
and pearls arise in Chìyě.
To the east, west, south, and north,
they are seven thousand eight hundred lǐ away from Zhōu.
Waters are cut off and terrains are severed;
boats and carts cannot pass through.
The former kings, because the paths were distant
and arrival was difficult,
therefore attributed utility to their value.
They made pearls and jade the highest currency,
gold the middle currency,
and knife-coins and cloth the lowest currency.
These three currencies,
if held in the hand, do not contribute to warmth;
if eaten, do not contribute to fullness.
The former kings used them to control goods and materials,
to manage the affairs of the people,
and to bring peace to the world.
Nowadays, when a ruler levies requirements from the people,
the order says:
"Prepare them within ten days,"
and the price of goods and materials drops by one-tenth.
The order says:
"Prepare them within eight days,"
and the price of goods and materials drops by two-tenths.
The order says:
"Prepare them within five days,"
and the price of goods and materials drops by half.
If the order is given in the morning and the goods must be prepared by evening,
then the price of goods and materials drops by nine-tenths.
The former kings knew this was so;
therefore, they did not make demands of the myriad people but levied requirements through commands and orders.
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zǐ, saying:
"May I ask about the administration of the state?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"There is a register for the fields,
a register for the people,
a register for expenses,
a register for the townships,
a register for human affairs,
a register for currency,
a register for the districts, and
a register for the state.
If one does not master the methods of the registers
yet wishes to govern a state,
it is impossible."
Huán Gōng said:
"How should the methods of the registers be implemented?"
He replied:
"How much field is in a certain township?
What is the standard for human affairs?
How heavy is the grain?
Ask:
How many people are in a certain district?
How much field?
How much currency is sufficient for use?
How heavy is the grain relative to the currency?
Estimating the food for the people throughout the year, how much surplus is there?
Ask:
Among the women of a certain township who are capable of work,
how much do they spin throughout the year?
Valuing their labor according to the season and standardizing it,
at the end of the year, after the people have been clothed,
how much surplus clothing is there?
Distinguish the various registers
and examine the suitability of the land."
Huán Gōng asked:
"What is meant by 'distinguishing the various registers
and examining the suitability of the land'?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"There is land for rushes and reeds;
there is land for bamboo, arrows, sandalwood, and mulberry;
there is low-lying land prone to flooding;
there is land for swamps, fish, and turtles.
Now, regarding the accounts of these four types of land,
if the ruler manages and guards them well,
then he levies from goods and materials
and does not levy from the people.
As for land that yields ten drums of grain per mǔ,
if the ruler does not guard it through registers,
then the people will take possession of it.
When the people trade and transport long knives as currency
and do not rely on fundamental labor to gain,
this is the fault of the ruler."
Huán Gōng asked:
"Where does the meaning of the register come from?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"If one does not secretly rely on the registers,
those below will control those above."
Huán Gōng asked:
"What do these words mean?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"How much field is in a certain township?
How many people are eating?
How much work is done by the women of a certain township?
How much surplus clothing is there?
Carefully inspect the states and villages, saying:
'There are this many fields,
this many people,
and if the population is large and the fields are insufficient for food, by how much?'
Or saying:
'There are this many fields,
and this much surplus food.'
One must obtain the standards of the register.
This is called the Tài Guǐ."
Then regulate and establish the circulating currency.
For the Tián Guǐ where there is a surplus of grain beyond the people's consumption needs,
carefully place public currency there.
Large households get more,
small households get less.
For mountain fields and fallow fields, it is said:
"If their annual food supply is insufficient for the people by a certain amount,
then place public currency there
to reach the standard level." In the following
year of bounty,
when the five grains flourish,
say to the commoners of the high fields:
"How much currency did I entrust to you?
What is the local price of grain?
I request a reduction of thirty percent for you."
Grain is the superior commodity,
and currency is the inferior.
High fields are managed, and while fallow fields
and mountain fields are not covered, grain prices increase tenfold.
For the mountain fields, because the ruler entrusted currency
to relieve their insufficiency,
they did not fall into ruin or loss.
High fields are managed at the proper time by the sovereign,
naturally increasing in value tenfold.
For the women's tribute of woven silk,
if it matches the state's requirements,
all should be kept and recorded with vouchers.
Using the local market prices as a standard
it is said:
"The superior has no currency, but has grain.
Use grain to match the currency value."
Circulate grain and respond with strategies,
and the state's requirements are fulfilled. Grain
returns to the standard price. Distribute the district currency;
grain is stored in granaries, its value increasing tenfold again.
Say to the large wealthy households:
"The sovereign is about to go on a tour;
each person shall contribute a certain amount of currency."
Say to neighboring counties:
"Those with grain stores should not move them to the left or right.
If there is insufficiency,
then for the sake of people and horses, food will be lent to the people."
When neighboring counties on all sides are at high prices, grain
naturally increases tenfold.
The superior issues an order saying:
"Wealthy households who lent currency
shall all use grain as the standard for currency,
and be repaid in grain at its current value."
Grain is the inferior commodity,
and currency is the superior.
The hundred capitals and hundred counties
are regulated and secured. Grain
naturally increases tenfold.
Circulate grain to meet the borrowed currency.
Nine parts of the state's currency are held by the sovereign,
and one part is with the commoners below.
When currency is heavy and the myriad things are light,
collect the myriad things
and respond to them with currency.
When currency is with the commoners below,
and the myriad things are all held by the superior,
the myriad things increase in value tenfold.
Government officials, using market prices, release
and elevate the myriad things, then stop.
Guó Guǐ is spread before things take shape,
secures them after they are completed,
and uses orders to advance or retreat,
making no demands on the people.
This is called Guó Guǐ."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zǐ:
"Is there a way to provide for the state without levying taxes?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"If regulation observes its seasons
and officials manage the Tiān Cái,
what need is there to seek from the people?"
Huán Gōng said:
"What do you mean by 'officials managing Tiān Cái'?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"In Tài Chūn,
it is the time for the people's labor;
in Tài Xià,
it is where the people's orders stop,
and where orders are issued.
In Tài Qiū,
it is where the people's orders stop,
and where orders are issued.
In Tài Dōng,
it is where the people's orders stop,
and where orders are issued.
These are all the times that the people must observe;
these are the times of the rise and fall of things;
these are the times when people compete to annex one another.
The ruler must guard these Sì Wù."
Huán Gōng said:
"What are the four duties?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"In Tài Chūn,
the things the people will use,
the ruler has already stored in granaries;
in Tài Xià,
the things the people will use,
the ruler has already stored in granaries;
in Tài Qiū,
the things the people will use,
the ruler has already stored in granaries;
in Tài Dōng,
the things the people will use,
the ruler has already stored in granaries.
When the days for Tài Chūn labor are distributed:
spring silk clothes,
summer unlined robes,
shovels, baskets, baskets for earth, winnowing baskets, rice baskets, bags, hampers, and bundles—
for a certain number of days of work,
how many people are used?
Families without resources
are all lent tools and equipment:
rice baskets, bundles, bags, hampers, and public clothing.
When the work is done, they return them to the public and cancel the vouchers.
Therefore, the labor comes from the people,
while the tools for use come from the superior.
Ten days in spring
do not harm the plowing;
ten days in summer
do not harm the weeding;
ten days in autumn
do not harm the harvest;
twenty days in winter
do not harm the field clearing.
This is called timely labor."
Huán Gōng said:
"Good.
I wish to establish a Guǐ Guān.
How should it be done?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"The strategies for salt and iron
are sufficient to establish a Guǐ Guān."
Huán Gōng said:
"How so?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"In the land of Lóng Xià,
distribute nine thousand units of gold,
using currency to match the gold.
Large households use gold,
small households use currency.
From Mount Zhōu Qí to the western passes of Sè Qiū and Zhēng Qiū,
these are the lands of mountain settlements;
distribute currency to regulate them according to poverty or wealth.
From Zhōu Shòu Líng eastward to Shǎo Shā,
these are middle-grade fields.
Secure them with currency:
large households with gold,
small households with currency.
Once the three types of soil are managed,
the state's grain will double and increase tenfold.
The oxen and horses from Liáng Wèi and Yáng Suǒ fill the plains of Qí.
Please categorize them by their teeth,
measure their height and strength,
and say:
'The state is forming an army;
war chariots are being prepared
to collect your oxen and horses.
The superior has no currency,
so please use grain according to market prices to compensate you.'
Oxen and horses are the superior goods,
and the grain goes to the owners.
When the owners disperse their grain,
it returns to the standard price. The oxen and horses return to the superior."
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"I request to establish a property tax for the people.
Those with land pay double.
If there is nothing within,
the outside lands will all become taxable territories."
Saddled horses for a thousand chariots,
and the equipment for the war chariots of Qí,
are all prepared here
without seeking anything from the people.
This was how the tax registration of the districts and villages was abolished.
"The morning and evening fluctuations of the state's grain are controlled by the superior;
the high and low prices of mountain forests, granaries, and equipment are controlled by the superior;
and the weight of values in spring, autumn, winter, and summer is controlled by the superior.
When inspecting the fields,
if there are trees in the fields,
they are called 'grain thieves.'
In the palace's four corners,
planting anything else is said to harm women's work.
Palaces and equipment
have nothing to rely on but the mountains.
Therefore, the ruler establishes three grades of tax on the mountains,
saying:
'Those below a hand's grip are for firewood;
those above a handful are for building houses;
and those of three girths or more
are for coffins.'
The tax for firewood is so much,
the tax for building houses is so much,
and the tax for coffins is so much."
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"With salt and iron regulated by the standards,
if grain is bought at one and stored until it is worth ten,
the ruler always holds nine parts.
The people have clothing and food while performing labor, and those below
are peaceful without resentment or blame.
Abolish their land tax
and tax their mountains instead:
great families who bury their relatives grandly
pay heavy taxes;
small families who bury their relatives simply
pay small taxes.
Great families who beautifully renovate their palaces
pay heavy taxes;
small families who build simple huts
pay small taxes.
The superior establishes standards in the state, and the poverty or wealth of the people
is as if measured by a string.
This is called Guó Guǐ."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zǐ:
"May I ask about the methods of power?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Heaven uses the seasons as its power,
Earth uses resources as its power,
Man uses labor as his power,
and the Ruler uses commands as his power.
If the power of Heaven is lost,
then the powers of Man and Earth are destroyed."
Huán Gōng said:
"Why is it that if the power of Heaven is lost, the powers of Man and Earth are destroyed?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Tāng had seven years of drought;
Yǔ had five years of flooding.
Among the people, those who had no grain sold their children.
Tāng used the metal of Zhuāng Shān to cast currency
to redeem those who had sold their children because they had no grain.
Yǔ used the metal of Lì Shān to cast currency
to redeem those who had sold their children because they had no grain.
Therefore, when Heaven's power is lost,
the powers of Man and Earth are both lost.
Thus, a king keeps three-tenths every year; in three years and a fraction,
he completes one year's worth. In thirty-seven years, he stores eleven years and a fraction.
Storing one-third
is not enough to harm the people,
while farmers diligently work at their labor.
Therefore, when Heaven destroys the Earth with drought or floods,
the people do not fall into ditches or become beggars.
This is the way of keeping watch over the seasons to await the power of Heaven."
Huán Gōng said:
"Good.
I wish to implement the methods of the three powers.
How should I do it?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"On the south side of Liáng Shān,
there are qìngqiàn and yèshí currencies
which are found nowhere else in the world."
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"By guarding the state's grain and keeping one-tenth every year,
if this is done for five years,
the value of the state's grain
will be ten times what it was before."
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"I request to establish currency.
Use the state's copper to purchase grain stored for two years,
and establish village registers.
Implement the policy of 'light and heavy' and harmonize with the world.
If their prices are high, they are targeted;
if low, they leak out.
Thus we harmonize with the world.
Leaking means losing power;
being targeted means losing strategy.
If you do not prepare for Heaven's power,
subordinates will seek preparation from each other,
and lower standards will secretly bind them.
This is where punishments arise
and the root of chaos lies.
Therefore, what should be balanced becomes unbalanced;
the people being wealthy becomes worse than being poor;
and the grain reserves become empty.
This is the loss of the three powers."
Huán Gōng said:
"How do we maintain the methods of the three powers?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"In times of great abundance, store a portion;
in times of scarcity, also store a portion."
Huán Gōng said:
"Scarcity is when things should be supplemented.
Why store a portion then?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"In scarcity, it is easy to increase value;
one can become ten,
and ten can become a hundred.
By using scarcity to control abundance,
the standard number for scarcity is one rising to ten;
the strategic number for abundance is to take nine out of ten,
so that our nine becomes the surplus. By calculating
for abundance, the three powers are all with the ruler.
This is called Guó Quán."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zǐ:
"May I ask about the state system?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"The state has no fixed system;
the land has measurements."
Huán Gōng said:
"What does it mean that the state has no fixed system and the land has measurements?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"High fields yield ten dàn;
middle fields five dàn;
common fields three dàn;
the rest are all wild fields.
Measuring the land, one hundred mǔ
is the labor of one man.
Grain prices may be one,
grain prices ten,
grain prices thirty,
or grain prices a hundred.
In the shifting strategies,
one hundred mǔ follows the strategy of a thousand mǔ.
Thus, a hundred chariots follow a thousand chariots,
and a thousand chariots follow ten thousand chariots.
Therefore, land has no fixed measure,
and the state has no fixed strategy."
Huán Gōng said:
"Good.
Now, for one who wishes to make his state great,
and for a great state that wishes to govern the world,
if one does not master power and strategy,
he will be incapable."
Huán Gōng said:
"How shall we implement power now?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"The ruler understands the calculations of size and narrowness,
so he does not fear the large because of his smallness;
he understands the calculations of price fluctuations,
so he does not fear the many because of his fewness.
This is the greatness of national strategy."
Huán Gōng said:
"Good.
To cover the world,
look upon all within the seas,
and maintain lasting fame without end,
is there a way to do this?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"There is.
It is said: Regulations maintain the numerical calculations,
standardizing and balancing the flow,
acting before things have taken shape,
and maintaining affairs already accomplished.
One thing becomes
ten; thus nine are for use.
The calculation of fast and slow
is the strategy of light and heavy;
one can be made into ten,
and ten can be made into a hundred.
Withdraw half of the ten and store four;
use five to manage affairs;
it depends on the ruler's deciding or blocking."
Huán Gōng said:
"What do you mean by deciding or blocking?"
Guǎnzǐ said:
"If the ruler does not exalt benevolence,
then inquiries will not reach one another;
if the ruler does not exalt kindness and filial piety,
then the people will neglect their kin and treat transgressions lightly.
This is the height of disorder.
Then let the ruler take one-tenth of the state strategy
to erect markers and establish honors;
recruit the filial sons of the villages with gifts of silk,
and whether the filial son's brothers are many or few,
they shall not participate in military affairs.
By erecting markers and establishing honors
to elevate benevolence, kindness, and filial piety,
wealth is dispersed and becomes light.
Take advantage of this lightness and maintain it with strategy,
then five-tenths will remain at the disposal of the ruler.
Employing these five is like performing tasks,
like the cycles of the sun and moon.
This is the way to possess the world for a long time;
it is called the Way of the Standard, Zhǔndào."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎnzǐ:
"May I ask about the calculations for education?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"For those among the people who are clear-sighted in agricultural matters,
provide them with one jin of gold,
equal to the value of eight shi of grain.
For those among the people who can breed the six types of livestock,
provide them with one jin of gold,
equal to the value of eight shi of grain.
For those among the people who can plant and cultivate,
provide them with one jin of gold,
equal to the value of eight shi of grain.
For those among the people who can plant melons, gourds, pungent vegetables, and various fruits to make them flourish and multiply,
provide them with one jin of gold,
equal to the value of eight shi of grain.
For those among the people who can cure the illnesses of the people,
provide them with one jin of gold,
equal to the value of eight shi of grain.
For those among the people who know the seasons:
saying
'the year will be difficult,'
saying
'a certain grain will not ripen,'
saying
for those,
'who say a certain grain is abundant,' provide them with one jin of gold,
equal to the value of eight shi of grain.
For those among the people who are skilled in sericulture and mulberry,
making it so the silkworms do not fall ill,
all shall be provided with one jin of gold,
equal to the value of eight shi of grain.
Listen carefully to their words and record them in the offices,
making them not participate in military affairs;
this is the state's strategy.
State expenditures will be mutually adjusted and sufficient,
(mutually following calculations to be sufficient) and mutually calculated and adequate.
Then establish the four limits, high and low,
command them with speed, drive and screen
the myriad things, maintain them with strategy,
and the skills of the Five Officials."
Huán Gōng said:
"What are called the skills of the Five Officials?"
Guǎnzǐ said:
"The Shī is for recording things;
the Shí is for recording the year;
the Chūnqiū is for recording success and failure;
the Xíng is for guiding the people's benefits and harms;
the Yì is for maintaining good and bad fortune, success and failure;
the Bǔ is for divining good and bad fortune, benefits and harms.
For those among the people who are capable in these,
give each of them the land for one horse
and clothing worth one jin of gold.
This is the calculation to keep the ruler from being deluded.
These five categories of experts,
once they appear: for their time,
have them prepare in advance and receive them on early leisure days,
so the ruler never misses the seasons,
never misses the strategy,
and the myriad things flourish and are abundant;
for the Chūnqiū,
predicting gains and losses from afar,
to serve as the final instruction;
for the Shī, record people without missing their words;
for the Xíng, exhaustively guide without missing righteousness;
for the Yì, maintain fortune and misfortune, good and bad luck, so they do not become confused.
This is called the Ruler's Handle."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎnzǐ:
"I have already heard the calculations of the power handle;
how about the firmness of protecting the state?"
He said:
"When ability is fully officialized,
when time is fully officialized,
when the calculations of gain and loss,
and the beginning and end of the myriad things
are all officialized by the ruler,
the rest will all proceed according to calculations."
Huán Gōng said:
"What do you mean by 'proceed according to calculations'?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Grain is the master of the people's lives;
wisdom is the aid of the people.
If the people are wise and the ruler is foolish,
if those below are rich and the ruler is poor,
if those below are poor and the ruler is rich,
these are called the two aspects of affairs.
The mechanism of the state
is simply a matter of fast and slow.
The Way of the Ruler
is simply a matter of measuring the laws.
The human heart
is simply a matter of forbidding errors."
Huán Gōng said:
"What is measuring the laws?
What is forbidding errors?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Measuring the laws
means measuring human strength and then undertaking work.
Forbidding errors
means taking what has gone before to warn of what is to come.
Thus, disaster does not sprout or spread,
and the people have no worries or calamities."
Huán Gōng said:
"I wish to hear about the prohibition of the mind."
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"In Jìn, there were subjects who were disloyal to their ruler,
planning to kill their lord;
this was called public transgression.
Members of all families with public transgressions
were not allowed to serve the ruler.
This was the error of Jìn.
In Qí, public transgression
involves seating and standing in a hierarchy;
hating the hateful brings punishment,
admiring the good brings glory.
This is a warning.
This is called the State Warning."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎnzǐ:
"The standard of 'light and heavy' has been applied;
is strategy exhausted here?"
Guǎnzǐ said:
"Not yet.
You must manage the divine and use treasures."
Huán Gōng said:
"What do you mean by managing the divine and using treasures?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"In Běiguō, someone dug an opening and found a turtle;
this is equivalent to several hundred li of land."
Huán Gōng said:
"What do you mean by finding a turtle being worth a hundred li of land?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"For the one who found the turtle in Běiguō,
order it to be placed in a flat basin.
May the ruler dispatch an envoy with ten chariots
and a gift of a hundred jin of gold,
ordering the family in Běiguō that found the turtle:
'We bestow upon you the rank of Zhōng Dàfū.'"
He said:
"The son of the Dōnghǎi resembles a tortoise,
and he has taken lodging with you.
I bestow upon you the robes of a Dàfū
to last for the rest of your life,
and reward you with one hundred gold pieces."
This tortoise was deemed priceless,
and it was stored in the Tàitái.
Every day it was fed four oxen,
and he established it as a treasure named 'Priceless'.
After four years had passed,
the campaign against Gūzhú began.
The grain of the Dīng family
could feed the host of the three armies
for five months on the march.
He summoned the head of the Dīng family and commanded him, saying:
"I have the 'Priceless' treasure here.
I am now about to undertake a great military endeavor;
I ask to use this treasure as collateral for you
in order to borrow the grain from your estate."
Dīng faced north and bowed twice, then handed over the grain,
but did not dare to accept the treasure as collateral.
Huán Gōng commanded Dīng, saying:
"I am old;
as for you, you do not understand this strategy.
You must accept my collateral!"
Dīng returned home,
renovated and built a chamber, and used tax registers to store and guard the tortoise.
After four years had passed,
during the campaign against Gūzhú,
it was said that the grain of the Dīng family
provided enough food for the three armies for five months.
Huán Gōng established the tribute values:
Those with patterned markings were worth seven thousand gold pieces; those with years
of age, tortoises are worth four thousand gold pieces;
and black and white ones are worth one thousand gold pieces.
Regarding the system of tribute,
it was used to balance the land of the two Qí
and was a strategy. By using tribute:
when the state is in danger, issue treasures;
when the state is at peace, circulate currency."
Huán Gōng asked:
"What is meant by 'circulation'?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"When goods are stockpiled in advance,
the ruler loses strategy and the people lose their livelihood.
Therefore, those good at governing the realm
operate outside of the two forms of advance stockpiling."
Huán Gōng asked:
"What is meant by 'outside the two forms of advance stockpiling'?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"A state of ten thousand chariots
cannot be without ten thousand gold pieces worth of accumulated stores;
a state of one thousand chariots
cannot be without one thousand gold pieces worth of accumulated stores;
a state of one hundred chariots
cannot be without one hundred gold pieces worth of accumulated stores.
Using these to manage advance and retreat according to orders—
this is called 'riding the timing'."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zǐ:
"Liáng Jù said to me:
'In ancient times, they lightened taxes and duties but increased household levies;
there is no more compliant way to take from those below than this.'
What do you think of Liáng Jù's words?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Liáng Jù's words are wrong.
If he lightens taxes,
the granaries will be empty.
If he increases household levies,
tools and equipment will not be supplied,
and the Zhū
hóu's skins and silks will not be worn as attire.
When granaries are empty,
